events.title: Adam
events.description: Adam was the chosen man, formed of the dust of the ground outside the garden and set inside it, and given the breath of life, which is the commandments. The serpent is Satan the deceiver, who played on the woman’s envy and taught her a doctrine: that she would not die, and that her eyes would be opened and she would be as gods. She ate the lie and taught it to her husband. Their nakedness was sin, and the sin was idolatry; the fig leaves were a covering of transgression, and the trees they hid among were the other people in the garden. Judgment fell on the serpent, the woman and the man; God covered them with the first sacrifice and drove them out, and set a flaming sword turning every way to keep the way back.
events.article:
Adam and Eve

Hearkening to the serpent’s doctrine, that ye shall not surely die; and eating the fruit of lies

Cursed

Adam was the chosen of the Most High. Out of all the people created on the earth he had a favourite from the beginning: he formed him of the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and that breath is the commandments (Genesis 2:7; 2 Esdras 3:5; Proverbs 7:2). He was formed of the soil, and the richer the soil the darker. He was formed outside the garden and then placed inside it, eastward in Eden, where the river Gihon compassed Ethiopia (Genesis 2:8-14). No help meet was found for him among the women already on the earth, which is more proof the earth was peopled beyond that house, so the woman was made of his rib (Genesis 2:18-23). He was set there with one commandment concerning the tree, and some of those trees are literal trees while some represent men (Genesis 2:16-17; Mark 8:24).

The serpent is not a snake; serpents do not speak. Another word for serpent is deceiver, and the serpent is Satan, who transforms himself into an angel of light (Genesis 3:1; 2 Corinthians 11:14). Satan taught her doctrine and played on the words: she had been taught that breaking the commandment meant death, and he told her she would not die at all, but that her eyes would be opened and she would be as gods (Genesis 3:4-5). What he worked on was envy, for through envy of the devil came death into the world; there was one God in that house and she wanted to be equal with her husband (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). Good for food is good to learn, and the fruit she ate was the lie; she taught her husband what the serpent taught her, and he broke the commandment also (Genesis 3:6; Hosea 10:13). The first attack in the scriptures is on a household, and it began with the woman: of the woman came the beginning of sin (Ecclesiasticus 25:24). Adam’s charge is that he listened to his wife’s voice against the command given him (Genesis 3:17).

They were not literally naked. Nakedness is sin, and the sin is named elsewhere: when Aaron made the calf, Moses saw the people naked, for Aaron had made them naked to their shame among their enemies, and the worshipping of idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil (Genesis 3:7; Exodus 32:25; Wisdom of Solomon 14:12, 27). The fig leaves are Adam covering his transgressions and hiding his iniquity within himself (Job 31:33; Lamentations 1:8). They hid among the trees of the garden, and the trees are people: they tried to hide their sin among the others in the garden with them, and no cedar in the garden of God could hide him (Genesis 3:8; Ezekiel 31:8). The question of where he was was a call to self-examination. Adam blamed the woman, and in saying she was given him blamed the Most High also; then Eve blamed the serpent (Genesis 3:9-13).

The serpent was cursed above all cattle and above every beast of the field, and the cattle and the beasts are the nations. Going on the belly and eating dust is a very low estate, a vagabond upon the earth, and the prophets say the nations will lick the dust like a serpent (Genesis 3:14; Micah 7:16-17; Isaiah 49:23). Verse fifteen is prophecy. The woman is the nation of Israel; the enmity between Satan’s seed and her seed remains; the bruised heel is Israel made to stumble, and the bruised head is Christ destroying the works of Satan under the feet of his people (Genesis 3:15; Jeremiah 3:2; Romans 16:20). To the woman it was said that her desire would be to her husband and that he would rule over her: her desire had been to learn from the serpent, and she was sent back to learn from her husband, one of the first commandments given (Genesis 3:16; 1 Corinthians 14:34). To Adam the ground was cursed, with sorrow and sweat all his days, and death was appointed in him and in his generations, of whom came nations and tribes out of number (Genesis 3:17-19; 2 Esdras 3:7-8).

The coats of skins were the first sacrifice, ordaining the sacrificial law: a beast slain to clothe them and cover their sin, and that lamb, slain from the foundation of the world, is Christ (Genesis 3:21; Leviticus 16:27; Isaiah 61:10; Revelation 13:8). Then the man was driven out to till the ground he was taken from, and cherubims and a flaming sword turning every way were set at the east of the garden to keep the way of the tree of life; a sword turning every way is confusion, so the way back could not be found (Genesis 3:22-24).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/adam-and-eve

events.title: Cain
events.description: Cain was the firstborn of the house after it was put out of the garden, a tiller of the ground and a man of the field. He knew the sacrifice ordained in the garden and in process of time brought fruit of the ground instead. Corrected, he grew bitter; called to repent, he refused. He talked with his brother as a friend, drew him out to the field and killed him, then lied to God’s face and took no accountability. Cursed from the earth, marked, and made a fugitive and a vagabond, he built a city in the east among the people already on the earth, and his line carried the music and the weapons until the earth was filled with violence.
events.article:
Cain

Bringing of the fruit of the ground when the sacrificial law required a firstling; refusing correction; and murder of his brother Abel

Cursed

Cain was born first, a tiller of the ground and a man of the field, and the ground had been cursed in chapter three, so it did not yield easily (Genesis 4:1-3; Genesis 3:17). He knew the Most High required animal sacrifice, because the sacrificial law was ordained when Adam was clothed with skins (Genesis 3:21; Genesis 9:5). In process of time he brought fruit of the ground; the words in process of time say the falling off was gradual, not sudden. The Lord had no respect to it, and Cain was very wroth and his countenance fell (Genesis 4:3-5). What started it was correction. Correction is grievous to the man who leaves the way, and only by pride comes contention; that grievous spirit nourished envy into bitterness, and Cain is the first hater the scriptures record (Proverbs 15:10; Proverbs 13:10).

The Most High called him to repent: if he did well he would be accepted, and if not, sin lay at the door, and the door is his own mind, and the desire of that sin would be toward him and it would rule over him (Genesis 4:7). Cain talked with his brother, playing the friend while Abel, a prophet, urged him to repent, and drew him out to the field where he spent his days, and killed him there (Genesis 4:8). Christ named the line when he told the men who were plotting his death that they were of their father the devil, a murderer from the beginning, who did not abide in the truth, a liar and the father of it: Satan murdered nobody in the beginning, Cain did, and Cain lied (John 8:44). John says the same, that he was of that wicked one, and killed

his brother because his own works were evil and his brother’s righteous (1 John 3:12). Where envying and strife are, there is confusion and every evil work, and confusion is where every evil work hides (James 3:16). Asked where his brother was, he answered with a lie and a taunt and took no accountability at all (Genesis 4:9).

Abel’s blood cried from the ground. Cain was cursed from the earth, the ground would no longer yield him her strength, and he was made a fugitive and a vagabond: the same low estate spoken to the serpent (Genesis 4:10-12; Genesis 3:14). A fugitive is a man who kills and escapes the sentence; a vagabond wanders from land to land and settles nowhere that belongs to him, and wherever he goes the ground does not answer him. The curse reached the man himself. Adam was formed of the ground, and the ground was cursed for Cain; the mark set upon him changed him, for at the beginning he looked like everybody else, and his own fear that anyone finding him would kill him says both that the earth was already peopled and that he now stood out among them (Genesis 4:14-15). Vengeance sevenfold was threatened against his killer, and the Most High reserved the matter to himself. From the face of God he would be hid: the Most High stopped dealing with him, and the father he had left was the wicked one.

He went out from the presence of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Nod, east of Eden, the same ground where the cherubims and the flaming sword were set; he found a wife among the people already there and built a city, which is not built for three people, and called it after the name of his son, as the wicked call their lands after their own names (Genesis 4:16-17; Psalms 49:11). The older scholars of Assyria identified that city with Unug, which the Akkadians called Uruk and which scripture calls Erech, and Nimrod later built the beginning of his kingdom on the same ground in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:8-10). His line kept the trades. Jubal fathered all such as handle the harp and the organ, and music in the wrong hands is a weapon; Tubalcain instructed every craftsman in brass and iron, which is the making of arms, and the Most High says he created the smith that blows the coals and created the waster to destroy (Genesis 4:20-22; Isaiah 54:16). Wisdom says the unrighteous man who went away from her in his anger perished in the same fury with which he murdered his brother, and names his cause as the cause for which the earth was drowned (Wisdom of Solomon 10:3-4; Genesis 6:1-2). The way of Cain stands condemned (Jude 1:11), and the same spirit appears again in Esau, the firstborn, the man of the field, who purposed in his heart to kill his brother (Genesis 27:41).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/cain

events.title: Abel
events.description: With Cain and Abel comes the birth of trade and of religion. Abel kept the sacrifice ordained when God clothed his father with skins, bringing the firstlings of his flock and the fat, the first and the best, and the Lord had respect to him and to his offering. He was a prophet; when Cain talked with him he was calling his brother to repent, and Cain killed him in his fury. Christ counts righteous Abel first of all the righteous blood shed on the earth, and Seth was appointed another seed in his place.
events.article:
Abel

Bringing the firstlings of his flock and the fat thereof, according to the sacrifice ordained in the garden

Kept the law

Abel kept sheep and Cain tilled the ground, and there is the birth of trade and of religion (Genesis 4:1-2). The sacrificial law was ordained when the Most High made coats of skins for Adam and his wife; the beast stood in the place of the sinner, taking the wrongdoing of another upon itself, and the same requirement of blood at the hand of every beast was still standing in Noah’s day, so the law passed down from father to son (Genesis 3:21; Genesis 9:5). That is why the sons were bringing offerings at all. Abel brought the firstlings of his flock and the fat of them, the first and the best, and the later law names the firstborn and the fat as the Lord’s (Genesis 4:3-5; Exodus 13:12; Leviticus 3:16). Hebrews calls it a more excellent sacrifice, offered by faith, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts (Hebrews 11:4). His own works were righteous where his brother’s were evil (1 John 3:12).

Abel was a son of God, of the lineage made in the likeness of Adam, and Abel was a prophet (Genesis 5:1-3). When Cain talked with his brother, Abel was working to bring him to repentance, and Christ counts righteous Abel at the head of all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, together with the blood of the prophets (Genesis 4:8; Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:49-51). It was not a quiet death; wisdom says the unrighteous brother perished in the same fury with which he murdered him, which tells you what the fury was (Wisdom of Solomon 10:3). Correction is the most dangerous word a man can carry to a brother who has already left the way, and Abel carried it.

The Lord had respect to Abel and to his offering, which is the whole blessing of the case: a righteous standing before God (Genesis 4:4). It did not buy him protection from his brother’s hatred; the murder of the righteous became the pattern repeated against every prophet after him (Matthew 23:35). Being dead, he yet speaks: his faith stands on record long after his life was taken, and his blood cried to God from the ground (Hebrews 11:4; Genesis 4:10).

Seth was appointed another seed in his place, for God, not the woman, appoints seed; and in the days of Seth’s son Enos men began to call upon the name of the Lord, because wickedness had spread so far that they had stopped (Genesis 4:25-26). Adam fathered Seth in his own likeness and after his image, which is said of no other son: Seth came out the man Adam had been before the fall. The Most High chose that line. It is the line of the sons of God, running through Shem to Israel, and Christ’s own line on his mother’s side runs back through Seth to Adam, the son of God (Genesis 5:3; Luke 3:36-38). The righteous is always born inside the wickedness, never outside it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/abel

events.title: Enoch
events.description: Enoch stands seventh from Adam in the direct lineage of the sons of God. He walked with God three hundred years after Methuselah was born, which is to say he walked in the statutes and kept the commandments through the whole of a household life, and he prophesied the judgment coming upon the ungodly. Ecclesiasticus holds him up as an example of repentance to all generations. God took him, and he did not taste death.
events.article:
Enoch

Walking with God three hundred years

Kept the law

Genesis 5 is the direct lineage of Adam, who was made in the likeness of God, and Adam fathered Seth in his own likeness and after his image. That lineage is the sons of God read of in the next chapter, and it runs down through Shem to Israel; Christ’s line on his mother’s side runs back through Seth to Adam, the son of God (Genesis 5:1-3; Luke 3:36-38). Cain’s line carried the same names and not the same spirit: there is a wicked Enoch in that line, and a city named after him, and there is this one (Genesis 4:17). Enoch walked with God for three hundred years after Methuselah was born, and had sons and daughters (Genesis 5:21-24). Walking with God is not long walks and talks; it is the same charge given to Abram, to walk before the Most High and be perfect, which means to walk in his statutes and to keep his commandments (Genesis 17:1). The walk was carried through the whole weight of a household, not on one occasion.

Jude preserves his prophecy that the Lord would come with ten thousands of his saints to execute judgment upon all, and to convince the ungodly of their ungodly deeds and of their hard speeches (Jude 1:14-15). Walking with God included testifying against the wicked of his generation, and the word he carried is the word Methuselah, Lamech and Noah were still carrying when the flood came. Ecclesiasticus holds him up as an example of repentance to all generations, which says plainly that he had something to repent of, and repented, and that is the example (Ecclesiasticus 44:16).

Genesis says only that he was not, because God took him. The Most High took him up and he did not taste death, the same way Elijah was carried up to heaven by a whirlwind, and as Christ was taken up and received by a cloud (Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:9-11; Acts 1:9). Hebrews says that by faith he was translated so that he should not see death, that before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God, and that without faith it is impossible to please him (Hebrews 11:5-6).

Ecclesiasticus sets him among the famous men and the fathers of our line, men renowned for their power, giving counsel by their understanding and declaring prophecies, whose righteousness has not been forgotten, whose seed stands fast and whose children are within the covenant (Ecclesiasticus 44:1-13). His days were three hundred sixty and five years, short beside every other man in that chapter, and the shortness was no mark of disfavour. The others are recorded dying; he is not.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/enoch

events.title: Lamech
events.description: Lamech of Cain’s line was the first man in scripture to take two wives. His house carried the trades of that line, the harp and the organ in one son and the working of brass and iron in another, which is the first making of weapons. He boasted to his wives that he had killed a man, with the weapon his own son had made, and claimed seventy and sevenfold against Cain’s sevenfold. He knew the commandment against killing and appealed past it. No sentence is recorded.
events.article:
Lamech

Taking two wives, the first in scripture; killing a man and boasting of it; claiming seventy-sevenfold vengeance

Sentence not recorded

Lamech took two wives, Adah and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). This is the first time scripture records a man taking multiple wives, and it is the sons of the wicked who did it; in the beginning it was one wife, and the line of Seth in the next chapter is not read of doing so (Genesis 2:24; Genesis 5:3-5). His house carried the trades of Cain’s line. Jabal fathered such as dwell in tents and have cattle, Jubal fathered all such as handle the harp and the organ, and Zillah bare Tubalcain, an instructor of every craftsman in brass and iron, which is the first making of weapons (Genesis 4:20-22). Music and warfare both sat in that one household, and the Most High takes the credit for neither man but for the making: he says he created the smith that blows the coals and brings forth an instrument for his work, and created the waster to destroy (Isaiah 54:16).

Lamech told his wives that he had slain a man to his wounding and a young man to his hurt (Genesis 4:23). He did it with what was to hand, and what was to hand was what his own son had forged. He knew the commandment against killing was in force in his day; that is exactly why he appealed to Cain’s sevenfold and claimed seventy and sevenfold for himself (Genesis 4:24; Genesis 4:15). They knew the commandments in that time. The word the Most High had spoken to restrain bloodshed was turned into a man’s boast of his own vengeance, though vengeance belongs to the Lord (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19). What he was announcing is the rule his line has kept ever since: touch one of us and we answer seventy times over, a household or a whole city for one man, because we hold the weapons.

Genesis records no sentence upon this Lamech. His speech stands as the testimony of Cain’s line, growing in violence and self-exaltation, before the account turns to Seth and to those who began to call upon the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:25-26). Two lines carry the same names and not the same spirit. Cain’s Lamech fathered a son of destruction; Seth’s Lamech fathered Noah, and named him for the comfort he would bring concerning their work and the toil of their hands, because of the ground the Lord had cursed (Genesis 5:28-29). Good is set against evil, and life against death, and all the works of the Most High are two and two, one against another (Ecclesiasticus 33:14-15). The line of Cain went on in wickedness until the sons of God mingled with it, the earth was filled with violence, and the flood came (Genesis 6:1-5; Wisdom of Solomon 10:3-4). The absence of a narrated punishment does not turn his claim into God’s promise; delay is not acquittal.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/lamech

events.title: Noah
events.description: Noah found grace, a just man, perfect in his generations, who walked with God when the sons of God had mingled with the daughters of men. Out of all the sons of God of his time he was the one who did not, and he took a wife of his own kindred as the fathers did from the beginning. He built the ark by faith for rain that had never fallen, preached righteousness for about a hundred years, kept the clean and the unclean as commanded, and was left as a remnant to the earth under the covenant of the bow.
events.article:
Noah

Doing according to all that God commanded him

Kept the law

Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord: a just man, perfect in his generations, and he walked with God (Genesis 6:8-9). Perfect is not a claim no man can reach; it means to walk in his statutes and keep his commandments, the same word afterward given to Abram (Genesis 17:1). He was himself one of the sons of God, and while that whole line went after the daughters of men he did not; he took a wife of his own kindred, and so did his sons, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all did from the beginning (Genesis 6:1-5; Tobit 4:12). Ecclesiasticus counts him found perfect and righteous, taken in exchange for the world in the time of wrath, and left as a remnant to the earth when the flood came (Ecclesiasticus 44:17-18).

He did according to all that the Most High commanded him, and he did it by faith. Up to that time it had never rained upon the earth; a mist went up and watered the whole face of the ground. It takes faith to build an ark against a thing that has never happened, and faith is the evidence of things not seen (Genesis 6:22; Genesis 2:5-6; Genesis 7:4; Hebrews 11:1, 7). He was five hundred years old when his sons were born and six hundred when the flood came, so he preached for around a hundred years; while the ark was preparing he was a preacher of righteousness, telling his people to repent, and the longsuffering of God waited on them (Genesis 5:32; Genesis 7:6; 2 Peter 2:5; 1 Peter 3:20). He took the clean beasts by sevens and the unclean by twos. The dietary law was not yet written down, but the Most High had already made the difference between the clean and the unclean, and Moses only said it again; that Noah knew which was which is proof he was keeping the laws (Genesis 7:2-3; Leviticus 11:46-47).

The Lord shut him in, and eight souls were saved while the ones out in the water died; of all that dwelt in the world only Noah and his household were left, and of them came all righteous men, through Shem to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their line (Genesis 7:16; 1 Peter 3:20; 2 Esdras 3:11). He stood inside a closed door and heard what he heard outside it, and the door was not his to open. Afterward he builded an altar and offered of every clean beast and every clean fowl, and the Lord smelled a sweet savour and said he would not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake (Genesis 8:20-22). Noah, Daniel and Job are named together as men who by their righteousness delivered their own souls, and that is what every soul in that ark did (Ezekiel 14:14).

The everlasting covenant made with him and with all flesh was that the waters should never again become a flood; the bow in the cloud is the token of it, and it compasses the heaven about with a glorious circle, and the hands of the Most High have bended it (Genesis 9:9-15; Ecclesiasticus 43:11-12). The world has taken that same token and made it the sign of sodomy, which is one of the marks of the place spiritually called Sodom and Egypt (Revelation 11:8). The bow also answers to Israel: as he swore that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so he swore that his kindness should not depart nor the covenant of his peace be removed, and that is the promise that this captivity is the last one (Isaiah 54:9-10). Before it was water; next time it is fire (2 Peter 3:9-10).

The renewed earth carried the laws that stood before Moses: replenish the earth, and one just child is better than a thousand ungodly; eat no flesh with the blood in it; and whoever sheds man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed (Genesis 9:1-6; Ecclesiasticus 16:1-3). The word is true from the beginning, and Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil, and not one jot or tittle passes from it (Psalms 119:160; Matthew 5:17-18). The coming of the Son of man will be as the days of Noah were, and a household is prepared for it by exactly the same faith and the same works (Matthew 24:37-39; Hebrews 11:7).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/noah

events.title: Ham
events.description: Noah, still righteous, drank of the wine with a heavy heart after a hundred years of preaching to a world that drowned. Ham saw his father’s nakedness and mocked him, telling his two brothers outside instead of covering him; Shem and Japheth covered him without looking, applying the laws concerning nakedness, and carried the matter to him as witnesses are bound to do. Noah, a prophet, was shown what his younger son had done and cursed Canaan to be a servant of servants. The curse is servitude, not a colour, and the Messiah was to come through Shem.
events.article:
Ham and the curse on Canaan

Seeing the nakedness of his father and not covering him

Cursed

Noah began to be a husbandman and planted a vineyard, drank of the wine, and was uncovered within his tent (Genesis 9:20-21). He was still perfect and righteous: a just man falls seven times and rises up again, and one fall does not undo righteousness (Proverbs 24:16). Understand the man’s heart. He had preached repentance for about a hundred years, and everyone he knew outside his own house drowned while he stood behind a door he had not closed himself; strong drink is given to him that is ready to perish, and wine to those that be of heavy hearts (Proverbs 31:6-7; 2 Peter 2:5).

Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brethren outside. Shem and Japheth took a garment upon both their shoulders, went backward with their faces turned away, and covered their father, and did not see his nakedness (Genesis 9:22-23). The commandments concerning nakedness were already being kept; Leviticus 18 opens those laws and forbids uncovering the nakedness of a father (Leviticus 18:6-8). Nothing in the text says Ham touched his father. He looked and he talked; he mocked him. His brothers covered without looking, and they also carried the matter to their father, because the law lays the iniquity on a witness who has seen or known a thing and does not utter it (Leviticus 5:1). The honour due a father did not lapse because his weakness was in plain view (Exodus 20:12; Ecclesiasticus 3:10-11).

Noah was asleep, so how did he know what his younger son had done to him? God speaks once, yea twice, in a dream, in a vision of the night, and reveals his secret to his servants the prophets; Noah was a preacher of righteousness, and the Lord told him (Genesis 9:24; Job 33:14-16; Amos 3:7). Cursed be Canaan: a servant of servants shall he be to his brethren (Genesis 9:25). Read what the curse actually is. It is servitude, not a skin. Every man in that tent was dark, and the first change of colour recorded in the scriptures comes later, with Esau. The sentence names Canaan, and the text does not carry it past the son it names.

Then Noah blessed the Lord God of Shem, and named no other God for the other two: it was revealed that the Messiah and the righteous seed would come through Shem. Japheth would be enlarged and dwell in the tents of Shem, and Canaan would be servant to both (Genesis 9:26-27). Whatever a servant has belongs to his master, which is why the children of Israel taking the land of Canaan was no robbery; the land was already theirs by that word. The sons of Ham are Cush, which is Ethiopia; Mizraim, which is Egypt; Phut, which is Libya; and Canaan, whose land is the land where Jerusalem sits (Genesis 10:6). Ham inhabited what men now call Africa, so the land of Israel is part of Africa; and Israel is of Shem, the father of all the children of Eber, Shemites scattered among the children of Ham (Genesis 9:18-19; Genesis 10:21).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/01-primeval/ham

events.title: Job
events.description:
Job lived in the land of Uz but was not of that nation; he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam, as Israel lives among the nations today and is not of them. He sanctified his children after every one his day and offered for them in case they had sinned. Satan, who took his orders from the Lord and needed his permission, was given all that Job had and then his flesh, and Job blessed the name of the Lord and answered his wife that we receive both good and evil at the hand of God. When the Lord answered him he repented in dust and ashes and prayed for his friends, and the Lord turned his captivity.

Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite came from their own places by appointment to mourn with Job and comfort him, and sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word. Then they reasoned from his suffering back to his guilt, and Eliphaz at last invented the sins outright. The Lord answered them by name: they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had, and he sent them with sacrifice to the man they had condemned, that he might pray for them.
events.article:
Job

Perfect and upright, fearing God and eschewing evil; and in all his loss he sinned not with his lips

Kept the law

Job was a man of the land of Uz, blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned from evil, the greatest of all the men of the east (Job 1:1-3). Living in the land of Uz did not make him of that nation, for he was a son of God, of the lineage of Adam. Some say he was an Edomite on the strength of a paragraph the Greek copy adds at the end of the book out of a Syriac writing, making him Jobab of the kings of Edom; the Hebrew, the Latin and the English all end at the same place, and that addition is commentary, not scripture. Job settles it himself: his skin was black upon him (Job 30:30). The law of sacrifice was never given to Esau, yet the Lord sends three men at the end of the book to offer through Job (Numbers 28:1-2); Ezekiel ranks him with Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14, 20).

Job 29 shows who he was before the trial: he prepared his seat in the street as a judge, delivered the poor and the fatherless, and broke the jaws of the wicked (Job 29:4-17; Deuteronomy 16:18). His sons feasted in their houses, every one his day, which is their birthdays, the only birthdays the scriptures record being kept by the heathen; and Job offered burnt offerings for each of them, in case they had sinned in their hearts (Job 1:4-5; Job 8:4).

When the sons of God came before the Lord, Satan came among them (Job 1:6); the sons of God are the lineage of Adam, also called angels, for another word for angel is messenger. The Lord asked Satan whether he had considered his servant Job, since there was none like him. The more good works a man does, the harder Satan comes at him. Satan asked whether Job feared God for nothing, and whether a hedge had not been made about him; the hedge is the angel of the Lord that encamps round about them that fear him (Job 1:8-10; Psalms 34:7). He is subject to God and took his orders: all Job had was put in his power, but not Job himself (Job 1:12). Both good and evil come from the Lord, who makes peace and creates evil (Isaiah 45:7). In one day the Sabeans, fire from heaven, the Chaldeans and a great wind took his herds, his servants and all ten children (Job 1:13-19). Job tore his mantle, fell to the ground and worshipped: he had come naked and would return naked, the Lord had given and the Lord had taken away, and he blessed the name of the Lord; in all this he did not sin or charge God with wrong (Job 1:20-22). Then the Lord bragged on him, that he still held fast his integrity; Satan was given his flesh but not his life (Job 2:3-7). His wife told him to curse God and die: if Satan cannot get to a man he comes through his woman, as he went to Eve. Job answered that she spoke as one of the foolish women, and asked whether they should receive good at God’s hand and not evil (Job 2:9-10).

When the Lord answered out of the whirlwind, Job laid his hand on his mouth; he had uttered what he did not understand, and having now seen with his eye what he had heard by the ear, he repented in dust and ashes (Job 40:4; Job 42:3-6). The Lord’s wrath was kindled against the three friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, and the sacrifice for their sin had to be carried to the righteous one in the matter (Job 42:7-9).

The Lord turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before, and seven sons and three daughters, Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, the fairest women in all the land, to whom he gave inheritance among their brothers. He lived a hundred and forty years and saw four generations (Job 42:10-16). James points to the patience of Job and the end the Lord gave, to show that the Lord is full of compassion and tender mercy (James 5:11). And Job looked past the restoration: he knew that his redeemer lived and would stand at the latter day upon the earth, and that though worms destroyed his body, in his flesh he would see God, with his own eyes (Job 19:25-27). His life is the pattern for every son of God: prepare the soul for temptation, for the trial comes by the Lord’s permission and inside his limits, and he will not suffer a man to be tempted above what he is able (Ecclesiasticus 2:1; 1 Corinthians 10:13).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/job

Job’s three friends

Speaking of God the thing that is not right; condemning the righteous, having found no answer

Restitution

When Job’s three friends heard of all the evil that had come on him, each came from his own place by appointment to mourn with him and to comfort him. They lifted up their voice and wept, rent every man his mantle, sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven, and sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word, for they saw that his grief was very great (Job 2:11-13). Friends who come to a man’s affliction with correction and hard truth are not the fault here. What is wanted is people who give straight facts and not people who butter a man up while he is in the wrong. The fault is the conclusion they reached and would not abandon.

Eliphaz began where it cuts deepest: Job had instructed many, strengthened the weak hands, upheld him that was falling and strengthened the feeble knees, and now that it had come on him, he fainted (Job 4:3-5). There is one that is wise and teaches many and yet is unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19): you were the man who comforted everybody, and now your own turn has come and you want to give up. That much was fair warning. Then he went further and asked who ever perished being innocent, or where the righteous were cut off (Job 4:7), which turns every affliction into proof of sin. Bildad asked whether God perverts judgment, pointed at Job’s dead children as cast away for their transgression, and promised a latter end that would greatly increase if Job were pure and upright, on the false premise that he was not already upright (Job 8:3-7; Job 1:1, 5). Zophar told him God exacted of him less than his iniquity deserved (Job 11:6). Then Eliphaz stopped inferring and began inventing: he said Job’s wickedness was great, that he had taken a pledge from his brother for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing and withheld bread from the hungry (Job 22:5-7), none of which the record supports. Job named it while it was being done: they were forgers of lies and physicians of no value and miserable comforters, and he asked whether they would speak wickedly for God and talk deceitfully for him (Job 13:4, 7; Job 16:2). Defending God with false accusations against his servant is the thing this case is entered for. Elihu’s wrath was kindled against the three because they had found no answer and yet had condemned Job (Job 32:3); and it was Elihu who spoke the word that reaches to our own day, that by reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry, and they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty (Job 35:9).

The Lord told Eliphaz the Temanite that his wrath was kindled against him and against his two friends, because they had not spoken of him the thing that was right, as his servant Job had (Job 42:7). The remedy was sacrifice and intercession, and it had to be carried to the man they had accused: seven bullocks and seven rams, brought to his servant Job, a burnt offering offered for themselves, and Job would pray for them, for the Lord would accept him, or else he would deal with them after their folly (Job 42:8). That is how the priesthood always worked in Israel: the sacrifice is brought to the righteous one and offered on the sinner’s behalf, and the man who does not bring it is not forgiven.

The three who had argued so long for Job’s guilt now depended on the prayer of the man they had condemned, and the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16). It was not the prayer by itself, but the prayer of a righteous man; the Most High deals with those who are dealing in righteousness. They did as the Lord commanded them, and the Lord also accepted Job; and it was in the praying for these friends that his own captivity was turned (Job 42:9-10). Afterward his brethren and sisters and former acquaintances came and ate bread with him and comforted him, every man bringing him a piece of money and an earring of gold (Job 42:11). The friends were restored along with everything else.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/jobs-friends

events.title: Abraham
events.description:
Called alone out of Ur of the Chaldees, out of his country, his kindred and his father’s house, Abraham went. He believed the Lord and it was counted to him for righteousness, and his faith showed itself in his works: the covenant sealed in his flesh the same day it was commanded, the household commanded after him, the only son offered. The Lord’s own account of him, given afterward to Isaac, is the law kept: Abraham obeyed his voice and kept his charge, his commandments, his statutes and his laws.

Abraham, old and blessed in all things, made the eldest servant of his house swear by the Lord that he would take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred. The servant asked a sign at the well, and before he had done speaking Rebekah came out, gave him drink and drew for all his camels, and he bowed his head and worshipped. Her family inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said she would; when she saw Isaac she lighted off the camel and covered herself with a vail. Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent, and she became his wife, and he loved her.
events.article:
Abraham

Obeying the Lord’s voice; keeping his charge, his commandments, his statutes, and his laws

Kept the law

The Most High called Abram to get out of his country, from his kindred and from his father’s house. He called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him (Genesis 12:1; Isaiah 51:2). Ur of the Chaldees is old Babylon, the same country where Cain built and where Nimrod built after him, and it was so far gone that one man had to be taken out of it. Kindred did not hold him back from the blessing, and confessing the Most High before men sets a man at variance with his own household (Matthew 10:32-37). The promise that all families of the earth would be blessed in him is not everybody: the children of the prophets and of the covenant are Israel, and Israel would be scattered into all nations, so through his seed the kindreds of the earth are blessed in being turned every one from his iniquities (Genesis 12:2-3; Acts 3:25-26; Amos 2:11). The nations that dealt well with him prospered in their fields and their cattle; the ones that laid a hand on him were cursed, and that is how the promise worked in his own lifetime. He departed at seventy and five years old into the land of Canaan (Genesis 12:4-5).

He believed in the Lord, and it was counted to him for righteousness. Righteousness is defined by the law, for it shall be our righteousness if we observe to do all these commandments, and righteousness is immortal; his faith showed itself in his works (Genesis 15:5-6; Deuteronomy 6:25; Wisdom of Solomon 1:15; Romans 4:1-3). He offered the divided sacrifice, and in the deep sleep and the horror of great darkness the Lord showed him what was coming: his seed a stranger in a land not theirs, afflicted four hundred years, the nation they served judged, and the seed brought out with great substance in the fourth generation, when the iniquity of the Amorites was full (Genesis 15:9-16; Job 33:15-16; Amos 3:7; Acts 7:6). That word was fulfilled at the exodus, when the sojourning of the children of Israel ended on the selfsame day and they spoiled the Egyptians (Exodus 12:40-41).

At ninety and nine he was commanded to walk before the Most High and be perfect; perfect means to walk in his statutes and keep his commandments, and there is no age excuse in it (Genesis 17:1; 1 Kings 8:61). Circumcision is the token of the covenant, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he already had while yet uncircumcised, and he circumcised every male of his house the selfsame day he received the commandment (Genesis 17:10-14, 23-27; Romans 4:11). When the son of the promise was demanded he rose up early in the morning, and the Lord swore by himself because Abraham had obeyed his voice (Genesis 22:3, 16-18). He was a peacemaker who let his nephew take the better land, a man who would not take a thread from the king of Sodom, and a man with trained servants of his own house and arms for them, who went to war and brought his brother’s son back (Genesis 13:8-9; Genesis 14:14-23). And the Lord said he knew him, that he would command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to do justice and judgment (Genesis 18:19).

His name was changed to Abraham, a father of many nations, and kings should come out of him; the same words passed to Jacob, named Israel, so the nations of the covenant are the tribes of Israel, and the blessing of all men and the covenant were made to rest upon the head of Jacob and were divided among the twelve tribes (Genesis 17:4-6; Genesis 35:10-11; Ecclesiasticus 44:19-23). The covenant is with his seed after him, literal offspring, and Israel is the servant, Jacob the chosen, the seed of Abraham the friend of God (Genesis 17:7; Isaiah 41:8). It passed to Isaac and not to Ishmael: in Isaac shall the seed be called, and the children of the promise are counted for the seed (Genesis 17:20-21; Romans 9:7-9). The land was covenanted to his seed from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates (Genesis 15:18).

What he carried was wisdom, and the wisdom was the law, for the law of the Most High is the truth (Psalms 119:142). Josephus records that in Egypt he reasoned down their customs and taught them arithmetic and the science of astronomy, which went from Egypt to the Greeks; the man Egypt is supposed to have taught had taught Egypt. And the oath sworn to him stood for his children on one stated ground, that Abraham obeyed his voice and kept his charge, his commandments, his statutes and his laws (Genesis 26:5).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/abraham

Rebekah and Abraham’s servant

Abraham: making his servant swear to take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites. The servant: asking a sign at the well and worshipping when it came to pass. Rebekah: drawing for the camels, saying, I will go, and covering herself with a vail

Kept the law

Abraham was old and well stricken in age, and the Lord had blessed him in all things; he made the eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all he had, swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that he would not take a wife for his son of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred (Genesis 24:1-4). The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, long before Moses wrote the law, and the law states its own reason, that they turn the son away from following the Lord to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Solomon is the prime example: he loved women of the other nations, went after their gods, and had to repent. Tobit says the same to his son: take a wife of the seed of your fathers, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did from the beginning, and their seed shall inherit the land (Tobit 4:12). The forefathers arranged marriages, because the building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young people left to their own accord. Abraham told the servant that the Lord God of heaven, who swore to give the land to his seed, would send his angel before him (Genesis 24:7).

At the well the servant prayed for good speed and for kindness to his master, and asked a sign: let the damsel who, being asked to let down her pitcher, answered that she would give his camels drink also be the one appointed for Isaac (Genesis 24:12-14). Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out, born to Bethuel the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder, very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: undefiled and beautiful, the kind of wife the forefathers had from the beginning (Genesis 24:15-16). He ran to meet her and asked to drink a little water; she hasted, let down her pitcher and gave him drink, then said she would draw for his camels also, and emptied her pitcher into the trough and ran again to the well (Genesis 24:17-20). She gave a stranger drink and then watered ten camels; that kind and easily entreated spirit is the pattern for the daughters of Israel. When the sign came to pass exactly, the man bowed his head and worshipped, and blessed the God of his master, who had not left him destitute of his mercy and his truth: being in the way, the Lord had led

him to the house of his master’s brethren (Genesis 24:26-27).

Her family asked to keep her ten days, and the servant said not to hinder him, seeing the Lord had prospered his way; so they called Rebekah and inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said, I will go (Genesis 24:55-58). They sent their sister away with her nurse and blessed her: to be the mother of thousands of millions, and that her seed might possess the gate of those which hate them, which is the blessing of Israel and a prophecy (Genesis 24:59-60). Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide, a custom of the forefathers showing the Lord dealt with them long before Sinai (Genesis 24:63). When she saw him she lighted off the camel, and when the servant told her it was his master, she took a vail and covered herself (Genesis 24:64-65). The four mothers covered their heads with actual material as a sign of submission; the power a woman has upon her head is her obedience, the custom the apostle goes into (1 Corinthians 11:5-10).

The servant told Isaac all things that he had done, and Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her, and he was comforted after his mother’s death, for he received a righteous wife like his mother (Genesis 24:66-67). He was forty when he took her; brothers waiting on a wife can be patient, because the right sister was appointed (Genesis 25:20).

When she was barren, Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, and the Lord was entreated of him, and Rebekah conceived (Genesis 25:21). A barren sister is not to nag her husband but to pray, and a husband is to pray for his wife, because only the Lord opens a womb. The oath against the daughters of Canaan, the sign at the well and the woman who said she would go were all answered inside one house. And the covenant narrows again here: it runs through her children, and of her two sons it is Jacob who carries it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/rebekah

events.title: Sarah
events.description: Twice Abraham called Sarah his sister, and twice a king took her into his house. The Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues; to Abimelech he came in a dream by night and told him he was a dead man, because the woman he had taken was a man’s wife. Adultery was sin in Genesis, long before Sinai, and the word spoken over Abraham, that the Most High would curse him that cursed him, worked here: a household plagued and every womb closed over the prophet’s wife.
events.article:
Pharaoh and Abimelech, who took Sarah

Taking another man’s wife into the king’s house

Plague

Entering Egypt, Abram feared that the men of the place would kill him for his wife’s sake, for Sarai was a very fair woman to look upon even in her sixties, and he told her to say she was his sister; Pharaoh’s princes commended her and she was taken into Pharaoh’s house (Genesis 12:10-15). Years later in Gerar, with Sarah still that fair at ninety, Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took her on the same word (Genesis 20:1-2). She was in fact his sister, the daughter of his father but not the daughter of his mother, and the saying was their standing agreement in every strange land (Genesis 20:12-13). The laws that name such a marriage a wicked thing were written down through Moses some four hundred years after this (Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 27:22).

Adultery was sin in Genesis, long before the seventh commandment was written at Sinai. God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and told him he was but a dead man, for the woman he had taken was a man’s wife; and the Most High said that he had withheld him from sinning against him, and suffered him not to touch her (Genesis 20:3-6). Abimelech called it what it is, a great sin, one of the weightier matters, for which there is no animal sacrifice that atones (Genesis 20:9). Abraham had thought the fear of God was not in that place (Genesis 20:11). The king was told to restore the man his wife, because the man was a prophet and would pray for him; and that if he did not restore her he would surely die, he and all that were his (Genesis 20:7).

The Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, and Pharaoh called Abram and sent him away with his wife and all that he had; and Abram came up out of Egypt very rich in cattle, in silver and in gold, so that the very household the wrong was done in paid for it (Genesis 12:17-20; Genesis 13:1-2). Behind the scenes with Abimelech the Lord had fast closed up all the wombs of his house because of Sarah; the king restored her with sheep, oxen, servants and a thousand pieces of silver, Abraham prayed, and God healed Abimelech, his wife and his maidservants, and they bare children (Genesis 20:14-18).

It happened both times she was taken, which is the point. The word given over Abraham was that the Most High would bless them that blessed him and curse him that cursed him, and here is that word working on two kings in two countries (Genesis 12:3). The Most High plagues a household over his prophet’s wife, and he does not play about it. The marriage stood under his protection whatever account the man had given of it, and neither king got past a dream and a plague before he let her go.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/pharaoh-and-abimelech-with-sarah

events.title: Lot
events.description:
Lot was a just man, one that does what is lawful and right, and living in Sodom he vexed his righteous soul from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked. He sat in the gate, pressed the two angels into his house because he knew the men of the city, made them a feast, and went out to the door and shut it behind him to stand between the mob and his guests. When he lingered, the men took him by the hand, the Lord being merciful to him, and brought him out before the fire fell.

The angels told them to escape for their lives and not look behind them. Brought out of the city by the hand, his wife looked back from behind him and became a pillar of salt, a standing monument of an unbelieving soul. She looked back because she loved what was burning; for her to look back at all says she had never agreed to leave. Christ made her a proverb in three words: Remember Lot’s wife.
events.article:
Lot

A just man, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked; pressing the strangers into his house and standing at the door

Kept the law

To be just is to do that which is lawful and right, which is a commandment keeper; and just Lot was a righteous man who, dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds (Ezekiel 18:5; 2 Peter 2:7-8). A righteous man cannot be at home in that conduct. He was Abram’s brother’s son, out of the same house that was called out of Ur of the Chaldees (Genesis 11:27, 31). Two angels came to Sodom at even while he sat in the gate; he rose up to meet them, bowed himself with his face toward the ground, and pressed upon them greatly to turn in to his house, because he knew the men of Sodom, and he made them a feast and they did eat. Angels have bodies and eat as men do; Abraham had fed three of them under the tree, and their appearance is likened to burning coals of fire (Genesis 19:1-3; Genesis 18:8; Ezekiel 1:13).

When the men of the city, old and young, compassed the house and demanded the men, Lot went out at the door, shut the door after him, and begged them as brethren not to do so wickedly (Genesis 19:4-7). He named the deed for what it was before the law was written at Sinai. They pressed sore upon him and came near to break the door, and the men put forth their hand, pulled him into the house and shut the door, and struck those at the door with blindness (Genesis 19:9-11). Then he went out and warned his sons in law to get up and get out of the place, and to them he seemed as one that mocked (Genesis 19:12-14).

While he lingered, the men laid hold upon his hand and upon the hand of his wife and of his two daughters, the Lord being merciful to him, and brought him out and set him outside the city, and told him to escape for his life, not to look behind him, not to stay in all the plain, and to escape to the mountain (Genesis 19:15-17). The angel could do nothing until he had come to Zoar; the judgment of a whole plain waited on one righteous man being brought out (Genesis 19:22). The Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptations and to reserve the unjust to the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9). God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow (Genesis 19:29). Noah, Daniel and Job are named as men who deliver their own souls by their righteousness, and that is what Lot did; the sons in law who laughed did not, and no man’s righteousness covered them (Ezekiel 14:14).

Afterward he feared to dwell in Zoar and went up into the mountain with his two daughters, and dwelt in a cave. They thought Sodom had been the whole world and that there was not a man left in the earth to come in to them, so they made their father drink wine and lay with him, the firstborn one night and the younger the next, and he perceived it not when they lay down nor when they arose (Genesis 19:30-36). Take no wayward idea from it: uncovering the nakedness of a father was unlawful then and is unlawful now (Leviticus 18:7). The firstborn bare Moab, the father of the Moabites, and the younger bare Benammi, the father of the children of Ammon, to this day; in this teaching those nations are identified with the peoples known today as the Chinese and the Japanese (Genesis 19:37-38).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/lot

Lot’s wife

Looking back toward Sodom against the angel’s command

Put to death

The instruction came with the rescue and it was specific: escape for your life, look not behind you, stay not in all the plain, escape to the mountain, or be consumed (Genesis 19:17). She had already been taken out by the hand together with her husband and her two daughters, the Lord being merciful to them (Genesis 19:16). The city she was leaving was the city whose men, old and young, from every quarter, had compassed her own house to know the two strangers, and had pressed against her own door (Genesis 19:4-7). Yet she looked back from behind him, against the word given to her (Genesis 19:26).

Ask why any woman would look back at that. The place was not a ruin: it was rich, glorious, full of the things the eyes want, and she loved that life. Somebody in that house was not vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked (2 Peter 2:7-8). For her to turn at all says she had never agreed to leave in the first place; she was grieving what was burning. Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world, for all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not of the Father but is of the world, and the world passes away (1 John 2:15-17). The psalm asks who will rise up for the Lord against the evildoers and who will stand up against the workers of iniquity, and she had not (Psalms 94:16).

She became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). Wisdom keeps that standing pillar as a monument of an unbelieving soul, and the waste land that smokes as a testimony of the wickedness to this day (Wisdom of Solomon 10:6-7). Christ set her among the weightiest words in the scriptures. He said it would be as in the days of Lot, when they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and builded, until the same day that Lot went out of Sodom and it rained fire and brimstone from heaven and destroyed them all; and so shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed, and in that day the man upon the housetop is not to come down for his goods, nor the man in the field to turn back. Remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:28-32).

Babylon has an end, and whoever wants to carry Babylon into the kingdom is looking back the way she looked back; a man that puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). She was not left behind. She was led out by the hand, by angels, ahead of the fire, with the mercy of the Lord upon her, and still she did not make it, because being led out is not the end of obedience.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/lots-wife

events.title: Laban
events.description: Laban of the house of Nahor, an idolater as his fathers were, received Jacob as his own bone and flesh, then took seven years of work for Rachel and delivered Leah, charged seven more, and changed the wages ten times over twenty years while the Lord blessed him for Jacob’s sake. When Jacob left, he pursued him seven days with the power in his hand to hurt him, and God came to him in a dream by night and told him to speak to Jacob neither good nor bad.
events.article:
Laban and the changed wages

Changing his hired servant’s wages ten times, and giving the elder daughter in place of the younger

Reprieve

Jacob went up out of Canaan north and then east to Haran, back to the family Terah had left there when he brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldees, and Laban said he was surely his bone and his flesh, which in the scriptures means, we are family (Genesis 29:1-5, 14; Genesis 11:26-31). Jacob loved Rachel, beautiful and well favoured, and served seven years for her, and they seemed to him but a few days for the love he had to her; men gather gold and silver and every goodly thing and then let it all go and fix their eyes fast on a comely woman, and many have run out of their wits for a woman and become servants for their sakes (Genesis 29:16-20; 1 Esdras 4:18-26). In the evening Laban brought him Leah, and in the morning it was Leah; his answer, that it must not be so done in their country to give the younger before the firstborn, was a rule he had known before he took the seven years (Genesis 29:23-26). He required seven other years (Genesis 29:27-30).

Laban had learned by experience that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob’s sake, and Jacob reminded him how little he had before he came, and that it was now increased to a multitude, and asked when he should provide for his own house also (Genesis 30:27-30). Jacob asked no gift. He set terms that could be checked in the open, the speckled and the spotted and the brown to be his hire, so that his righteousness would answer for him in time to come; and Laban agreed and that same day removed those very cattle into the hand of his own sons and set three days journey between them (Genesis 30:31-36). Then he changed the wages ten times. Jacob’s account, which Laban does not deny, is that but for the God of his father he would have been sent away empty: twenty years, the drought consuming him by day and the frost by night, and his sleep departing from his eyes (Genesis 31:7, 38-42). When Laban’s sons said Jacob had taken away all that was their father’s, Laban’s countenance was not toward him as before (Genesis 31:1-2). The Lord told Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and to his kindred, and he would be with him (Genesis 31:3). Laban pursued him seven days journey and asked why he had stolen his gods. That question tells what Laban was: an idolater of the house of Nahor, whose fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood and served other gods, the very kindred the Most High had separated Abram from (Genesis 31:23, 30; Joshua 24:2; Genesis 12:1).

The pursuer was restrained before he could use the power he had. God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night and warned him to take heed that he speak not to Jacob either good or bad (Genesis 31:24). He admitted it to Jacob’s face: he had the power to do Jacob harm, but the God of Jacob’s father had spoken to him the night before (Genesis 31:29). He searched every tent and found nothing. Jacob answered that God had seen his affliction and the labour of his hands, and had rebuked him the night before (Genesis 31:42).

They made a covenant at the heap and the pillar, that neither would pass over it to the other for harm, and Laban rose up early, kissed his sons and his daughters, blessed them and returned to his place (Genesis 31:44-55). The record does not reduce him to poverty, and it does not need to. It shows a man with the power and the numbers to take everything, stopped in his sleep by one sentence, and Jacob walking away with the household and with the substance the Most High had preserved for him out of twenty years of changed wages.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/laban

events.title: Isaac
events.description:
A famine came, and the natural road was Egypt, where his father had gone. The Lord appeared and told him not to go down into Egypt but to sojourn in that land, where he would be with him, and performed to him the oath sworn to Abraham, because Abraham obeyed his voice and kept his charge, his commandments, his statutes and his laws. Isaac stayed, sowed in a famine year and reaped a hundredfold, dug his wells over again rather than fight for them, and the nations envied him for the blessing itself.

Before either child was born the Lord told Rebekah that two nations were in her womb, two manner of people, and that the elder shall serve the younger. Esau sold the birthright himself and despised it. When Isaac, whose eyes the Lord let grow dim, sent Esau for venison to bless him, Rebekah moved on the word she carried, took the curse upon herself, and sent Jacob in with the kid skins and his brother’s raiment. Isaac tested him four ways and blessed him, and when the deception was known he confirmed it knowingly: he shall be blessed. The supplanting was of the Holy Ghost, not of Jacob’s trickery.
events.article:
Isaac

Dwelling in the land the Lord told him of, and not going down into Egypt in the famine

Kept the law

In the famine Isaac was told not to go down into Egypt, but to dwell in the land which the Lord would tell him of, and to sojourn there, and he would be with him and bless him (Genesis 26:1-3). The oath sworn to Abraham was performed to him: seed as the stars of heaven, all those countries, and in his seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. That does not put everybody in the covenant. The seed is Christ, and the children of the prophets and of the covenant are Israel, scattered into every nation; through Christ, scattered Israel in all the kindreds of the earth gets the blessing, which is being turned every one from his iniquities (Genesis 26:4; Galatians 3:16; Acts 3:25-26; Amos 2:11). The reason the oath stood is stated in the text: because Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes and my laws (Genesis 26:5). Isaac dwelt in Gerar in obedience to that word (Genesis 26:6).

He said of Rebekah that she was his sister, fearing the men of the place, as his father had done before him; and Abimelech looked out at a window and saw him sporting with Rebekah his wife, and knew (Genesis 26:7-11). Take the lesson from the sporting: love your wife, play with your wife, keep the flirting and the freshness in the marriage, and live joyfully with the wife you love all the days of your life (Ecclesiastes 9:9). When the herdmen of Gerar strove for the wells he had digged again after his father, at Esek and at Sitnah, he removed and digged again, until at Rehoboth they strove not, and he said that now the Lord had made room for them (Genesis 26:17-22). He did not assimilate among a people that hated him; he separated from them. And when Abimelech came claiming they had done him nothing but good, though his people had stopped the wells and sent him away, he answered plainly and asked why they came to him, seeing they hated him (Genesis 26:26-27). Words can be smoother than butter while war is in the heart, and he dealt with their covenant with his eyes open.

Then Isaac sowed in that land and received in the same year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him; the man waxed great and went forward and grew until he became very great (Genesis 26:12-13). The Philistines envied him and stopped up all his wells with earth; the nations envy the prosperity of Israel, and it is not for anything done to them, for the blessing itself is what is hated (Genesis 26:14-15). The king of the country came to him seeking terms, and gave his reason: they had seen certainly that the Lord was with him (Genesis 26:28). The blessing was public and legible to outsiders.

He made them a feast, exchanged an oath and sent them away in peace without pretending he had been well treated, and that same day his servants came and told him of the well (Genesis 26:30-33). The Lord had appeared to him the night before at Beersheba as the God of Abraham his father, told him not to fear, and promised to be with him and bless him and multiply his seed for his servant Abraham’s sake; and he builded an altar there, called upon the name of the Lord and pitched his tent (Genesis 26:24-25). He lived an hundred and fourscore years and died old and full of days, and his two sons buried him (Genesis 35:28-29).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/isaac

Jacob, deceiving Isaac for the blessing

Obeying his mother’s voice, who carried the word of the Lord that the elder shall serve the younger; receiving the blessing prophesied before his birth

Kept the law

The children struggled together within Rebekah, and when she went to inquire of the Lord he told her that two nations were in her womb, that two manner of people should be separated from her bowels, that one people should be stronger than the other, and that the elder shall serve the younger (Genesis 25:22-23). Two manner means two different peoples in look, in thought and in behaviour, which is not how twins usually come. Good is set against evil, and life against death, so is the godly against the sinner, and all the works of the Most High are two and two, one against another (Ecclesiasticus 33:14-15). Rebekah loved Jacob because the Lord had told her which son was the chosen, and she was the only one who had been told (Genesis 25:28). Esau had already sold the birthright for a meal and sworn to it; it was not taken from him, he threw it away himself, and that is how Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:29-34).

Isaac’s eyes were dim so that he could not see, and the Lord allowed that blindness for a purpose, that the blessing could pass to Jacob; what looks like evil can be meant for good, as Joseph’s slavery was meant for good (Genesis 27:1; Genesis 50:20). How else was the elder going to serve the younger, if the elder took the whole blessing? Rebekah heard and moved, because she carried the word from the Lord and knew this was the moment. Jacob objected that his father would feel him, and he would seem a deceiver and bring a curse upon himself and not a blessing, and his mother took the curse upon herself, telling him to let it fall on her and only obey her voice (Genesis 27:5-13). She made the savoury meat such as his father loved, put Esau’s raiment upon him so that he would carry the smell of the field, and put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands and upon the smooth of his neck (Genesis 27:14-16). Isaac was not simple. He asked how the venison was found so quickly, he felt him and said the voice is Jacob’s voice but the hands are the hands of Esau, he asked outright whether he was his very son Esau, and he called him near to kiss him so that he could smell his raiment (Genesis 27:20-27). Jacob is called a supplanter, but the supplanting was of the Holy Ghost: the purpose of God according to election stood, not of works but of him that calleth, and the word had been spoken to her and not to him (Romans 9:11-13). It was not his plan. He obeyed his mother, and she obeyed the word she had been given.

The blessing is rulership of the earth: the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, plenty of corn and wine, people serving him and nations bowing down to him, lordship over his brethren, and a curse upon every one that cursed him and a blessing upon every one that blessed him (Genesis 27:28-29). When Esau came in, Isaac trembled very exceedingly and then confirmed it knowingly: he had blessed him, and he shall be blessed; he had made him his lord and given him all his brethren for servants (Genesis 27:33, 37). That is how the elder shall serve the younger, and the blessing does not come into fruition until the appointed time. Esau cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry and said that Jacob had supplanted him these two times, telling a pity story about a birthright he had sold himself (Genesis 27:34-36).

Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing, and said in his heart that the days of mourning for his father were at hand and then he would slay his brother, which is the same hatred Cain bore Abel; and Rebekah sent Jacob to Laban her brother, and away from the daughters of Heth, saying she was weary of her life because of them (Genesis 27:41-46). God appeared to him at Bethel, showed him the ladder set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven and the angels ascending and descending on it, confirmed the covenant to him, and promised to bring him again into that land (Genesis 28:12-15; 1 Chronicles 16:15-17). Christians read this chapter and call Jacob the evil son and Esau the good one; the scriptures call Esau the profane one and the fornicator, and call this son the chosen.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/jacob-deceiving-isaac

events.title: Rebekah
events.description: Abraham, old and blessed in all things, made the eldest servant of his house swear by the Lord that he would take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred. The servant asked a sign at the well, and before he had done speaking Rebekah came out, gave him drink and drew for all his camels, and he bowed his head and worshipped. Her family inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said she would; when she saw Isaac she lighted off the camel and covered herself with a vail. Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent, and she became his wife, and he loved her.
events.article:
Rebekah and Abraham’s servant

Abraham: making his servant swear to take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites. The servant: asking a sign at the well and worshipping when it came to pass. Rebekah: drawing for the camels, saying, I will go, and covering herself with a vail

Kept the law

Abraham was old and well stricken in age, and the Lord had blessed him in all things; he made the eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all he had, swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that he would not take a wife for his son of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred (Genesis 24:1-4). The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, long before Moses wrote the law, and the law states its own reason, that they turn the son away from following the Lord to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Solomon is the prime example: he loved women of the other nations, went after their gods, and had to repent. Tobit says the same to his son: take a wife of the seed of your fathers, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did from the beginning, and their seed shall inherit the land (Tobit 4:12). The forefathers arranged marriages, because the building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young people left to their own accord. Abraham told the servant that the Lord God of heaven, who swore to give the land to his seed, would send his angel before him (Genesis 24:7).

At the well the servant prayed for good speed and for kindness to his master, and asked a sign: let the damsel who, being asked to let down her pitcher, answered that she would give his camels drink also be the one appointed for Isaac (Genesis 24:12-14). Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out, born to Bethuel the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder, very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: undefiled and beautiful, the kind of wife the forefathers had from the beginning (Genesis 24:15-16). He ran to meet her and asked to drink a little water; she hasted, let down her pitcher and gave him drink, then said she would draw for his camels also, and emptied her pitcher into the trough and ran again to the well (Genesis 24:17-20). She gave a stranger drink and then watered ten camels; that kind and easily entreated spirit is the pattern for the daughters of Israel. When the sign came to pass exactly, the man bowed his head and worshipped, and blessed the God of his master, who had not left him destitute of his mercy and his truth: being in the way, the Lord had led

him to the house of his master’s brethren (Genesis 24:26-27).

Her family asked to keep her ten days, and the servant said not to hinder him, seeing the Lord had prospered his way; so they called Rebekah and inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said, I will go (Genesis 24:55-58). They sent their sister away with her nurse and blessed her: to be the mother of thousands of millions, and that her seed might possess the gate of those which hate them, which is the blessing of Israel and a prophecy (Genesis 24:59-60). Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide, a custom of the forefathers showing the Lord dealt with them long before Sinai (Genesis 24:63). When she saw him she lighted off the camel, and when the servant told her it was his master, she took a vail and covered herself (Genesis 24:64-65). The four mothers covered their heads with actual material as a sign of submission; the power a woman has upon her head is her obedience, the custom the apostle goes into (1 Corinthians 11:5-10).

The servant told Isaac all things that he had done, and Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her, and he was comforted after his mother’s death, for he received a righteous wife like his mother (Genesis 24:66-67). He was forty when he took her; brothers waiting on a wife can be patient, because the right sister was appointed (Genesis 25:20).

When she was barren, Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, and the Lord was entreated of him, and Rebekah conceived (Genesis 25:21). A barren sister is not to nag her husband but to pray, and a husband is to pray for his wife, because only the Lord opens a womb. The oath against the daughters of Canaan, the sign at the well and the woman who said she would go were all answered inside one house. And the covenant narrows again here: it runs through her children, and of her two sons it is Jacob who carries it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/rebekah

events.title: Esau
events.description: The first came out red, all over like a hairy garment, and his birth had to be documented because a nation comes out of him; from him comes Edom, which is red, and this teaching reads his seed as the return of Cain’s line. He was the firstborn as Cain was the firstborn, a man of the field as Cain was, and carnal minded: he sold the birthright for a meal, took Hittite wives to his parents’ grief, and when the blessing went to Jacob he purposed in his heart to kill him. His own anger turned away; his children’s never did.
events.article:
Esau

Despising his birthright; marrying the daughters of Heth against the fathers’ law; purposing to kill his brother

Cursed

The first came out red, all over like a hairy garment, and they called his name Esau; Jacob is not described, because he looked like his father and his mother and like everybody from the time of Adam (Genesis 25:25-26). The scribes wrote down the colour of the one who was different, because a nation comes out of him. Esau means wasted away, and what was wasted away was the pigment; the hair over him covers a body with no protection of its own from the sun, and it is thin and goatlike, which is why goat skins passed for it. Jacob’s hand took hold on Esau’s heel, and that is prophecy: Esau is the end of this world, and Jacob the beginning of it that follows (2 Esdras 6:7-9). He was a cunning hunter, a man of the field, as Cain was a man of the field; Cain was the firstborn and Esau was the firstborn, and it is the same spirit (Genesis 25:27; Genesis 4:2).

He came from the field faint and asked to be fed with that same red pottage, which had red meat in it, and that is why his name was called Edom, red; he asked what profit the birthright should do him, sware, sold it for bread and pottage of lentiles, rose up and went his way (Genesis 25:29-34). He wanted the carnal thing and threw away the thing from above; it was not taken from him.
