Hebrews names him a profane person and a fornicator, and the fornication is in the law he broke: at forty he took to wife Judith and Bashemath, daughters of the Hittites, which were a grief of mind to Isaac and to Rebekah, and later he went to Ishmael and took Mahalath also (Hebrews 12:16; Genesis 26:34-35; Genesis 28:8-9; Tobit 4:12). That is the nature of the vessel, and Hebrews names the root: a root of bitterness springing up, and thereby many defiled (Hebrews 12:15).

When the blessing went to Jacob he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry and wept aloud, which is worldly sorrow; he told his father that Jacob had supplanted him these two times, playing the victim over a birthright he sold (Genesis 27:34-38; Psalms 50:19-20). He found no place of repentance, though he sought it with tears (Hebrews 12:17). He hated Jacob because of the blessing, and said in his heart that the days of mourning for his father were at hand and then he would slay his brother (Genesis 27:41). Cain killed Abel; Esau purposed to kill Jacob. Rebekah knew that if he did it she would be deprived of both in one day, because the man who kills his brother dies for it (Genesis 27:45; Wisdom of Solomon 10:3).

His portion was given him: his dwelling should be the fatness of the earth and of the dew of heaven from above, and by his sword he should live, and he should serve his brother; and when he should have the dominion he should break his brother’s yoke from off his neck (Genesis 27:39-40). What his kingdoms have, they took by war and by ever more advanced weaponry, the same inheritance Cain’s line carried through Tubalcain (Genesis 4:22). He broke the yoke in the days of Jehoram, when Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah and made a king over themselves (2 Kings 8:20); this present time is the time of his dominion, and when his rule is done, Jacob comes into power.

His own anger turned away; his children’s did not, and the perpetual hatred remained in his seed (Ezekiel 35:5). In the day that the strangers carried Judah away he stood as one of them, rejoiced over their destruction, laid hands on their substance and cut off those that escaped, and the Edomites burned the temple (Obadiah

1:11-14; 1 Esdras 4:45). The Lord said he loved Jacob and hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste; though Edom says they will return and build the desolate places, they shall build and he will throw down, and they shall be called the border of wickedness, the people against whom the Lord has indignation for ever (Malachi 1:2-4). For his violence against his brother Jacob shame shall cover him, and the house of Esau shall be stubble, with none remaining (Obadiah 1:10, 18). Though he exalt himself as the eagle and set his nest among the stars, from there he shall be brought down (Obadiah 1:3-4). The descendants of Esau, sworn enemies of the descendants of Jacob even to the end of the world, went out from Mount Seir and founded Rome and its empire, and hold dominion over Europe, Esau detaining his brother Jacob in captivity; those prophecies have not yet received their full accomplishment.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/esau

events.title: Rachel
events.description: Rachel stole the images that were her father’s, hid them in the camel’s furniture and sat upon them, and told her father she could not rise up before him, so he searched and found them not. Jacob, not knowing, had said that whoever was found with them should not live. No sentence for the theft is announced. The strange gods stayed hidden in the household until Jacob commanded them put away before Bethel, and the beguiling of the mothers from Eve to Rachel is the warning the record leaves.
events.article:
Rachel and the stolen teraphim

Stealing her father’s images, and hiding them under her while she sat upon them

Sentence deferred

When Laban went to shear his sheep, Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s (Genesis 31:19). Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that fears the Lord shall be praised: she was fine, and she was a thief (Proverbs 31:30). Laban’s own question, why he had stolen his gods, tells what house she came out of: an idolater of the line of Nahor, whose fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time and served other gods, and that is why the Most High had told Abram to get out from his country and from his kindred (Genesis 31:30; Joshua 24:2).

Jacob, who did not know that Rachel had stolen them, answered that with whoever his gods were found, let him not live, and invited Laban to search before their brethren (Genesis 31:32). She had taken the images and put them in the camel’s furniture and sat upon them, and said to her father, let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before you, for the custom of women is upon me; and he searched all the tent and found not the images (Genesis 31:34-35). Idolatry was carried hidden into the covenant household, and a lie covered it, and her own husband had unknowingly pronounced a sentence over her head.

No sentence for the theft is recorded, and Jacob’s oath was spoken in ignorance. The images stayed in the camp. Before going up to Bethel, Jacob said to his household and to all that were with him, put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments; the strange gods were there because she had stolen them and hidden them, and she gave them up then, and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem (Genesis 35:1-4). Idolatry hidden in a household has to be put away before a man can stand at Bethel.

What followed was protection, not punishment: the terror of God was upon the cities round about, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob, for the angel of the Lord encamps round about them that fear him and delivers them (Genesis 35:5; Psalms 34:7). From Eve to Rachel the scriptures show how sin comes into a house through the household, for of the woman came the beginning of sin, and the warning left here is for the mothers of Israel to guard against the same beguiling (Ecclesiasticus 25:24). Rachel died in hard labour bearing Benjamin in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem, and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave (Genesis 35:16-20); the record does not name that death as the penalty for the theft, and it is not given as one. Delay is not acquittal.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/rachel-and-the-teraphim

events.title: Reuben
events.description: Jacob’s firstborn went up to his father’s bed and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it. Paul calls that a fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, and the law had already forbidden it, because a father’s wife is the father’s own nakedness. Nothing more is said until the deathbed, where it cost Reuben the birthright: unstable as water, he would not excel.
events.article:
Reuben

Lying with Bilhah, his father’s concubine

Cursed

While Israel dwelt in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it (Genesis 35:22). Paul names the same offense among the Corinthians and calls it a fornication not so much as named among the Gentiles, that a man should have his father’s wife (1 Corinthians 5:1). The law had already forbidden it: the nakedness of a father’s wife is the father’s own nakedness, and the wicked mind that reasons she is not the biological mother is answered before it opens its mouth (Leviticus 18:8). The chapter sets it in the middle of a household being cleaned up. Before going up to Bethel, Jacob had told his house to put away the strange gods among them and be clean, and the terror of God was on the cities round about so that they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:2-5). Sin entering the household is the running warning of the chapter. The brief report on Reuben is not an acquittal by silence.

Jacob called him his firstborn, his might and the beginning of his strength, the excellency of dignity and the excellency of power; then, unstable as water, he would not excel, because he went up to his father’s bed and defiled it (Genesis 49:3-4). The firstborn is the father’s posterity, and dignity and power belonged to him. The chronicle states the transfer plainly: because he defiled his father’s bed his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, and the genealogy is not reckoned after the birthright; Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came the chief ruler (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). The firstborn lost the place of the heir, as Esau came out first and did not keep it.

Reuben remained a son and a tribe of Israel, and one good line runs through his record. At the pit he delivered Joseph out of his brothers’ hands, telling them to shed no blood, because he meant to bring him back to his father (Genesis 37:21-22); years later, in Egypt, he offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin (Genesis 42:37). The tribe itself went a-whoring after the gods of the people of the land, the very thing the fringes were given to prevent, so that Israel would look on them and remember the commandments and not go after their own eyes; therefore the Most High stirred up the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria, who carried Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh into captivity, where they remain to this day (1 Chronicles 5:25-26; Numbers 15:39). The blessings of Jacob tell who the tribes are in the last days. Reuben is the so-called Seminole Indian today: great warriors carrying the excellency of power, and unstable as water, nomads always moving, exactly as the scripture said.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/02-patriarchal/reuben

events.title: Aaron
events.description:
Not forty days after they heard the voice from the mount, the people told Aaron to make them gods, since they did not know what had become of this Moses. Aaron, who had seen every plague, made the calf and proclaimed a feast to the Lord, and the people feasted and rose up to play. The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left. Moses stood in the breach, the sons of Levi drew the sword, and the Lord plagued the people because of the calf that Aaron made.

Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, who was Zipporah the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom the Lord had allowed him. The woman was the excuse; what they actually said was a claim of equal standing with the man God had set over them, and the Lord heard it. He came down and declared the difference to their faces, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow: a father’s spit in her face, seven days without the camp, while the whole nation waited.
events.article:
Aaron and Israel at the golden calf

Idolatry within weeks of the covenant: the spirit of Egypt still in Israel

Plague

When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, they gathered to Aaron and told him to make them gods to go before them, since as for this Moses they did not know what had become of him (Exodus 32:1). Any time deliverance did not come when Israel wanted it, the nation turned, and the leadership got the blame; the same spirit works against the leadership of Israel to this day. Aaron told them to break off the golden earrings in the ears of their wives, their sons and their daughters, which men and women both wore in the scriptures and which is not the sin here; he received the gold, fashioned it with a graving tool and made a molten calf, and they declared it the god that had brought them up out of the land of Egypt, and he built an altar before it and proclaimed a feast to the Lord for the next day (Exodus 32:2-5). Aaron had seen the miracles in Egypt and was set up as high priest, and he still succumbed to the pressure of the people.

The people rose up early, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play; that play was fornication, the same play as at Peor (Exodus 32:6; 1 Corinthians 10:7-8). The Lord told Moses that they had turned aside quickly out of the way he commanded them, and that he had seen this people and it is a stiffnecked people (Exodus 32:8-9). Not forty days gone from the mount, and they had already left his commandments. The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left, and the same holds coming into this truth: the evil carried in from the world will corrupt a man and turn him from the Lord if it is not put off (Ecclesiastes 5:1). They had broken the first two commandments that had just been given at Sinai (Exodus 20:3-5).

The Lord told Moses to let him alone, that his wrath might wax hot against them and consume them, and he would make of Moses a great nation; Moses was of Levi and of the seed of Jacob, so the Lord could have started over with him (Exodus 32:10). Moses stood in the middle and pleaded the name and the oath: why should the Egyptians say that for mischief he brought them out to slay them in the mountains; and he asked the Lord to remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel, to whom he swore by his own self. And the Lord repented of the evil which he thought to do to his people (Exodus 32:11-14). He was never going to break that covenant, for consuming the people would have destroyed the very seed he had sworn to, and his counsel stands from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10).

Joshua heard the noise of the people and said there was a noise of war in the camp, and Moses answered that it was not the voice of them that shout for mastery nor the voice of them that cry for being overcome, but the noise of them that sing (Exodus 32:17-18): they were feasting and dancing around the idol, and Joshua’s loyalty at the mount is one of the main reasons the Lord chose him to follow Moses. When Moses came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, his anger waxed hot; he brake the tables beneath the mount, burnt the calf, ground it to powder, strawed it on the water and made the children of Israel drink of it (Exodus 32:19-20). Aaron answered exactly as Saul would answer afterward, blaming the congregation: they are set on mischief, I cast the gold into the fire, and there came out this calf (Exodus 32:22-24). A leader cannot blame the people he was left in charge of. The people were naked, for Aaron had made them naked to their shame among their enemies, the same nakedness of the

garden, sin uncovered (Exodus 32:25). The sons of Levi answered the call to the Lord’s side, and about three thousand men fell that day, entered separately as their blessing (Exodus 32:26-28). Moses returned to mediate, asking to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if the sin was not forgiven, and the Lord answered that the man who sinned against him is the man he would blot out, and that in the day of his visitation he would visit their sin upon them; and the Lord plagued the people because they made the calf, which Aaron made (Exodus 32:32-35). They changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eats grass, and forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt (Psalms 106:19-21).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/04-wilderness/the-golden-calf

Aaron and Miriam

Speaking against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, and claiming an equal standing: hath he not spoken also by us?

Temporal judgment

Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman he had married (Numbers 12:1). This is still Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom Moses married in the forty years he dwelt outside Egypt, when he was in a land by himself with none of his own people around him, and whom the Lord allowed him (Exodus 2:16, 21); a place being called Midian and the woman being called an Ethiopian is no contradiction. They had said nothing about her when Moses was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of what was at hand.

The woman was the excuse. The charge is what they actually said: they asked whether the Lord had spoken only by Moses, and not also by them, and the Lord heard it (Numbers 12:2). Was the Most High dealing with Aaron and Miriam? He was. He was dealing with Moses more, and that is what could not be borne, so the real matter was a covetousness for his standing dressed up as a complaint about his wife. The teaching names the pattern: a man who has a problem with the leadership goes looking for something in the leadership to hold up, so that when he gossips and murmurs about the body he looks like the righteous one; pull the curtain back and it was never about the thing he named, it was about power. The man Moses was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3), so this was no hard man provoking them. Those who despise government are presumptuous and selfwilled, and are not afraid to speak evil of dignities (2 Peter 2:10).

The Lord spoke suddenly to Moses, Aaron and Miriam, calling the three of them out to the tabernacle; He came down in the pillar of the cloud, called Aaron and Miriam forward, and declared the difference: to a prophet among them He would make Himself known in a vision and speak in a dream, but His servant Moses was not so, being faithful in all His house; with him He spoke mouth to mouth, plainly and not in dark speeches; so why were they not afraid to speak against His servant Moses (Numbers 12:4-5, 6-10). He had to let them know that He does not deal with everyone the same. They were a prophet and a prophetess and He spoke with them, but in visions and dreams; some spirits are greater than others, and a nation has to learn to accept it. The anger of the Lord was kindled, the cloud departed from the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow. Aaron pleaded that the sin not be laid on them, and Moses cried to the Lord to heal her (Numbers 12:11, 13-15).

The Lord answered that if her father had only spat in her face she would have been ashamed seven days, so she was to be shut out of the camp seven days and then received in again. The spit is correction, a father putting his child in her place; had she been raised to respect the men of the Lord, this would not have come on her. Miriam was shut out, and the people did not journey until she was brought in again: a whole nation held in place over one tongue. This is a charge to raise the children in the fear of the Lord and teach them to respect the elders and the men of the Lord. Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, and fathers are not to provoke their children to wrath but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:1-4); parents who let their children speak evil to the men of the Lord bring the judgment on their own household. Moses made it a standing warning: Israel was to remember what the Lord their God did to Miriam by the way (Deuteronomy 24:9).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/04-wilderness/aaron-and-miriam

events.title: Moses
events.description:
Things were not bad for Moses in Egypt; he made them bad for himself by choosing his people. By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, chose affliction with the people of God over the pleasures of sin for a season, and led a stiffnecked house forty years. The Lord’s testimony on him is unmatched: his servant Moses was faithful in all his house, and he spoke with him mouth to mouth. He was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth, and God buried him.

Raised in Pharaoh’s house but nursed by his own mother, Moses always knew who he was. At forty it came into his heart to visit his brethren, and he looked on their burdens and saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and killed him. He did not merely marvel at the oppression; he used his position for his people, supposing his brethren would understand that God would deliver them by his hand. They did not understand, the man in the wrong threw the killing in his face, and Moses fled to Midian a stranger in a strange land forty years, until the God of his fathers sent back the man they had refused.

Sent back to Egypt with the rod of God in his hand and the message that Israel was the Lord’s son, his firstborn, whom Pharaoh must release or lose his own firstborn, Moses went with his wife and his sons. On the way, at the inn, the Lord met him and sought to kill him, because his own son was uncircumcised. Zipporah took a sharp stone and circumcised the child, and the Lord let him go. The laws did not begin at Sinai, and the covenant of circumcision still stands.

There was no water, and the people chode with Moses, loud and angry, wishing they had died when their brethren died. Moses had to deal with all twelve tribes at once, and a stomach can only take so much of a rebellious people. Told to speak to the rock, he called them rebels, asked whether he and Aaron must fetch them water out of this rock, and smote it twice. That we is how the record shows he was out of the spirit: he put himself in the place of the One giving the water. The water still came, and the sentence with it.
events.article:
Moses

Refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; faithful in all the Lord’s house; very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth

Kept the law

By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he had respect to the recompence of the reward (Hebrews 11:24-26). Everybody in ancient Egypt was not badly off. Some of our people had money and standing and were comfortable with the oppression they lived under, like the officers of the children of Israel whom the taskmasters had set over their own brethren, until the beatings came to them too (Exodus 5:14); the same men live in spiritual Egypt now. In Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and his customs Egyptian, and he laid every bit of it down to be what he was called to be.

He was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22). He did not stutter, as is commonly taught; he was not fluent in the Hebrew of his brethren, having been raised in Pharaoh’s court and then spent forty years in Midian, and a language moves on in forty years, so Aaron was given him for a mouth and he stood to Aaron instead of God (Exodus 4:10-16). From the royal court he went to keeping his father in law’s flock for forty years, and when the Lord called him out of the bush his answer was, who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh (Exodus 3:11). A man’s goings are of the Lord (Proverbs 20:24). He built the tabernacle exactly as the Lord commanded him (Exodus 40:16), bore a congregation that murmured at every stage, and stood between the people and the wrath they provoked, asking to be blotted out of the Lord’s book if their sin was not forgiven (Exodus 32:11-14, 32). The man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3).

When Miriam and Aaron spoke against him because of the Ethiopian woman, who was Zipporah the daughter of the priest of Midian, and asked whether the Lord had spoken only by Moses and not also by them, the Lord heard it, came down in the pillar of the cloud, and declared the difference: to a prophet among them he would make himself known in a vision and speak in a dream, but his servant Moses was not so, being faithful in all his house; with him he would speak mouth to mouth, even apparently and not in dark speeches, and Moses beheld the similitude of the Lord; why then were they not afraid to speak against his servant (Numbers 12:1-8). They that despise government and speak evil of dignities are presumptuous and selfwilled (2 Peter 2:10). Miriam became leprous, white as snow, and was shut out of the camp seven days, and the people did not journey until she was brought in again. The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend (Exodus 33:11).

He was refused the land for Meribah, which is entered separately, and the Lord buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, and no man knows of his sepulchre to this day (Deuteronomy 34:5-6). He was a hundred and twenty years old when he died, and his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated (Deuteronomy 34:7): he was not a weak, sickly old man; he was in full strength, and still he had to go up and die, because he could not enter. There arose not a prophet since in Israel like him, whom the Lord knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10). That verse also answers a doctrine. Some say Joshua was the prophet raised up like Moses, and therefore there is no Christ; but the same passage that says Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom says in the next breath that there arose not a prophet like Moses. Joshua was a mighty prophet, and he did not fit that word; Christ did (Deuteronomy 18:18). And Moses himself stood on the mount with Elijah at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/03-egypt/moses

Moses, and the Egyptian in the sand

Slaying the Egyptian that smote his brother, and hiding him in the sand

Sentence not recorded

A man of the house of Levi took to wife a daughter of Levi, Amram and Jochebed, and the child was goodly, exceeding fair; by faith his parents hid him three months and were not afraid of the king’s commandment (Exodus 2:1-2; Exodus 6:20; Acts 7:20; Hebrews 11:23). Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out of the river and knew at once that this was one of the Hebrews’ children, because the Most High puts a difference between the Egyptians and Israel, though both peoples were dark of skin (Exodus 2:5-6; Exodus 11:7). His sister Miriam was crafty, and by her offer his own mother was called and paid wages to nurse him, so that his first years were spent with her (Exodus 2:7-9). He was raised in the royal court and received one of the finest educations in the world, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and mighty in words and in deeds (Acts 7:22).

When he was full forty years old it came into his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel; he went out to them and looked on their burdens, and he spied an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, one of his brethren (Exodus 2:11; Acts 7:23). He did not act as though the palace had made him something else. This was not ordinary correction on a work site; it was an abuse of power in which his brother’s life was in danger. He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand (Exodus 2:12). He did not kill out of hatred, and the law weighs the other side of it: if a man forbears to deliver them that are drawn to death and those that are ready to be slain, and says he did not know it, the one that ponders the heart considers it, and he that keeps the soul knows it, and renders to every man according to his works (Proverbs 24:11-12). He did not merely marvel at the matter as the preacher warns (Ecclesiastes 5:8); he used his position for his people, supposing his brethren would have understood that God by his hand would deliver them, but they did not understand (Acts 7:25).

The second day two men of the Hebrews strove together, and he asked the one that did the wrong why he smote his fellow. The man answered by asking who made him a prince and a judge over them, and whether he meant to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian (Exodus 2:13-14). When a people is oppressed they take the oppression out on one another, and the same spirit answers correction among our people now, pointing the finger at the one who corrects. Moses was afraid, and knew that the thing was known.

When Pharaoh heard of it he sought to slay Moses, but Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian (Exodus 2:15). By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:24-26). At the well he stood up for the seven daughters of the priest of Midian against the shepherds and watered their flock, a man of war and not a weak man, and they told their father that an Egyptian had delivered them, for Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same colour as the Egyptians (Exodus 2:16-19). He married Zipporah and named his son Gershom, because he had been a stranger in a strange land (Exodus 2:21-22).

No sentence upon the killing is recorded. Forty years later, at eighty, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire in a bush at Sinai, and the man they had refused with the question, who made him a ruler and a judge over them, is the same man God sent to be a ruler and a deliverer (Acts 7:30-35). The people he had tried to help turned on him; the God of his fathers sent him back to deliver them.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/03-egypt/moses-and-the-egyptian

Moses and the uncircumcised son

Neglecting the token of the covenant in his own house, on the road to demand the release of God’s firstborn

Reprieve

Circumcision was not a Sinai ordinance. It was given to Abraham as the token of the covenant: every man child in every generation circumcised at eight days, and the uncircumcised man child whose flesh is not circumcised cut off from his people, because he has broken the covenant (Genesis 17:10-14). Moses had spent forty years in Midian and had married Zipporah, a daughter of the priest of Midian and not a daughter of Israel, and the son of that house carried no token of the covenant. The Egyptians did not practise it either; they were a nation of uncleanness, and Israel was afterward told plainly not to do after the doings of the land of Egypt where they had dwelt (Leviticus 18:3).

The word he was carrying makes the neglect weigh more. He was to tell Pharaoh that Israel is the Lord’s son, even his firstborn, and that Pharaoh must let that son go to serve him, and if he refused, the Lord would slay Pharaoh’s son, his firstborn (Exodus 4:22-23). Israel was not the first nation created; Israel was the first nation the Most High chose, the apple of his eye from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob down, and the firstborn is the heir. Moses was going to demand another man’s firstborn on pain of death while his own son bore no token of the very covenant he was invoking. That is why he was worthy of death.

By the way in the inn, the Lord met him and sought to kill him (Exodus 4:24). Zipporah took a sharp stone and cut off the foreskin of her son and cast it at his feet, and called him a bloody husband; so the Lord let him go, and she said again that he was a bloody husband because of the circumcision (Exodus 4:25-26). Bloody because she had to take the stone and do it herself. The thing had to be set right in his own house before he could carry a word from God into Pharaoh’s house.

This shows the laws did not begin at Sinai, and the covenant still stands. A son of Israel is circumcised on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), and a man who comes to the truth grown is still circumcised at forty, fifty or sixty years, as Abraham himself was circumcised at ninety and nine, and as Paul took Timothy, whose father was a Greek, and circumcised him (Genesis 17:24; Acts 16:3). Joshua had to circumcise again the generation born in the wilderness before they took the land (Joshua 5:2-5). Romans does not do away with circumcision of the flesh: circumcision profits if a man keeps the law, and the man circumcised who breaks the law has made his circumcision uncircumcision, while the uncircumcised who keeps the righteousness of the law is counted for circumcision (Romans 2:25-29). The circumcision of the heart is commanded alongside it and not instead of it, Israel being told to circumcise themselves to the Lord and take away the foreskins of their heart (Jeremiah 4:4; Deuteronomy 10:16). Nothing that defiles enters the kingdom (Revelation 21:27).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/03-egypt/moses-uncircumcised-son

Moses at the waters of Meribah

Failing to sanctify the Lord before the people: must we fetch you water out of this rock?

Reprieve

The congregation came into the desert of Zin in the first month and abode in Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there (Numbers 20:1). There was no water for the congregation, and they gathered together against Moses and against Aaron. The people chode with Moses, which is to say they raised their voices in a loud, angry, shouting argument: they wished they had died when their brethren died before the Lord, and asked why they had been made to come up out of Egypt into this evil place, with no seed, figs, vines or pomegranates, and no water to drink (Numbers 20:2-5). Taken out of Egypt by the hand of the Most High and headed to the promised land, they forgot so quickly how they were brought out, and anything out of the ordinary they complained about. Moses had to deal with twelve tribes at once, twelve personalities and twelve attitudes, and that brother deserves all the honour he is given.

The command was exact: take the rod, gather the assembly with Aaron, and speak to the rock before their eyes, and it would give forth its water for the congregation and their beasts (Numbers 20:7-8). At this point Moses got out of the spirit; a stomach can only take so much of a rebellious people. He called them rebels and asked, must we fetch you water out of this rock? The Lord never told him to say that. That we is how you know he was off: he put himself alongside the One who was giving the water. Then he lifted up his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod (Numbers 20:9-11). The psalm gives the cause: they provoked his spirit, so that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips (Psalms 106:32-33). Anger is what clouds a man’s judgment; it takes him out of the spirit, and then he leans on his own understanding instead of trusting the Lord with all his heart and keeping to the instruction he was given (Proverbs 3:5). A wrathful man stirs up strife, but the man slow to anger appeases it (Proverbs 15:18).

The water came out abundantly, and the congregation and their beasts drank; the people lost nothing by it (Numbers 20:11). The Lord told Moses and Aaron that because they had not believed Him, to sanctify Him in the eyes of the children of Israel, they would not bring this congregation into the land He had given them (Numbers 20:12-13). This is the water of Meribah, which means strife, because the children of Israel strove with the Lord, and He was sanctified in them. Set beside it the war with Og a short time later, when the people said that the Lord their God delivered the king of Bashan into their hands (Deuteronomy 3:3): they were doing the fighting, and they gave the praise, the glory and the victory to the Most High, and did not boast in their own swords. That is what sanctifying Him looks like, and at the rock Moses did the opposite.

Forty years of carrying the nation ended with the two men kept out of the land for a sentence spoken out of the spirit. At mount Hor, by the coast of the land of Edom, the Lord said Aaron would be gathered to his people because they had rebelled against His word at the water of Meribah; Moses stripped him of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son, and Aaron died there on the top of the mount, and all the house of Israel mourned him thirty days (Numbers 20:23-29). Moses was told to go up into mount Abarim and see the land, and then be gathered to his people as Aaron was, for the same cause (Numbers 27:12-14). He begged to go over and see the good land beyond Jordan, and the answer was final: let it suffice, and speak no more of this matter (Deuteronomy 3:23-26), the way a parent tells a child who keeps asking that the matter is closed. His charge was to strengthen and encourage the man appointed to take the people over in his place.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/04-wilderness/moses-at-meribah

events.title: Othniel
events.description: Caleb, given Hebron for wholly following the Lord, drove out the three sons of Anak and offered his daughter to whoever smote Kirjath-sepher. Othniel the son of Kenaz, his younger brother, took it and was given Achsah. She moved him to ask her father for a field, and asked well: he had given her a south land, so she asked also for springs of water, and Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs. When Israel served Chushan-rishathaim eight years, the Spirit of the Lord came on Othniel, and he judged Israel and went out to war, for the Lord is a man of war.
events.article:
Othniel and Achsah

Taking Kirjath-sepher at Caleb’s word; and asking for the springs as well as the land

Kept the law

Caleb the son of Jephunneh was given a part among the children of Judah according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua, the city of Arba the father of Anak, which is Hebron, and Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (Joshua 15:13-14). He had been promised that mountain and he went and claimed it. He went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir, whose name before was Kirjath-sepher, and promised his daughter Achsah as wife to the man who smote it and took it; Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, took it, and Caleb gave him Achsah (Joshua 15:15-17). He took a fortified city on the strength of a word.

Achsah’s obedience is one of speech. When she came to him she moved him to ask her father for a field, then got down off her ass, and when Caleb asked what she wanted she asked for a blessing, because he had given her a south land, and asked also for springs of water (Joshua 15:18-19). Given a lawful portion in the dry south, she did not resent it; she asked the right person, at the right moment, framing it as a blessing rather than a complaint, and asked for the one thing the land needed. The record carries the whole account twice, at the opening of Judges as at the end of Joshua, because the history is worth reviewing (Judges 1:12-15).

Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs (Joshua 15:19): more than she had asked for. Then the Lord left nations in the land to prove Israel, nations that had not known the wars of Canaan, so that the generations of the children of Israel might know war and be taught it, and so that it would be seen whether they would hearken to His commandments (Judges 3:1-4). They did not. The children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, the very people they had been told to destroy, took their daughters to wife and gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods; so the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel and He sold them into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, whom they served eight years (Judges 3:5-8).

When the children of Israel cried to the Lord, He raised up a deliverer, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother; the Spirit of the Lord came on him, and he judged Israel and went out to war, and the Lord delivered Chushan-rishathaim into his hand, and his hand prevailed (Judges 3:9-10). He judged Israel, and today our people say that no one can judge them. And he went out to war, because the Lord is a man of war, and that is His name (Exodus 15:3); that also answers the question asked of the men out on the street about where their women are. The war now is spiritual: though we walk in the flesh we do not war after the flesh, and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:3-5). The weapon is this Bible. The land had rest forty years, until Othniel the son of Kenaz died (Judges 3:11). The first deliverer in the book of Judges came out of the household of the man who wholly followed the Lord, where a daughter asked well and a father gave more than was requested.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/05-conquest/othniel-and-achsah

events.title: Boaz
events.description: In the days when the judges ruled, a Moabite widow would not go back to her people and to Chemosh, but bound herself to Naomi’s road, Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God. She came to Bethlehem with a mother in law who called herself Mara, gleaned in the field of Boaz, and called herself what she was to Israel, a stranger. Boaz went up to the gate, called ten elders as witnesses, carried out the law of inheritance and the law of the husband’s brother, and bought the field and Ruth with it, to keep the dead man’s name alive. Their son was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David.
events.article:
Ruth and Boaz

Ruth: cleaving to Naomi and joining herself under Israel and Israel’s God. Boaz: the law of the land conducted at the gate before witnesses, and love thy neighbour as thyself

Kept the law

When the judges ruled, famine drove Elimelech of Bethlehem-judah to Moab with Naomi and their two sons, who married the Moabite women Orpah and Ruth and died there (Ruth 1:1-9). Were the sons of Israel supposed to marry the women of Moab? No. A Moabite was not to enter the congregation of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:3), and Israel had already gone whoring with the daughters of Moab at Shittim (Numbers 25:1-2); but this was the era of no king, when every man did what was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25), and even in Ezra’s day the Moabites had not been put away (1 Esdras 8:69). Naomi prayed that each daughter in law find rest in a husband’s house. That rest is an inheritance; a good man leaves one to his children’s children, not a gang of bills (Proverbs 13:22). Behind her words stands the law of the husband’s brother, the widow’s firstborn carrying on the dead man’s name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). We are not under that

law now, having no land inheritance in this captivity, and it is wicked to pull that scripture today to get with a brother’s widow; but we are still to build a legacy and pass it down.

Orpah went back to her people and her gods, to Chemosh (Numbers 21:29), for all the gods of the nations are idols (Psalms 96:5). Ruth clung to Naomi, her people and her God until death (Ruth 1:14-22). Does that make her an Israelite, or an heir of the kingdom? No. Both daughters in law knew exactly what they were, and Ruth never claimed otherwise. She joined herself under Israel and acknowledged her place, like the woman of Canaan who accepted the crumbs from the masters’ table (Matthew 15:24-28), and like Rahab, who knew the God of Israel was the true living God (Joshua 6:25). Naomi came home to Bethlehem calling herself Mara, bitter.

Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Elimelech, who kept her with his young women and charged his men not to touch her (Ruth 2:1-16). She asked why he took notice of her, since she was a stranger, the word the law uses for the nations round about (Leviticus 25:44-46). Boaz had heard how she left her own parents and land for her mother in law, prayed that the Lord under whose wings she had taken refuge would reward her, and had handfuls dropped on purpose for her. Naomi then sought that same rest for her, sending her to lie at Boaz’s feet on the threshing floor (Ruth 3:1-18), where Ruth asked him to spread his skirt over her as near kinsman. The skirt is male clothing, the edge of the garment; she was asking the near kinsman to take her under his covering. He blessed her for not going after young men: even as a Moabitess she was keeping the customs of Israel, seeking her dead husband’s kinsman to keep his name in the earth.

Boaz sat at the gate with the nearer kinsman and ten elders as witnesses, for the record (Ruth 4:1-12). The kinsman had first right to redeem Elimelech’s land, under the law that no inheritance pass from tribe to tribe (Numbers 36:5-9); a man could marry outside his own tribe but not outside the nation. But whoever took the land took the dead man’s wife with it, to keep his name on his inheritance, the duty of the husband’s brother and the loosed shoe. The kinsman declined and drew off his shoe, and Boaz bought all that was Elimelech’s and took Ruth, Mahlon’s widow, as his wife. What law was Boaz exercising in all of that? Loving his neighbour as himself (Leviticus 19:18). That is why he is mentioned in the scriptures.

The elders blessed the marriage, naming Rachel and Leah who built the house of Israel and Pharez whom Tamar bore to Judah; in that blessing they were prophesying of David to come. Ruth bore a son, and Naomi took the child to her bosom and became his nurse (Ruth 4:13-22). Why? Because it is not the custom of Israel to allow a child to be raised under the hand of a heathen. A child’s first teacher is the mother; he takes on her ways, which is what Nehemiah found among the children of the wives of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, who could not speak the Jews’ language (Nehemiah 13:23-24). Ruth was brought in to keep Mahlon’s name alive in Israel, and she had no hand in raising the child; Naomi raised him so he would learn the ways of Israel. His name was Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David, the line of Judah running down to the king and on to Christ (Matthew 1:5-6).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/ruth-and-boaz

events.title: Gideon
events.description:
Israel hid in dens and caves in the mountains of their own land while Midian, Amalek and the eastern peoples swarmed in like locusts and destroyed the crops. An angel sat under an oak in Ophrah while Gideon threshed wheat in the winepress to hide it, and greeted him as a mighty man of valour with the Lord at his side; the Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat. He tore down his father’s altar of Baal by night, sent home thirty-one thousand seven hundred men because the Lord said the army was too big, and broke the host of Midian with three hundred, with pitchers, lamps and trumpets. The victory of battle comes from the Lord.

The men of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them, and his son and grandson after him, for saving them from Midian, and he refused: the Lord would rule over them. Then he asked every man for the earrings from his plunder, because the enemy were Ishmaelites and wore gold earrings, and made an ephod of seventeen hundred shekels of gold and set it up in his city. All Israel went after it there in spiritual whoredom, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house. As soon as he was dead the people went after the Baals again and made Baal-berith their god.

Gideon’s son by his concubine in Shechem went to his mother’s kin and told them to remember he was their own flesh and blood, and they chose him by kinship rather than by righteousness. With seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith he hired worthless, reckless men and killed his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham, the youngest, escaped, and stood alone on mount Gerizim and prophesied the fire. Three years later God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and both sides were destroyed. A woman in a tower at Thebez broke his skull with a piece of a millstone.
events.article:
Gideon

Throwing down his father’s altar of Baal; going against Midian with three hundred, as the Lord said

Kept the law

Israel did evil, and the Lord handed them to Midian for seven years; they hid in dens, caves and strongholds in the mountains of their own land (Judges 6:1-16). Whenever Israel planted, Midian, Amalek and the eastern peoples swarmed in like locusts, destroyed the crops, and left no food and no livestock: the curse of blight and mildew gone into famine (Deuteronomy 28:21-22). When Israel cried, the Lord first sent a prophet to remind them that He had brought them out of bondage and told them not to fear the gods of the Amorites, and that they had not listened; the judgment came with a reason attached, and those Amorites trace back through Canaan into the Hamites (Genesis 10:15-16). Then an angel of the Lord sat under an oak in Ophrah while Gideon threshed wheat in the winepress to hide it from Midian, and greeted him as a mighty man of valour with the Lord at his side. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon asked why, if the Lord was with them, all this had happened, and where were the miracles their fathers told of. Many of us ask the same today, watching our people judged in the streets over and over. But God has not forsaken us; we forsook Him, abandoning the spring of living water for broken cisterns that hold nothing (Jeremiah 2:13), and the Lord disciplines those He loves (Hebrews 12:6). Sent to save Israel, Gideon answered with his pedigree: his family the poorest in Manasseh, himself the least in his father’s house. That is a defeated mentality, and every one of us has to overcome it. God calls few of the wise, mighty or noble; He chooses the foolish, weak and lowly to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:26-28), and what men prize is detestable to Him (Luke 16:15). Fire rose out of the rock to consume his offering, and the same night the Lord told him to tear down his father’s altar of Baal and cut down the grove beside it (Judges 6:17-32). The tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal before the kingdom split, which made Jeroboam’s golden calves an easy transition (1 Kings 12:28). He did it by night, and when the men of the city demanded his death, Joash told them to let Baal defend himself if he was a god, He asked the fleece sign twice (Judges 6:34-40), but we do not ask for signs like that any more, for Christ called sign seeking the mark of a wicked and unfaithful generation (Matthew 12:39).

The Lord said the army was too large, or Israel would boast that its own hand had saved it (Judges 7:1-8). That is Israel: look at what I did. They had been warned before entering the land not to credit their own power and strength for their wealth (Deuteronomy 8:14-18). The fearful were sent home, and twenty-two thousand left; the Lord tested the rest at the water, and kept the three hundred who lapped from the hand, men still upright and alert with their eyes on what was around them. You have to be willing to let go of some people, as the Lord told Abraham to leave his country and kindred (Genesis 12:1), and as Christ came to set a man against his own household (Matthew 10:34-36).

That night the Lord sent Gideon down to the edge of the camp. There he overheard a man tell a dream of a barley loaf tumbling into the camp and flattening a tent, and his companion say it could only be the sword of Gideon, into whose

hand God had given Midian. The Lord put that dream in the enemy’s mind and sent Gideon to hear it, so he would go in without doubt (Judges 7:9-25). Look around us and it is the same picture, enemies as far as the eye can see. He split the three hundred into three companies with trumpets and lamps hidden in empty pitchers, and struck at the start of the middle watch, right as the watchmen changed; they blew the trumpets, smashed the pitchers, and shouted a battle cry for the Lord and for Gideon, and the Lord turned every man’s sword against his companion. The enemy destroyed itself. The trumpets go into the law: when Israel goes to war against an oppressor they sound an alarm, and the Lord remembers and saves them (Numbers 10:9). Midian was subdued and never raised its head again, and the land was quiet forty years (Judges 8:28). Victory does not come by numbers, by how many guns or bullets; it is easy for many to be delivered into the hands of a few, for strength comes from heaven (1 Maccabees 3:18-19).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/gideon

Gideon’s ephod

Making an ephod of the golden earrings of the spoil, and putting it in Ophrah; all Israel going a whoring after it

Temporal judgment

The men of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them, he and his son and his grandson, because he had saved them from Midian (Judges 8:22-27). Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep and wander off the path without somebody to guide us in the way we must go. Gideon refused the throne for himself and his son, because the Lord was their ruler. He knew that if thrones were set up in Israel the people would put their trust and their faith in the king instead of in the Most High. Those were right words, and the man who spoke them had already torn down his father’s altar of Baal and cut down the grove beside it (Judges 6:25-27). The test did not end when he refused the crown.

He made one request: that every man give him the earrings from his plunder, since the enemy, being Ishmaelites, wore gold earrings. They gave gladly, spreading a garment and throwing the earrings on it, and the gold weighed seventeen hundred shekels, not counting the ornaments, pendants and purple garments of the Midianite kings and the chains from their camels’ necks. Gideon made an ephod of it and set it up in his city of Ophrah, and all Israel went after it there in spiritual whoredom, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house. Paul names the love of money as the root of evil (1 Timothy 6:10); the gold Gideon gathered turned into the very snare that trapped his own house.

The judgment is already in the word the record chooses: a snare. No sentence is passed on Gideon in the chapter, and none needed to be written; the man who had pulled down one idol furnished the people with another object to go after, and his own house was caught in it. Midian stayed subdued and the land was quiet forty years in Gideon’s days; he fathered seventy sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem also bore him a son he named Abimelech, and Gideon the son of Joash died at a good old age (Judges 8:28-35).

As soon as Gideon was dead, the children of Israel turned again to spiritual whoredom after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god (Judges 8:33-35). Baal means lord and berith means covenant, so the god they set up was the lord of the covenant, a counterfeit put over the people in place of the One who had just delivered them. They forgot the Lord their God who had rescued them from all the enemies around them, and showed no kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, that is Gideon, for all the good he had done Israel. The same cycle turned again the moment the judge was gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. The son born of the concubine in Shechem, and the silver out of the house of Baal-berith, are the next case.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/gideons-ephod

Abimelech son of Gideon

Slaying his seventy brethren upon one stone with silver out of the house of Baal-berith; making himself king at Shechem

Put to death

Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to his mother’s kin in Shechem and had them ask the men of the city whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man, reminding them he was their own blood (Judges 9:1-6). His very name means my father is king; the ambition was carried in what he was called. When people remind you that blood is thicker than water, they want you to back them whether or not the thing is right. The men of Shechem leaned toward him because he was their brother: they chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol’s house, and with it he hired worthless, reckless men to follow him. At Ophrah he killed his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham the youngest survived, by hiding. Then the men of Shechem and the house of Millo made him king, endorsing the man who had used their money to murder his seventy brothers.

When Jotham heard, he stood on the top of mount Gerizim and shouted for the men of Shechem to listen to him, so that God would listen to them (Judges 9:7-21). This young brother was fearless, standing alone to rebuke them. In his parable the trees went out to anoint a king. The trees are Israel; the olive tree is Gideon, who would not give up his richness to rule over the trees; the fig tree and the vine are Gideon’s sons, who would not give up their sweetness and their wine. Only the bramble accepted, a thistle that pricks and tears, and its answer carried a threat of fire. Jotham applied it: their father had risked his life for them, and they had killed his sons on one stone and made the slave woman’s son king because he was their brother. If they had acted in good faith, let them enjoy Abimelech; if not, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume Shechem, and fire out of Shechem consume Abimelech. That was a prophecy, and it came to pass.

After Abimelech had ruled Israel three years, God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, and they betrayed him, so that the blood of the seventy sons of Jerubbaal would fall on Abimelech who killed them and on the men of Shechem who helped him (Judges 9:22-24). Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody’s spirit suddenly turns against you, we tend to think it is just that person. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, not karma, not mother nature; the Lord of hosts musters the army for battle (Isaiah 13:4), both peace and evil come from His hand as light and darkness do (Isaiah 45:7), and He put a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets (1 Kings 22:22-23). Abimelech ran three years and everything looked good, and he was not getting away with it.

Gaal the son of Ebed came to Shechem and, with wine in him, talked big against Abimelech (Judges 9:22-49). Zebul the ruler of the city sent word to Abimelech, strung Gaal along, then asked him where his big mouth was now. All the big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Abimelech drove him out, took the city, killed its people, razed it and sowed it with salt; and when the men of the tower of Shechem took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of Berith, he burned the stronghold over them with branches from mount Zalmon, so that about a thousand men and women died. The people who made him king were burned by him; the fire out of the bramble was doing exactly what Jotham said. At the tower of Thebez a woman dropped a piece of millstone on his head and cracked his skull; he quickly told his armourbearer to kill him so no one would say a woman had done it, and the young man ran him through (Judges 9:50-57). It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by a woman’s hand, as when Jael drove the peg into Sisera’s temple (Judges 4:21). Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull. So God repaid Abimelech and the men of Shechem for their evil, and Jotham’s curse came upon them. Trace the pattern in the man and you can name it anywhere: preeminence, manipulation, hatred, murder. It begins in wanting to be the head and it ends in blood, and the warning to us is plain: do nothing out of rivalry or conceit (Philippians 2:3), and know that your sin will catch up with you (Numbers 32:23).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/abimelech

events.title: Eli
events.description: The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord. Levites and priests in the house of the Lord, doing the work of the Lord, and yet they did not know Him, because they kept the commandments only on the surface where men could see. They sent a servant with a three-pronged fork to take the priest’s portion raw before the fat was burned, by force if the man refused, so that men despised the offering of the Lord; and they lay with the women who served at the door of the tabernacle. Eli said something, but he took no action. In one day both sons died, the ark was taken, and the old man fell backward from his seat and broke his neck.
events.article:
Eli and his sons

Sons of Belial in the priest’s office, strong-arming the offering of the Lord and lying with the women at the tabernacle door; and a father who honoured his sons above the Lord

Put to death

The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord (1 Samuel 2:12-17). They were the devil. Priests in the house of the Lord, they still did not know Him, because they kept the commandments on the surface where you can see it and not true in their spirit. They looked the part, the fringes, the beard, showing up on the sabbath day, and their spirit was not right with the Lord. Do not let that be you, Israel. The custom was that while a man’s sacrifice was boiling, the priest’s servant plunged a three-pronged fork into the pot and the priest took whatever it brought up. That is how the Lord took care of Levi, who had no land inheritance among the tribes; He provided for them out of Israel’s sacrifices, so that they needed nothing. But these men would not wait. Before the fat was even burned the servant demanded raw meat, by force if the worshipper objected. So the young men’s sin was very great before the Lord, for men came to despise the Lord’s offering. Devils serving in the house of the Lord, strong-arming the offerings of the people.

Eli was very old, and he heard everything his sons did to Israel, and that they lay with the women serving at the door of the tabernacle, the harlots hanging around the temple (1 Samuel 2:22-25). He asked why they did such things, and told them they were making the Lord’s people sin. The Levites were the leaders, so the people followed their actions, saying it must be all right, look at how they live in the temple. But the sons would not listen to their father, because the Lord meant to put them to death. Eli said something to his children, but he did not remove them from the priesthood. He did not go further than words, and you have to watch what happened to his children.

A man of God reminded Eli that the Lord had chosen his father’s house out of all the tribes as priests and given it Israel’s offerings (1 Samuel 2:27-36). Why then did they scorn His sacrifices, and why did Eli honour his sons above Him? Take that into account: do you honour your children above what the Lord says to do? Can they do no wrong, even when they keep no commandments and never show up on the sabbath day while living grown under your roof? Joshua resolved that he and his house would serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15), and the Lord dealt with Abraham as He did knowing he would command his children and household after him to keep the way of the Lord (Genesis 18:19). The Lord had promised Eli’s house would serve before Him for ever, but now He said He would honour those who honour Him, and those who despise Him would be lightly esteemed. Lightly esteemed means He is not looking out for you: you are not thinking about me, so I am not thinking about you. He would cut off the strength of Eli’s house, so that no man in it would reach old age. Cutting off the arm is cutting off the strength, and the strength was his children. Why judge the generations after? Not because a son dies for his father; each son lives or dies by his own doings (Ezekiel 18:10-17). Because Eli did not reprove his sons, the generations after them were going to follow in the same footsteps.

The sign was that his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, would both die on one day, and the Lord would raise up a faithful priest who would act according to His heart and mind. That is the same man we all have to be, not leaning on our own understanding or our own emotions (Proverbs 3:5). Whoever was left in Eli’s house would come begging for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread: Levi had no inheritance of land, and cut off from the priesthood there was nothing left but to beg. The Lord confirmed it to the child Samuel: Eli’s house was judged because his sons disgraced themselves and he did not stop them, and Eli accepted it as the Lord’s will (1 Samuel 3:13-18). When the Philistines fought Israel again, thirty thousand Israelite soldiers fell, the ark was taken, and both sons of Eli were killed (1 Samuel 4:10-22). When the news reached Shiloh that the ark was taken, Eli fell backward off his seat, broke his neck and died, for he was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years. His daughter in law named her newborn Ichabod, for the glory had departed from Israel.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/eli-and-sons

events.title: Samuel
events.description:
Given to the Lord as a child, he served before Eli in days when the word of the Lord was precious and visions were rare. The Lord came and stood and called him by name, and the child did not yet know the Lord until Eli taught him how to answer. His first test as a judge was to carry a judgment against the house that raised him, and he told Eli all of it and held nothing back. The Lord made every one of his words come to pass; he judged Israel all the days of his life, established the kingdom, and by his faithfulness was found a true prophet.

When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel in Beersheba, and they did not follow his ways: they chased dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice. The elders of Israel used them as the reason to demand a king like all the nations. No sentence upon the two men is recorded anywhere in the chapter; the sentence that is recorded fell on the nation that used them as an excuse.
events.article:
Samuel

Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth: telling Eli every whit and hiding nothing; and an accounting no man could contradict, whose ox have I taken?

Kept the law

The child Samuel served the Lord under Eli when the word of the Lord was precious and visions were rare (1 Samuel 3:8-14). Precious means the Lord was not dealing with everybody; not with the priests, and there were no prophets around saying what the Lord had spoken. Twice the Lord called and the child ran to Eli, because Samuel did not yet know the Lord. He had been in the house of the Lord since he was weaned, and he still did not know the Lord. That goes in on those playing church with their children: just because your children come and sit and listen does not mean they know the Lord; they are there because you brought them. Your job is the training, raising a child in the path he should keep (Proverbs 22:6); the revealing belongs to the Most High, for only the Son knows the Father, and He reveals Him to whom He chooses (Matthew 11:27). The third time Eli understood, and taught the child to answer that the Lord’s servant was listening.

The Lord came and stood and called as before, Samuel, Samuel. He did not simply call out of the heavens; He came down and stood by him. Samuel could not see Him, but he heard Him, and that is what happens in the spirit to all of us. The Lord is merciful with us even in this wickedness, standing at the door and knocking, calling numerous times until we wake up (Revelation 3:20). Those who heed His correction receive His spirit and His words; those who refuse, and the day comes when they call and He will not answer (Proverbs 1:23). The word given to the child was a judgment against the house that raised him: Eli’s house judged for ever, its sin beyond the reach of any sacrifice. When the Lord is angry, He is angry; do not sin a sin so great that it cannot be prayed for.

In the morning Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the vision, but Eli charged him to hide nothing, and Samuel told him all of it (1 Samuel 3:18-21). He was going to be a judge of Israel, and this was his first test: do not sugarcoat what the Lord has said, and do not trim your words to seek love. Years later he put his own record before the nation, and the people agreed he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Samuel 12:3-4). Nor did he abandon them: he would count it a sin against the Lord to stop praying for them, and he would keep teaching them the good and right way (1 Samuel 12:23). Marinate on that. For a leader of Israel, ceasing to pray for the nation is itself a transgression.

Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him. What Samuel said, it came to pass. All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew he was confirmed as a prophet of the Lord (1 Samuel 3:18-21). At Mizpeh he told Israel that if they were returning to the Lord with all their hearts they must get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth and serve Him only, and they did (1 Samuel 7:3-6). That is repentance. When the Philistine lords came up and Israel was afraid, this time the people did not run for the ark; they begged Samuel not to stop crying to the Lord for them, because they knew the earnest prayer of a righteous man is powerful and effective (James 5:16).

Samuel offered a lamb and cried to the Lord for Israel, and as the Philistines closed in, the Lord thundered against them and routed them (1 Samuel 7:8-13). That was no regular thunder; that was the Lord entering the battle Himself.

They had repented and put away the false gods, and the prayer of a righteous man reached His ears. Samuel set up a stone and named it Ebenezer, and the Philistines were held back all his days. He judged Israel all his life, circling each year through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpeh and home to Ramah (1 Samuel 7:15-17). That yearly circuit is leadership making its rounds, establishing the people and coming back to check on them, as Paul went back to visit the brethren in every city (Acts 15:36). Ecclesiasticus remembers him as beloved of his Lord, proved a true prophet by his faithfulness (Ecclesiasticus 46:13-15). Faithfulness translates loyalty. He came up under Eli, watched Eli’s sons go wicked, watched Eli die and the nation take losses, and stayed loyal to the Most High. Prayer is a superpower, and that is how our forefathers rolled, from Moses to Samuel all the way to Christ. What was written before was written to teach us (Romans 15:4).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/samuel

Joel and Abiah, the sons of Samuel

Turning aside after lucre, taking bribes, and perverting judgment in the seat of the judge

Sentence deferred

When Samuel was old he made his sons judges over Israel, Joel the firstborn and Abiah the second, judging in Beersheba. But his sons did not follow his ways: they chased dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:1-3). The law for the judges in the gates was plain. They were to judge the people justly, not twist judgment, not show partiality, and take no gift, because a bribe blinds even the wise and corrupts the cause of the righteous (Deuteronomy 16:18-20; Exodus 23:8). That gift is what goes into the pocket of a judge and comes back out as a perverted sentence against the man who could not pay.

We see that same thing going on now in this political climate, and even in the church system. It is why the churches will not teach us who we are or teach the commandments of the Most High, and why, when riots and unrest break out, it is those same pastors who are sent out to calm the people down. The contrast with their father was public and undeniable. Samuel could stand before all Israel and ask whose ox or donkey he had taken, whom he had cheated, and from whom he had taken a bribe, and the whole congregation answered that he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Samuel 12:3-4). The sons made the seat of judgment serve their own increase.

Then all the elders of Israel came to Samuel at Ramah, saying he was old and his sons did not follow his ways, and asking him to appoint a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Your sons are not righteous like you, so instead of them judging us, give us a ruler like the other nations have. The corruption was real and the complaint was real; the remedy the people insisted on is its own case, entered next, because the Lord told Samuel that they had not rejected him but had rejected the Lord as their king (1 Samuel 8:7).

No penalty upon Joel or Abiah is recorded. Their own end is not written, and the silence does not turn bribery into righteousness. If a man sees the poor oppressed and justice violently perverted in a province, he is not to be astonished, for a higher official watches over the high one, and One higher still is over them both (Ecclesiastes 5:8). What the record does show is the damage: an office handed down without the character the office requires, a nation that had been delivered by judges for four hundred years handed its excuse, and a demand made at Ramah that cost Israel far more than two corrupt men in Beersheba ever took in bribes.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/the-sons-of-samuel

events.title: Samson
events.description: A Nazarite to God from the womb, with a lust for heathen women that is the infamy his story is known for. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether no woman among his own people would do, but he insisted, and the Lord used the flaw as an occasion against the Philistines who ruled Israel. Three times Delilah tried to have his life taken and he stayed with her; then he told her everything in his heart, woke shaven in her lap, and did not know that the Lord had left him. Blinded and grinding grain in the prison at Gaza, he prayed once more, and killed more Philistines in his death than in his life.
events.article:
Samson

Lusting after Philistine women: a wife at Timnath against his parents’ counsel, a harlot at Gaza, and Delilah, to whom he told all his heart

Put to death

Samson saw a Philistine woman at Timnath and told his parents to get her for him. This brother had a lust issue with heathen women. His parents answered him rightly, asking whether no woman among his own people would do; there were twelve tribes and no shortage of women in Israel, and the forefathers always charged their sons against it, as Isaac charged Jacob not to marry a Canaanite (Genesis 28:1). Samson insisted, because she pleased him (Judges 14:1-6). His parents did not know it was from the Lord, who sought an occasion against the Philistines then ruling Israel. The Most High was using Samson’s own flaw to destroy the nation oppressing His people, and that is the basis of the whole story. His thinking is higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8-9); both the one misled and the one misleading are under His rule (Job 12:16); no counsel stands against the Lord (Proverbs 21:30); no calamity comes on a city unless the Lord has done it (Amos 3:6).

At the wedding feast his thirty companions threatened to burn his wife and her father’s house unless she got his riddle out of him. She turned to tears and manipulation, crying through the feast that he did not love her, until he gave in and she passed it to her people (Judges 14:15-18). This big strong mighty brother caved in under the tears of a woman, and knew it, saying they had plowed with his heifer. Never trust the enemy. Her loyalty belonged to her husband, and she carried his business straight to her heathen people, which is why it makes no sense to marry the enemy. Later he slept with a harlot at Gaza and carried off the city gate at midnight (Judges 16:1-14). Then he loved Delilah, and each Philistine lord offered her eleven hundred pieces of silver to

learn the secret of his strength. It was a setup. Once they learn where a man’s strength lies they can bind him and plunder his goods, and that is the method used on this whole nation, the same reason Holofernes wanted to know what held Israel up. The weapon they used on Samson was his weakness for sex. She asked him outright how he could be bound and subdued, asking for the formula to get him killed. Three times she tried it with men waiting in the room, and a man of war should have recognised the setup and cut her off; he was still there.

She nagged him daily, asking how he could say he loved her when his heart was not with her, until he told her everything: he was a Nazarite from the womb, and if shaved his strength would leave him (Judges 16:15-22). That is where he messed up. This is the scriptural example of why a man does not tell his wife every single thing in his heart; we do not go by the philosophies of men that say your wife is your best friend you tell everything to. Scripture says to guard your words even from the woman who lies in your arms (Micah 7:5); counsel on those things belongs among the brothers. His downfall was compromise: emotional attachment, a physical relationship, and every warning sign ignored. She lulled him to sleep on her knees and had his seven locks shaved, and he woke not knowing the Lord had left him. They gouged out his eyes and set him grinding in the prison at Gaza, a blind slave put on show; but his hair began to grow back.

The Philistine lords gathered to sacrifice to Dagon, crediting their god with delivering Samson to them (Judges 16:23-31). They gave the glory to an idol that had not done a thing; it was Samson’s own transgression that caused the Most High to allow them to afflict him, and that praise to a fake god did not please Him. They brought Samson out to entertain them and stood him between the pillars, with all the lords in the house and about three thousand on the roof. He called on the Lord to strengthen him just this once, to be avenged for his two eyes, pushed on the two middle pillars with all his might, and the house fell, so that he killed more in his death than in his life. Even with all his failings the Most High used him as a vessel of vengeance on the oppressor who gave the glory of the victory to a devil. Israel’s salvation in scripture is always joined with the destruction of the enemy, the two received together (Wisdom of Solomon 18:7). He had judged Israel twenty years. When Satan whispers to a fallen man that God cannot use somebody like him, remember that He used Samson.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/06-judges/samson

events.title: Saul
events.description:
The first king of Israel began to show his simplicity at Gilgal: told to wait seven days until Samuel came, he panicked when the people scattered, offered the burnt offering that was not his office to offer, and answered the prophet with excuses. Sent to wipe out Amalek, he spared Agag and the best of the flocks, greeted Samuel claiming he had carried out the Lord’s command while the sheep were bleating in the prophet’s ears, and laid it on the people. Obeying counts for more than sacrifice, and rebellion ranks with witchcraft. The kingdom was torn from him that day, and it ended on mount Gilboa.

Jonathan and his armourbearer climbed a rock face on their hands and feet and took a Philistine garrison, and the Lord sent a trembling through the host until the Philistines turned their swords on one another. In the middle of that deliverance Saul bound the army with a curse on any man who ate before evening, and the men of Israel were distressed. Jonathan, who had not heard the charge, tasted honey and argued against the order, and the famished people fell on the spoil and ate flesh with the blood. When the lot fell on Jonathan the king swore he should die, and the people would not let him kill the man who had wrought with God that day.

Saul had set an Edomite over his servants. Doeg reported that Ahimelech had enquired of the Lord for David, given him the hallowed bread and the sword of Goliath, and Saul, who by then read any loyalty to David as treason against himself, would not hear the priest’s defence. The king’s own footmen would not put forth their hand against the priests of the Lord, so he got the Edomite to do what his own men would not: Doeg slew eighty-five men that wore a linen ephod and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword. David wrote the Edomite’s sentence in a psalm.

Samuel was dead, Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land, and when he saw the host of the Philistines his heart greatly trembled.
