He enquired of the Lord and was not answered, not by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets, so he asked his servants to find him a woman with a familiar spirit: that is necromancy, and it was the very thing he had outlawed. He disguised himself, went by night, and heard from Samuel that the Lord had become his enemy and that the next day he and his sons would be with him. Chronicles names this as the cause of his death.

A young man came out of the camp of Israel to Ziklag with his clothes rent and earth upon his head, and fell before David with the crown and the bracelet of Saul: he said he had come by chance upon mount Gilboa, found Saul leaning on his spear, and slew him at his own asking. The earlier chapter says Saul fell on his own sword. He was an Amalekite, of the seed of Esau, the nation written of as fearing not God, and he expected a reward for the deed. His own mouth testified against him, and David had him slain.

A famine of three years sent David to enquire of the Lord, who answered that it was for Saul and his bloody house, because Saul had slain the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn by the Lord in Joshua’s day to let live (2 Samuel 21:1-2; Joshua 9:15-20). The lesson the Most High was teaching Israel through the famine was to pay what you vow. The Gibeonites refused silver and gold and asked for seven of Saul’s sons; David spared Jonathan’s son for his own oath, delivered the seven, and after the burial of Saul’s house the Lord was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:3-14).
events.article:
Reign

c. 1030–1010 BC

United

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

King Saul

Offering the burnt offering himself at Gilgal; sparing Agag and the best of the spoil; and stubbornness, which is as iniquity and idolatry

Put to death

Chapter thirteen is the beginning of Saul showing his simplicity, the proof he was not fit to be king. Samuel had told him to wait seven days at Gilgal (1 Samuel 10:8). When the Philistines massed, the chosen nation hid in caves and pits, though the Lord had just defeated the Philistines for them; the spirit God gives is not fear but power, love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7). With Samuel not yet come and the people scattering, Saul offered the burnt offering himself, Samuel’s office, not his, and Samuel arrived as he finished (1 Samuel 13:8-14). Brothers do the same today: leadership said ten o’clock, it is five past, so we go home. Wait as you were instructed; the Lord may be testing your patience, and a man is not to rush in time of trouble (Ecclesiasticus 2:2).

Then came the excuses: the people scattering, Samuel late, the Philistines gathering. That is the pattern of the man; he never holds himself accountable, he always deflects, going out to meet the man before he gets to where he messed up. Samuel told him he had acted foolishly and his kingdom would not last, for the Lord had sought a man after His own heart (Acts 13:22). Disobeying the prophet’s instruction was disobeying the commandment of the Lord.

Then Saul was sent to destroy Amalek completely for what it did to Israel on the way out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:3), the war sworn from generation to generation (Exodus 17:16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Christianity says forgive and forget; the Most High said remember. But Saul spared Agag and the best of the flocks, destroying only what was worthless (1 Samuel 15:9), killing what looked like it deserved killing so he could say he did some killing. Saul did most of it, and the Lord counted that as not carrying out His commands at all (1 Samuel 15:10-11). Whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given to you. At Carmel he raised a monument to himself, then claimed he had obeyed while sheep bleated nearby, and blamed the people, as at Gilgal. The Lord’s commands are kept with nothing added or taken away (Deuteronomy 12:32). Still insisting he had obeyed, he boasted of bringing back Agag; a man who justifies himself is condemned by his own mouth (Job 9:20).

Samuel made it plain: the Lord delights in obedience more than in burnt offerings (1 Samuel 15:22). Spoil taken against His will made the offering ridiculous; the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, worse when brought with evil intent (Proverbs 21:27). Rebellion ranks with witchcraft and stubbornness with idolatry, and because Saul rejected the Lord’s word, the Lord rejected him as king (1 Samuel 15:23). A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway, and according to this verse that rebellion is witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction is the Lord’s commandment carried by leadership, and stubbornness against it puts what I want before what God wants.

The confession finally came and was still not sincere: he feared the people and did what they said (1 Samuel 15:24). Fear of man is a trap, but whoever trusts the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25); a leader in fear of his people is being led by them. Saul tore Samuel’s robe, and Samuel told him the Lord had torn the kingdom from him that day for a better man; God does not lie or change His mind (Numbers 23:19). Then he asked to be honoured before the elders anyway, hiding the demotion: the spirit of vanity, caught up in a title and forgetting it came for pleasing the Lord.

Samuel mourned for him, for he had seen his potential. The Spirit of the Lord left Saul and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him (1 Samuel 16:14), and instead of repenting he went down into envy of David. It all traces back to bashfulness: he looked in the mirror and saw a kitty cat where God had said there was a lion, self-willed because he was afraid, and would not ask, wait or take counsel with the prophet at his side. A man can ruin his own soul through bashfulness and bring himself down by respecting persons (Ecclesiasticus 20:22). At the end, with the Lord silent, he consulted a medium, the very thing he had driven out of the land, and heard that he and his sons would die the next day (1 Samuel 28:19). They fell on mount Gilboa, Saul on his own sword (1 Samuel 31:4-6), dying for his unfaithfulness and for seeking a medium, and the kingdom went to David (1 Chronicles 10:13).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/saul

Saul’s rash oath, and the people at the blood

A strange oath that distressed the army; the people eating flesh with the blood; the king ready to kill the son who had wrought the salvation

Spared

Jonathan told the young man who bore his armour to come over to the garrison of the uncircumcised, since it might be that the Lord would work for them, for there is no restraint on the Lord to save by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6). The Most High put that spirit on him; He loves to show His power by having a small number defeat a very large number, and that is why it will be the hundred and forty-four thousand taking over the whole world. Judas Maccabeus said the same thing, that with the God of heaven it is all one to deliver with a great multitude or a small company (1 Maccabees 3:18-19). Jonathan climbed up on his hands and his feet with his armourbearer after him, and that first slaughter was about twenty men within half an acre of land. Some hold a doctrine that Jonathan was a homosexual; scaling a rock face to rush a garrison two deep is a bold, manly act of war that most men are not cut out for. There was trembling in the host and in the field, the earth quaked, the Philistines went on beating down one another, the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines turned back to Israel, and the men who had hidden in mount Ephraim followed hard after them; so the Lord saved Israel that day (1 Samuel 14:13-23).

In the middle of that deliverance the king adjured the people with a curse on any man who ate food before evening, until he was avenged on his enemies, and the men of Israel were distressed that day (1 Samuel 14:24-30). A vow is not a light thing: a man that vows a vow to the Lord is not to break his word, but to do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth (Numbers 30:2), and it is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay, for God has no pleasure in fools (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). They came into a wood where honey dropped on the ground, and no man put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath; but Jonathan had not been there when the charge went out, and he dipped the end of his rod in a honeycomb, and his eyes were enlightened. He said his father had troubled the land, and argued that the slaughter of the Philistines would have been far greater if the people had eaten freely of the spoil. The scripture says to fear the Lord and the king and to meddle not with them that are given to change (Proverbs 24:21); the king’s order was folly, but the talk against it led the people into a worse thing. Very faint, they flew on the spoil, took sheep, oxen and calves, slew them on the ground, and ate them with the blood (1 Samuel 14:29-32).

When they told Saul that the people were sinning against the Lord, he answered that they had transgressed, had a great stone rolled to him, and made every man bring his ox and his sheep and kill them there and eat, and not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood; and he built an altar to the Lord, the first altar he ever built to Him (1 Samuel 14:31-35). Then he proposed to go down after the Philistines by night, and when he asked counsel of God, God did not answer him that day. When the Lord ignores a man the scriptures give only one reason: if a man regards iniquity in his heart the Lord will not hear him (Psalms 66:18), and our iniquities have separated between us and our God, and our sins have hid His face so that He will not hear (Isaiah 59:2). Saul swore by the Lord who saves Israel that the guilty man would surely die, even if it were his own son; the lot fell between him and Jonathan, and Jonathan was taken. Jonathan said he had only tasted a little honey with the end of the rod in his hand, and Saul swore that God should do so and more to him if Jonathan did not surely die (1 Samuel 14:36-46). The people would not have it: should the man who had wrought this great salvation in Israel die? Not one hair of his head would fall to the ground, for he had wrought with God that day, and so the people rescued him. Weigh it as they weighed it: yes, he crossed the order, but he had just saved all their lives. Judgment without mercy comes on the man who has shown no mercy, and mercy rejoices against judgment (James 2:13).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/sauls-oath-and-jonathan

Saul and Doeg at Nob

Slaughter of the priests of the Lord on an Edomite’s report

Cursed

David came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest, three days out in the field and fearful of king Saul, and the priest gave him hallowed bread, for there was no bread there but the shewbread that had been taken from before the Lord (1 Samuel 21:6-7). Christ recounted this very history when the Pharisees challenged his disciples for plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, asking whether they had never read what David did when he had need and was an hungred (Mark 2:25-26); precept it in your bibles if it is not there already. A certain servant of Saul was detained before the Lord that day: Doeg, an Edomite, the chief of Saul’s herdmen (1 Samuel 21:7). The scriptures tell us never to trust an enemy (Ecclesiasticus 12:10), yet here is a king of Israel with an Edomite set over his servants. Doeg answered and reported that he had seen the son of Jesse come to Nob to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, who enquired of the Lord for him, gave him victuals, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine (1 Samuel 22:9-10). Saul sent for Ahimelech and all his father’s house, the priests in Nob, and charged them with conspiracy; Ahimelech answered that no one among all the king’s servants was as faithful as David, the king’s son in law, who went at his bidding and was honourable in his house, and that it was hardly the first time he had enquired of God for him, and the king should impute nothing to his servant nor to all his father’s house (1 Samuel 22:13-16). Saul had become so desperate that he read loyalty to David as betrayal of himself, because he wanted everybody against David. That is no new thing under the sun: men put slander out to turn whole congregations against a man they have never sat down with and broken bread with.

The king told the footmen standing about him to turn and slay the priests of the Lord, because their hand also was with David, but the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the Lord. So the king said to Doeg, turn and fall upon the priests; and Doeg the Edomite turned and fell upon them and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod, and smote Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, oxen, asses and sheep (1 Samuel 22:13-19). Saul was able to get the Edomite to do what his own men would not do. Go back to Genesis and see the spirit that has been on this man from the beginning: Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing, and comforted himself with the purpose of slaying his brother (Genesis 27:41). That comfort in killing is the same thing seen in Doeg; when Saul appointed him to the task you can best believe he found pleasure in it. Eighty-five priests and a whole city destroyed because they showed affinity to David, all out of hatred and envy. The servant is not greater than his lord, and if they persecuted Christ they will persecute us (John 15:20), and not only by the heathen but by our own kinsmen.

One of the sons of Ahimelech, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David, and told him that Saul had slain the Lord’s priests. David answered that he had known that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul, and that he had occasioned the death of all the persons of his father’s house; Abiathar was to abide with him and fear not, for the man who sought David’s life sought his life, and with David he would be in safeguard (1 Samuel 22:20-23). Where the reigning king had become a threat, the fugitive became a shelter.

Doeg’s own sentence is written in the psalm David made about him, the psalm inscribed for the day when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul that David was come to the house of Ahimelech: his tongue devised mischief like a sharp razor, working deceitfully, loving evil more than good and lying rather than speaking righteousness; therefore God would likewise destroy him for ever, take him away, pluck him out of his dwelling place, and root him out of the land of the living (Psalms 52:5). David did not tell the Edomite he could come and rule with him in the kingdom. That is the sentence, and it stands over the nation Doeg came from.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/doeg-and-the-priests-of-nob

Saul and the witch of Endor

Seeking a woman with a familiar spirit after he had himself put them out of the land

Put to death

Samuel was dead and buried in Ramah, and Saul had put away those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land. When the Philistines gathered and pitched in Shunem, Saul was afraid and his heart greatly trembled (1 Samuel 28:3-7). This is the king; if the king is afraid, so goes every man under him. As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers, and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein (Ecclesiasticus 10:2). Fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason offers (Wisdom of Solomon 17:12): a man tricks himself into being afraid of what is not there, because his faith is in what his eyes can see. Saul had been bashful from the beginning, little in his own sight, and bashfulness made him self willed, full of excuses, and easy to manipulate.

When Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. Then he told his servants to seek him a woman that had a familiar spirit, that he might go to her and enquire of her, and they told him of one at Endor (1 Samuel 28:3-7). He had just rid the land of the familiar spirits and the wizards, and now he says, find me one; his mind was all over the place, double minded. What he was doing is called necromancy, and the commandment he broke is written plainly: there shall not be found among the people any that uses divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a necromancer, for all that do these things are an abomination to the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); and the law says not to suffer a witch to live (Exodus 22:18). Saul disguised himself and came to the woman by night with two men, asking her to divine by the familiar spirit and bring up whoever he named. She answered that he knew what Saul had done, cutting off those that had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land, and asked why he was laying a snare for her life; and Saul swore to her by the Lord that no punishment would happen to her for it (1 Samuel 28:8-14). He swore by the name of the Lord to protect her in the doing of what the Lord calls abomination.

Samuel asked why he had disquieted him, and Saul answered that he was sore distressed: the Philistines made war on him and God was departed from him and answered him no more, so he had called Samuel to make known what he should do. Samuel asked why he asked of him, seeing the Lord was departed from him and was become his enemy (1 Samuel 28:15-19). Imagine that: the Lord is your enemy now. The Lord had done to him as He spoke by Samuel, rending the kingdom out of his hand and giving it to his neighbour David, because he obeyed not the voice of the Lord nor executed His fierce wrath upon Amalek; that is the law concerning Amalek he did not carry out (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Moreover the Lord would deliver Israel with him into the hand of the Philistines, and the next day he and his sons would be with Samuel: a prophecy from the grave that he and his sons would die. Saul fell straightway all along on the earth, sore afraid, and there was no strength in him (1 Samuel 28:15-20).

The Philistines followed hard upon Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua; the archers hit Saul and he was sore wounded, and rather than be taken and abused by the uncircumcised he asked his armourbearer to thrust him through, and when the man would not, Saul took a sword and fell upon it; so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together (1 Samuel 31:2-6), exactly as Samuel said. The chronicle states the cause: Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the Lord, against the word of the Lord which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it, and enquired not of the Lord; therefore He slew him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse (1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The Philistines cut off his head, put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth and fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan, until the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead went all night, took down the bodies and buried the bones at Jabesh (1 Samuel 31:8-13).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/saul-and-the-witch-of-endor

The Amalekite who claimed to kill Saul

Claiming to have slain the Lord’s anointed, and bringing his crown for a reward

Put to death

After the death of Saul, when David had returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and abode two days in Ziklag, a man came out of the camp from Saul with his clothes rent and earth upon his head and fell to the earth before David. He said the people were fled from the battle, many were fallen and dead, and Saul and Jonathan his son were dead also. Asked how he knew it, he said he happened by chance upon mount Gilboa and found Saul leaning upon his spear with the chariots and horsemen following hard after him; Saul asked who he was, and he answered that he was an Amalekite; then Saul asked him to stand upon him and slay him, because anguish was come upon him while his life was yet whole in him, so he stood upon him and slew him, being sure he could not live after he was fallen, and took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm and brought them to his lord (2 Samuel 1:2-10). The earlier account says Saul took a sword and fell upon it (1 Samuel 31:3-5). The man was an Amalekite: Amalek came of Eliphaz the son of Esau (Genesis 36:12). He carried the crown and the bracelet as tokens of a deed he expected to be paid for.

David took hold on his clothes and rent them, and so did all the men with him, and they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan his son, and for the house of Israel, because they were fallen by the sword. The renting of garments was the sign of mourning, but the Most High looks for a rent heart and not rent garments only, for true repentance is inward (Joel 2:13). The opening of the throne was no occasion for celebration, and the man who brought the crown had misjudged the king he brought it to.

David asked the young man where he was from, and he answered that he was the son of a stranger, an Amalekite. Then David asked how he was not afraid to stretch forth his hand to destroy the Lord’s anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-16). The answer to that question is written in the law: Amalek met Israel by the way, smote the hindmost when they were faint and weary, and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:18). That nation has had a perpetual hatred and has shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity (Ezekiel 35:5), pursuing his brother with the sword, casting off all pity, and keeping his wrath for ever (Amos 1:11). The man who had twice refused to put forth his hand against Saul, saying the Lord forbid it (1 Samuel 26:11), was not going to reward a stranger for claiming the act. David called one of his young men and told him to go near and fall upon him, and he smote him that he died; his blood was upon his own head, for his own mouth had testified against him. Whether or not he had done what he claimed, his mouth condemned him; he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword (Revelation 13:10). David remembered this messenger when Rechab and Baanah brought him the head of Ish-bosheth: the man who thought he brought good tidings of Saul was taken hold of and slain in Ziklag, and that was the reward he got for his tidings (2 Samuel 4:10).

Then David lamented over Saul and over Jonathan, and bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, which is written in the book of Jasher (2 Samuel 1:17-18). The book of Jasher is not in the canon because the Most High did not will us to have it; He put in the book exactly what His people need in the last days. And this walk is not by the bow nor by

the gun: not by might, nor by power, but by His spirit (Zechariah 4:6); here is the patience of the saints, they that keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus (Revelation 14:12). There is nothing wrong with knowing how to defend yourself, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms. The lament itself is prophecy given in the spirit: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions (2 Samuel 1:23). Before the devil jumped on Saul he was a good man, and the forefathers died only when the Most High said it was time; the man who boasted of hastening it lost his own life for it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/the-amalekite-messenger

Saul’s house and the Gibeonites

Breaking the oath Israel sware to the Gibeonites by slaying them in zeal for Israel and Judah

Put to death

There was a famine in the days of David, three years, year after year, and David enquired of the Lord. The answer was that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he killed the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). The Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Israel had sworn to them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 21:2). Saul broke his word.

The oath went back to the conquest. The Gibeonites heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai and worked by craft: old sacks, torn wine skins, worn shoes and garments, dry and mouldy bread, and a story that they came from a far country. Israel was commanded to

destroy the nations of the land, so their only hope was to pretend they were not of it. The men of Israel took of their provisions and did not ask counsel of the Lord. That was the first mistake, and it became a snare to the people, for the Most High says counsel before every action (Joshua 9:3-14). Joshua made peace with them and a league to let them live, and the princes of the congregation swore to it (Joshua 9:15). When the deceit came out three days later the congregation murmured, but the princes held the line: they had sworn by the Lord God of Israel, so they could not touch them, and would let them live lest wrath come on Israel for the oath (Joshua 9:16-20). Our forefathers were wrong in one situation, but upright men in holding to their word. A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile. The Gibeonites were made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God (Joshua 9:21-27).

Saul undid what the princes had kept. When a vow is made to God it is not to be put off; He has no pleasure in fools, it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, and a man is not to tell the angel afterward that it was a mistake (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6). Christ made it simple: let your yes be yes and your no be no (Matthew 5:37). The teaching on this says your word is your bond, and it is better not to swear at all than to cause yourself to sin by an oath you cannot live up to. Saul gave his yes to the Amorites and went back on it, and the whole house paid for it. Blood defiles the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood shed in it except by the blood of the one who shed it (Numbers 35:33).

David asked the Gibeonites what he should do for them and how he could make atonement, so that they would bless the inheritance of the Lord. The study notes are careful here: the blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through the famine. The Gibeonites would take no silver or gold of Saul or his house, and did not ask for any man in Israel to be killed for them. They asked for seven sons of the man who had consumed them and plotted to wipe them out of every border of Israel, to be hanged before the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, and the king agreed (2 Samuel 21:3-6).

David kept his own oath while he settled Saul’s broken one. He spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the oath of the Lord between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). David did not go back on his word; he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David’s table. The king delivered the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal to the Gibeonites, who hanged them in the hill before the Lord, all seven together, at the beginning of barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:8-9). Rizpah kept watch over the bodies until the rain, which is entered as her own case, and when David heard it he gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan with the bones of the hanged and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish; after that God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:10-14). Saul’s death on Gilboa did not wipe the breach out of the land. The king who came after him had to enquire into the cause and settle what lay beneath three years of famine.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/sauls-house-and-the-gibeonites

events.title: Jonathan
events.description: Jonathan’s soul was knit with David’s, and he loved him as his own soul; the same word describes the church, hearts knit together in love. The king’s son and heir stripped off his own robe and gave it to the shepherd, with his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle. He warned David of his father’s intent, spoke good of him to Saul and had a javelin cast at him for it, and went out to him in the wood at Ziph to strengthen his hand in God. His loyalty exceeded his own desires, and the kindness he asked for reached his lame son at the king’s table.
events.article:
Jonathan

Stripping himself of his robe for the man whom the Lord would make king; standing between his father and David’s innocent blood; thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee

Kept the law

When David had made an end of speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul; they made a covenant, and Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him and gave it to David, with his garments, even to his sword, his bow and his girdle (1 Samuel 18:1-4). Souls being knit is not speaking of anything unnatural between the two men. The same word describes the church, whose hearts are comforted by being knit together in love (Colossians 2:2), and the body, knit together by joints and bands (Colossians 2:19). Note the estate of the two men: Jonathan was the prince and the heir, David was an armourbearer out of Bethlehem, and a true friend does not rejoice in standing higher. A faithful friend is a strong defence and the medicine of life, and he that has found such a one has found a treasure (Ecclesiasticus 6:14).

Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants that they should kill David; the Philistines could not get him, so now the king wanted Israelites to kill an Israelite. But Jonathan delighted much in David and told him plainly that his father sought to kill him, and told him to take heed until the morning, abide in a secret place and hide himself (1 Samuel 19:1-7). Jonathan would have been next in line for the throne, and you would think his loyalty lay with his father, but he saw that the spirit was not on his father, it was on his brother David. Do not be ashamed to defend a friend, nor hide from him in the time of his trouble (Ecclesiasticus 22:25). He spoke good of David to Saul: let not the king sin against his servant, who had not sinned against him and whose works toward him had been very good, for he put his life in his hand and slew the Philistine and the Lord wrought a great salvation for all Israel, which Saul saw and rejoiced at; so why sin against innocent blood and slay David without a cause? The innocent and righteous are not to be slain (Exodus 23:7), and hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17). Saul listened and swore that David would not be slain, and Jonathan brought him back. At the new moon, when David’s seat was empty and Jonathan covered for him, Saul’s anger was kindled against his own son, telling him that as long as the son of Jesse lived on the ground neither he nor his kingdom would be established, and he cast a javelin at him to smite him; by that Jonathan knew it was determined of his father to slay David (1 Samuel 20:30-33). He would not buy a throne with his friend’s blood. When David was hunted in the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan rose up and went to him into the wood and strengthened his hand in God, telling him not to fear, for the hand of Saul his father would not find him, and David would be king over Israel and Jonathan would be next to him, and Saul his father knew it too (1 Samuel 23:16-17).

Jonathan had asked that the kindness of the Lord continue toward his house and never be cut off from it (1 Samuel 20:12-17). The covenant outlived him. The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons and slew Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua on mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). David lamented over them in the spirit, a eulogy and a prophecy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives and in their death they were not divided, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions; and

he was distressed for his brother Jonathan, whose love to him was wonderful, passing the love of women (2 Samuel 1:23-26). There is a friend that sticks closer than a brother (Proverbs 18:24); that is what Jonathan was. When David was king he asked whether any of the house of Saul was left, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, fetched Mephibosheth, lame on both his feet, out of Lo-debar, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually (2 Samuel 9:1-13). When seven of Saul’s house were delivered to the Gibeonites, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan because of the oath of the Lord that was between them (2 Samuel 21:7). Jonathan did not live to stand next to David, but his bones were gathered with his father’s into the sepulchre of Kish (2 Samuel 21:12-14), and the kindness he asked for was still being served at the king’s table years after he died.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/jonathan

events.title: David
events.description:
Samuel named the replacement at Gilgal before he had ever met him: the Lord had sought a man after His own heart and commanded him to be captain over His people. Twice Saul was delivered into David’s hand, in the cave at Engedi and in the trench at Hachilah, and twice David would not stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed, leaving the judgment with the Most High. He reverenced the man who was hunting him, and he judged the men who shed blood in his name. When he fell he had godly sorrow and rose again; his one great fall is its own case, and this is the rest.

In the season when kings went out to war, David stayed behind in Jerusalem, saw a woman bathing from his roof, was told plainly that she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and sent for her anyway. When she conceived he called Uriah home to cover it, and when Uriah would not go down to his house he sent him back carrying his own death warrant. Nathan came with a parable, David pronounced sentence on himself, and Nathan told him he was the man. The Lord took away his sin, but the sword never left his house, and the child died.

The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah; the Chronicles account says Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to do it (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The king’s word prevailed over Joab’s objection, and when the count came in David’s conscience struck him. Offered three judgments by the prophet Gad, he chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, and seventy thousand men died of the pestilence before the Lord stayed the angel at the threshing floor of Araunah, which David bought for an altar (2 Samuel 24:10-25).
events.article:
Reign

c. 1010–970 BC

United

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

David

A man after the Lord’s own heart: twice sparing the Lord’s anointed, leaving vengeance with the Lord, and repenting when he fell

Kept the law

Samuel told Saul at Gilgal that his kingdom would not continue, because the Lord had sought a man after His own heart and commanded him to be captain over His people (1 Samuel 13:14); the prophet said it without ever having met the replacement, and the apostle repeated the testimony, that the Lord had found in David the son of Jesse a man after His own heart who would fulfil all His will (Acts 13:22). What that heart looks like is shown while Saul hunted him. Saul took three thousand chosen men to the rocks of the wild goats and went into a cave to cover his feet, which is the scripture’s way of saying he was in there relieving himself, and David and his men were staying in the sides of it (1 Samuel 24:2-13). David rose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily, the corner of a man’s garment where the fringes are attached, and afterward his heart smote him even for that, and he stayed his servants, saying the Lord forbid that he should do such a thing to his master, the Lord’s anointed (1 Samuel 24:4-7). Then he went out after him, called him his lord the king, bowed with his face to the earth, laid the proof in his hand, and left the case with the Most High to judge between them, since his own hand would not touch him. Saul wept and admitted that David was more righteous, having repaid him good for evil, and that he knew well David would surely be king (1 Samuel 24:16-20). A king shall reign in righteousness (Isaiah 32:1); that is what Saul was acknowledging.

It happened again in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul lay sleeping in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster and Abner and the people round about him, and Abishai

asked leave to pin him to the earth with one stroke and not need a second. David answered that no man could stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless; as the Lord lived, the Lord would smite him, or his day would come to die, or he would go down into battle and perish (1 Samuel 26:7-11). These were warriors and they were itching for it, but David took the bigger position: this man was chosen before me, so let God deal with him. Saul had men around him whispering that David thought himself better and wanted the throne,, and he fed into it instead of saying that David was a man of God. David cried from the hill that if the Lord had stirred Saul up against him, let Him accept an offering, but if it was the children of men, let them be cursed before the Lord, and Saul confessed that he had played the fool and erred exceedingly (1 Samuel 26:19-21). The same spirit met Shimei on the road out of Jerusalem, and David let him curse, saying it might be that the Lord would look on his affliction and repay him good for the cursing that day (2 Samuel 16:10-12).

The Lord built him a house: his house and his kingdom would be established for ever before Him, and his throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:16). When a stranger claimed the crown of Saul, and when two captains carried in the head of Ish-bosheth, he did not accept wickedness done in his name; both were put to death for taking a life not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king (2 Samuel 1:14-16; 2 Samuel 4:9-12), because all things are to be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40). When Nathan told him he was the man, he confessed that he had sinned against the Lord (2 Samuel 12:13), and his sorrow was the godly sorrow that works repentance to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10); a just man falls seven times and rises up again (Proverbs 24:16). Fleeing from Absalom he sent the ark back into the city in faith: if he found favour in the eyes of the Lord, He would bring him again to see it, and if not, let Him do what seemed good (2 Samuel 15:25-26). The Lord took away his sins and exalted his horn for ever, giving him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel (Ecclesiasticus 47:11). The throne stands on the stipulation he gave Solomon at the last, to keep the charge of the Lord his God and walk in His ways and keep His statutes and commandments as written in the law of Moses (1 Kings 2:3-4); and the throne of his father David is the one given to Christ, whose kingdom shall have no end (Luke 1:32-33).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/david

David and Bathsheba

Adultery with the wife of Uriah, and setting Uriah up to be murdered on the battlefield to cover it

Temporal judgment

While Joab and all Israel were sent to destroy the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah, David stayed in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 11:1). Walking on the roof of his house in the evening he saw a woman bathing, asked after her, and was told she was Bath-sheba the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 11:2-3). He was told plainly that she was a married woman, and he had known the law from his youth up. He sent for her and lay with her, and she conceived and sent him word that she was pregnant (2 Samuel 11:4-5). Bath-sheba was not innocent either; when the king called she went, and she did not refuse.

David sent for Uriah and told him to go down to his house, with a gift of food following him from the king; but Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with the servants and did not go home (2 Samuel 11:6-9). He answered that the ark and Israel and Judah were living in tents and his lord’s servants were camped in the open field, so how could he go into his own house (2 Samuel 11:11). David made him drunk, and even drunk he would not go down (2 Samuel 11:13). That loyalty was killing David all the more.

In the morning David wrote to Joab and sent the letter by Uriah’s own hand, ordering that he be put at the front of the fiercest fighting and abandoned there to be killed (2 Samuel 11:14-15). Joab placed him where he knew the valiant men were, and Uriah died along with some of David’s servants (2 Samuel 11:16-17); other men of Israel died with that sin. The curses at Ebal are for this: a curse lies on the man who strikes his neighbour in secret and on the man who takes a reward to kill an innocent person, and the reward here was the woman (Deuteronomy 27:24-25). David sent word to Joab not to be troubled, since in battle the sword kills this man or that one (2 Samuel 11:25). When the mourning was over he married her, but the Lord was displeased with what David had done (2 Samuel 11:27).

The Lord sent Nathan with a parable of a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man’s one ewe lamb, dear to him as a daughter, to feed a traveller. David burned with anger and swore the man deserved to die, because he had no pity (2 Samuel 12:1-5); judging that man, he was pronouncing sentence on himself. Nathan told him he was the man: the Lord had anointed him, delivered him from Saul, given him his master’s house and all Israel and Judah, and would have given him more; why then had he despised the Lord’s commandment, killing Uriah and taking his wife (2 Samuel 12:7-9)? If he had only asked, the Lord would have given him anything.

So the sword would never leave his house; the Lord would raise up trouble from within it and give his wives to another man in broad daylight, because he had acted in secret and this would be done before all Israel (2 Samuel 12:10-12). It came to pass exactly, on a roof, by Ahithophel’s counsel. David confessed his sin against the Lord, and Nathan told him the Lord had taken it away and he would not die, but because the deed had given the Lord’s enemies great cause to blaspheme, the child would die (2 Samuel 12:13-14). That child was the judgment: the Lord shows mercy and forgives iniquity, yet does not clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7). He was pardoned; he was not cleared. He fasted and lay on the ground all night while the child lived; when it died he rose, washed, worshipped and ate, saying he would go to the child but the child would not come back to him (2 Samuel 12:16-23). His was the godly sorrow that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10); a just man who falls seven times gets up again (Proverbs 24:16). Through the judgment Solomon was still born and the Lord loved him (2 Samuel 12:24-25). People who want to justify wrongdoing run straight to this history; but you are not King David, and this is the mess up, not the licence.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/david-and-bathsheba

David’s numbering of the people

Numbering Israel and Judah against Joab’s counsel; seventy thousand men dead of the pestilence

Plague

Two accounts tell one event. Second Samuel says the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel and he moved David against them to number Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 24:1). First Chronicles says Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number Israel (1 Chronicles 21:1). The teaching reconciles them: it is all saying the same thing. The Most High wanted to judge Israel, and he used David and used Satan to do it. Satan cannot come into a man’s life without the okay from God: God chooses him, and Satan uses him. The Lord already knew the lust that was in David, and it was Satan’s work to feed that desire and keep tempting him until he carried it out.

The lust was pride, the desire of a man in power to know how many he is over. Only God is supposed to know the number of his people. Numbering was not the king’s work but the Levites’, and when Israel was counted under the law, every man from twenty years old and up gave a ransom for his soul, half a shekel, rich and poor alike, so that no plague would come on them (Exodus 30:11-16). Joab tried to talk sense into the king. He asked why the king took delight in this thing when God already knew the number, but the king’s word prevailed against Joab and the captains of the host (2 Samuel 24:3-4). Chronicles adds that Joab called it a cause of trespass to Israel and left Levi and Benjamin uncounted, because the king’s word was abominable to him (1 Chronicles 21:3-6).

The count took nine months and twenty days from Dan to Beer-sheba, and Joab brought back eight hundred thousand valiant men of Israel who drew the sword and five hundred thousand of Judah, not counting the women and children (2 Samuel 24:5-9). The teaching sets this beside the census of today. The powers that control the earth count the people not for their good but to know what level of force to use against them. A leader aligned with God does as Joab said and keeps the number to God.

As soon as it was done it hit him. David’s conscience struck him; he confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly, and asked the Lord to take away his servant’s iniquity (2 Samuel 24:10). In the morning the word came to Gad, David’s seer, with three judgments and a choice of one: famine in the land, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence (2 Samuel 24:11-13). Samuel gives the famine as seven years and Chronicles as three (1 Chronicles 21:11-12). David was in a great strait and chose to fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, rather than into the hand of man, knowing that man would not show him the mercy the Most High would (2 Samuel 24:14; 1 Chronicles 21:13).

The pestilence ran from the morning to the time appointed, and seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beer-sheba (2 Samuel 24:15). God killed seventy thousand because David decided to number the people, and the same way God used the nations back then to correct us when we were disobedient, it is the same thing today. The notes send the reader back to the first verse: the reason for the seventy thousand is that the Most High was angry at Israel. When the angel stretched out his hand over Jerusalem, the Lord repented of the evil and told him it was enough. David saw the angel, something we cannot see today, for this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. He and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces, and he pleaded that he alone had sinned and that the sheep had done nothing (2 Samuel 24:16-17; 1 Chronicles 21:16-17).

Gad sent him to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. Araunah offered the floor, the oxen and the threshing tools as a free gift, but David would not offer the Lord burnt offerings that cost him nothing. He paid, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the plague was stayed from Israel (2 Samuel 24:18-25). Samuel gives the price as fifty shekels of silver for the floor and the oxen; Chronicles gives six hundred shekels of gold for the place, and adds that the Lord answered by fire from heaven and the angel put up his sword (1 Chronicles 21:25-27). True worship costs us something. That threshing floor on mount Moriah is where Solomon later built the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 3:1).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/davids-census

events.title: Mephibosheth
events.description: He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, because a new king customarily killed the descendants of the old one, and in her haste he fell and became lame. David fetched him out of Lo-debar for Jonathan’s sake, restored him all the land of Saul, and set him at the king’s table continually. When David fled from Absalom, his servant Ziba slandered him and took the estate; when the king came again in peace, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven and said, let him take all.
events.article:
Mephibosheth

What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am? and, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace

Kept the law

Jonathan the son of Saul had a son that was lame of his feet. He was five years old when the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she made haste to flee he fell and became lame; his name was Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4). She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill the descendants of the former king, so that none could overthrow him. But David asked whether there was yet any left of the house of Saul, that he might show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake, because they had made a covenant, loving each other as their own souls (1 Samuel 18:3). Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, told him that Jonathan had yet a son, lame on his feet, in Lo-debar, and the king sent and fetched him. When Mephibosheth came he fell on his face and did reverence, and David told him to fear not, for he would surely show him kindness for Jonathan his father’s sake, restore him all the land of Saul, and have him eat bread at the king’s table continually; and he bowed and asked what his servant was, that the king should look upon such a dead dog as he (2 Samuel 9:1-8). His standing rested on a covenant between his father and the king, not on anything he could do.

During Absalom’s rebellion Ziba met David past the top of the hill with asses saddled and bread and raisins and summer fruits and wine; when the king asked where his master’s son was, Ziba said he abode in Jerusalem, saying that the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father that day. It was not true, and on that word David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 16:1-4). When the king came again, Mephibosheth came down to meet him, having neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace: he had mourned the whole time. He told the king that his servant had deceived him, for he was lame and had asked for an ass to be saddled that he might ride to the king, and Ziba had slandered him; but the king was as an angel of God, and all his father’s house were but dead men before the king, yet he had set his servant among them that ate at his own table, so he had no right to cry any more to the king. When David said that he and Ziba should divide the land, Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take all, forasmuch as his lord the king was come again in peace to his own house (2 Samuel 19:24-30).

The king called Ziba and told him he had given his master’s son all that pertained to Saul and to all his house; Ziba, his sons and his servants were to till the land and bring in the fruits, that his master’s son might have food, but Mephibosheth would eat bread always at the king’s table. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Samuel 9:9-13). That shows the riches Israel had as a nation: Saul’s servant had servants of his own, all set to work the land for a lame man out of the respect David had for Jonathan. So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem and did eat continually at the king’s table, and was lame on both his feet. This is what we need to bring back into Israel, that same love and care for the people we lose: we take care of their family as if they were there themselves. That is a large part of why the Most High called David a man after His own heart.

When the famine came for Saul’s bloody house and the Gibeonites required seven of his sons, the king spared Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, because of the oath of the Lord between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). Set the two houses side by side. Saul had given his word to the Gibeonites and gone back on it, and the whole house paid for it, because when a man vows a vow to God he must not defer to pay it, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). David had given his word to Jonathan and kept it, and Jonathan’s crippled son was pulled out of that judgment by the promise. Jonathan was gone, Saul’s rule was gone, the kingdom had passed; the word of kindness had not passed, and a lame man at the king’s table made a kept promise visible every day.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/mephibosheth

events.title: Amnon
events.description: David’s firstborn was so tormented over his half sister that he made himself ill, and his crafty friend Jonadab told him how to get her alone: play sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for him where he could watch. He cleared the room so there would be no witnesses. She begged him not to force her, because Israel does not do such things, and called it folly; being the stronger, he forced her, then hated her more than he had loved her and had her thrown out and the door bolted. David was very angry and did nothing. Two years later Absalom had him killed at a sheepshearing.
events.article:
Amnon

Forcing his sister Tamar, then hating her and putting her out

Put to death

Amnon the son of David was so tormented over Tamar, Absalom’s beautiful sister, that he fell ill, because she was a virgin and it seemed impossible for him to do anything to her; but he had a friend, Jonadab the son of David’s brother Shimeah, a very crafty man (2 Samuel 13:1-2; 2 Samuel 13:1-3). He was the grimy sort who knows exactly how to get over on somebody, and Tamar was Amnon’s sister by another mother. Jonadab told him to lie in bed and pretend to be sick, and when his father came, to ask for Tamar to prepare food in front of him so he could eat from her hand (2 Samuel 13:5). David sent Tamar, and she made cakes where he could see; he refused to eat and sent every man out (2 Samuel 13:7-9). He emptied the room so there would be no witnesses, then took hold of his own sister and told her to lie with him.

She begged her brother not to force her, because Israel does not do such things, and not to commit this folly; she would have nowhere to carry her shame, and he would be counted among the fools of Israel; let him rather speak to the king, who would not keep her from him. He would not listen, and he overpowered her and forced her (2 Samuel 13:6-14; 2 Samuel 13:12-14). Tamar herself calls it folly and sin. Any man talking about forcing a woman is wicked, and the law is plain: if a man forces a betrothed young woman in the field, only the man dies and nothing is done to her, for the case is like a man attacking his neighbour and killing him (Deuteronomy 22:25-26). Rape is murder, and it falls under the commandment against killing. On top of that it was his sister, whose nakedness the law forbids uncovering (Leviticus 18:9), and a curse stands on the man who lies with his sister (Deuteronomy 27:22). Then Amnon’s hatred for her was greater than his love had been, and he told her to get out; she answered that sending her away was a worse wrong than the first, but he would not listen, and had his servant put her out and bolt the door behind her (2 Samuel 13:15-19; 2 Samuel 13:15-18; 2 Samuel 13:15-17). She wore a robe of many colours, the dress of the king’s virgin daughters (2 Samuel 13:18), part of the order of the kingdom, and it is why we wear garments today.

Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her robe and went away crying. Absalom asked whether Amnon had been with her, told her to keep quiet for now, since he was her brother, and she stayed desolate in his house. David was very angry when he heard, and Absalom said nothing at all to Amnon, for he hated him for forcing his sister (2 Samuel 13:19-22). David

was upset at what happened to Tamar and did nothing about it; Absalom was one of those men who holds a grudge for years just to get somebody back, and these are people who know the law and know they are Israel. After two full years Absalom held a sheepshearing at Baal-hazor and pressed the king until Amnon and all the king’s sons came; he ordered his servants to wait until Amnon was merry with wine and then strike him down at his word, and they did (2 Samuel 13:23-29; 2 Samuel 13:23-33). He was killed for what he did to Tamar, by a brother’s revenge and not by a hearing under the law; his guilt did not make every act against him righteous. Word reached David that all his sons were slain, and he tore his clothes and lay on the ground, until Jonadab told him only Amnon was dead, and that Absalom had settled on it from the day Amnon forced Tamar (2 Samuel 13:30-33). The king and his servants wept bitterly, Absalom fled to Talmai king of Geshur, and David mourned for his son every day (2 Samuel 13:36-37). The sword Nathan had announced was working inside the house: Tamar desolate, Amnon dead, Absalom gone.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/amnon

events.title: Absalom
events.description: David’s son killed his brother, fled, was brought home, then provided himself chariots, horses and fifty runners and stood by the road to the gate, telling every man who came for judgment that his case was good and right but the king had appointed no one to hear it. He kissed their hands and stole the hearts of the men of Israel. Under cover of a vow at Hebron he raised a rebellion, drove his father out barefoot and weeping up Olivet, and by Ahithophel’s counsel lay with the royal concubines on the roof in the sight of all Israel. He was left hanging by his head in an oak, and Joab drove three darts through his heart.
events.article:
Absalom

Murder of Amnon; stealing the hearts of the men of Israel; conspiracy and rebellion against the king his father; lying with his father’s concubines before all Israel

Put to death

Absalom took his sister into his house after Amnon forced her, nursed his hatred two full years, had Amnon killed at his sheepshearing, and fled to Geshur (2 Samuel 13:11-14; 2 Samuel 13:15-22; 2 Samuel 13:23-29; 2 Samuel 13:20-38). Joab brought him home by the wise woman of Tekoah; he lived two years in Jerusalem without seeing the king, and when Joab would not come he set Joab’s barley field on fire to force a meeting (2 Samuel 14:23-33). His complaint was that his father had rendered no justice for Tamar, but he had already taken that justice into his own hand, and now he wanted the seat. He then provided himself chariots and fifty runners, stood early by the gate, and told every man bringing a case to the king that his cause was good and right but no one was appointed to hear it, wishing aloud that he were judge in the land. When anyone bowed to him he took his hand and kissed him, and so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel (2 Samuel 15:1-6; 2 Samuel 15:1-12).

That is the sneakiness: instead of going to the king and resolving the matter, he got into the king’s good graces and then went around patting people on the back behind his back. That is what the bishop calls friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend. After forty years he asked leave to pay a vow at Hebron, and sent spies through all the tribes to proclaim at the trumpet that Absalom reigned in Hebron; two hundred men went with him in their simplicity, knowing nothing, and with Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, the conspiracy grew strong (2 Samuel 15:7-12). That is the simplicity of a lot of brothers: a man who says all the nice things goes completely out of order against leadership, and men follow him carnally because he kissed their hand and told them their cause was good. Others follow for what they can get, grumblers and faultfinders driven by their own desires, flattering people to gain an advantage (Jude 1:16). When word came that Israel’s heart was with Absalom, the king fled barefoot and weeping up Olivet (2 Samuel 15:13-30). Ahithophel then counselled Absalom to go in to the concubines David had left to keep the house, so all Israel would know he had made himself odious to his father; they pitched a tent on the roof and he did it in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:21-22). That fulfilled exactly what the Lord said by Nathan, that David’s wives would be given to another in broad daylight (2 Samuel 12:11); and the son who fulfilled it fell under the curse himself, which lies on a man who lies with his father’s wife (Deuteronomy 27:20).

David prayed that the Lord would turn Ahithophel’s counsel to foolishness and sent Hushai back to defeat it (2 Samuel 15:31-34), and the Lord had determined to overthrow that counsel so as to bring evil on Absalom (2 Samuel 17:1-14). David divided the army under Joab, Abishai and Ittai and charged them in everyone’s hearing to deal gently with the young man for his sake; even after the concubines and the stolen hearts, the father still sought to make amends with his son (2 Samuel 18:1-5).

In the battle in the wood of Ephraim the forest took more lives than the sword. Absalom, riding a mule, was caught by the head in the thick branches of a great oak and left hanging between heaven and earth as the mule went on (2 Samuel 18:6-9). The man who saw it would

not touch him for a thousand shekels, because of the king’s charge; Joab took three darts and drove them into Absalom’s heart while he was still alive in the oak, and ten of his armour bearers finished him (2 Samuel 18:10-15; 2 Samuel 18:1-15). Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought him back alive for his father to make amends, and he did what he wanted. In his lifetime he had set up a pillar in the king’s dale and named it after himself, because he had no son to keep his name alive (2 Samuel 18:17-18). He sought a monument and a kingdom, and his rebellion ended in a pit under stones. When Cushi brought the news, the king went up to the room over the gate and wept for his son, wishing he had died in his place (2 Samuel 18:31-33). Promotion comes from the Most High, who places every member in the body as He pleases (1 Corinthians 12:18), and not from a man stealing hearts at the gate.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/absalom

events.title: Solomon
events.description:
At Gibeon the Lord appeared to the young king in a dream and told him to ask what He should give him. Solomon called himself a little child set over a people too many to count, and asked for an understanding heart to judge them and to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:5-9). The request pleased the Lord, who gave him a wise and understanding heart like none before or after him, added the riches and honour he had not asked for, and promised length of days on condition that he walk in the commandments as David had (1 Kings 3:10-14).

Two harlots who lived in one house each bore a son three days apart; one woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it, and she exchanged it for the living child while the other slept (1 Kings 3:16-22). There was no witness, and before the king each claimed the living child. Solomon called for a sword and ordered the child divided; the true mother gave up her claim to save the child’s life, the other would have it cut in two, and the king gave the child to its mother, so that all Israel saw the wisdom of God in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:23-28).

Solomon, the wisest of kings, loved many strange women besides Pharaoh’s daughter, from the very nations the law said would surely turn Israel’s heart after their gods, and he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:1-3). When he was old they turned his heart, and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:4-8). The Lord, who had appeared to him twice, said He would rend the kingdom out of his son’s hand, leaving one tribe for David’s sake, and stirred up adversaries against him (1 Kings 11:9-40).
events.article:
Reign

c. 970–931 BC

United

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Solomon at Gibeon

Asking for an understanding heart to judge thy people, and not long life, nor riches, nor the life of his enemies

Kept the law

The chapter opens on the setting. Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and took his daughter, and the people still sacrificed in high places because no house had yet been built to the name of the Lord. Solomon loved the Lord and walked in the statutes of David his father, only he too sacrificed and burnt incense in high places, and he went to Gibeon, the great high place, and offered a thousand burnt offerings there (1 Kings 3:1-4). The study notes read this as a king who loved the Lord in a time before the temple. The classes press the other side of the same verses: marrying Pharaoh’s daughter went against the law that forbade marriages with the nations because they would turn the heart to other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), so the Lord came to him while he was already mixing, and History in the AM counts Gibeon as the first of the two times the Lord appeared to him to admonish him (1 Kings 11:9).

God said to ask. Solomon began with the great mercy shown to David, who had walked before the Lord in truth, righteousness and uprightness of heart, and the kindness of giving him a son to sit on his throne. He said he was only a little child who did not know how to go out or come in, set in the midst of a chosen people too great to be numbered, and he asked for an understanding heart to judge them, that he might discern between good and bad, for no one could judge so great a people without it (1 Kings 3:6-9). The teaching hears a young man saying, Lord, how do I guide these people; tell me what to do. This is what we still need to pray for: that the Most High endows our leadership with wisdom, and that we ourselves learn wisdom in these scriptures and how to judge matters among one another. The saints will judge the world and even angels, so they ought to be able to judge the smallest matters of this life (1 Corinthians 6:1-3).

The speech pleased the Lord. Because Solomon had not asked for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, but for understanding to discern judgment, God gave him a wise and understanding heart, so that there was none like him before him and none would arise after him, and added what he had not asked, riches and honour above all the kings of his days (1 Kings 3:10-13). Length of days was conditional: if he would walk in God’s ways and keep His statutes and commandments as his father David had, the Lord would lengthen his days (1 Kings 3:14). The gift did not cancel the command. Solomon woke, came to Jerusalem, and offered before the ark of the covenant (1 Kings 3:15).

The wisdom was seen in judgment. When the two women came before him, which is entered as its own case, all Israel feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). It was seen in government: princes and twelve officers, each man in his position of order, the same pattern of captains and officers set up in the days of Moses (1 Kings 4:1-7). Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and fig tree from Dan to Beer-sheba, because the wars of David had put down the surrounding nations and put them to tribute (1 Kings 4:20-25).

God gave him wisdom and understanding exceeding much and largeness of heart like the sand on the seashore. His wisdom excelled all the children of the east country and all the wisdom of Egypt; he spoke three thousand

proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and people of all nations came to hear him (1 Kings 4:29-34). Since his wisdom already excelled Egypt’s, there is no need to dabble in Egyptology or any doctrine outside the scriptures; the classes ask whether we do not want our own understanding to pass the nations the same way, by keeping the Lord’s ways, statutes and commandments. The Most High gave him knowledge of how the world was made, the working of the elements, the natures of living creatures, the diversities of plants and the virtues of roots, and the reasonings of men (Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-21). The reasonings of men is what would be called psychology today, spiritual discernment, and it is the gift he used to see through the claims brought to his throne. The Lord appeared to him a second time after the temple was finished with the same condition (1 Kings 9:2-5); what he did with his wives when he was old is another case.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/solomon-at-gibeon

The two women before Solomon

Two harlots, one living child, and a claim that only a sword could sort out

Restitution

The case came before the throne soon after Gibeon, when Solomon had asked for an understanding heart to judge the people and to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:9). Two women who were harlots stood before the king. The first said that she and the other woman lived in one house, that she gave birth there, and that three days later the other woman gave birth as well, with no one else in the house but the two of them. The other woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it. She rose at midnight, took the living son from beside the first woman while she slept, laid him in her own bosom, and laid her dead child in the first woman’s bosom. In the morning the first woman rose to nurse her child and found him dead, but when she looked closely in the light she knew it was not the son she had borne (1 Kings 3:16-21). The teaching notes that a child dying under its sleeping mother is something that happens, and it hurts the mothers greatly; and that to an untrained eye one small baby can look like another, but a mother knows her own.

The other woman answered that the living child was hers and the dead one belonged to the first, and the first said the opposite, and so they argued before the king (1 Kings 3:22). How was Solomon to know who was lying and who was telling the truth? He was king over all Israel and did not know these women. There was no stranger in the house to bear witness, both women claimed the same right, and both laid the dead child on the other. The classes add that during the time of Solomon, the Kingdom of Heaven on earth, there were still harlots, and they came to the king in a pair: all flesh keeps company with its own kind.

The king repeated both claims back to them, called for a sword, and when it was brought he ordered the living child divided in two and half given to each (1 Kings 3:23-25). Then the woman whose child it was spoke, because her heart yearned over her son. She begged the king to give the other woman the living child and by no means kill it. The other said to let it be neither hers nor her rival’s, but divided (1 Kings 3:26). The teaching reads the second woman plainly: she did not care whether the baby was put to death, because she had already lost her own; she wanted company in her misery. It compares her spirit to that of women today who have abortion after abortion and have no love for the child. The king answered that the living child was to be given to the first woman and by no means killed, for she was its mother (1 Kings 3:27).

The Jurisprudence class asks what law Solomon had to go on, since no statute covers one woman taking another’s baby, and answers that he went on the strength of common sense. From the moment he called for the sword he knew the real mother would react in a way the false one would not; he judged by what he had seen of a mother’s love for her child. Wisdom knows things of old and can conjecture aright what is to come; she knows the subtleties of speeches (Wisdom of Solomon 8:8). Conjecture is a conclusion formed on incomplete information, and Solomon had only each woman’s version of the story; by wisdom, experience and the law he reached a right conclusion and recognised the subtlety in the false woman’s speech. Most in the congregation will never be judges, the class says, but they still have to understand judgment, and study is how that wisdom is gained.

All Israel heard of the judgment the king had judged, and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). This was the answer to what he had asked at Gibeon, made visible to the whole nation through a household dispute between two women. The Lesser and the Greater class then turns to Christ, the greater Solomon, who did not need anyone to testify of man, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24-25). Solomon had to hear the women out and watch their countenance; Christ perceives the thoughts of men before they speak (Luke 5:22). The record gives no separate punishment for the false claimant. It ends with the living child given to his mother.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/the-two-women-before-solomon

King Solomon

Loving many strange women of the nations the Lord had forbidden; multiplying wives against the law of the king; building high places for Chemosh and Molech

Temporal judgment

Sirach sums up his life: he reigned in a peaceable time, was as wise as a flood of understanding, gathered gold as tin and silver as lead, and then bowed his loins to women, was brought into subjection by his body, stained his honour and polluted his seed (Ecclesiasticus 47:13-20). History in the AM calls the lesson Simping Solomon, from his own words. He knew better. He wrote that understanding would deliver a man from the strange woman who flatters with her words, whose house leads down to death (Proverbs 2:16-19); that her lips drip honey but her end is bitter as wormwood, and a man should not embrace the bosom of a stranger (Proverbs 5:3-20); that many strong men have been slain by her (Proverbs 7:24-27). His own mother told him not to give his strength to women (Proverbs 31:3). One may be wise and teach many and yet be unprofitable to himself (Ecclesiasticus 37:19).

The law was plain. Israel was to make no marriages with the nations, for they would turn their sons away to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4), and their daughters would lead Israel’s sons after their gods (Exodus 34:16). The study notes stress that it was not a maybe but a will. The king in particular was not to multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away, nor greatly multiply silver and gold (Deuteronomy 17:17). Tobit told his son to take a wife of the seed of his fathers, for despising the sons and daughters of your people by not taking a wife of them is pride, and pride is destruction (Tobit 4:12-13). Nehemiah later saw children who could not speak the Jews’ language because their mothers were of Ashdod, and reminded the people that even Solomon, beloved of his God, was caused to sin by outlandish women (Nehemiah 13:23-26).

Solomon clung to these in love, and when he was old his wives turned his heart after other gods, and it was not perfect with the Lord as David’s had been. David sinned, but he repented and turned back; Solomon kept going. He went after Ashtoreth of the Zidonians, the fertility goddess behind Easter, and Milcom of Ammon, and built high places for Chemosh and Molech and for all his strange wives to burn incense to their gods (1 Kings 11:3-8). He did this after building the Lord’s house. The six-pointed star belongs here: the star of their god that Israel carried with Molech (Amos 5:26), the star of Remphan still carried in the apostles’ day (Acts 7:43), not a star of David. His sin was not his alone, for he was the greatest influence on the earth. He gave his heart to know madness and folly, and kept nothing from his eyes (Ecclesiastes 1:17; Ecclesiastes 2:10).

The Lord was angry, because Solomon’s heart had turned from Him who had appeared to him twice and commanded him not to go after other gods (1 Kings 11:9-10). The teaching sets it beside the rule for a heretic, to be rejected after a first and second admonition (Titus 3:10): the third time is judgment. The Lord said He would surely rend the kingdom from him and give it to his servant, not in his days for David’s sake, but out of his son’s hand, leaving one tribe for David and for Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:11-13). The study notes call this the pivotal moment in Israel’s history, the sin that divided the kingdom under Jeroboam and Rehoboam.

Peace had held while he kept the commandments; when he broke them, the Lord gave strength to his enemies. He stirred up Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a child when Joab cut off every male in Edom, for Esau was always the first hater of Israel, and Rezon, who reigned in Damascus and was an adversary all Solomon’s days (1 Kings 11:14-25). Then the prophet Ahijah tore Jeroboam’s new garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten, for ten tribes; Solomon sought to kill him, and he fled to Shishak in Egypt until Solomon died (1 Kings 11:26-40).

Sirach says he left behind him the foolishness of the people and a son without understanding who turned the people away (Ecclesiasticus 47:23); the classes observe that a king searching out every folly had no time to raise Rehoboam in the law. Had he walked in the way of God, he would have dwelt in peace forever (Baruch 3:13). At the end he came full circle: he found more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares (Ecclesiastes 7:26), called it all vanity, and gave the conclusion of the whole matter, to fear God and keep his commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/07-united-monarchy/solomon

events.title: Rehoboam
events.description: All Israel came to Shechem to make Solomon’s son king and asked him to lighten the heavy yoke his father had laid on them (1 Kings 12:1-4). Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men who had served Solomon, took the counsel of the young men he grew up with, and answered the people roughly, and ten tribes left the house of David that day, for the cause was from the Lord (1 Kings 12:6-20). Once his kingdom was strong he forsook the law of the Lord and all Israel with him, and Shishak of Egypt came up against Jerusalem until king and princes humbled themselves (2 Chronicles 12:1-12).
events.article:
Reign

931–913 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Rehoboam

Forsaking the counsel of the old men for the young men he grew up with; and forsaking the law of the Lord when the kingdom was established

Temporal judgment

Sirach names him plainly: Solomon left behind him even the foolishness of the people, one that had no understanding, who turned away the people through his counsel (Ecclesiasticus 47:23). Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel came to make him king; Jeroboam came back from Egypt, and the congregation asked Rehoboam to lighten the grievous service and heavy yoke his father had put on them, and they would serve him (1 Kings 12:1-4). The study notes say the yoke was the labour of the building; Solomon did not enslave his own people as he did the nations, but they had to put in that work. Our Hidden History reads it as the taxes Solomon laid on the people to finance his wives’ temples.
