He told them to come back in three days, which was wisdom, for it is right to take time and get counsel before giving an answer (1 Kings 12:5). He consulted the old men who had stood before Solomon, and they told him that if he would be a servant to the people that day and speak good words to them, they would be his servants forever. He forsook their counsel and turned to the young men who had grown up with him (1 Kings 12:6-8). Solomon was the wisest man on earth and still had counsellors, yet Rehoboam forsook the counsellors of the wisest man for his peers; the problem is getting counsel from those on your own level rather than from your elders. The classes call it pride, and add that his father, busy with his own pleasures, had not been there to guide him. The young men told him to say that his little finger would be thicker than his father’s loins, and that where his father chastised them with whips he would chastise them with scorpions (1 Kings 12:9-11). On the third day he spoke to the people roughly in just those words (1 Kings 12:12-14). You are where you are based on the decisions you made.

The study notes on Chronicles show the second offense. When Rehoboam had established the kingdom and strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him (2 Chronicles 12:1). One who leads goes astray and carries many with him. Judah built high places, images and groves on every high hill, and sodomites were in the land (1 Kings 14:22-24). He did evil because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14); Solomon had prepared his heart at Gibeon, and his son did not follow those footsteps.

The king did not listen to the people, for the cause was from the Lord, that the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam might come to pass (1 Kings 12:15). Israel answered that they had no portion in David, and went to their tents; Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute, and all Israel stoned him to death, and the king fled in his chariot to Jerusalem. So Israel rebelled against the house of David to this day, and only Judah followed the house of David (1 Kings 12:16-20). Rehoboam gathered a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men to bring the kingdom back, but the word came through Shemaiah not to fight their brethren, for this thing was from the Lord, and they listened and went home (1 Kings 12:21-24).

In his fifth year, because they had transgressed, Shishak king of Egypt came up with a great host and took the fenced cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 12:2-4). Shemaiah told them that because they had forsaken the Lord, He had left them in Shishak’s hand. The princes and the king humbled themselves and said the Lord is righteous (2 Chronicles 12:5-6). When correction comes, the right response is to confess that the Most High is righteous in what He does. Because they humbled themselves He would not destroy them, but they would be Shishak’s servants, to learn the difference between His service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). If Israel confesses its iniquity and accepts the punishment, He remembers His covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42). The people today must likewise humble themselves and accept their condition as righteous judgment.

Shishak carried off the treasures of the Lord’s house and the king’s house and all the shields of gold Solomon had made, and Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, a fall from gold to brass (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Because he humbled himself, the wrath turned from him, and in Judah things went well (2 Chronicles 12:12). There was war with Jeroboam all his days, and after seventeen years Abijah his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:13-16).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/rehoboam

events.title: Baasha
events.description: Baasha conspired against Nadab the son of Jeroboam, killed him, and destroyed all the house of Jeroboam as Ahijah had foretold, then reigned twenty-four years walking in the same way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:27-34). He built Ramah to stop the people of the north from going over to Asa and the Lord (2 Chronicles 16:1). The word came by Jehu the son of Hanani that the Lord, who had lifted him out of the dust, would make his house like the house of Jeroboam, and it was fulfilled when Zimri killed his son Elah and all his kin (1 Kings 16:1-13).
events.article:
Reign

909–886 BC

Israel

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Baasha

Walking in the way of Jeroboam after being exalted out of the dust to destroy Jeroboam’s house

Put to death

Nadab the son of Jeroboam reigned two years and did evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him and struck him down at Gibbethon, reigned in his place, and struck all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word the Lord spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite, because of the sins by which Jeroboam made Israel to sin (1 Kings 15:25-30). The study notes mark it as the fulfilment, years later, of the judgment on Jeroboam’s descendants. Then he reigned twenty-four years in Tirzah and did evil in the sight of the Lord, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin he made Israel commit (1 Kings 15:33-34). The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

He also made war on Judah. There was war between Asa and Baasha all their days, and Baasha came up and built Ramah to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah (1 Kings 15:16-17). The study notes on Chronicles give the reason: tribes out of Israel had been turning their hearts back to the Most High and joining Asa, and Baasha was trying to stop the northern kingdom from coming down to Judah (2 Chronicles 16:1). Asa, instead of crying to the Most High as he had against Zerah, hired Benhadad of Syria with the treasures of the Lord’s house to break his league with Baasha; Benhadad struck the cities of Israel, and Baasha left off building Ramah (2 Chronicles 16:2-6).

The word of the Lord came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha: the Lord had exalted him out of the dust and made him prince over His people Israel, and he had walked in the way of Jeroboam and made Israel sin, provoking Him with their sins. Therefore He would take away the posterity of Baasha and make his house like the house of Jeroboam; the dogs would eat those of his who died in the city, and the birds those who died in the field (1 Kings 16:1-4). The same judgment falls because the same sin is repeated, just as descendants keep the pattern of their fathers though they saw the ruin it brought. The word came against him both for all the evil he did in walking like Jeroboam and because he killed him (1 Kings 16:7). Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned (1 Kings 16:6).

Elah reigned two years. His servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, killed him while he was drunk in a steward’s house, and as soon as Zimri sat on the throne he killed all the house of Baasha, leaving not one male, nor his kinsfolk nor his friends, according to the word spoken by Jehu (1 Kings 16:8-12). It all came for the sins of Baasha and of Elah his son, who provoked the Lord God of Israel to anger with their vanities (1 Kings 16:13). Moses saw it in the spirit: Israel grew fat and kicked, forsook the God who made him, and provoked Him to jealousy with strange gods (Deuteronomy 32:15-21). A generation later the same sentence was pronounced on Ahab, that his house would be made like the house of Jeroboam and like the house of Baasha (1 Kings 21:22).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/baasha

events.title: Ahab
events.description: Ahab the son of Omri did evil above all the kings before him: he married Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, served Baal, and built him an altar and a house in Samaria (1 Kings 16:30-33). He blamed Elijah for the drought his own sin brought, spared Ben-hadad whom the Lord had appointed to destruction, and took Naboth’s vineyard after Jezebel had him murdered, selling himself to work wickedness (1 Kings 18:17-18; 1 Kings 20:31-42; 1 Kings 21:19-25). His humbling delayed the ruin of his house to his son’s days, but he died at Ramoth-gilead and the dogs licked his blood (1 Kings 21:27-29; 1 Kings 22:34-38).
events.article:
Reign

874–853 BC

Israel

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Ahab

Marrying Jezebel and serving Baal above all the kings before him; letting go Ben-hadad whom the Lord appointed to destruction; selling himself to work wickedness

Put to death

As if walking in the sins of Jeroboam were a light thing, he took Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians to wife, served and worshipped Baal, reared an altar for Baal in the house of Baal he built in Samaria, and made a grove, provoking the Lord more than all the kings of Israel before him (1 Kings 16:29-33). The study notes see Solomon in it, whose wives turned his heart after Ashtoreth of the Zidonians (1 Kings 11:4-5), against the law on marriage outside the people (Deuteronomy 7:3). History in the AM adds that Omri had made the alliance with the Zidonians of Tyre and Zidon by marrying his son to their daughter, so that Samaria became a little Zidon in Israel. The teachers call Ahab the weak, woman-led king: the Jezebel spirit cannot exist without a man who enables it, and Ahab let Jezebel reign through him, kill the prophets, and feed Baal’s prophets at her table.

When Elijah appeared after three years of drought, Ahab asked whether he was the one who troubled Israel. That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the ordained prophet of God for the trouble instead of his own wickedness. Elijah answered that Ahab and his father’s house had troubled Israel by forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). Into a malicious soul wisdom will not enter; sin comes in and wisdom goes out, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4-5).

When Ben-hadad besieged Samaria, the study notes call it Ahab’s judgment for trying to kill Elijah, serving Baal, and letting Jezebel run him. Yet a prophet told him the Lord would deliver that great multitude into his hand that he might know He is the Lord, and He did it twice, the second time because the Syrians said the Lord was a god of the hills and not of the valleys (1 Kings 20:13; 1 Kings 20:28). The Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, but he did not check Jezebel or destroy the idols. When Ben-hadad’s servants came in sackcloth with ropes on their heads, Ahab called him his brother, took him into his chariot, and sent him away with a covenant (1 Kings 20:31-34). Look at his wickedness: this Syrian had just tried to kill him. A prophet in disguise drew from Ahab his own sentence, that because he let go a man appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for that man’s life (1 Kings 20:39-42). Then he coveted Naboth’s vineyard and when Jezebel had Naboth stoned on false witness he rose up and went down to take it; he shares the guilt, for he let her commit the crime and went to claim the reward (1 Kings 21:1-16).

Elijah met him in the vineyard. Ahab called him his enemy, and Elijah answered that he had found him because he had sold himself to work evil in the sight of the Lord; the Lord would cut off every male of his house and make it like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, and dogs would lick his blood where they licked Naboth’s (1 Kings 21:19-24). There was none like Ahab, stirred up by Jezebel his wife (1 Kings 21:25). When he heard it he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted and walked humbly, and the Lord said He would not bring the evil in his days but in his son’s days (1 Kings 21:27-29). The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and moved to the next generation; genuine humbling before the Most High moves His hand.

Three years later he wanted Ramoth-gilead, and four hundred prophets told him with one mouth to go up. Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab admitted there was Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him (1 Kings 22:6-8). Micaiah saw Israel scattered on the hills as sheep with no shepherd, and a lying spirit put in the mouths of all Ahab’s prophets; the Most High used the lie to bring the judgment He had already declared (1 Kings 22:17-23). Ahab jailed Micaiah and went into battle in disguise (1 Kings 22:27-30). An arrow drawn at a venture struck him between the joints of his armour, he died at evening propped up in his chariot, and when they washed it in the pool of Samaria the dogs licked up his blood, according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:34-38). In Jehu’s day the rest came: seventy sons of Ahab beheaded and every one of his house cut off, that nothing of the word spoken by Elijah would fall to the ground (2 Kings 10:7-11).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/ahab

events.title: Jehoshaphat
events.description:
The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the first ways of David and did not seek Baal; he took away the high places and groves and in his third year sent princes, Levites and priests through all the cities of Judah with the book of the law to teach the people (2 Chronicles 17:3-9). The fear of the Lord fell on the kingdoms round about so that they made no war with him (2 Chronicles 17:10). When Moab, Ammon and mount Seir came against him he fasted and prayed, was told the battle was not his but God’s, sent singers before the army, and found the enemy dead (2 Chronicles 20:1-24).

Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord and taught the law through Judah, joined affinity with Ahab by marrying his son to Ahab’s daughter, and went up with him to Ramoth-gilead after the true prophet Micaiah had foretold defeat (2 Chronicles 18:1-16). Ahab disguised himself and sent Jehoshaphat into the battle in his royal robes, and only the Lord’s help saved him (2 Chronicles 18:29-31). Jehu the son of Hanani rebuked him for helping the ungodly, and when he later joined with Ahaziah to build ships, the Lord broke his works (2 Chronicles 19:1-3; 2 Chronicles 20:35-37).
events.article:
Reign

870–848 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Jehoshaphat

Walking in the first ways of his father David and seeking not unto Baalim; sending princes and Levites with the book of the law to teach in all the cities of Judah; and setting singers before the army

Kept the law

Jehoshaphat reigned in his father Asa’s place, strengthened himself against Israel, and set garrisons in the fenced cities, securing the land before trouble came (2 Chronicles 17:1-2). The Lord was with him because he walked in the first ways of David and sought the God of his fathers and His commandments, not the doings of Israel (2 Chronicles 17:3-4). David was a man after God’s own heart because he kept the commandments, and the way we must walk is set by the ordinances and laws we are taught (Exodus 18:20). His heart was lifted up in the ways of the Lord, not in pride but in devotion, and he took the high places and groves out of Judah, the false idols and their little churches (2 Chronicles 17:5-6).

In the third year of his reign he sent his princes, and with them Levites and priests, and they taught in Judah with the book of the law of the Lord, going through all the cities and teaching the people (2 Chronicles 17:7-9). What Christ did in sending out the twelve was not new, and what is done in the streets today is not new. In Jehoshaphat’s day our people were worshipping Molech, Chemosh and Baal, and the remedy was to tear down the groves and send teachers through the land with the book. Christ said to go into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in (Luke 14:23), and wisdom cries at the gates and the entry of the city, calling to men (Proverbs 8:1-4). He also went out himself from Beer-sheba to mount Ephraim bringing the people back to the Lord, and set judges city by city, telling them they judged not for man but for the Lord, with whom there is no iniquity, no respect of persons and no taking of gifts (2 Chronicles 19:4-7). These judges are soldiers with biblical education; it is easy to get caught up in popular persuasion even among our own people, and God says take heed and do what the book says.

When Moab, Ammon and those with them came against him, Jehoshaphat feared, set himself to seek the Lord, proclaimed a fast and stood in the congregation and prayed that they had no might against this great company and did not know what to do, but their eyes were on Him (2 Chronicles 20:1-12). Then the spirit of the Lord came on Jahaziel, a Levite, in the midst of the congregation. The spirit is not always there; the Lord watches how His people respond and then sends the right word. Jahaziel told them not to fear the great multitude, for the battle was not theirs but God’s; they would not need to fight, but should stand still and see the salvation of the Lord (2 Chronicles 20:14-17). Do not be scared of armies and people;

teach the word no matter what they threaten, for those with us are more than those with them (2 Kings 6:15-17). Jehoshaphat bowed with his face to the ground and all Judah worshipped, the Levites praised with a loud voice, and in the morning he told them to believe in the Lord and be established, believe His prophets and prosper, and set singers before the army to praise the beauty of holiness (2 Chronicles 20:18-21).

The fear of the Lord fell on all the kingdoms round about so that they made no war against him; Philistines brought presents and tribute silver and Arabians brought flocks, and he built castles and cities of store (2 Chronicles 17:10-12). Teaching the law had a real effect on the nations: wisdom is better than weapons of war (Ecclesiastes 9:18), and strengthens the wise more than ten mighty men in a city (Ecclesiastes 7:19). Cities of store are cities of provision, like Joseph’s storehouses; the diligent tend to plenty.

When they began to sing and praise, the Lord set ambushments against Ammon, Moab and mount Seir, and they turned on one another until every one was destroyed; when Judah came to the watchtower the multitude were dead bodies on the ground and none escaped (2 Chronicles 20:22-24). They spent three days gathering the spoil, blessed the Lord in the valley of Berachah, and returned to the house of the Lord with harps and trumpets; the fear of God was on all the kingdoms when they heard that the Lord fought against the enemies of Israel, and his realm was quiet (2 Chronicles 20:25-30). Some battles you have to let the Lord fight; your job on this earth is to fear God and keep His commandments. His affinity with the house of Ahab, and what it cost him, is the next case.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoshaphat

Jehoshaphat’s alliances

Joining affinity with Ahab and going up with him to Ramoth-gilead against the word of the prophet; joining himself with Ahaziah to make ships

Temporal judgment

Jehoshaphat had riches and honour in abundance, and joined affinity with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1): he married his son Jehoram to Ahab’s daughter, and through that marriage the daughter of Jezebel brought Baal worship into the southern kingdom, where even righteous kings after that could never fully purge it out. After some years he went down to Samaria, and Ahab killed sheep and oxen for him in abundance, good northern kingdom hospitality, and persuaded him to go up to Ramoth-gilead, a war Judah had nothing to do with. Jehoshaphat answered that he was as Ahab was and his people as Ahab’s people (2 Chronicles 18:2-3). You cannot join affinity with people just because they are your people; this was a war God had not sanctioned. Some men are friends for their own occasion and will not stay in the day of your trouble (Ecclesiasticus 6:7-8), and a friend cannot be known in prosperity (Ecclesiasticus 12:8).

He was making a bad decision in being with the wicked, yet the spirit was still on him: he asked to enquire of the Lord first, and when four hundred prophets said go up, he asked whether there was not a prophet of the Lord besides. Ahab said there was one, Micaiah, but he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him, which meant he told the truth (2 Chronicles 18:4-7). A rebellious people tell the seers to prophesy smooth things (Isaiah 30:9-11), and the time comes when men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:3-4). Micaiah told them he saw all Israel scattered on the mountains as sheep with no shepherd (2 Chronicles 18:16), and Jehoshaphat went up anyway.

At the point of no return Ahab told him that he would disguise himself, but Jehoshaphat should wear his robes. The king of Syria had ordered his captains to fight no one but the king of Israel, and Ahab knew it; he was setting Jehoshaphat up for the kill. The captains saw the robes, took him for the king of Israel and surrounded him, and if it had not been for the Lord he would have died in Ahab’s place (2 Chronicles 18:28-31). Beware of a counsellor who counsels for himself, who tells you your way is good and then stands on the other side to see what will happen to you (Ecclesiasticus 37:8). After Ahab was dead he did it again, joining himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly, to make ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:35-36).

The Lord helped him and moved the Syrians away from him (2 Chronicles 18:31), but his rescue was mercy, not approval. When he returned in peace, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and asked whether he should help the ungodly and love those who hate the Lord; therefore wrath was on him from before the Lord. Nevertheless good things were found in him, for he had taken away the groves and prepared his heart to seek God (2 Chronicles 19:1-3). We have to be careful not to bring wrath on ourselves or on the congregation; the Lord does not like that thing right there. Do not strive in a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10).

Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah prophesied that because he had joined himself with Ahaziah, the Lord had broken his works, and the ships were wrecked and never went to Tarshish (2 Chronicles 20:37). Good works are being done, and all praise for the leadership that labours before us; but the scripture says that if we join with those doing wickedness, the Lord will break our works. The marriage he made outlived him: Jehoram his son took the daughter of Ahab, walked in the way of the kings of Israel and killed all his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4-6), and Athaliah later destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:10). The judgment on his alliances was written in his ships and in his grandchildren.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoshaphats-alliances

events.title: Elijah
events.description: Elijah the Tishbite of Gilead stood before Ahab and declared, by the Lord God of Israel before whom he stood, that there would be no dew nor rain but by his word (1 Kings 17:1). The Lord fed him by ravens and by a widow of Zarephath, raised her son at his prayer, and at Carmel answered him by fire before all Israel and the prophets of Baal, then sent rain (1 Kings 17:2-24; 1 Kings 18:17-46). Fleeing Jezebel, he asked to die, but the Lord fed him, spoke to him at Horeb in a still small voice, told him seven thousand had not bowed to Baal, and gave him Elisha; he was taken up by a whirlwind (1 Kings 19:1-19; 2 Kings 2:11-13).
events.article:
Elijah

As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand: shutting the heaven by prayer, standing alone against eight hundred and fifty at Carmel, and running before the king in the hand of the Lord

Kept the law

The session on these chapters frames everything on the power of the Most High, set on display through His prophet. Elijah told Ahab there would be no dew nor rain those years but according to his word; he prayed, and it did not rain (1 Kings 17:1). The history the class reads calls him a man of tempestuous nature, guided by no consideration of expediency, who thundered against the weak, woman-led Ahab and was gone before anyone could seize him; he wore a leather girdle and a hairy cloak, unlike the effeminate dress of the worshippers of Baal, and he was known by it (2 Kings 1:8). The Lord sent him to hide by the brook Cherith, where the ravens brought him bread and flesh morning and evening, for He can command the animals to feed a man (1 Kings 17:2-6). When the brook dried up He sent him to a widow at Zarephath, whose meal and oil did not fail, and at his prayer her dead son revived (1 Kings 17:7-22). She said that now she knew he was a man of God and the word of the Lord in his mouth was truth (1 Kings 17:24): a man of God is known because the word in his mouth is the word of truth.

In the third year he showed himself to Ahab, and when Ahab called him the troubler of Israel, he answered that Ahab and his father’s

house were, for forsaking the commandments and following Baalim (1 Kings 18:17-18). At Carmel he asked the people how long they would halt between two opinions; if the Lord is God, follow Him. They answered not a word (1 Kings 18:21). It is a call for us to examine ourselves and not keep one foot in and one foot out, for the lukewarm are spewed out (Revelation 3:15-16). The prophets of Baal cried from morning until past noon, leaped on their altar and cut themselves till the blood gushed out, and Elijah mocked them; no one answered, because the Lord will not give His glory to another and the gods of the nations are idols (1 Kings 18:26-29; Isaiah 42:8; Psalms 96:5). He repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones for the twelve tribes, drenched the sacrifice three times until the trench was full, and at the evening sacrifice prayed that the people would know the Lord is God in Israel and that He had turned their heart back again (1 Kings 18:30-37).

The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones and the dust, and licked up the water. The people fell on their faces crying that the Lord, He is the God, and at Elijah’s word the prophets of Baal were taken down to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:38-40). The false shepherds of today stand under the same woe (Jeremiah 23:1-2). Then he prayed on the top of Carmel with his face between his knees until a cloud like a man’s hand rose from the sea, and there was a great rain; the hand of the Lord was on him and he ran before Ahab to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:41-46).

When Jezebel swore to take his life he fled, sat under a juniper tree, and asked to die, saying he was no better than his fathers (1 Kings 19:1-4). The notes say our forefathers had ultimate faith and understood regeneration, trusting the Most High to raise them when He chose. An angel fed him twice, and in the strength of that food he went forty days and nights to Horeb (1 Kings 19:5-8). The Lord passed by in wind, earthquake and fire, and was not in them, and then came a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11-12); we do not know who we are dealing with. He said he alone was left, and the Lord sent him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha in his place, and told him He had left Himself seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:14-18). Elijah was not by himself; the Lord had people reserved who had not yet awakened, and the classes say that is why we pray for more labourers and preach, for we never know which flyer or video will wake one. He cast his mantle on Elisha (1 Kings 19:19), founded a circle of disciples who kept the ancient law alive, and was taken up by a whirlwind while Elisha cried after him as his father (2 Kings 2:11-13). Christ said Elias had come already, and the disciples understood He spoke of John the Baptist (Matthew 17:11-13), who came in his spirit before the great day (Malachi 4:5).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/elijah

events.title: Athaliah
events.description: Athaliah of the house of Ahab counselled her son Ahaziah king of Judah in wickedness, and when Jehu killed him she destroyed all the royal seed of Judah to keep the power that had come to her through him (2 Chronicles 22:2-3; 2 Kings 11:1). Jehosheba hid the infant Joash in the house of the Lord six years; in the seventh, Jehoiada the priest crowned him under guard, and when Athaliah tore her clothes and cried treason, she was taken out and killed (2 Kings 11:2-16). Jehoiada renewed the covenant, and the people tore down the house of Baal (2 Kings 11:17-18).
events.article:
Reign

841–835 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Athaliah

Destroying all the seed royal of the house of Judah to reign herself; crying treason when the rightful king was crowned

Put to death

Ahaziah king of Judah was the son of Athaliah, of the house of Omri and Ahab, and he walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, because his mother counselled him in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:2-3; 2 Kings 8:18, 26). He went to his mother for counsel instead of to the priests and the judges; a woman with a grudge can rule a kingdom through her son. A mama’s boy is not ready to rule, and the Lord does not deal with men who follow behind a woman into sin. When Jehu killed Ahaziah and Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she rose and destroyed all the royal seed (2 Kings 11:1). A mother gave orders to kill anyone next in line, because her power came through her son and she meant to keep it; to stay in power, such women will destroy the men. She did not do it alone; she had weak men helping her run over everything. The teaching reads her as the Jezebel of Thyatira, with the children who follow her (Revelation 2:20-23).

But Jehosheba, daughter of king Joram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, took Joash the son of Ahaziah from among the king’s sons who were being murdered, and hid him and his nurse in a bedroom, and he stayed hidden with her in the house of the Lord six years while Athaliah reigned over the land (2 Kings 11:2-3; 2 Chronicles 22:11-12). The rightful king was kept hidden the whole time the usurper sat on the throne. Her sons, meanwhile, broke up the house of God and gave its dedicated things to the Baals (2 Chronicles 24:7).

In the seventh year Jehoiada brought the captains of hundreds and the guard into the house of the Lord, made a covenant with them, showed them the king’s son, and set armed men around him on every side with King David’s spears and shields, with orders to kill anyone who came within the ranks (2 Kings 11:4-11). That was order and strategy. He brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, gave him the testimony, and anointed him, and the people clapped and cried, God save the king (2 Kings 11:12). The saying comes from our forefathers, not from Europe: the priest had to establish a king against a wicked woman who had interfered with the rulership of men.

Athaliah heard the noise and came into the house of the Lord, saw the king standing by the pillar as the custom was, with the trumpeters and all the people rejoicing, and tore her clothes and cried, Treason, treason (2 Kings 11:13-14). She had just killed all the royal seed, and when the rightful king was anointed she screamed treason. When someone tries to restore order, that is how some look at it, as treason against them; they do not see that they are out of order. Jehoiada ordered her taken out between the ranks, and anyone who followed her killed with the sword, because she was not to be slain in the house of the Lord; they seized her, and at the horse entrance to the king’s house she was killed (2 Kings 11:15-16). Twice in the history, when wicked women rose up in power to devour, Jezebel and Athaliah, God sent men of the Lord to remove them for not listening to Him.

Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king and the people, that they should be the Lord’s people; the people tore down the house of Baal, smashed its altars and images, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars, and the city was quiet (2 Kings 11:17-20). This same covenant is what happens today: as a person repents, keeps the commandments and comes out of idolatry, they become the Lord’s people again. The weapons then were physical; today Israel’s weapon is the scriptures.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/athaliah

events.title: Elisha
events.description: Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and cast his mantle on him; Elisha killed his oxen, fed the people with them, and followed (1 Kings 19:19-21). He would not leave his master, asked for a double portion of his spirit, saw him taken up, and parted the Jordan with his mantle (2 Kings 2:1-15). The spirit of Elijah worked through him in healings, provision and deliverance; he refused Naaman’s gifts, and after his death a dead man who touched his bones revived (2 Kings 5:15-16; 2 Kings 13:20-21).
events.article:
Elisha

Leaving the oxen and following; asking a double portion of the spirit; and refusing Naaman’s reward, as the Lord liveth, before whom I stand

Kept the law

Elijah passed by Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and cast his mantle on him without a word. Elisha left the oxen, ran after him, and asked to kiss his father and mother first. Then he went back, killed a yoke of oxen, boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, gave it to the people, and went after Elijah and ministered to him (1 Kings 19:19-21). The Mantle class draws the lesson. The mantle was the prophets’ garment, and the spirit in Elisha told him this was a special calling. He had faith: husbandry was his living, yet he destroyed the oxen and the instruments and did not turn back. No man who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom (Luke 9:57-62). Twelve oxen under one goad are the twelve tribes, and guiding them takes the tunnel vision of a straight furrow, and the class asks where that faith is in brothers today who give up their post when home life pulls at them.

When the Lord was about to take Elijah up, at Gilgal, Bethel and Jericho Elijah told him to stay behind, and each time Elisha swore he would not leave him. The sons of the prophets, a prophetic order and not blood sons, told him his master would be taken, and he told them he knew it. Elijah struck the Jordan with his mantle and they crossed on dry ground, and when Elijah asked what he should do for him, Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit (2 Kings 2:1-10). He saw him go up in a whirlwind with a chariot and horses of fire, cried after him as his father, took up the mantle that fell from him, struck the waters, and they parted; the sons of the prophets said the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha and bowed before him (2 Kings 2:11-15). Walking in Elijah’s Footsteps, reading the history of the prophetic schools, says Elisha then placed himself at the head of Elijah’s disciples at Bethel, Gilgal and Jericho, lived at first on Mount Carmel, and later roused the man who destroyed the house of Omri and ended the worship of Baal.

The spirit that was on Elijah worked through him where the people were in need. He healed Jericho’s waters with salt (2 Kings 2:19-22). For a widow of the sons of the prophets whose sons were to be taken for her dead husband’s debt, the oil ran until every borrowed vessel was full, and she paid the debt and lived on the rest (2 Kings 4:1-7). The Shunammite who made him a chamber bore a son at his word, and when the child died, Elisha shut the door, prayed, and stretched himself on him until he sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kings 4:8-37). He took the death out of the pot at Gilgal and fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, with some left over, according to the word of the Lord (2 Kings 4:38-44).

When Naaman the Syrian was cleansed and came back confessing that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, Elisha swore by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive nothing, though Naaman urged him (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi ran after the gifts and went out a leper, for that was not the time to receive (2 Kings 5:20-27; Ecclesiastes 3:6). When Syria sent a host by night to Dothan for one prophet, he told his servant that those with them were more than those against them, and the Lord opened the young man’s eyes to a mountain full of horses and chariots of fire; the angel of the Lord encamps round those who fear Him (2 Kings 6:15-17; Psalms 34:7). He led the blinded Syrians into Samaria and had them fed and sent home, and their raids stopped (2 Kings 6:18-23).

On his deathbed King Joash wept over him as the chariot of Israel, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands for the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance from Syria; the king struck the ground only three times, and Elisha was angry, for he would now beat Syria only three times (2 Kings 13:14-19). Elisha died and was buried, and when a dead man was thrown into his sepulchre and touched his bones, he revived and stood on his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). History in the AM reads Sirach on him: filled with Elijah’s spirit, he was not moved by any prince, no one could bring him into subjection, and after his death his body prophesied (Ecclesiasticus 48:12-14).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/elisha

events.title: Ahaziah
events.description: Ahab’s son Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and sent to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover, and Elijah met the messengers with the Lord’s question: was there no God in Israel (2 Kings 1:2-3)? Two captains of fifty who ordered the prophet down were burned up by fire from heaven, and the third fell on his knees and begged for his life (2 Kings 1:9-14). Ahaziah died in his bed according to the word Elijah spoke (2 Kings 1:16-17).
