Israel

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Ahaziah of Israel

Sending to enquire of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron, as though there were not a God in Israel

Put to death

After Ahab died, Moab rebelled against Israel (2 Kings 1:1). The nations David had subdued and put under tribute began to break away, because Israel no longer walked in the blessing that came from serving the Most High (2 Samuel 8:2). If Israel listened diligently and did His commandments, the Lord would set them on high and strike down their enemies before them; if not, they would be struck down before their enemies and their bodies left to the birds, the same judgment spoken on the house of Ahab (Deuteronomy 28:1, 7, 15, 25-26).

Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper chamber and lay sick, and he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub the god of Ekron whether he would recover (2 Kings 1:2). Baal-zebub is the lord of the flies, and the teaching calls him plainly Satan, a god of the Hamites at Ekron. It frames the act as a choice, like Joshua’s call to choose whom they would serve (Joshua 24:15): Ahaziah thought God was not listening and went to another nation’s god, and he could not blame God for that. He should have known the history. When the ark of God was brought to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out that it had come to kill them, and the hand of God was heavy there; the god of Ekron could not even defend his own people (1 Samuel 5:10-11).

The angel of the Lord sent Elijah to meet the messengers and ask whether it was because there was no God in Israel that they were going to inquire of Baal-zebub; the Lord’s word was that the king would never rise from his bed; he would die (2 Kings 1:3-4). Elijah was quick to the point, and left. The messengers described a hairy man with a leather belt, a man in a garment of hair like the camel’s hair John the Baptist later wore, and the king knew it was Elijah (2 Kings 1:7-8; Mark 1:6). Then he sent a captain with his fifty men, who found Elijah on top of a hill and told the man of God that the king ordered him to come down (2 Kings 1:9).

Elijah answered that if he was a man of God, fire would come down from heaven and consume the captain and his fifty, and it did. The king sent another captain with fifty, who spoke the same way, and fire from heaven consumed them too (2 Kings 1:10-12). This is our history, not a Marvel movie: Elijah brought down fire three times, once on Carmel and then on the captains back to back (Ecclesiasticus 48:3). The Lord did not let His prophet’s words fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19). The third captain was a wise one. Having heard that a hundred men had been burned, he humbled himself quickly, went up, fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged that his life and the lives of his fifty be precious in the prophet’s sight (2 Kings 1:13-14). The angel of the Lord told Elijah to go down with him and not be afraid (2 Kings 1:15). The teaching draws the lesson: humble yourself and seek the prayers of the Lord’s leaders rather than scorning correction.

Elijah went to the king himself and delivered the same word: because he had sent to ask Baal-zebub as though Israel had no God to ask, he would never rise from that bed; he would die (2 Kings 1:16). He died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken, and since he had no son, Jehoram reigned in his place (2 Kings 1:17). The prophet brought kings to destruction and honored men from their beds (Ecclesiasticus 48:6). The same Ahaziah had joined with Jehoshaphat king of Judah to build ships, and because Jehoshaphat joined himself with a king who did very wickedly, the Lord broke the ships (2 Chronicles 20:35-37). If we join with the wicked, the Lord breaks our works.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/ahaziah-of-israel

events.title: Gehazi
events.description: When Elisha refused Naaman’s gifts, his servant Gehazi ran after the Syrian’s chariot, invented a message from his master asking silver and clothing for two young prophets, and hid the two talents and the garments in the house (2 Kings 5:20-24). He lied again to Elisha’s face, and Elisha told him his heart had gone with him; Naaman’s leprosy would cling to him and his descendants for ever, and he went out a leper white as snow (2 Kings 5:25-27).
events.article:
Gehazi

Running after Naaman to take what his master refused; lying to Naaman and then to the prophet’s face

Cursed

Elisha had refused Naaman’s gifts, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood (2 Kings 5:16). Gehazi, his servant, told himself his master had let this Syrian off too lightly, and swore by the Lord to run after him and get something from him (2 Kings 5:20). He had been Elisha’s understudy and seen all the miracles, and he was still looking at all that glitter. When Naaman saw him running he got down from his chariot and asked whether all was well. Gehazi said it was, and that his master had sent him to ask a talent of silver and two changes of clothing for two young men of the sons of the prophets just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim (2 Kings 5:21-22). Naaman told him to be content and take two talents, and pressed them on him; Gehazi should have woken up then (2 Kings 5:23). At the hill he took the bags from Naaman’s servants, hid them in the house like a thief, and sent the men away (2 Kings 5:24).

Then he went in and stood before his master, and when Elisha asked where he had been, he said he had gone nowhere (2 Kings 5:25). Covetousness makes a man lie, and Gehazi lied twice, adding sin to sin, because he would not control it. The study notes say it shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks, hasty to grasp things by unjust means. Elisha had asked Elijah for a double portion of his spirit, not for money and clothes. The real men of God do not do the Lord’s work for a reward; they trust Him to provide.

Elisha asked whether his heart had not gone with him when the man turned from his chariot to meet him (2 Kings 5:26). God sees it all; the spirit of the Lord reveals what is done in secret, so do not lie before righteous men, but come correct. He asked whether this was a time to take money and clothes, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, and servants (2 Kings 5:26). There is a season for everything, a time to get and a time to lose (Ecclesiastes 3:1, 6), and Elisha explained that there was a time to receive, and this was not it.

The leprosy of Naaman would cling to Gehazi and to his descendants for ever, and he went out from Elisha’s presence a leper, white as snow (2 Kings 5:27). The same sickness that had just left Naaman came on him. He was judged immediately. Many think they are fine because judgment is slow, but the money they love will destroy them. The work of one sinner cost his whole lineage: he destroyed not only himself

but his children. The teaching applies it to generational curses, telling the hearers to examine whether they are paying for the sins of their parents. The class on generational curses reads the leprosy white as snow as the whole skin with its pigment gone, which the law calls the clean leprosy when it covers the body from head to foot (Leviticus 13:12-13). It teaches that this is how Cain was cursed from the ground and how Esau was born, and that the look of white people is that curse. Because it was laid on his seed for ever, the class teaches that Gehazi’s descendants are here today and carry it. The remedy the law gives for a generational curse is to confess the iniquity of the fathers and accept its punishment, and then the Lord remembers His covenant (Leviticus 26:40-42).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/gehazi

events.title: Ahaziah
events.description: Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, reigned one year and walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:1-4). He went with Joram son of Ahab to war at Ramoth-gilead and then down to Jezreel to visit him, and so came into the path of Jehu, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:5-7). Jehu’s men killed him, and his mother then destroyed the seed royal (2 Chronicles 22:8-10).
events.article:
Reign

841–841 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Ahaziah of Judah

Walking in the ways of the house of Ahab, his mother being his counsellor to do wickedly; going down to Jezreel to see Joram

Put to death

The Arabians had killed all the elder sons, so the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king. He reigned one year, and his mother was Athaliah, called the daughter of Omri (2 Chronicles 22:1-2); scripture often calls a grandparent father, and the other translations make it plain that she was Omri’s granddaughter, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. As is the mother, so is her daughter (Ezekiel 16:44). Jezebel was a heathen, but her daughter was an Israelite with the same wicked spirit, the spirit that works through weak men.

He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly, and after his father died the house of Ahab were his counsellors, to his destruction (2 Chronicles 22:3-4). As Jezebel stirred up Ahab, Athaliah stirred up Ahaziah. This is a warning against being ruled by the wrong counsel: instead of going to the priests and the judges, as the law set for hard matters (Deuteronomy 17:9-11), he went to his mother, and a woman with a grudge ruled a kingdom through her son. He was the son-in-law of the house of Ahab (2 Kings 8:27), a picture of the curse passed from father to son.

He walked after their counsel and went with Joram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead; the Syrians wounded Joram, who went back to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah went down to see him (2 Chronicles 22:5-6; 2 Kings 8:28-29). His descent from Jehoshaphat did not make his own conduct righteous; he joined the cause of Ahab’s house at the hour its judgment was arriving.

The destruction of Ahaziah was of God, by his coming to Joram, for he went out with Joram against Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Chronicles 22:7). Joram asked Jehu whether it was peace, and Jehu answered, what peace, so long as the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel were so many? There is no peace as long as a wicked woman is in power. Joram turned and fled, crying treachery to Ahaziah, and Jehu drew his bow and shot him through the heart (2 Kings 9:22-24). Ahaziah fled by the garden house and was struck in his chariot at the going up to Gur, and died at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27).

Jehu also found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who served him, and killed them; they caught Ahaziah hiding in Samaria, brought him to Jehu and killed him, and buried him because he was the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord with all his heart. The house of Ahaziah had no power to keep the kingdom (2 Chronicles 22:8-9). The remembered faithfulness of his grandfather bought him a grave, not a deliverance, and the same hand the Most High anointed to avenge Israel on Ahab cut off the king of Judah who rode with Ahab’s son.

When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah (2 Chronicles 22:10), killing her own grandsons, or so she thought, because her power had come through her son and she meant to rule. Back then a woman was only empowered through the man. The counsellor to do wickedly finished the ruin she had counselled, and only one child, hidden in the house of God, was left of the house of David.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/ahaziah-of-judah

events.title: Jehoahaz
events.description: Jehu’s son Jehoahaz reigned seventeen years in Samaria and kept Jeroboam’s sins, and the Lord gave Israel into the hand of Hazael and his son Ben-hadad all his days (2 Kings 13:1-3). He pleaded with the Lord, and the Lord heard him, because He saw how Syria oppressed Israel, and gave Israel a saviour; but the people still did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, and the king was left with fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers (2 Kings 13:4-7). The teaching reads the saviour as coming after his death, in the reigns of his son and grandson (2 Kings 13:22-25; 2 Kings 14:25-27).
events.article:
Reign

814–798 BC

Israel

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Jehoahaz of Israel

Doing evil in the sight of the Lord and following the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, departing not therefrom; beseeching the Lord under the oppression of Syria, and not departing from the sins of the house of Jeroboam when the saviour came

Temporal judgment

In the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years; the teaching dates it about 814 to 798 BC (2 Kings 13:1). He did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin (2 Kings 13:2). His father had cut off Baal but kept the calves (2 Kings 10:28-31), and the son walked in them. The Lord’s anger burned against Israel, and He gave them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and Ben-hadad his son all their days (2 Kings 13:3). When we sin, the Lord brings an adversary, other nations, to correct us.

Jehoahaz pleaded with the Lord, and the Lord listened to him, because He saw the oppression of Israel (2 Kings 13:4). Even though he was wicked, the Lord hears the prayer of the oppressed (Ecclesiasticus 35:13). Yet they did not depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam but walked in them, and the grove also stood in Samaria (2 Kings 13:6). The prayer was heard; the idolatry stayed.

Syria left Jehoahaz no army but fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers, for the king of Syria had destroyed them and made them like the dust of threshing (2 Kings 13:7). Fifty horsemen is what remains after a people takes a major loss: the curse of the law, to go out against the enemy one way and flee seven (Deuteronomy 28:25). Threshing here means thrashing. Hazael oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 13:22).

The saviour is written ahead of time. What is read there is not what was happening in his reign but what was going to happen: the Lord heard him in his lifetime and answered in the days of his son and his grandson, as the commentators the teacher reads explain it, when Jehoash took back the cities and Jeroboam the second restored Israel’s border (2 Kings 13:5, 24-25; 2 Kings 14:25-27). He gave them saviours when they cried to Him in their trouble, as the Levites later confessed (Nehemiah 9:27). The Lord put a plan of salvation in place; He did not send a Clark Kent.

The mercy is named with its reason: the Lord was gracious to them and had compassion and regard for them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and would not destroy them or cast them from His presence as yet (2 Kings 13:23). God has a chosen people and has regard for His chosen (Wisdom of Solomon 4:15), but He is no respecter of persons in judging them. The words as yet carry the rest of the story, for the northern kingdom was later cast off (2 Kings 17:18). Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, was buried in Samaria, and Joash his son reigned in his place (2 Kings 13:8-9).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoahaz-of-israel

events.title: Jonah
events.description:
The word of the Lord sent Jonah the son of Amittai to cry against Nineveh, and he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord (Jonah 1:1-3). The storm found him asleep in the ship; he confessed he was the cause and was cast into the sea, and the Lord prepared a great fish in which he lay three days and three nights, praying, until he was put out on dry land (Jonah 1:4-17; Jonah 2:1-10). Sent the second time he went and cried against the city, and when the Lord spared it he was angry; the Lord reproved him with the gourd, and Christ made his three days the sign given to His generation (Jonah 3:1-4; Jonah 4:1-11; Matthew 12:39-40).

Jonah was sent to cry against Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, because its wickedness had come up before the Lord; after fleeing and being brought back from the belly of the fish, he went in and cried that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 1:1-2; Jonah 3:1-4). The people believed God and fasted in sackcloth, and the king decreed that every one turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands (Jonah 3:5-9). God saw their works and did not bring the evil He had spoken, and when Jonah was angry He answered that He would spare that great city (Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:1-11).
events.article:
Jonah

Rising up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the Lord instead of going to Nineveh to cry against it

Reprieve

Jonah the son of Amittai prophesied in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, who restored Israel’s border by his word (2 Kings 14:25). The word came to him to go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for its wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Christians read Ninevites and think Assyrians, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were the captives of the ten tribes led into Nineveh, as Tobit of Naphtali shows, who was carried there and heard Jonah and took heed (Tobit 1:1-3; Tobit 14:8); the study note on Acts 1 likewise says Jonah preached to Nineveh, where the northern kingdom was exiled. Our people in Nineveh were observing lying vanities, one class says, as they keep Christmas and a white Jesus today (Jonah 2:8).

Jonah said no, as the teacher puts it: he rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, went down to Joppa, found a ship, paid the fare and went aboard (Jonah 1:3). The study note on Genesis 10 places Tarshish in Spain, first among the merchants of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:12); one history teaching reads from a book that Jonah looked to it as a safe haven where Hebrew traders had been since Solomon’s time, and another says most place it at Sicily. Two classes say he fled because he was afraid of the people of Nineveh; he himself later says he fled because he knew the Lord was gracious and merciful and would relent (Jonah 4:2), and the teaching adds that he feared being taken for a false prophet. Both can stand; like Adam, one class says, he tried to hide.

The Lord sent a great wind and the ship was near breaking; the mariners cried each to his own god, and Jonah lay fast asleep in the sides of the ship (Jonah 1:4-5). The study note calls him the picture of the slack spirit, asleep while the ship breaks, and America the spiritual ship going down with our people asleep in it. The lot fell on Jonah, and he confessed he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord, the God of heaven who made the sea and the dry land (Jonah 1:7-10).

He told them to throw him into the sea, for the storm was on his account (Jonah 1:11-12). That is accountability and integrity, the teaching says, owning that you are the cause, the opposite of Achan, whose hidden sin troubled the camp (Joshua 7:1). They rowed hard, prayed not to be charged with innocent blood, and cast him in, and the sea ceased her raging (Jonah 1:13-16). The Lord had prepared a great fish and Jonah was in its belly three days and three nights (Jonah 1:17). He cried to the Lord out of the belly of hell, which the teaching explains is the grave; cast out of His sight, he would look again toward the holy temple and pay what he had vowed (Jonah 2:1-9). The man who fled the Lord now sought Him, as in their affliction they will seek Him early (Hosea 5:15); in the fish, one class says, he repented of his fear and his doubt, and the teaching reads his rising from the pit as pointing to Christ, whose soul would not be left in the grave (Psalm 16:10).

The word came the second time, and he went and cried what he was given, that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown (Jonah 3:1-4). When the Lord spared the city he was very angry and asked to die (Jonah 4:1-3). Jonah had an attitude problem, one class says, self-willed, mad that God did not destroy the people, like James and John wanting fire from heaven (Luke 9:54-55). With the gourd, the worm and the east wind the Lord showed him that he pitied a plant he had not laboured for, and asked whether He should not spare Nineveh (Jonah 4:4-11). Your spirit is not right, the teacher says; we do not preach for our own glory, and His thoughts are not our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8). The Lord held off because His people were there, the Luke 11 teaching says, but the word still stood and the city was destroyed (Tobit 14:4).

Christ gave that generation no sign but the sign of Jonas: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the fish, the Son of man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, and one greater than Jonah was there (Matthew 12:39-41). Three days and three nights, the teaching says, rules out Good Friday to Sunday. Jonah is actually about us, one class says: the God who heard him in the fish does not change (Malachi 3:6), so pray.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jonah

Nineveh under Jonah

Wickedness come up before the Lord; and turning every one from his evil way, and from the violence that was in their hands

Reprieve

Jonah the son of Amittai prophesied in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, whose restoring of Israel’s coast from the entering of Hamath was according to the word the Lord spoke by him (2 Kings 14:23-25). He was in the same time frame as Hosea and Amos, and the prophets were all seeing the same thing: the disorder in Israel, and the Lord always sending His prophets to correct His people. The word came to him to arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it, for their wickedness had come up before the Lord (Jonah 1:1-2). Nineveh was the seat of the kings of Assyria; Sennacherib went home to dwell there after the angel struck his camp (2 Kings 19:36). But the Ninevites to whom Jonah was a sign were not the Assyrians, the teaching says (Luke 11:29-30). They were the captives of the ten tribes led into Nineveh: Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali of the northern kingdom, was carried away in the time of Enemessar king of the Assyrians and came to Nineveh with his brethren and his nation (Tobit 1:1-3).

Jonah fled toward Tarshish, and when the storm came he was asleep in the ship. When the lot fell on him he confessed he was a Hebrew who feared the Lord, and told them to cast him into the sea; that is accountability and integrity, standing up when you know you are the cause of the trouble, the opposite of Achan hiding the accursed thing (Jonah 1:3-12; Joshua 7:1). In the fish’s belly he sought the Lord, as Hosea says they will seek Him early in their affliction (Jonah 2:1-9; Hosea 5:15), and Christ made those three days and nights the sign of His own burial (Matthew 12:39-40).

The word came the second time to preach the preaching the Lord gave him, and a true prophet speaks the words of the Lord, not his own (Jonah 3:1-2; 1 Peter 4:11). Nineveh was a city of three days’ journey; he went a day’s journey in and cried that in forty days it would be overthrown (Jonah 3:3-4). The king’s decree named what had to change: the evil way and the violence in their hands (Jonah 3:8). The prophets of that day named the same sins in Israel, swearing, lying, killing, stealing and adultery until blood touched blood, and selling the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of shoes (Hosea 4:1-2; Amos 2:6-8).

The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth from the greatest to the least. The king rose from his throne, laid aside his robe, sat in ashes, and decreed that neither man nor beast taste anything or drink water, but cry mightily to God and turn from their evil way and their violence (Jonah 3:5-8). That is what a true fast is: not holding back one food, but no food and no water. They did not presume on God: who could tell whether He would turn from His fierce anger (Jonah 3:9)? Judith warned the elders of Bethulia the same way not to bind the counsels of the Lord to their own time (Judith 8:12-16). God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way, and He repented of the evil He had said He would do and did not do it (Jonah 3:10).

It displeased Jonah, and he said this was why he had fled, for he knew the Lord was gracious, merciful, slow to anger and of great kindness (Jonah 4:1-2). He had gone in on fire, and now he felt he would look like a false prophet, and twice he asked to die. The Lord answered with the gourd: Jonah had pity on a plant he did not labour for, and should not the Lord spare Nineveh, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand who could not discern their right hand from their left, and much cattle (Jonah 4:3-11)? His thoughts are not our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8-9). We preach so that God gets the glory, not ourselves; as He turned from punishing when the fathers provoked Him, He can turn to do well (Zechariah 8:14-17).

The reprieve was not the end of the word against Nineveh. Tobit, a captive of Naphtali in Nineveh, told his son to leave the city, because what the prophet Jonah spoke would surely come to pass: the captives had heard Jonah and taken heed, and the Lord held off because His people were there, but the word still stood, and before Tobit died he heard of the city’s destruction and rejoiced over it (Tobit 14:4, 8, 15). The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment and condemn the generation that heard a greater than Jonah and did not repent (Matthew 12:41).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/nineveh-repents

events.title: Amaziah
events.description: Amaziah did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart; he punished his father’s murderers but spared their children as the law commands, and at the word of a man of God sent home the hundred thousand men he had hired out of Ephraim (2 Chronicles 25:1-10). After the Lord gave him victory over Edom he brought home the gods of Seir and worshipped them, and threatened the prophet sent to rebuke him (2 Chronicles 25:11-16). He then provoked Joash of Israel, was defeated and captured, saw Jerusalem’s wall broken and the temple plundered, and was later killed by conspirators at Lachish (2 Chronicles 25:17-27).
events.article:
Reign

796–781 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Amaziah

Bringing home the gods of the children of Seir, setting them up to be his gods, and bowing down before them; threatening the prophet sent to him; provoking Israel to his hurt

Put to death

Amaziah was twenty-five when he began to reign, and he did right in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart (2 Chronicles 25:1-2). Kings says he did right, yet not like David his father, but according to all his father Joash did (2 Kings 14:3), and Joash did right only while Jehoiada instructed him. David praised the Lord with his whole heart (Psalm 111:1), while Solomon’s heart was not perfect with the Lord (1 Kings 11:4). Do not come to the Lord with a double heart (Ecclesiasticus 1:28): when circumstances change, a double heart changes on the Lord.

When the kingdom was established he took vengeance on the servants who had killed his father, but did not kill their children, as written in the law of Moses that every man dies for his own sin (2 Chronicles 25:3-4; Deuteronomy 24:16). That is a foundational law: a man answers for his own sin. He mustered three hundred thousand of Judah and Benjamin and hired a hundred thousand mighty men out of Israel for a hundred talents of silver, like mercenaries. A man of God told him not to take them, for the Lord was not with Israel, with all the children of Ephraim; if he went with them, God would make him fall. When he asked about the hundred talents, the man of God answered that the Lord could give him much more than that, and he sent them home (2 Chronicles 25:5-10). Moses had warned Israel the same way not to go up when the Lord was not among them (Numbers 14:41-43). The hired men went home in great anger and fell on the cities of Judah while he was at war, and a brother offended is harder to win than a strong city (2 Chronicles 25:13; Proverbs 18:19).

He went to the valley of salt and struck ten thousand of the children of Seir, and cast another ten thousand from the top of the rock (2 Chronicles 25:11-12). Then he brought home the gods of the children of Seir, set them up to be his gods, bowed down to them and burned incense to them (2 Chronicles 25:14). It makes no sense: the Lord gave him the victory,

and he took the gods of the people who had just lost while praying to them. The law said to consume those nations and not serve their gods, for that would be a snare (Deuteronomy 7:16). In mercy the Lord sent a prophet to ask why he sought gods that could not deliver their own people out of his hand, and the king asked whether he had been made the king’s counsellor and told him to stop before he was struck. The prophet stopped, and said he knew God had determined to destroy him because he had done this and would not listen to counsel (2 Chronicles 25:15-16). Pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18), and there is more hope for a fool than for a man wise in his own conceit (Proverbs 26:12).

Someone boosted his head, and he sent to Joash king of Israel to meet him face to face. Joash answered with the parable of the thistle in Lebanon that asked the cedar for his daughter and was trampled by a wild beast: he had struck Edom and his heart was lifted up; why stir up trouble to his own harm? Amaziah would not listen, for it came of God, to deliver them into the hand of their enemies because they had sought the gods of Edom (2 Chronicles 25:17-20). Judah was routed at Beth-shemesh, Amaziah was captured, four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem were broken down, and the gold, silver and vessels of the house of God and the king’s treasures were carried to Samaria with hostages (2 Chronicles 25:21-24). The spoil taken from Edom was snatched away, brother stripping his own brother’s temple.

He lived fifteen years after Joash, and from the time he turned away from following the Lord they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; he fled to Lachish, and they sent after him and killed him there (2 Chronicles 25:25-27). Like father, like son: he did right for a time without a whole heart, went off, and his own people conspired against him as they had against his father. Power is given by the Lord, who will search out the counsels of kings who do not walk after the counsel of God, and a sharp judgment comes to those in high places (Wisdom of Solomon 6:1-5). When a man departs from the Most High, the protection departs with him.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/amaziah

events.title: Uzziah
events.description: Uzziah was made king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years; as long as he sought God in the days of Zechariah, God made him prosper, against the Philistines, Arabians and Mehunims, in towers, wells, husbandry and a great army with engines of war (2 Chronicles 26:1-15). When he was strong his heart was lifted up, and he went into the temple to burn incense, which belonged only to the priests (2 Chronicles 26:16). When Azariah and eighty priests withstood him he raged with the censer in his hand, and leprosy broke out on his forehead; he lived as a leper, cut off from the house of the Lord, until he died (2 Chronicles 26:17-21).
events.article:
Reign

781–740 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Uzziah

Going into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense, which appertaineth not unto the king but to the priests the sons of Aaron; and raging at the priests who withstood him

Temporal judgment

All the people of Judah made Uzziah king at sixteen in place of Amaziah, and he did right and sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God; as long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper (2 Chronicles 26:1-5). This Zechariah was a different man from the priest Joash killed. Uzziah is like Joash, who did well while he had the guidance of Jehoiada. All the wise kings consulted with spiritual men; David consulted with every leader (1 Chronicles 13:1), and by wise counsel you make your war (Proverbs 24:5-6). Prosperity comes from the Most High, and it lasts only as long as a man keeps seeking Him.

He broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod and built cities among the Philistines, God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabians and the Mehunims, the Ammonites paid gifts, and his name spread to the entrance of Egypt (2 Chronicles 26:6-8). Jehoram had lost Edom and Elath; Uzziah restored Elath to Judah (2 Chronicles 26:2). He built towers, dug wells for his cattle and loved husbandry, a picture of the blessings of Deuteronomy 28 as the Lord made the land fruitful. His army numbered three hundred and seven thousand five hundred, with shields, spears, helmets and slings, and engines invented by cunning men to shoot arrows and great stones; his fame spread far, for the Lord helped him wonderfully until he became strong (2 Chronicles 26:9-15). Together with Jeroboam II in the north, the two kingdoms held borders close to those of David and Solomon; the Lord was giving His people another chance before He began to unleash judgments.

But when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense (2 Chronicles 26:16). He got big-headed, a Judahite acting like a Levite. The king was to write a copy of the law and read it all the days of his life, so that his heart would not be lifted up above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18-20); the greater you are, the more you should humble yourself (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). Only the seed of Aaron could offer incense, lest a man end like Korah (Numbers 16:40), and the stranger who came near the priest’s office was to die (Numbers 18:7). Azariah the priest and eighty valiant priests withstood him and told him it did not belong to him, to leave the sanctuary, for he had trespassed and it would not be for his honour. Then Uzziah was angry, with a censer in his hand (2 Chronicles 26:17-19). He had beaten nations and would not be corrected by men he counted lower than himself, and he was ready to set fire to the priests of God.

While he was angry with the priests, the leprosy rose up in his forehead before them beside the incense altar. The priests saw it and thrust him out, and he hurried out himself, because the Lord had struck him (2 Chronicles 26:19-20). He that is soon angry deals foolishly (Proverbs 14:17); one act out of a quick temper cost him a lifetime. The fear of the Lord goes before the obtaining of authority, but roughness and pride is the losing of it, and the Lord brings strange calamities on the proud (Ecclesiasticus 10:13, 21).

He was a leper to the day of his death and lived in a separate house, cut off from the house of the Lord, and Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people (2 Chronicles 26:21). The law said the leper must dwell alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46); he was still king in name but could no longer sit on the throne, and leprosy is not merely white skin but a slow deterioration of the whole body. The Lord puts down the mighty from their seats (Luke 1:52). Isaiah wrote the rest of his acts, and they buried him in the field of burial belonging to the kings, not in their sepulchres, because they said he was a leper (2 Chronicles 26:22-23). Stay in the spirit, stay humble, and never forget who put you in the position you are in. In the year king Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/uzziah

events.title: Jotham
events.description: Jotham, son of Uzziah, reigned sixteen years and did right as his father had done, but he did not go into the temple as his father had; the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, cities, castles and towers, and put the Ammonites under tribute (2 Chronicles 27:3-5). He became mighty because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6).
events.article:
Reign

740–736 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Jotham

Preparing his ways before the Lord his God; doing according to all that his father Uzziah did, howbeit he entered not into the temple of the Lord

Kept the law

Jotham judged the people from the king’s house while his father lived as a leper in a separate house, so the last years counted to Uzziah were really his son’s (2 Chronicles 26:21). He was twenty-five when he began to reign in his own right and reigned sixteen years; he did right according to all his father Uzziah did, except that he did not enter the temple of the Lord (2 Chronicles 27:1-2). He was like his father, industrious and a builder, but he did not make his father’s mistake of going in to burn incense as though he were a Levitical priest.

Yet the people still did corruptly (2 Chronicles 27:2). The high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there (2 Kings 15:35); since Solomon brought in the gods of his wives, the land was never the same. Micah began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, and this is the corruption he describes: they built up Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, the heads judged for reward, the priests taught for hire, the prophets divined for money, and still they leaned on the Lord and said no evil could come on them; therefore Zion would be ploughed as a field (Micah 1:1; Micah 3:10-12). A righteous king in Jerusalem did not mean the whole realm was clean, any more than the lower parts of the capital are clean today.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord and much on the wall of Ophel, and cities in the mountains of Judah, and castles and towers in the forests (2 Chronicles 27:3-4). He cut down the forests and made towns; we always built castles, that is Judah. He fought the king of the Ammonites and prevailed, and they paid him a hundred talents of silver and ten thousand measures each of wheat and barley that year and the next two, putting the heathen under tribute as his father had done (2 Chronicles 27:5).

So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God (2 Chronicles 27:6). That is what Ezra did when he prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, to do it, and to teach it in Israel (Ezra 7:10), and it is the opposite of Rehoboam, who did evil because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14). That is why he had favour during his reign. The Most High was with our forefathers when they followed the commandments.

In those days the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah (2 Kings 15:37). Syria had been the northern kingdom’s oppressor, and now the two were joining against Judah; it began under Jotham and came to its height under his son. Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, not in the field where his leper father lay, and Ahaz his son reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 27:7-9). A good reign does not pass to the next by blood, and the son who followed him would burn his children in the fire.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jotham

events.title: Isaiah
events.description: In the year king Uzziah died Isaiah saw the Lord on His throne, confessed himself a man of unclean lips, was cleansed by a coal from the altar, and answered the call to go (Isaiah 6:1-8). He was sent to a people who would hear and not understand, until the land was desolate; he walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia; and when Assyria blasphemed he told Hezekiah not to fear, and the word came to pass exactly (Isaiah 6:9-12; Isaiah 20:2-4; Isaiah 37:5-7, 36-38).
events.article:
Isaiah

Here am I; send me: a prophet unto a people whose heart was made fat, who walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign, and stood beside the king when Assyria blasphemed

Kept the law

Isaiah the son of Amoz prophesied concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), in the same period as Hosea and Micah, which is why so much of what is read in one is found in the others. In the year Uzziah died he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and His train, His garment, so long that it filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims, high ranking angels that cover the throne as the cherubims covered the mercy seat, each with six wings, crying to one another that the Lord of hosts is holy and the whole earth full of His glory (Isaiah 6:1-4). The King he saw, the Lord of hosts, is Christ.

Isaiah cried that he was undone, a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips, the Israelites (Isaiah 6:5). When men see the Most High or the day of the Most High, terror comes on them. A seraphim took a live coal from the altar with the tongs and laid it on his mouth, and his iniquity was taken away. Then the Lord asked whom He should send, and Isaiah offered himself (Isaiah 6:6-8). Nowhere in that scripture does it say he was sent to be liked. That is not the job and not the mission: he was sent to wake up the people, to tell them how evil they are, to repent and come back to Messiah.

His message was hard. The people would hear and not understand, see and not perceive; their heart was made fat and their ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed (Isaiah 6:9-10). Christ spoke in parables for the same reason, fulfilling this prophecy, because it is not meant for everybody to get the understanding (Matthew 13:13-14). When he asked how long, the answer was until the cities were wasted and the land desolate, and the Lord had removed men far away, yet a tenth would return, and the holy seed would be its substance (Isaiah 6:11-13).

In the year Tartan took Ashdod for Sargon, the Lord told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and take off his shoes, and he walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign that Assyria would lead Egypt and Ethiopia away captive, young and old, uncovered to their shame (Isaiah 20:1-4). An 1844 history by a coloured man, R. B. Lewis, reads it as a sign that went further: as the prophet was naked, so the people were led away barefoot into captivity, and their descendants from Africa are led away by a wicked people into slavery even to this day.

When Rabshakeh blasphemed, Hezekiah sent to Isaiah for prayer, and Isaiah answered that he should not fear, for the king of Assyria would hear a rumour, return home and fall by the sword in his own land (Isaiah 37:1-7). The Lord would defend Jerusalem for His own sake and for David’s sake; not an arrow would be shot into it; and the angel of the Lord struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in one night, and Sennacherib was killed by his own sons in the house of his god (Isaiah 37:33-38). Every word Isaiah spoke stood. Ben Sira says the Holy One delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah, who was great and faithful in his vision; in his days the sun went backward, and by an excellent spirit he saw what would come to pass at the last and comforted those who mourned in Sion (Ecclesiasticus 48:20-24).

The answer Here am I is also a prophecy that Isaiah would return. Long after he was dead, the Lord said by Esdras that for the help of Jerusalem He would send His servants Isaiah and Jeremiah (2 Esdras 2:17-18), and He named the prophets He would give as leaders to the people coming from the east (2 Esdras 1:37-40). John too was told he must prophesy again before many peoples and nations (Revelation 10:11). We do not know who is who, but those prophets are back in these last days, grown up in a grimy state and now coming to the fulfilment of their spirit, and no amount of money spent against this awakening can stop what the Most High Himself is doing.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/isaiah

events.title: Ahaz
events.description: Ahaz son of Jotham walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, made molten images for Baalim and burned his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom (2 Chronicles 28:1-4). The Lord gave him into the hands of Syria and of Pekah, and instead of believing Isaiah he sent the Lord’s treasure to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, who distressed him and did not help him (2 Chronicles 28:5-21). In his distress he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, cut up the vessels of God’s house, shut its doors and set up altars on every corner of Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 28:22-25).
events.article:
Reign

736–716 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Ahaz

Molten images for Baalim; burning his children in the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom; hiring Assyria with the treasure of the Lord’s house; sacrificing to the gods of Damascus that smote him; cutting the vessels in pieces and shutting up the doors of the house of the Lord

Temporal judgment

Ahaz was twenty when he began to reign and did not do right like David his father, but walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and made molten images for Baalim (2 Chronicles 28:1-2). His grandfather and father had Judah making progress, and he came on the scene and set them five steps back. He burned incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom and burned his children in the fire, after the abominations of the heathen the Lord had cast out (2 Chronicles 28:3). Hinnom was a place of burning south of Jerusalem, where Tophet stood and children were sacrificed to Molech; its Greek name, Gehenna, became the word for hell. The Lord said He never commanded it, nor did it come into His heart (Jeremiah 7:31). The Canaanites were driven out for their witchcraft, wicked sacrifices and merciless murders of children (Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-6), and Ahaz did the very thing that got them evicted. Baal was worshipped as the sun and storm god who gave power, crops and children, with ritual prostitution and the sacrifice of the firstborn; wealth and power for a sacrifice, and it sounds familiar today.

When Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah came against Jerusalem they could not overcome him, as Isaiah said, for within sixty-five years Ephraim would be broken; but if Ahaz would not believe, he would not be established (2 Kings 16:5; Isaiah 7:7-9). He did not believe the Lord; he believed the king of Assyria. He sent to Tiglath-pileser saying he was his servant and his son, and asked him to save him (2 Kings 16:7). That is the mind of the Negro today, wanting the one who enslaved him to save him. Isaiah pronounced woe on the rebellious children who seek counsel and protection anywhere but from the Lord and His spirit, adding sin to sin (Isaiah 30:1). He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and sent it as a present (2 Kings 16:8). At Damascus he saw a heathen altar that captivated him and had Urijah the priest build one on its pattern to replace the altar the Lord had designed (2 Kings 16:10-16).

In the time of his distress he trespassed yet more: he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had struck him, reasoning that since the gods of the kings of Syria helped them, they would help him; but they were the ruin of him and of all Israel (2 Chronicles 28:22-23). Why not serve your own God? He cut the vessels of the house of God in pieces, shut up the doors of the house of the Lord, made altars in every corner of Jerusalem and high places in every city of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:24-25).

The Lord delivered him to the king of Syria, who carried a great multitude captive to Damascus, and to the king of Israel: Pekah killed a hundred and twenty thousand valiant men of Judah in one day because they had forsaken the Lord, and Israel carried away two hundred thousand of their brethren, women and children, to Samaria (2 Chronicles 28:5-8). It was brother against brother. The prophet Oded met the army and told them they had slain their brethren in a rage that reached to heaven and now meant to make them bondmen, with sins of their own; the heads of Ephraim agreed, and they clothed, fed and anointed the captives, carried the feeble on asses and brought them to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). A brother sold for poverty was not to serve as a bondservant (Leviticus 25:39-41); even in the division these men feared the Most High.

The Edomites struck Judah and the Philistines took the cities of the low country, for the Lord brought Judah low because of Ahaz, who made Judah naked (2 Chronicles 28:17-19). Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and killed Rezin, as Amos had foretold (2 Kings 16:9; Amos 1:3-5), but he came to Ahaz and distressed him and did not strengthen him, though Ahaz stripped the house of the Lord, the king’s house and the princes to pay him (2 Chronicles 28:20-21). Never trust your enemy. Running to another nation with the Lord’s treasure bought only distress, and Isaiah warned that the Assyrian would overflow Judah up to the neck (Isaiah 8:6-8). This history shows why we went into captivity: despite every warning of the prophets we begged the Most High to send us there. Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but not in the sepulchres of the kings, and Hezekiah his son reigned (2 Chronicles 28:27).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/ahaz

events.title: Hezekiah
events.description:
Hezekiah trusted in the Lord God of Israel so that no king of Judah before or after him was like him; he broke down the high places and the bronze serpent the people burned incense to, and kept the commandments given to Moses (2 Kings 18:3-7). In his first month he reopened and cleansed the house of the Lord, and he called all Israel and Judah to a second-month Passover whose joy had not been seen since Solomon (2 Chronicles 29:3-5; 2 Chronicles 30:1, 26). The teaching calls him a king of God’s mercy: the Lord heard him for the people, for the city, and on his sickbed (2 Chronicles 30:20; 2 Kings 20:5).

Healed of a mortal sickness, given fifteen years, and shown the shadow going back ten degrees, Hezekiah did not repay the benefit done to him, for his heart grew proud (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). When the king of Babylon sent letters and a present, Hezekiah showed his envoys everything in his treasuries and armoury, and Isaiah declared that all of it would be carried to Babylon and some of his sons made eunuchs in the palace there (2 Kings 20:12-18). Hezekiah humbled himself, and the wrath did not come in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26).
events.article:
Reign

716–687 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Hezekiah

Trusting in the Lord God of Israel, so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah; cleaving to him and keeping his commandments; breaking the brasen serpent; opening the doors of the house of the Lord and keeping the passover

Kept the law

Hezekiah son of Ahaz began to reign in the third year of Hoshea, Israel’s last king, and did right in the sight of the Lord, as David had (2 Kings 18:1-3). Unlike his father, who multiplied idols even in the holy place, Hezekiah, whose name the teaching gives as the strength of God, refused to serve the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:7). He removed the high places, broke the images, cut down the groves, and smashed Moses’ bronze serpent, to which the people burned incense, calling it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). The Lord was with him and he prospered (2 Kings 18:5-7). Prospering here is not a mansion or luxury; it is the blessing that comes from keeping the covenant and doing it (Deuteronomy 29:9). Of all the kings, only David, Hezekiah and Josiah were not found defective (Ecclesiasticus 49:4).

In the first month of his first year he opened the doors of the house of the Lord, repaired them, and told the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves and carry the filth out of the holy place (2 Chronicles 29:3-5). He named the sin plainly: their fathers had shut the doors, put out the lamps and stopped the offerings of an everlasting statute, so wrath had come on Judah and Jerusalem, and they could see it (2 Chronicles 29:6-9; Leviticus 24:2-8). The confession came before the offerings, a broken spirit before sacrifice (Psalm 51:16-17), and he set his heart on a covenant with the Lord because Judah was about to go the way of the northern kingdom (2 Chronicles 29:10).

The cleansing ran past the Passover, so he sent letters through all Israel and Judah, Ephraim and Manasseh too, to keep it at Jerusalem in the second month, as the law allows for the unclean and those far off (2 Chronicles 29:17; 2 Chronicles 30:1-5; Numbers 9:10-11). Tiglath-pileser had carried off most of the north, and the letters called the remnant that escaped Assyria to turn back; it was their last chance, some six years before Samaria fell (2 Chronicles 30:6-9). The runners went from city to city and were laughed to scorn, the same mockery Israel meets today when the truth is preached; yet some of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came (2 Chronicles 30:10-11).

Many who came had not cleansed themselves and ate the Passover otherwise than written, and Hezekiah prayed that the good Lord would pardon everyone who set his heart to seek Him; the Lord listened and healed the people (2 Chronicles 30:18-20). Grace and mercy were already there. They kept the feast seven days with gladness and chose seven more, and there had been no joy like it in Jerusalem since Solomon (2 Chronicles 30:21-26). In every work he began he sought his God with all his heart, and prospered (2 Chronicles 31:21); no one can halfway walk in the truth and expect to grow.

The teaching calls him a king of God’s mercy. The Lord had said He would no longer have mercy on the house of Israel but would have mercy on Judah and save them without bow or sword (Hosea 1:6-7), and the king who trusts in the Lord will not be moved (Psalm 21:7). Hoshea was moved; Hezekiah was not. When the nation was threatened, he went to the house of the Lord and to the man of God, and Isaiah brought word that God had heard; the deliverance from Assyria is entered as its own case (2 Kings 19:1-7, 14-20). He made a pool and a conduit and brought water into the city, which the study notes call vision and planning like no other: nation building (2 Kings 20:20). The class reads the same works through Isaiah: when Sennacherib came they stopped the fountains, gathered the lower pool and broke down houses for the wall, but did not look to their Maker; they did everything but return to the Lord (2 Chronicles 32:2-4; Isaiah 22:9-11).

Sick to death and told to set his house in order, that is, settle his inheritance, he did not trust the physicians as Asa had (2 Chronicles 16:12). He turned his face to the wall and prayed and wept, and the Lord heard his prayer, saw his tears, and added fifteen years (2 Kings 20:1-6). A lump of figs was laid on the boil, for remedies go together with prayer, but it was the Lord’s word that healed him (2 Kings 20:7; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). For a sign the shadow went back ten steps on the dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:8-11): the Lord, who can turn back time itself, showed that everything is subject to the Most High. After such mercy he did not repay the benefit done to him (2 Chronicles 32:25), a failing entered under the envoys of Babylon.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/hezekiah

Hezekiah and the ambassadors of Babylon

Rendering not again according to the benefit done unto him, for his heart was lifted up; shewing all his treasures to the men of Babylon

Reprieve

Hezekiah was sick to death, and Isaiah told him to set his house in order. He turned to the wall and wept, and asked the Lord to remember how he had walked before Him in truth, and before Isaiah had left the middle court the word came back: fifteen years added, and the city defended for David’s sake (2 Kings 20:1-6). A lump of figs was laid on the boil, for remedies go together with prayer, though it is the word of the Lord that heals (2 Kings 20:7; Wisdom of Solomon 16:12). For a sign the shadow went back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz, reversing the course of the sun (2 Kings 20:8-11). Sickness humbles the mightiest man; in his writing afterward Hezekiah said the grave cannot praise the Lord, but the living will, and the father will make the truth known to the children (Isaiah 38:9-19).

Yet he did not repay the kindness shown him, for his heart swelled with pride, and wrath came on him and on Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:24-25). When things go well, do not get puffed up and make it about yourself. Berodach-baladan king of Babylon, then only a province under Assyria, sent letters and a present because he had heard Hezekiah had been sick. Hezekiah was glad of them and showed them the whole house of his precious things, the silver, the gold, the spices, the ointment and all his armour; nothing in his house or dominion was held back (2 Kings 20:12-13; Isaiah 39:1-2). A flattering letter and a gift, and he gave the heathen a tour of everything, not knowing they were scouting what they meant to take. A gift destroys the heart (Ecclesiastes 7:7).

This was a trial. In the business of the ambassadors who came to enquire of the wonder done in the land, God left him, to try him and know all that was in his heart (2 Chronicles 32:31). The Lord does the same with us: you have been doing well, and then a strange scenario is before you, and you have to stop and ask whether the Lord is trying you right now, and not get carried away in the moment. He tried Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the same way (Judith 8:25-27).

Isaiah asked what the men had said and what they had seen, and Hezekiah answered that they had seen everything. Then came the word: the days would come when all in his house, and all his fathers had stored up, would be carried to Babylon with nothing left, and some of his own descendants would be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (2 Kings 20:14-18; Isaiah 39:3-7). It is like a family that left you houses, and you show a stranger all the deeds; everything you showed them you are going to lose. It was fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar carried out the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house (2 Kings 24:13), and when Daniel and his companions, of the king’s seed and the princes, were taken to stand in the palace of Babylon under the master of the eunuchs (Daniel 1:3-6). Some are made eunuchs by men (Matthew 19:12). Each time we were conquered we were made to take on another tongue and customs not our own.

Hezekiah called the word of the Lord good and took comfort that there would be peace and truth in his own days (2 Kings 20:19). He did not argue or justify himself. He humbled himself for the pride of his heart, he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the wrath of the Lord did not come on them in his days (2 Chronicles 32:26). That is how to take correction: when your elders show you that what you did was foolish, say you are right and fix it. The humbling held the judgment back for his lifetime, but the prophecy still came to pass. He slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place (2 Kings 20:21).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/hezekiahs-pride

events.title: Sennacherib
events.description: After Assyria carried the northern kingdom away, Sennacherib came against the fenced cities of Judah, and his captain Rabshakeh stood at the conduit of the upper pool and shouted in the Jews’ language that Hezekiah could not make them trust in the Lord, since no god of the nations had delivered his land from Assyria (2 Kings 18:13-35). Hezekiah spread the blasphemous letter before the Lord, and the answer came through Isaiah that Sennacherib had reproached the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:14-22). That night one angel killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib was later killed by his own sons in the house of his god (2 Kings 19:35-37).
events.article:
Sennacherib and Rabshakeh

Reproaching the living God; setting the Holy One of Israel among the gods of the nations that could not save

Put to death

Assyria was a rising empire. It had carried the northern kingdom away in stages, and in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them (2 Kings 18:9-13). Judah seems to have joined a revolt against the tribute; Hezekiah admitted he had offended and, to pay it, cut the gold off the doors of the temple (2 Kings 18:14-16). Tribute did not satisfy the king of Assyria. He wanted the land, and sent Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh with a great host to Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17).

Rabshakeh asked what confidence Hezekiah was trusting in. He called Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of the man who leans on it, and then turned Hezekiah’s own reform against him: was this not the God whose high places and altars Hezekiah had taken away, and whose house he had just stripped to pay Assyria? He even claimed the Lord had sent him to destroy the land (2 Kings 18:19-25). Asked to speak in the Syrian language, he stood and cried in the Jews’ language so the people on the wall would hear: Hezekiah could not deliver them and should not make them trust in the Lord; make an agreement, eat from your own vine, until I come and take you to a land like your own (2 Kings 18:26-32). It is the same thing they try with us now: the enemy threatens your food and water, because once that is cut off most people will turn their backs on God.

He asked whether any of the gods of the nations had delivered his land, where the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Sepharvaim were, and whether they had saved Samaria (2 Kings 18:33-35), and his letter set the living God among the idols Assyria had burned (2 Kings 19:9-13). This is the puffed-up spirit the Lord allows the heathen to reach just before He destroys them, when their rulers say there is none other but us (Ecclesiasticus 36:10). Assyria was only the rod of His anger (Isaiah 10:5). The people held their peace and did not answer him a word, for the king had commanded it (2 Kings 18:36). Let him talk; that is why we do not do interviews with these people.

Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, went into the house of the Lord and sent to Isaiah, calling it a day of trouble, rebuke and blasphemy. Isaiah answered that he should not fear the words of the Assyrian servants; the Lord would send a blast on the king, he would hear a rumour, return to his own land, and fall by the sword there (2 Kings 19:1-7). While Rabshakeh was running his mouth, the Lord had already set an ambush on another front (2 Kings 19:8-9). Hezekiah spread the letter before the Lord and prayed that He would save them, so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know He alone is God (2 Kings 19:14-19). That is a righteous prayer, praying for the downfall of the enemy and for righteous judgment.

The answer came back through Isaiah: the virgin daughter of Zion laughed him to scorn, for he had lifted his eyes against the Holy One of Israel (2 Kings 19:20-22). The Lord had formed Assyria’s conquests long before; now He would put His hook in Sennacherib’s nose and His bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came (2 Kings 19:25-28). He would not shoot an arrow into the city, for the Lord would defend it for His own sake and for His servant David’s sake (2 Kings 19:32-34). That is why we honour our forefathers: God had a relationship with them before us.

That night the angel of the Lord struck a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and in the morning they were all dead (2 Kings 19:35). This was a celestial being, part of the army from heaven, and Judah did not lift a sword, for it is not by might nor by power but by His spirit (Zechariah 4:6). Ben Sira records that Sennacherib lifted his hand against Zion and boasted proudly, and the Holy One heard His people out of heaven and delivered them by the ministry of Isaiah (Ecclesiasticus 48:17-21). Sennacherib went home to Nineveh and took out his rage on the northern kingdom captives there, whom Tobit buried in secret, and within fifty-five days his own sons killed him as he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god (2 Kings 19:36-37; Tobit 1:18-21). The man who said no god could save Jerusalem could not be saved in the house of his own god. God sends strange punishments to the proud, even from inside their own house.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/sennacherib-and-rabshakeh
