events.title: Nahum
events.description: Nahum’s burden of Nineveh declares the Lord jealous and avenging, slow to anger but never clearing the guilty, and names the wicked counsellor who came out of Nineveh imagining evil against Him (Nahum 1:1-3; Nahum 1:11). The lions’ den that had emptied Jacob would be flooded, spoiled and left empty, and the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, would have no healing for its wound (Nahum 2:2-13; Nahum 3:1; Nahum 3:19). The teachers read it as the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC and, in several classes, as the sentence on Mystery Babylon, America.
events.article:
Nineveh under Nahum

A bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose prey departeth not; the dwelling of the lions that filled his holes with prey; the wicked counsellor that imagineth evil against the Lord

Put to death

The burden opens with who the Lord is: jealous, avenging, taking vengeance on His adversaries and reserving wrath for His enemies (Nahum 1:2). God reserves wrath for America, for China, for Europe, the class says, for what they did to our people. He is slow to anger and great in power and will not at all acquit the wicked (Nahum 1:3); somebody tell the white man, one teacher says. His way is in the whirlwind and the storm, and one teaching sees Him in today’s hurricanes and earthquakes; the mountains quake before Him, and none can stand before His indignation (Nahum 1:3-6).

Nineveh had been spared once. The Lord held off because His people were there, the Luke 11 teaching says, and the Empires class says Jonah stayed the destruction but Nineveh did not change the people there, which was us, and eventually Nineveh fell. Tobit, a captive of Naphtali there, saw the bodies of Israelites thrown out about the walls of Nineveh (Tobit 1:17-18); the Assyrians did much wickedness to our people, the teacher says. The emptiers had emptied Jacob and marred his branches (Nahum 2:2). Nineveh was the den of the lions, where the lion tore enough for his whelps and filled his holes with prey (Nahum 2:11-12). Out of her came one who imagined evil against the Lord, a wicked counsellor (Nahum 1:11); one class says that is America, another a system of people (Daniel 7:8).

Woe to the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose prey never departs (Nahum 3:1). Woe to the bloody city, this is America, one class says, and the heaps of carcasses are our forefathers. Another says the bloody city robbed our lands, our identity, our culture, even our minds, and we are the prey that is still here; the study note on Exodus 14 reads the prey that does not depart as the people in captivity who will not leave. She was the well-favoured harlot, mistress of witchcrafts, who sold nations through her whoredoms (Nahum 3:4), which one class reads as the harlot Mystery Babylon (Revelation 17:5).

The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and knows those who trust Him (Nahum 1:7): trouble is coming, the class says, and the Lord is good in the day of trouble if you keep the law, and we will have to depend on each other. With an overrunning flood He would make an utter end of the place, and affliction would not rise a second time (Nahum 1:8-9); one teacher sets it with Babylon, which shall not rise again (Jeremiah 51:64). He would break the yoke from off Judah and burst the bonds (Nahum 1:13): God will break the yoke of the white man and the nations off of us, the class says. No more of Nineveh’s name would be sown, her images would be cut off, and He would make her grave (Nahum 1:14), which one teaching reads of Esau (Isaiah 14:20). To Judah it was good tidings on the mountains: keep your solemn feasts (Nahum 1:15).

The one who dashes in pieces came up; the chariots raged in the streets, the gates of the rivers were opened and the palace dissolved, and though they cried stand, stand, none looked back; she was empty, void and waste (Nahum 2:1-10). The Lord of hosts was against her (Nahum 2:13; Nahum 3:5). Her shepherds would slumber and her bruise would have no healing, and all who heard of her fall would clap their hands, for her wickedness had passed on everyone continually (Nahum 3:18-19).

The history teachings give the fall: Babylon and the Medes teamed up to take down the Assyrian, Cyaxares the Mede with Nabopolassar, in 612 BC after about three months of siege; the Median army stormed the city and left ruined hills and heaps of debris, and by 600 BC Assyria was gone. Tobit had told his son to leave Nineveh, because what Jonas the prophet spoke would surely come to pass, and before he died he heard of its destruction and rejoiced (Tobit 14:4; Tobit 14:8; Tobit 14:15). The Disturbing Truth class reads Nahum 1 as not about ancient Assyria but about Babylon and her allies, and the other classes read the bloody city as Mystery Babylon: Nineveh and America are one and the same, one teacher says.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/nineveh-destroyed

events.title: Amon
events.description: Amon began to reign at twenty-two, reigned two years, and brought back all the idols his father Manasseh had served, without the humbling his father came to at the end (2 Kings 21:19-22; 2 Chronicles 33:21-23). He trespassed more and more, and his own servants conspired against him and killed him in his house; the people of the land killed the conspirators and made his son Josiah king (2 Kings 21:23-24).
events.article:
Amon

Sacrificing to all the carved images his father had made; humbling not himself as his father had humbled himself, but trespassing more and more

Put to death

Every time a king tried to remove the idolatry, Israel found its way back to folly; the Lord speaks peace to His people, but they are not to turn again to folly (Psalm 85:8). Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, and at most the last few were spent trying to put things right. Amon was twenty-two when he took the throne, so most of his life had been spent under his father’s worst years, watching the rituals and the orgies of Baal worship. That was what he was raised in, and as soon as his father died he brought it all back as if Manasseh had never tried to undo it. He did evil as his father had done, walked in all his ways, served the idols his father served, and forsook the Lord God of his fathers (2 Kings 21:19-22).

Chronicles sets him beside his father on purpose: he sacrificed to all the carved images Manasseh had made, and did not humble himself as his father had, but trespassed more and more (2 Chronicles 33:22-23). Ezekiel describes exactly this: a just man who has a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, who eats on the mountains and lifts his eyes to idols. It does not matter that the father repented; that son will surely die, and his blood is on himself (Ezekiel 18:10-13). The idols Amon served are named in Josiah’s cleansing: vessels made for Baal, for the grove and for all the host of heaven, idolatrous priests burning incense to the sun, moon and planets, and houses of the sodomites by the house of the Lord (2 Kings 23:4-7). Baal worship came with sexual rites, and it is thriving today under the name of Christianity and liberty, down to the daily horoscope beside the scripture. The worship of idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil, and with it come blood, theft, adultery and men slaying one another treacherously (Wisdom of Solomon 14:23-27). Because sentence against an evil work is not carried out speedily, men’s hearts are set to do evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11), and his sins abounded to his own destruction.

The servants of Amon, the people he kept close, conspired against him and killed the king in his own house (2 Kings 21:23). That was the fruit of his own work: the idolatry he enforced brought with it the spirit of slaying one another treacherously, and it came back on him. The traitors did not escape either; the people of the land killed all who had conspired against the king and made Josiah his son king in his place (2 Kings 21:24). Treason was not tolerated.

The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time He sets over it one that is profitable (Ecclesiasticus 10:4). Wicked rulership lasts only so long. The throne passed to a boy of eight who, while he was still young, began to seek the God of David his father (2 Chronicles 34:1-3). Ben Sira says that all the kings of Judah were defective, for they forsook the law, except David, Hezekiah and Josiah (Ecclesiasticus 49:4). Grandfather, father and son stood in a row: the one who went past the Amorites and then humbled himself, the one who saw it and trespassed more and more, and the one who turned to the Lord with all his heart.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/amon

events.title: Josiah
events.description:
Josiah began to reign at eight, sought the God of David while still young, and in his eighteenth year, while the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found (2 Chronicles 34:1-3; 2 Kings 22:8). When it was read to him he tore his clothes, and Huldah answered that the curses written in it would come, but because his heart was tender he would go to his grave in peace (2 Kings 22:11-20). He read the book to all the people, made a covenant, cleansed the land from the temple to Samaria, and kept a passover like none since the judges (2 Kings 23:1-25).

Some years after his great passover, Josiah went out against Necho king of Egypt, who was marching to Carchemish on the Euphrates to fight the Babylonians and told him plainly that his quarrel was not with Judah and that God was with him (2 Chronicles 35:20-21). Josiah would not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God, disguised himself, and was shot by the archers in the valley of Megiddo; he died in Jerusalem and all Judah mourned him (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). He got involved in a matter that did not concern him and lost his life in it.
events.article:
Reign

640–609 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Josiah

A tender heart at the reading of the book; rending his clothes; turning to the Lord with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses

Kept the law

Manasseh began to reign at twelve, Amon at twenty-two and Josiah at eight, and the youngest was the wisest; better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished (Ecclesiastes 4:13). He did what was right and turned neither to the right hand nor to the left, the charge given to Joshua (2 Kings 22:1-2; Joshua 1:7). In his eighth year he began to seek the God of David, and in his twelfth to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, groves and images (2 Chronicles 34:3-7). Jeremiah, a Levite and a priest’s son of Anathoth, was called in his thirteenth year, and Zephaniah prophesied in his days against the remnant of Baal (Jeremiah 1:1-2; Zephaniah 1:1-4).

In his eighteenth year he sent Shaphan to have the silver given to the carpenters and masons repairing the house, and he made sure the workmen were paid, for the workman is worthy of his hire (2 Kings 22:3-7). Hilkiah the high priest found the book of the law in the house of the Lord (2 Kings 22:8). Manasseh and Amon had been so wicked the very book was lost. When Shaphan read it, the king tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). The king was meant to read the law all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19), and the wicked kings had not. Josiah had been seeking the Lord for years and still had not heard the curses; what shook him was the wrath written for a people that will not listen (Deuteronomy 28:15). The same is true on the street today: people in Bible study their whole life know the Exodus, but never heard that the slave ships and the iron yoke are in the Bible.

He sent to enquire of the Lord, for great was the wrath kindled because the fathers had not kept the book (2 Kings 22:13). To enquire of the Lord you go to one who has the word. They went to Huldah the prophetess, who lived in Jerusalem in the college, the school where the sons of the prophets were trained in the scriptures, as the brothers go to the school on the Sabbath now. She answered that all the curses in the book would come on the place, as Micah had said Zion would be ploughed as a field for the sake of its heads, priests and prophets (2 Chronicles 34:22-25; Micah 3:9-12). But because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil (2 Kings 22:18-20).

He gathered all the people, small and great, read in their ears the whole book of the covenant, stood by a pillar and made a covenant to keep the commandments with all their heart and soul, and all the people stood to it (2 Kings 23:1-3). Our forefathers had the Bible, and the king read it openly. Then he cleaned house: the vessels of Baal and the host of heaven burned at the Kidron, the idolatrous priests put down, the grove burned to powder, the houses of the sodomites by the temple broken down, Topheth defiled so no child could be passed through the fire to Molech, the horses given to the sun taken away, and Solomon’s high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom defiled (2 Kings 23:4-14). He burned bones on Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel as the man of God had foretold by name (2 Kings 23:15-16; 1 Kings 13:2). The priests of the high places in Samaria he killed on their own altars (2 Kings 23:19-20). It was a bloody path to redemption: the king who will set no wicked thing before his eyes destroys early all the wicked of the land (Psalm 101:3-8). This is repentance in action, cleaning house of every idol that brings a people under punishment.

He commanded the passover as written in the book, and none like it had been kept since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-22); reading the law brought the nation back to the appointed feasts in order, as the feast is kept in order today. No king before or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul and might (2 Kings 23:25). His memory is like perfume and like honey in every mouth; he behaved uprightly in the conversion of the people, and in a time of the ungodly he established the worship of God. All the kings except David, Hezekiah and Josiah were defective, for they forsook the law (Ecclesiasticus 49:1-4). Yet the Lord did not turn from His wrath over Manasseh’s provocations (2 Kings 23:26-27); the promise to Josiah was that the evil would not come in his days.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/josiah

Josiah at Megiddo

Going out against Necho king of Egypt who had no quarrel with him; hearkening not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God; disguising himself to fight

Put to death

Josiah’s passover was right on time, on the fourteenth day of the first month as Moses instituted it (2 Chronicles 35:1), and it was greater than any since the days of Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:18); his works were upright, with a heart full of godliness (1 Esdras 1:23). It shows what order and unity in righteousness can restore, even after all we had done and suffered. The same history shows the other lesson: you can know all the precepts and be righteous and still get high minded, and you have to mind your God-given business.

The power of Assyria was slipping, and Babylon and Egypt were contending for what it had held. Nineveh had fallen to the Babylonians and Medes, and Pharaoh Necho led his army north to help what was left of Assyria at Carchemish, passing through Josiah’s kingdom on the way (2 Kings 23:29). Josiah went out against him (2 Chronicles 35:20). Necho sent ambassadors asking what he had to do with the king of Judah: he had not come against him but against the house he was at war with, for God had commanded him to make haste, and Josiah should stop meddling with God, who was with him, lest God destroy him (2 Chronicles 35:21). The Lord is not restricted in whom He speaks through; He spoke through a donkey and through Balaam, and He had spoken to Pharaoh. That did not mean He wanted Egypt to stop Babylon, for He had already foretold in Hezekiah’s day that Babylon would take Judah (Isaiah 39:5-7). Pharaoh was telling his Israelite brother to fall back, because this had nothing to do with him.

In Josiah’s eyes he was standing up to possible Egyptian oppression. Nevertheless he would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself to fight, and did not listen to the words of Necho from the mouth of God (2 Chronicles 35:22). Esdras says he did not regard the words of the prophet Jeremiah spoken by the mouth of the Lord (1 Esdras 1:28). Ben Sira warns not to strive in a matter that does not concern you, for if you meddle much you will not escape (Ecclesiasticus 11:9-10), and the one who meddles with strife not belonging to him is like a man who takes a dog by the ears (Proverbs 26:17). Grab a pit bull by the ears and you are going to get torn up.

He went into the battle in disguise, yet the archers shot at king Josiah himself. Pharaoh had warned that God would destroy him if he meddled, and among all the soldiers the Lord put it on the archers to find the king. He told his servants to take him away, for he was badly wounded; they moved him to his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in the sepulchres of his fathers (2 Chronicles 35:23-24). Megiddo is the place of troops, the place the Lord will gather all nations again in the last days. After Megiddo the Egyptians and Assyrians were destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish, Assyria ceased to be, and Babylon rose to take Judah as the prophets had said; the Bible is real history.

All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah; Jeremiah, who began to prophesy in the same years as Josiah’s reform, lamented for him, and the singing men and women spoke of him in their lamentations and made it an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:24-25). The promise through Huldah that he would be gathered to his grave in peace concerned the evil coming on Jerusalem, which he did not live to see (2 Kings 22:20). He meddled in a matter that did not belong to him, but he never went after another god, and he left a very good example. Virtue leaves a memorial that is immortal: when it is present men take example from it, and when it is gone they desire it (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1-2). Like David, whose righteous legacy stands over his transgressions, Josiah’s is praised among the famous men whose bodies are buried in peace and whose name lives for evermore (Ecclesiasticus 44:1-15). His death opened Judah’s last years: the people made Jehoahaz king, and within three months Pharaoh had him in bands (2 Chronicles 36:1-4).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/josiah-at-megiddo

events.title: Jeremiah
events.description: Jeremiah, of the priests in Anathoth, was known and ordained a prophet to the nations before he was formed in the belly, and he prophesied from the days of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1:1-5). Told not to plead his youth or fear their faces, he spoke against kings, princes, priests and people through the stocks, the burned roll and the miry dungeon (Jeremiah 20:1-2; Jeremiah 36:23; Jeremiah 38:6). The Lord made him a fortified city against the whole land: they fought against him and did not prevail, and when the city fell the enemy set him free (Jeremiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 40:1-6).
events.article:
Jeremiah

Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; be not afraid of their faces: speaking all that was commanded, though the word was a burning fire shut up in his bones and his own familiars watched for his halting

Kept the law

Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, of the priests in Anathoth, a Levite city in Benjamin, and the word came to him from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the carrying away of Jerusalem in the eleventh year of Zedekiah (Jeremiah 1:1-3; Joshua 21:17-18). The verse-by-verse teaching places his ministry at about 627 to 586 BC and calls him one of the mightiest prophets in the scriptures; he worked hand in hand with Josiah’s reform and lamented Josiah when he fell (2 Chronicles 35:25).

Before the Lord formed him in the belly He knew him, set him apart and ordained him a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:4-5). The teaching reads this with Paul, separated from his mother’s womb (Galatians 1:15), and the study note says the same thing is happening today: the brothers and sisters waking up were known from the beginning and are raised up to prophesy against the nations. Jeremiah answered that he could not speak, for he was a child, about eighteen by the teacher’s reckoning; the Lord told him not to say it, but to go where he was sent and speak what he was commanded, without fear of their faces (Jeremiah 1:6-8). The class puts it plainly: stop making excuses; he tried to run from it and the Lord did not let him. The Lord touched his mouth, put His words there, and set him over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant (Jeremiah 1:9-10). That is why we stay within these scriptures and never go wrong, the note says, and it is our job today, spiritual warfare. He was to gird himself and speak all he was commanded and not be dismayed, lest he be confounded before them; we cannot go out with a spirit of fear on us (Jeremiah 1:17; 2 Timothy 1:7).

The opposition came from his own. When he stood in the court of the Lord’s house and said the house would become like Shiloh, the priests, the prophets and the people seized him and said he must die; he answered that he was in their hand, but they would bring innocent blood on themselves (Jeremiah 26:8-16). Urijah, who prophesied the same words, was hunted down and slain by Jehoiakim, while the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:20-24). Pashur the priest struck him and put him in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:1-2). Mocked daily, he resolved to speak no more in the Lord’s name, but the word burned inside him like fire trapped in his bones and he could not hold it in (Jeremiah 20:7-9).

One class reads those verses as his thoughts in the stocks, encouraging himself; the fire is inescapable, not surface level. His familiar friends watched for him to stumble (Jeremiah 20:10): the people who watched you grow up, waiting for you to revert so they can plaster it over social media. Jehoiakim cut the roll and burned it, and the words were written again with more besides (Jeremiah 36:23-32). The princes let him down into the dungeon of Malchiah and he sank in the mire (Jeremiah 38:6); the class says that mire is dung, and it is not far fetched.

The promise of his ordination was kept: they fought against him and did not prevail (Jeremiah 1:19). He had the respect of a prophet and the contempt of a prophet, the teacher says; his own king, princes and priests gave him trouble for forty years and could not stop him, and he never lost his love for his people. Ebed-melech drew him out of the mire, and he stayed in the court of the prison until the day Jerusalem was taken (Jeremiah 38:7-13; Jeremiah 38:28). Nebuchadnezzar gave charge to look after him and do him no harm (Jeremiah 39:11-12); the teaching calls this the Lord’s mercy and grace, the enemies showing him favour, as the Lord had promised to make the enemy treat him well (Jeremiah 15:11; Proverbs 16:7).

Nebuzaradan, a heathen, told him the city fell because the people sinned and did not obey the voice of the Lord; the nations always knew why we went into captivity (Jeremiah 40:1-3; Judith 5:17-18). He had been bound in chains among the captives at Ramah, but he was loosed and given his choice, and he went to Gedaliah at Mizpah and dwelt among the people left in the land (Jeremiah 40:4-6). The verse-by-verse teaching stresses that Jeremiah was never a captive in Babylon. One class goes further, reading the word that he himself would lose his heritage and serve his enemies in a land he did not know as spoken to Jeremiah for the last days: that land, the class says, is called America today (Jeremiah 17:4).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jeremiah

events.title: Jehoiakim
events.description: Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son Eliakim, was set on the throne by Pharaoh-nechoh and taxed the land to pay him; he did evil, built his house with unpaid labour, slew Urijah the prophet, and cut and burned the roll of Jeremiah’s words (2 Kings 23:34-37; Jeremiah 22:13-17; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Jeremiah 36:23). He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and rebelled, and the Lord pronounced that none of his would sit on David’s throne and that he would have the burial of an ass (2 Kings 24:1; Jeremiah 22:18-19; Jeremiah 36:30).
events.article:
Reign

609–598 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Jehoiakim

Building his house by unrighteousness and his chambers by wrong, using his neighbour’s service without wages; eyes and heart set on covetousness, innocent blood, oppression and violence; slaying Urijah the prophet; cutting the roll of the Lord’s words with a penknife and burning it

Cursed

Pharaoh-nechoh bound Jehoahaz at Riblah and made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in his place, turning his name to Jehoiakim; Jehoiakim taxed the land to give Pharaoh the silver and gold he demanded, and did evil as his fathers had done, not as his father Josiah (2 Kings 23:31-37). The class calls him a puppet, Pharaoh’s vassal king, the way America goes into other countries and sets up puppet rulers; he paid his taxes to Pharaoh, the teacher says, but he taxed us to do it. The renaming, the Daniel 1 teaching notes, is a practice among all the nations when we are taken over: they give us a new name. The Three Waves teaching dates his reign from about 608 BC.

Jeremiah pronounced woe on the king who built his house by unrighteousness and his upper rooms by wrong, who used his neighbour’s labour without pay, and made himself a wide house panelled in cedar and painted with vermilion (Jeremiah 22:13-14). His father ate and drank and did justice, judged the cause of the poor and needy, and it was well with him; but Jehoiakim’s eyes and heart were only for covetousness, for shedding innocent blood, for oppression and violence (Jeremiah 22:15-17). The teaching reads it as Jehoiakim refusing Josiah’s example. The classes carry it to America: how was the White House built? By slaves. Did we get paid for our captivity? Not at all. The slaves who built the Capitol never lived in it, and woe means destruction.

Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim prophesied the same words as Jeremiah; when Jehoiakim sought to kill him he fled to Egypt, and the king sent men who brought him back, and he struck him with the sword and threw his body among the graves of the common people (Jeremiah 26:20-23). The study note sets the two kings side by side: Hezekiah knew the word came from God and spared Micah, and this king killed his prophet (Jeremiah 26:18-19). When the roll of Jeremiah’s words was read to him in the winter house, he cut it with the penknife and burned it in the fire until it was consumed, and neither he nor his servants were afraid or tore their garments, though three of his princes pleaded with him (Jeremiah 36:21-25). God always gives warning first, the class says, and some still wish they could burn this Bible up. He ordered Baruch and Jeremiah seized, but the Lord hid them (Jeremiah 36:26).

Jeremiah wrote the words again with the sentence added: Jehoiakim would have no one to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body would be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night; the Lord would punish him, his seed and his servants for their iniquity (Jeremiah 36:27-31). Congratulations, the teacher says, you played yourself. Jeremiah had already said no one would lament him, but he would be buried with the burial of an ass, dragged and thrown out beyond the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:18-19); the teacher reads it as dying outside the land because he was evil. His son Coniah would be pulled off like a signet ring and recorded as childless, none of his seed to prosper on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:24-30).

He served Nebuchadnezzar three years and then rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah to destroy it, the evil out of the north (2 Kings 24:1-2; Jeremiah 4:6). This man was so evil, the teacher says, the Lord was sending nations against us. The study note traces the removal of Judah to the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:3-4). Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim in fetters to carry him to Babylon and took vessels of the Lord’s house (2 Chronicles 36:6-7), and the teaching counts this as the first wave, when Daniel and the three Hebrew children were taken. The note draws the lesson: when His people will not rule in righteousness, the Most High raises up a Nebuchadnezzar over them (Ecclesiasticus 10:1-4). All these people and their offspring, the class says, paid for what this fool did.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoiakim

events.title: Daniel
events.description:
Daniel, of the king’s seed of Judah, was carried to Babylon with the best of Israel’s youth to be trained for the king’s service, and he resolved not to defile himself with the king’s meat and wine; God gave him favour, and he and his companions were found ten times wiser than all the king’s wise men (Daniel 1:1-20). Under Darius, when his rivals could find no fault in him except concerning the law of his God, he kept praying three times a day toward Jerusalem after the decree was signed, and God shut the lions’ mouths (Daniel 6:1-23). He prospered under Darius and Cyrus and was told he would stand in his lot at the end of the days (Daniel 6:28; Daniel 12:13).

The presidents and princes under Darius sought occasion against Daniel and found no fault in him except concerning the law of his God, so they had the king sign an unchangeable decree that no one petition any god or man but the king for thirty days (Daniel 6:4-9). They found Daniel praying toward Jerusalem as before, reported him, and pressed the king until Daniel was cast to the lions (Daniel 6:10-17). God shut the lions’ mouths, and the king had the accusers, their children, and their wives cast into the den, where the lions broke their bones before they reached the bottom (Daniel 6:22-24).
events.article:
Daniel

Purposing in his heart not to defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat nor with the wine which he drank; kneeling and praying three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, as he did aforetime, after the decree was signed

Kept the law

When Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem he carried off vessels of the house of God, as the prophets had warned, and Isaiah had told Hezekiah that his sons would be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon (Daniel 1:1-2; 2 Kings 20:16-18). The king had the master of his eunuchs bring children of the king’s seed and the princes, without blemish and skilled in wisdom, to be taught the tongue of the Chaldeans and fed from the king’s table (Daniel 1:3-5). The class teaches that Babylon did not take any old body; they took the best and most educated to build up their kingdom, and Esau did the same when he took the best of our people and put them in North America. The study note adds that our people still serve in governments and are used to build a system that is not their own, often assimilated and well rewarded for it. The prince of the eunuchs renamed Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (Daniel 1:6-7), part of the assimilation; the study notes compare it to Hadassah made Esther, and the teaching to our fathers in slavery whose names were changed.

But Daniel resolved in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s meat or his wine, and asked the prince of the eunuchs to spare him (Daniel 1:8). God brought him into favour, for the Lord causes the enemy to treat His remnant well in the time of evil (Jeremiah 15:11). The officer feared for his head if they looked worse than the others, so Daniel asked for a ten day proof on pulse, which the teaching explains as vegetables, the green herb given for meat in the beginning (Genesis 1:29), and water; at the end they looked fairer and fuller than all who ate the king’s meat (Daniel 1:9-16).

Under Darius, Daniel was first of three presidents over a hundred and twenty princes, preferred because an excellent spirit was in him, and when the others sought occasion against him they found no error or fault (Daniel 6:1-4). The study note says this is how our forefathers rolled, keeping a clear conscience before God and men (Acts 24:16), and the class says he lived up to a name, integrity. They could find nothing against him except concerning the law of his God, so they had Darius sign a decree that no one petition any god or man but the king for thirty days (Daniel 6:5-9). When Daniel knew it was signed he went home, and with his windows open toward Jerusalem he knelt three times a day and prayed and gave thanks, as he had done before (Daniel 6:10).

God gave the four children knowledge and skill in all learning, and Daniel understanding in all visions and dreams; the king found them ten times better than all his magicians and astrologers (Daniel 1:17-20). The verse by verse teaching says the Most High gave them that understanding and they could not be outdone, as with Moses before the magicians, and points to Susanna, where young Daniel exposed the lying elders (Susanna 1:45-62). He continued to the first year of Cyrus (Daniel 1:21).

Cast into the den, he told the king that God had sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, because he was found innocent, and he came up unharmed because he trusted in his God (Daniel 6:16-23). The study note joins to this the account of Habakkuk carried by an angel with food for Daniel in the den, for God does not forsake those who seek and love Him (Bel and the Dragon 1:33-39). His accusers went into the den in his place (Daniel 6:24), for when a man’s ways please the Lord He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Darius commanded all his dominion to tremble before the God of Daniel, and Daniel prospered under Darius and Cyrus the Persian (Daniel 6:25-28); a reference work read in class calls him one of the few well known men of the Bible of whom nothing negative is written.

Daniel was told that he would rest, and at the end of the days stand in his lot (Daniel 12:13). The study note reads rest as his death and the promise as the Most High sending these leaders back to us, and the verse by verse class teaches that Daniel is on the earth in the time of the end, raising up his people and understanding what was sealed from him, though no one knows who he is.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/09-exile-and-return/daniel

Daniel’s accusers

Seeking occasion against Daniel and finding none; procuring a decree by the law of the Medes and Persians that no man petition any god or man for thirty days save the king, to take him in the law of his God; assembling to find him praying and pressing the king to cast him to the lions

Put to death

Darius set a hundred and twenty princes over the kingdom and three presidents over them, Daniel first, and thought to set him over the whole realm because an excellent spirit was in him (Daniel 6:1-3). The presidents and princes sought occasion against him concerning the kingdom and found none, because he was faithful and no error or fault was in him (Daniel 6:4). The class renders their thinking: we cannot find fault with his work, so we will use his religion against him. The study note says they really hated Daniel and knew the only way to find fault was concerning the law of his God (Daniel 6:5).

They came to the king claiming that all the rulers had agreed, and persuaded him to sign a decree that anyone who asked a petition of any god or man but the king for thirty days be cast into the den of lions, by the law of the Medes and Persians, which does not change (Daniel 6:6-9). The teaching explains that in the Persian empire a decree once sent out could not be reversed, and the king’s counsellors held him to it. They gathered, found Daniel praying and making supplication to his God, reminded the king of his decree, and reported that Daniel, of the captivity of Judah, did not regard him or his decree (Daniel 6:10-13). The king laboured till sundown to deliver him, but they pressed him that no decree of the Medes and Persians could be changed (Daniel 6:14-15). The class reads beside this the account in Bel and the Dragon, where the people of Babylon said the king had become a Jew and threatened to destroy him and his house unless he delivered Daniel to them (Bel and the Dragon 1:28-30). The king, displeased with himself, commanded Daniel cast in, saying that the God he served continually would deliver him, and the den was sealed (Daniel 6:16-17).

The king passed the night fasting, with no music and no sleep, and hurried to the den at dawn; Daniel answered that God had sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths, because he was found innocent before God and had done the king no hurt (Daniel 6:18-22). The class sets beside it the Bel and the Dragon account, in which seven lions were kept hungry so they would devour Daniel, the prophet Habakkuk was carried by an angel to feed him in the den, and the king cried that the God of Daniel is great and there is none other (Bel and the Dragon 1:31-41).

Then the king commanded that the men who had accused Daniel be cast into the den, they, their children, and their wives, and the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones before they came to the bottom (Daniel 6:24). The class says the lions that had been held back from Daniel devoured those who set him up. The law of the false witness is to do to him as he thought to do to his brother (Deuteronomy 19:16-19), and the study note on that law says that whoever falsely accuses a man of a crime worthy of death is put to death, because that is what he intended for his neighbour, and that false witnesses arising among our own people were part of why the nation fell into captivity. When a man’s ways please the Lord, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him (Proverbs 16:7). Darius then wrote to every people that in all his dominion men should tremble before the God of Daniel, the living God whose kingdom shall not be destroyed (Daniel 6:25-27).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/09-exile-and-return/daniels-accusers

events.title: Jehoiachin
events.description:
After Josiah fell at Megiddo the people of the land anointed his son Jehoahaz, called Shallum, and in three months he did evil according to all his fathers had done (2 Kings 23:30-32). Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah, laid a tribute on the land, set his brother Eliakim on the throne as Jehoiakim, and carried Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34). Jeremiah told the people to weep not for the dead king but for the one who went away, for he would never see his native land again (Jeremiah 22:10-12).

Jehoiachin, called Coniah and Jeconiah, reigned three months and did evil as his father Jehoiakim had done (2 Kings 24:8-9). Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to him with his mother, servants, princes and officers; he was carried to Babylon in the second wave of the conquest with the temple treasures, the mighty men and the craftsmen (2 Kings 24:10-16). Jeremiah said that though Coniah were the signet on the Lord’s right hand he would be plucked off, and written childless as to the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:24-30).
events.article:
Reign

598–598 BC

Judah

Who's Who in the Bible, Joan Comay and Ronald Brownrigg, Chronology (the reigns of the kings, years BC); https://archive.org/details/whos-who-in-the-bible

Jehoahaz (Shallum) of Judah

Doing evil in the sight of the Lord according to all that his fathers had done

Captivity

Josiah was carried dead from Megiddo, and the people of the land took Jehoahaz his son, anointed him and made him king in his father’s place (2 Kings 23:30). The people did this themselves, and they passed over the elder brother: Jehoahaz was twenty-three and Jehoiakim twenty-five (2 Kings 23:31, 36). The curse had said the Lord would bring them and the king they set over themselves into a nation they had not known (Deuteronomy 28:36), and this king is an example of it. He reigned three months and did evil according to all that his fathers had done (2 Kings 23:31-32). He followed the wicked kings, not his father who had turned to the Lord with all his heart.

Ezekiel took up a lamentation for the princes of Israel: their mother was a lioness who raised a whelp among the young lions, and he learned to catch the prey and devoured men; the nations heard of him, he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains to the land of Egypt (Ezekiel 19:1-4). That is Jehoahaz. Like Nimrod, the mighty hunter, he led men, the nation, into evil. Jeremiah was sent to the king’s house in those days with the terms on which the house of David would stand: execute judgment and righteousness, deliver the oppressed, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless or the widow, and shed no innocent blood; if they would not hear, the house would become a desolation (Jeremiah 22:1-5).

Pharaoh Necho put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, in Syria, so that he could not reign in Jerusalem, and laid on the land a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He made Eliakim, Josiah’s other son, king and changed his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died (2 Kings 23:33-34; 2 Chronicles 36:3-4). Jehoiakim paid Pharaoh by taxing the people, exacting silver and gold from every man according to his assessment (2 Kings 23:35), and he too did evil like his forefathers.

The word concerning Shallum the son of Josiah, who reigned in place of his father, was that the people should not weep for the dead, but weep bitterly for the one who went away: he had gone out of that place and would not return, but would die where they led him captive and see the land no more (Jeremiah 22:10-12). Shallum means retribution. Josiah was buried among his fathers; his son was buried in Egypt, the house of bondage the Lord had brought Israel out of. A father’s crown could not keep a son who would not keep his father’s course.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoahaz-of-judah

Jehoiachin (Coniah)

Doing evil as his father Jehoiakim had done; a signet plucked from the Lord’s right hand

Captivity

Babylon took Judah in three waves. In the first, in the days of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar came up and Jehoiakim served him three years and rebelled, and the Lord sent bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah, as He had spoken by the prophets, for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood the Lord would not pardon (2 Kings 24:1-4); Daniel and his companions were taken then (Daniel 1:1-6). Jehoiakim built his house by unrighteousness, used his neighbour’s service without wages, and set his eyes on covetousness and innocent blood, so he was buried with the burial of an ass, dragged out beyond the gates (Jeremiah 22:13-19).

Jehoiachin his son was eighteen when he began to reign, reigned three months, and did evil according to all his father had done (2 Kings 24:8-9); Chronicles gives eight years, and three months and ten days (2 Chronicles 36:9). His mother, Nehushta, is named with him, as the mothers of these evil kings are named, and the teaching reads Isaiah’s word over them: children are their oppressors and women rule over them (Isaiah 3:12). Jeremiah was told to say to the king and the queen to humble themselves and sit down, for the crown of their glory would come down (Jeremiah 13:18). The queen in our custom was the king’s mother, not his wife, and the king and the queen went into captivity together (Jeremiah 29:2). The Lord said that though Coniah were the signet on His right hand, the closest place a man can hold, He would pluck him off and give him to Nebuchadnezzar, whose face he feared, and cast him and his mother into a country where they were not born (Jeremiah 22:24-26).

This was the second wave. Nebuchadnezzar’s servants besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his princes and his officers, and was taken in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign. All the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house were carried out, and the vessels of gold Solomon made were cut in pieces, as the Lord had said (2 Kings 24:10-13), the word to Hezekiah fulfilled (Isaiah 39:6). Those who plunder stripped the land and ruined its vines (Nahum 2:2); the Lord turned away the excellency of Jacob, and Judah was like Jeremiah’s linen girdle hidden by the Euphrates, marred and good for nothing (Jeremiah 13:1-11).

He carried away the princes and the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, seven thousand men of might, and a thousand craftsmen and smiths, all strong and fit for war; none remained but the poorest sort (2 Kings 24:14-16). They took the best of the best, the men who built in their own land, to build for Babylon. America did the same: it did not bring illiterate people to build a country; it had to pass laws against our reading and writing, because the dumbing down was made here. Among those captives was Ezekiel, whose visions by the river Chebar are dated by the years of king Jehoiachin’s captivity (Ezekiel 1:1-3), and to them Jeremiah wrote his letter after Jeconiah and the craftsmen had departed (Jeremiah 29:1-2).

The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, his father’s brother, king and changed his name to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). Over Coniah the Lord asked whether he was a despised and broken vessel, and had him recorded as childless: no descendant of his would prosper on the throne of David or rule in Judah again (Jeremiah 22:28-30). In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Evil-merodach lifted his head out of prison, spoke kindly to him, changed his prison garments and gave him a daily allowance for life (2 Kings 25:27-30), a mercy at the close of the account that did not put him back on the throne of David.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/08-divided-kingdom/jehoiachin

events.title: Belshazzar
events.description: At a feast for a thousand lords, Belshazzar had the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple at Jerusalem brought in, and he, his princes, his wives, and his concubines drank from them and praised gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone (Daniel 5:1-4). A hand wrote on the wall, and Daniel read it: God had counted out his kingdom and ended it, he was weighed and found lacking, and his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:5-28). That same night Belshazzar was slain, and Darius the Mede took the kingdom (Daniel 5:30-31).
events.article:
Belshazzar

Drinking wine from the gold and silver vessels taken out of the temple of the house of God at Jerusalem, with his princes, his wives, and his concubines, and praising the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone; lifting himself up against the Lord of heaven, having known how his father was humbled

Put to death

Belshazzar the king, not Belteshazzar, which is Daniel, made a great feast, and while tasting the wine commanded that the vessels of the temple be brought so that his lords, wives, and concubines might drink from them, and they praised gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood, and stone (Daniel 5:1-4). The study note recalls that even before the captivity Israel was warned it would see these gods of silver and gold in Babylon and was told not to fear or worship them (Baruch 6:3-6). The class says they were mocking the vessels stolen from the temple of the Lord. The text calls Nebuchadnezzar his father; the classes teach that Belshazzar was a later descendant, the margin reading father as grandfather, and one class names him the son of Nabonidus, the king then reigning.

Daniel set his sin before him. The Most High had given Nebuchadnezzar his kingdom and majesty, so that he slew whom he would and set up whom he would, the same power, the teaching says, that America has; but when his heart was lifted up in pride he was put down from his throne and driven out until he knew that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men (Daniel 5:18-21). Belshazzar knew all this and did not humble his heart, but lifted himself against the Lord of heaven, drank from His vessels, and praised gods that neither see nor hear, and did not glorify the God who holds his breath in His hand (Daniel 5:22-23). The teaching puts it to him plainly: you knew about your father being driven out of his kingdom and losing his mind, and you still chose to be arrogant. The study note adds that gods of silver and gold cannot even save themselves (Baruch 6:12-16).

In the same hour the fingers of a man’s hand wrote on the plaster of the palace wall, and the king’s face changed, his joints were loosed, and his knees knocked together (Daniel 5:5-6). The study note pictures him sitting back with his lords, wives, and concubines having a good time when a hand starts writing on the wall, and he is terrified out of everything. None of his wise men could read it, and he offered scarlet, a chain of gold, and the third place in the kingdom (Daniel 5:7-9); the class explains the third place, since Nabonidus ruled first and Belshazzar second as co-regent. The queen told him of Daniel, in whom was the spirit of the holy gods (Daniel 5:10-12), which the class identifies as the Holy Spirit, the spirit of truth given to those who keep the commandments (John 14:15-17). Daniel, old now after the seventy years in Babylon, told him to keep his gifts (Daniel 5:13-17).

Daniel read the writing: God had counted out the days of the kingdom and ended it; the king was weighed and found lacking; his kingdom was divided and given to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:24-28). The class reads it as the end of Babylon’s seventy years: your time is up. Belshazzar clothed Daniel in scarlet and proclaimed him third ruler, and that night Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans was slain, and Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old (Daniel 5:29-31). The study note marks that the kingdom passed to the Medes and Persians immediately after the interpretation. The teaching says it was an inside job, for the Medes had long been allied with Babylon and lived among them, so Babylon was taken rather than burned; the Babylon prophesied to burn is the one still to come, the one we live in now.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/09-exile-and-return/belshazzar

events.title: Esther
events.description: Mordecai would not bow to Haman, and when Haman’s wrath became a decree against all the Jews he mourned in sackcloth, prayed, and charged Esther to go in to the king for her people (Esther 3:2; Esther 4:1-8; Rest of Esther 13:8-18). Esther feared the law against coming to the king uncalled, but at Mordecai’s word she had the Jews of Shushan fast three days with her, prayed, and went in against the law, ready to perish (Esther 4:10-16; Rest of Esther 14:1-19). God turned the king’s heart, Haman fell, the Jews were delivered, Purim was ordained, and Mordecai was made next to the king (Esther 7:10; Esther 9:1-32; Esther 10:3).
events.article:
Mordecai and Esther

Mordecai: bowing not to Haman, nor doing him reverence. Esther: gathering the Jews to fast three days, and going in to the king not according to the law: if I perish, I perish

Kept the law

All the king’s servants bowed to Haman, but Mordecai would not bow, for he had told them he was a Jew (Esther 3:2-4). The class teaches that it is not our custom to bow to any man, the same as the three Hebrew children would not bow to the image. Mordecai’s own prayer gives the reason: not contempt, pride, or a desire for glory; he could have kissed the soles of Haman’s feet for the salvation of Israel, but he would not set the glory of man above the glory of God (Rest of Esther 13:12-14). The teaching sets it beside our people at work today, where the co-worker asks in front of everyone why you dress as you do and keep the Sabbath, and then goes to the supervisor.

When Mordecai learned of the decree he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried out through the city, and in every province there was mourning, fasting, and weeping (Esther 4:1-3). This was a law passed to kill every Israelite, and the teaching warns that such laws will be passed again. He prayed that the whole world is in God’s power and that if He has appointed to save Israel no man can stand against it, and all Israel cried out with him (Rest of Esther 13:8-18). He refused the clothes Esther sent and gave her messenger a copy of the decree, charging her to go to the king for her people (Esther 4:4-8).

Esther answered that whoever came to the king uncalled died unless he held out the golden sceptre, and she had not been called in thirty

days (Esther 4:10-11); the study note says she made an excuse. Mordecai would not take a weak answer: she would not escape in the king’s house more than the other Jews; if she kept silent, deliverance would come from another place and she and her father’s house would perish; and who could say she had not come to the kingdom for such a time as this (Esther 4:13-14). The deliverance of Israel cannot be held back, and the teaching applies it to anyone slothful in the work: the Lord will raise up somebody else. Esther had all the Jews in Shushan fast three days, she and her maidens with them, and resolved to go in against the law, and if she perished, she perished (Esther 4:15-17). She put off her royal apparel for mourning, covered her head with ashes, confessed that Israel was given to its enemies for worshipping their gods, asked for boldness and eloquent speech, and told God she abhorred the sign of her high estate (Rest of Esther 14:1-19). The teaching notes she was raised right, taught from her youth how the Lord took Israel from among all people.

On the third day she put on her royal apparel and stood in the inner court; the king looked on her fiercely and she fainted, and God changed his spirit into mildness, so that he held out the golden sceptre and comforted her (Esther 5:1-2; Rest of Esther 15:1-16). At her second banquet she named Haman, and he was hanged on the gallows he had made for Mordecai (Esther 7:3-10). The king gave Esther the house of Haman and Mordecai his ring, and a second decree let the Jews in every city stand for their lives (Esther 8:1-11). Mordecai went out in royal blue and white with a great crown of gold, and many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell on them (Esther 8:15-17): a picture, the study note says, of the time when the fear of Israel will be on all nations.

The day their enemies hoped to rule them was turned the other way, and no man could stand before them (Esther 9:1-2). Mordecai and Esther wrote to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar every year as Purim, days turned from sorrow to joy, and the Jews bound it on their seed so that it would not fail (Esther 9:20-32). The teaching reminds that Purim is a memorial of the destruction of Israel’s enemies and of the Lord’s deliverance, not a day about presents (Rest of Esther 16:21-23). Mordecai was made next to the king, great among the Jews, seeking the wealth of his people and speaking peace to all his seed (Esther 10:3), and he confessed that God had done all these things (Rest of Esther 10:4-5). What was written before was written for our learning (Romans 15:4): days of sorrow now, and joy coming for those who stay in the commandments.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/09-exile-and-return/mordecai-and-esther

events.title: Nehemiah
events.description: Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes in Shushan, heard that the remnant in Judah was in affliction and the wall of Jerusalem broken down, and he wept, fasted, and prayed, pleading the promise to gather a scattered people who return (Nehemiah 1:1-11). The king sent him with letters, timber, and an armed escort, and he built the wall in fifty-two days with the builders armed, refused the governor’s bread, ended the usury, and later cleansed the temple chamber and shut the gates on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 2:1-9; Nehemiah 4:13-23; Nehemiah 5:6-18; Nehemiah 6:15; Nehemiah 13:4-22). He never claimed the work as his own, and asked God to remember him for good (Nehemiah 13:31).
events.article:
Nehemiah

Fasting and praying before the God of heaven for the remnant; building the wall in fifty-two days with a sword in one hand; taking no governor’s bread; forbidding usury; shutting the gates on the Sabbath; remember me, O my God, for good

Kept the law

Nehemiah was born in captivity at Shushan and had never seen Jerusalem. He held a high place in the Persian court as cupbearer, whose work guarded the king from poison and kept him in the king’s presence every day. When Hanani came from Judah with word that the remnant was in great affliction and reproach, the wall broken down and the gates burned, he sat down and wept, mourned for days, fasted, and prayed (Nehemiah 1:1-4). No matter how high he went, he never forgot his people. He confessed the sins of Israel, his own father’s house included, and held the Most High to what He had told Moses: scattered among the nations for transgression, gathered from the uttermost parts when they turned and kept His commandments (Nehemiah 1:5-11; Deuteronomy 30:1-4).

A cupbearer had to keep a cheerful face before the king, and the class compares it to how our people are expected to smile before their employers today. When the king saw his sorrow Nehemiah was very afraid. Yet he told the king that the city of his fathers’ sepulchres lay waste, and he prayed to the God of heaven before he made his request (Nehemiah 2:1-4). He asked to be sent to build it, set the king a time, and received letters to the governors and to the keeper of the king’s forest, all by the favour of his God upon him (Nehemiah 2:5-8). It is not that the heathen love Israel; the Lord moves a king to deal well with His remnant (Jeremiah 15:11). After three days in Jerusalem he viewed the ruined walls by night, telling no man what God had put in his heart, then told the rulers how God’s hand had been with him, and they set their hands to the work (Nehemiah 2:11-18). He never said the work came from his own wisdom, and he put the same vision on the men around him.

Under mockery and conspiracy the people had a mind to work, and the wall rose to half its height (Nehemiah 4:1-6). He answered with

prayer and a watch day and night, set the people by their families with swords, spears, and bows, and told them not to fear but to remember the Lord, who is great and to be feared, and fight for their brethren, wives, and houses; half worked and half stood guard, every builder wore his sword, and no one put off his clothes except for washing (Nehemiah 4:9-23). When the nobles exacted usury of their brethren he rebuked them and made them restore it, and for twelve years as governor he refused the governor’s portion, because the bondage was heavy on the people and because of the fear of God (Nehemiah 5:6-18). The teaching draws the lesson that leaders must always deal right with the people. When a hired prophet urged him to hide in the temple, he asked whether a man like him should flee (Nehemiah 6:10-13). The teaching says real leaders do not run and hide while other men stand in the front. On his return from the king he threw Tobiah’s goods out of the temple chamber, restored the Levites’ portions, and shut the gates at dark before the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:4-22).

The wall was finished in fifty-two days, and when the enemies and the heathen round about saw it they were disheartened, for they saw that the work was done by God (Nehemiah 6:15-16). Ecclesiasticus counts him among the elect, a man of great renown who raised up the fallen walls, set up the gates and bars, and rebuilt the ruins (Ecclesiasticus 49:13), and he gathered a library of the records of the kings, the prophets, and David (2 Maccabees 2:13).

Again and again he asked God to think on him for good according to all he had done for the people, and not to wipe out his good deeds for the house of God (Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 13:14; Nehemiah 13:31). God is not unrighteous to forget the work and labour of love shown toward His name (Hebrews 6:10); Nehemiah is remembered for his good deeds to this day. He was humble enough to write down the names of everyone who built beside him, so that they too would be remembered by God, while the nobles of Tekoa who would not bend their necks to the work are remembered for that (Nehemiah 3:1-5). The pattern stands for today: be a people with a mind to work, and do not be the noble who would not put his hand to it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/09-exile-and-return/nehemiah
