events.title: Jesus
events.description: The angel Gabriel was sent to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. She was told she would bring forth a son and call his name Jesus, that he would be great and be called the Son of the Highest, and that with God nothing shall be impossible; she asked how it should be, and then answered as the handmaid of the Lord, that it be to her according to his word (Luke 1:26-38). Elisabeth gave the verdict on that answer: blessed is she that believed, for there shall be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:39-45).
events.article:
Mary, the mother of Jesus

Be it unto me according to thy word; blessed is she that believed

Kept the law

Her answer was the answer of a servant. She called herself the handmaid of the Lord and said, let it be to me according to your word (Luke 1:38). The same messenger had stood in the temple six months earlier and told Zacharias that his wife would bear a son, and the promise was performed in its season, in the order the Most High set, and the same order holds here (Luke 1:13; Luke 1:23-24). Mary went from there into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah, and saluted Elisabeth, who was then six months with child (Luke 1:39-40).

Everything done for the child was done after the law. He was circumcised when eight days were accomplished and his name was called Jesus, as the law of circumcision requires on the eighth day, a covenant older than the Levitical priesthood and given to Abraham (Luke 2:21; Leviticus 12:3; Genesis 17:9-12; John 7:22). When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord and to offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which is the offering the law appoints for a woman who cannot bring a lamb (Luke 2:22-24; Leviticus 12:6-8). He was made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those that were under the law (Galatians 4:4-5), and his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover (Luke 2:41). She kept the sayings spoken of him and pondered them in her heart (Luke 2:19). At the marriage in Cana she told him they had no wine, and when he answered that his hour was not yet come she turned to the servants and told them to do whatever he said (John 2:1-5). After the ascension she is named in the upper room with the eleven and the women and his brethren, continuing with one accord in prayer and supplication (Acts 1:14).

Elisabeth, filled with the Holy Ghost, called her blessed among women and blessed for believing, because there should be a performance of the things told her from the Lord (Luke 1:41-45). Mary answered with the song that magnifies the Lord for regarding the low estate of his handmaiden, and said that from that time all generations would call her blessed (Luke 1:46-48). The song does not stop with her. Her song says that God had shown the strength of his arm against the proud, brought the mighty down from their thrones and lifted the lowly, fed the hungry and sent the rich away empty, and helped Israel his servant in remembrance of his mercy, as he had promised the fathers, Abraham and his seed for ever (Luke 1:51-55). The mercy she was given is the mercy promised to the nation she belonged to.

Christ himself fixed where the honour goes. When a woman in the crowd blessed the womb that bare him, he answered that rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11:27-28), and when he was told his mother and his brethren stood outside, he said that his mother and his brethren are those who hear the word of God and do it (Luke 8:21). He turned the honour off the mother and onto the keeping of the word, which is the same thing his mother had done at Cana when she pointed the servants at him. And the blessing came with a sword in it. Simeon told her that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul also (Luke 2:34-35). John places her standing by the cross, and records the care of her committed to the disciple whom he loved (John 19:25-27). She was called blessed, and she was not spared the grief that came with it.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/11-gospels/mary-the-mother-of-jesus

events.title: Peter
events.description:
Peter said that though all men should be offended because of him he would never be offended, and that though he should die with him he would not deny him (Matthew 26:33-35). In the high priest’s hall he denied it to a damsel, then with an oath, and then with cursing and swearing that he did not know the man, and the cock crew (Matthew 26:69-75). The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and he remembered the word that had been spoken to him, and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62).

At Antioch Peter had eaten with the Gentiles until certain men came from James, and then he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision, and the other Jews dissembled with him, so that even Barnabas was carried away. Paul withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed, and said before them all that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel. This history is not recorded in Acts; Paul tells it himself to the Galatians.
events.article:
Peter’s denial

Denying Christ three times with cursing and swearing

Reprieve

Before the denial he was warned and he was prayed for. Satan had desired to have them, to sift them as wheat, and Christ told Peter he had prayed for him that his faith fail not, and that when he was converted he should strengthen his brethren (Luke 22:31-32). Peter had walked with him and was not yet converted. What converts a man is named in the psalm: the law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul (Psalms 19:7), and that is also what he was to strengthen his brethren with. Peter answered out of his own confidence that he was ready to go both into prison and to death, and was told what he would do before the cock crew (Luke 22:33-34). A man does not know tomorrow, for his life is a vapour that appears for a little time and then vanishes away (James 4:14-15).

He denied three times. The third time he was picked out by his speech, because he was a Galilaean; the way he talked gave him away, so that he sounded like the man he was denying (Luke 22:54-60). Matthew records the oath, and then the cursing and swearing that he did not know the man (Matthew 26:69-75). The warning about that stands in the same gospel: whoever confesses him before men, him will he confess before his Father, and whoever denies him before men will be denied (Matthew 10:32-33). It was the hour given to the other side, as Christ told the chief priests and the captains of the temple when they came out against him with swords and staves, that this was their hour and the power of darkness (Luke 22:52-53). Isaiah had written it plainly of the servant: he was despised and rejected of men, and we hid as it were our faces from him, and we esteemed him not (Isaiah 53:3). That verse is Peter in the courtyard.

The look and the tears are the first part of the answer. The Lord turned and looked on Peter, and Peter remembered the word and went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60-62). The difference between this case and the traitor in the same chapter is what came after the weeping. When Judas saw what he had done he did not go back and reconcile; he went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3-5). Peter reconciled. Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The reconciliation is recorded. After the resurrection Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved him and three times charged him to feed his lambs and his sheep, once for each denial, and Peter was grieved at the third asking (John 21:15-17). Then he was told by what death he should glorify God, that when he was old another would gird him and carry him where he would not (John 21:18-19), which answers what he had been told in the upper room, that where Christ was going he could not follow then but should follow afterwards (John 13:36). The history says he was held nine months in prison at Rome, converted the keepers and others while he was in there, and was scourged and crucified with his head downward, a position he asked for because he did not count himself worthy to die as his master died. The man who bounced back from that courtyard is the same man who stood at the gate called Beautiful and told a lame beggar that he had no silver and gold, but gave him what he had (Acts 3:1-8). The charge given with the warning stood: once converted, he was to strengthen his brethren. The fall did not cancel the man, and it did not cancel what he was sent to teach.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/11-gospels/peters-denial

Peter at Antioch

Dissembling: withdrawing from the Gentiles for fear of them of the circumcision

Reprieve

When James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace given to Paul, they gave him and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, that they should go to the heathen and the pillars to the circumcision (Galatians 2:9). The heathen there is the northern kingdom, the same people called the Gentiles and the uncircumcision; the scripture itself calls the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali Galilee of the Gentiles, and those are two tribes of Israel (Matthew 4:15-16). Paul was already at Antioch doing his ministry when Peter came along later. But when Peter was come to Antioch, Paul withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed; for before certain men came from James he did eat with the Gentiles, and when they were come he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision, and the other Jews dissembled likewise with him, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their dissimulation (Galatians 2:11-13). This history is not recorded in Acts at all. Peter was the head apostle, second in command from Christ, and he still made mistakes.

Four words carry the charge: he withdrew, he separated himself, the others dissembled, and Barnabas was carried away with their dissimulation. To dissimulate is to disguise or conceal under a false appearance, to hide the real motive behind a pretense; dissimulation is feigning and hypocrisy. In plain speech, Peter was being fake, and the reason given is fear. The men he had been eating with were Israelites of the northern kingdom living in a Gentile way of life; when

the southern kingdom arrived he separated himself from them out of respect of persons, not wanting to be seen eating with them, and Barnabas withdrew with him and would not sit or eat with them either. That withdrawing is the very thing that broke the nation in the first place, when the ten tribes told Rehoboam they had no portion in David and every man went to his tent (1 Kings 12:16). The law forbids respect of persons in judgment, neither respecting the person of the poor nor honouring the person of the mighty (Leviticus 19:15). And Peter knew better than any man there, because he was the one who had been told by God not to call any man common or unclean, and the one who had watched the same gift of the Holy Ghost fall on that household (Acts 10:28, Acts 11:2-3, Acts 15:7-9).

When Paul saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, he said to Peter before them all that if he, being a Jew, lived after the manner of Gentiles and not as do the Jews, he had no business compelling the Gentiles to live as do the Jews (Galatians 2:14). Paul confronted him in front of everybody. The charge was plain: you claim to be a Jew, salvation is of the Jews, you are supposed to be the example, and you are following their footsteps instead of setting one, showing respect of persons and living like them while trying to teach them to follow after the Jews. You are being a hypocrite in your actions. Paul did not let things slide; he had no respect of persons and feared no man regardless of his status. You already learned this, Peter. God showed you that you cannot call any man common or unclean. You sat with them, and you convinced many of the Jews that these men were all right, and now you are wavering.

The correction went no further than the rebuke. Galatians records no sentence taking Peter out of his work, and the next words of the letter are Paul including himself with him: we who are Jews by nature, knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ (Galatians 2:15-16). Peter was corrected in front of them all and would have been embarrassed and ashamed, and he repented; and as a teacher, what does a man teach after that? What he repented from. Do not be fake. Reproof between brethren is the law and not an injury, since the commandment is to rebuke a brother plainly and not to hate him in the heart (Leviticus 19:17), and Peter himself afterward wrote of the wisdom given to our beloved brother Paul (2 Peter 3:15-16). The case is kept in the book so that a so-called Christian cannot use it to excuse breaking the commandments, and so that a man with rank among us knows that rank is no cover for hypocrisy.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/12-apostolic/peter-at-antioch

events.title: Paul
events.description:
The witnesses who stoned Stephen laid their clothes at his feet, and he was consenting to the death; from that day he made havock of the congregation, entering every house and committing men and women to prison (Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1-3). Breathing out threatenings and slaughter, he went to the high priest for letters to Damascus so that he might bring any he found of that way bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). A light out of heaven struck him down on the road, and the voice asked why he was persecuting Christ; the man who came to lead others bound was led by the hand into the city, blind, and afterward was told he was a chosen vessel who would suffer for that name (Acts 9:3-9; Acts 9:15-16).

Paul wrote his last letter knowing he was ready to be offered and that the time of his departure was at hand (2 Timothy 4:6). He said he had fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith, and that a crown of righteousness was laid up for him, which the Lord the righteous judge would give him at that day, and not to him only but to all them also that love his appearing (2 Timothy 4:7-8). At his first answer no man stood with him, yet the Lord stood with him and strengthened him (2 Timothy 4:16-17).
events.article:
Saul of Tarsus

Persecuting the church; consenting to Stephen’s death; compelling the saints to blaspheme

Spared

The witnesses who stoned Stephen laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul, and he was consenting to his death (Acts 7:58; Acts 8:1). From that day he made havock of the congregation, entering into every house and haling men and women and committing them to prison (Acts 8:3). Still breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples, he went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1-2). Before the followers of Christ were called Christians at Antioch they were called this way, after the one who said he is the way (John 14:6). Authority from the chief priests gave the campaign an official face. It did not make it obedience to God.

His own account is heavier than Luke’s summary. He persecuted this way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women (Acts 22:4-5). He shut up many of the saints in prison, gave his voice against them when they were put to death, punished them often in every synagogue and compelled them to blaspheme, and being exceedingly mad against them, persecuted them even to strange cities (Acts 26:9-11). He thought he ought to do it. He had been brought up at the feet of Gamaliel and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers (Acts 22:3); he was of the stock of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, a Pharisee, and by his own reckoning blameless touching the righteousness which is in the law (Philippians 3:5-6); and he profited in that religion above many of his equals, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of his fathers, while he wasted the church of God beyond measure (Galatians 1:13-14). Learning, zeal and certainty did not keep him out of the gravest sin.

As he came near Damascus a light from heaven shined round about him, he fell to the earth and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him (Acts 9:3-5). Christ was already dead at that time, and the question still stands in the present tense, because what is done to one of his little ones is done to him. Trembling and astonished, the man who had set out to lead others bound asked what he would have him do, and was led by the hand into the city, and was three days without sight and neither ate nor drank (Acts 9:6-9). The men with him stood speechless, hearing a voice and seeing no man, while his own retelling says they saw the light and heard

not the voice, the other half of one event and no contradiction (Acts 22:9). Ananias objected that he had heard by many how much evil this man had done to the saints at Jerusalem, and was told to go, for he was a chosen vessel to bear the name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, and would be shown how great things he must suffer for it (Acts 9:13-16). Ananias went in, called him Brother Saul, and there fell from his eyes as it had been scales, and he received sight and was baptized (Acts 9:17-18).

He did it in ignorance, which is why the scripture says to judge nothing before the time (1 Corinthians 4:5). The things any of us did before this truth were worthy of death, so no man is written off as beyond repentance, and the enemies who can still repent are the ones inside our own nation (Romans 11:28). Straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, and all that heard him were amazed and asked whether this was not the man who destroyed them which called on that name; but he increased the more in strength and confounded the Jews at Damascus (Acts 9:20-22). The mercy did not cancel the cost. They took counsel to kill him and watched the gates day and night, and the disciples took him by night and let him down the wall in a basket (Acts 9:23-25). He afterward called himself the least of the apostles, not meet to be called an apostle, because he persecuted the church of God (1 Corinthians 15:9), and a blasphemer and a persecutor and injurious, who obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly in unbelief, and was set forth as a pattern of Christ’s longsuffering to them which should believe after (1 Timothy 1:12-16). The gospel he preached was not taught him by any man; he had it by revelation, went into Arabia, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem to see Peter and James (Galatians 1:11-12; Galatians 1:17-19).

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/12-apostolic/saul-of-tarsus

Paul, at the end of his course

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith

Kept the law

Paul was not guessing about the ending. Christ had said of him at the very beginning that he was a chosen vessel to bear his name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, and that he would be shown how great things he must suffer for that name (Acts 9:15-16), and Peter likewise knew he must shortly put off his tabernacle because Christ had showed him (2 Peter 1:14). So when Paul told the elders at Miletus that bonds and afflictions awaited him in every city, he could add that none of these things moved him, neither counted he his life dear to himself, so that he might finish his course with joy and the ministry he had received (Acts 20:22-24). He was not out to preserve his life; he was out to finish the work, because the man who saves his life loses it.

The course is itemised: stripes above measure, prisons more frequent, deaths often, five times forty stripes save one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three shipwrecks, a night and a day in the deep, perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen, of the heathen, in the city, in the wilderness, in the sea, among false brethren, and on top of all of it the care of all the churches daily (2 Corinthians 11:23-28). The stoning at Lystra was the worst of it: they drew him out of the city supposing he was dead, and he rose up and went back in (Acts 14:19-20). The teaching sets that hour beside the man caught up to the third heaven, into paradise, who heard unspeakable words not lawful for a man to utter (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Paul counted himself the least of the apostles, not fit to be called one because he persecuted the congregation of God, and said he laboured more abundantly than they all, yet not he but the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:9-10): he did more work because he had done more damage. He forgot the things behind and reached toward the mark for the prize of the high calling (Philippians 3:13-14), and kept his own body under, lest after preaching to others he himself should be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

He had fought a good fight, finished his course, and kept the faith, and there was laid up for him a crown of righteousness which the Lord the righteous judge would give him at that day (2 Timothy 4:7-8). The crown is not his alone. It is promised to all them also that love his appearing, which puts it in front of everybody who actually wants that day to come.

The ending itself was lonely. At his first answer no man stood with him and all men forsook him, and he prayed that it would not be laid to their charge (2 Timothy 4:16). Demas had gone, Crescens was in Galatia, Titus in Dalmatia, and only Luke was with him (2 Timothy 4:10-11). Notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him and strengthened him, so that by him the preaching might be fully known and all the Gentiles hear, and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:17). He said the Lord would deliver him from every evil work and preserve him to his heavenly kingdom (2 Timothy 4:18). He had also left the elders at Ephesus a clean account of how he had lived among them: he coveted no man’s silver, gold, or apparel, his own hands ministered to his necessities and to them that were with him, and he taught them that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:33-35). He was beheaded at Rome under Nero soon after the letter was sent.

Source: https://cyberjudah.io/cases/12-apostolic/paul-at-the-end

events.title: Zacchaeus
events.description: Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans at Jericho and rich, could not see Christ for the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree, and was called down by name and received him joyfully while the people murmured (Luke 19:1-7). Standing before him he said he gave half of his goods to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored it fourfold, which is the rate the law names (Luke 19:8; Exodus 22:1). Salvation came to his house, and he was named a son of Abraham, since the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10).
events.article:
Zacchaeus

Extortion as chief of the publicans

Restitution

Jesus entered and passed through Jericho, and a man named Zacchaeus, who was chief among the publicans and rich, sought to see who he was and could not for the press, because he was little of stature; so he ran before and climbed up into a sycamore tree on the road he would take (Luke 19:1-4). He had been hearing the reports. A cleansed leper had published the matter and blazed it abroad until Christ could no more openly enter a city (Mark 1:40-45), and this man wanted to see for himself who everybody was talking about. The office and the money are the setting of the case; the interest that put him up that tree was already faith.

Christ came to the place, looked up, called him by his name and told him to make haste and come down, for he must abide at his house that day; he made haste and came down and received him joyfully, while the onlookers murmured that he had gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner (Luke 19:5-7). Receiving a man carries a promise with it: he that receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward, and even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple does not lose its reward (Matthew 10:40-42). That cold water is good news from a far country to a thirsty soul (Proverbs 25:25). The murmurers had already been answered once: the whole need no physician, but they that are sick, and they were sent to go and learn what it means that God will have mercy and not sacrifice (Matthew 9:11-13; Hosea 6:6).

Zacchaeus stood and said that half of his goods he gave to the poor, and that if he had taken anything from any man by false accusation he restored him fourfold (Luke 19:8). That is a man applying the law to himself. Fourfold is the rate the statute names for a stolen sheep, where an ox requires five (Exodus 22:1); the law of the trespass requires the principal restored with a fifth part added, paid to the man who was wronged (Leviticus 6:1-5; Numbers 5:6-7); and David passed the same fourfold sentence on himself when Nathan set the parable before him (2 Samuel 12:5-6). John had already told publicans coming to his baptism to exact no more than was appointed them, and to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance (Luke 3:8; Luke 3:12-13). A sacrifice cannot stand in the place of dealing justly with the man a person has robbed.

Salvation came to that house that day, and he was called a son of Abraham, because the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:9-10). Sonship there is by faith, not by the sacrifice: Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, and circumcision was afterward the seal of a righteousness of faith he already had (Romans 4:1-3; Romans 4:11). A rich young ruler heard a like word about selling and giving to the poor and went away sorrowful because he had great possessions (Matthew 19:16-22); a rich man hardly enters the kingdom, and yet this rich man did, because his hand was already open. And the salvation spoken over the house is the one Zacharias named, to be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all that hate us (Luke 1:68-74), for the lost that the Son of man came after are the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24).

events.title: The first Africans in the Americas and the 1518 asiento
events.description: Africans reached Hispaniola with the Spanish from about 1502; as the Taíno died out, Las Casas proposed African labour in their place, the Crown let colonists import African slaves in 1517, and in August 1518 granted the first asiento, a monopoly to import up to 4,000 enslaved Africans.
events.article:
Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and Spain

1502–1518

Documented history

Juan Garrido, born in the Kingdom of Kongo, arrived in Santo Domingo, Hispaniola, in 1502 or 1503, among the earliest Africans to reach the Americas; he later fought in Puerto Rico, Cuba, Florida and the siege of Tenochtitlan.

Las Casas, who had come with Ponce de León to Puerto Rico, protested the Spanish treatment of the Taíno at court in 1512. When colonists complained that they needed labour for the mines, forts and sugar, Las Casas suggested African slaves instead, and in 1517 the Crown permitted its subjects to import twelve slaves each. In early writings Las Casas advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour; later in life he repented, judging 'black slavery … as unjust as Indian slavery'.

The first asiento was drawn up in August 1518, giving Charles I's Flemish favourite Laurent de Gouvenot a monopoly on importing enslaved Africans for eight years, to a maximum of 4,000; he sold it to Genoese merchants for 25,000 ducats. events.title: The encomienda, and the New Laws that were revoked
events.description: From 1503 the Spanish Crown granted conquistadors encomiendas, the labour of whole Indigenous communities; the New Laws of 20 November 1542 limited them, but the restriction was repealed in 1545 after the encomenderos resisted.
events.article:

Documented history

Governor Nicolás de Ovando set up the formal encomienda on Hispaniola. Although Isabella I had declared the natives free vassals of the Crown in 1501, in 1503 the Crown began formally granting encomiendas to conquistadors and officials as rewards: a monopoly on the labour of particular Indigenous groups, which devolved into a form of communal slavery. Natives were forced into hard labour and punished, even killed, if they resisted.

Following the protests of Bartolomé de las Casas and others, Charles V issued the New Laws on 20 November 1542 to limit the encomenderos' power; encomiendas were to end on the holder's death. The encomenderos resisted: in Peru Gonzalo Pizarro led a revolt, and the first viceroy, Blasco Núñez Vela, was killed in 1546. The laws, passed in 1542, were repealed in 1545. The encomienda was legally ended only in 1720.

events.title: Ponce de León conquers Borinquen and parcels out the Taíno
events.description: In 1508 Juan Ponce de León led the first official Spanish expedition to Puerto Rico, founded Caparra, became governor in 1509 and parcelled out the Taíno among the settlers in encomienda to mine gold and grow food.
events.article:
Caparra and San Juan Bay, Puerto Rico

Caribbean

12 July 1508 – 1511

Documented history

Ponce de León had first seen the island on Columbus's second voyage in 1493 and had helped crush a Taíno rebellion on Hispaniola. In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to the island the Spanish called San Juan Bautista; about 50 men in one ship left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 and anchored in San Juan Bay, and placer gold was found in the west of the island. Archival documents suggest an earlier, quieter expedition as early as 1506.

He built a storehouse and fortified house about two miles from the bay, the first settlement, Caparra, in late 1508; it is a U.S. National Historic Landmark, the oldest known European settlement in the United States. Ovando appointed him governor, confirmed by Ferdinand II on 14 August 1509, with instructions to extend the settlement and continue mining for gold.

Ponce de León parcelled out the native Taínos among himself and other settlers under the forced-labour system of encomienda, putting them to work growing food and mining gold; his own encomienda searched for gold in the Toa Valley. Many Spaniards treated the Taínos very harshly and death rates were very high, and the demand for slaves kidnapped from other islands grew. By June 1511 the Taínos began a rebellion, put down by Ponce de León with crossbows and arquebuses. A 1530 story from Caparra tells of two Spaniards each with 40 Taíno slaves searching the rivers for gold.

events.title: Velázquez conquers Cuba; the massacre at Caonao
events.description: Diego Velázquez sailed from Hispaniola in January 1511 with about 300 men, defeated the Taíno resistance, founded Baracoa and six more towns by 1515, and apportioned the Native people in encomienda; Las Casas witnessed the massacre of the people of Caonao.
events.article:
Baracoa, Bayamo, Caonao (Camagüey) and Havana, Cuba

Caribbean

January 1511 – 1515

Documented history

Las Casas estimated the Taíno population of Cuba at 350,000 by the end of the 15th century. Velázquez sailed for Cuba in January 1511 with four ships and 300 men, among them Hernán Cortés and Pedro de Alvarado, and landed in the province of Mayci. The Taínos, organized by the cacique Hatuey, were outmatched by Spanish weapons and defeated after two months of intermittent fighting. Baracoa was founded by August 1511, and Pánfilo de Narváez brought thirty Spanish archers and Native auxiliaries from Jamaica; within three years the Spanish controlled the island.

Las Casas observed a number of massacres, notably near Camagüey of the inhabitants of Caonao: by his account some three thousand villagers who had come to greet the Spanish with food were "without provocation, butchered". Survivors fled to the mountains or small islands before being captured and forced into reservations such as Guanabacoa.

In 1513 Ferdinand II decreed the encomienda system, and Velázquez apportioned the land and the Indigenous peoples among the colonists. Bayamo was founded in 1513 and Trinidad, Sancti Spíritus and Havana in 1514; gold deposits set off a gold rush until about 1520. The native population was largely destroyed as a culture after 1550; under the New Laws of 1552 Indigenous Cubans were freed from encomienda.

events.title: Pedro de Alvarado conquers the Maya of Guatemala and Cuzcatlán
events.description: Sent by Hernán Cortés, Pedro de Alvarado invaded the Maya kingdoms of Guatemala in 1524, burned the Kʼicheʼ kings alive and their capital Qʼumarkaj, and campaigned against the Pipil of Cuzcatlán in present-day El Salvador until 1528.
events.article:
Guatemalan Highlands and western El Salvador

Central America

1524–1528 (Qʼumarkaj burned March 1524)

Documented history

Cortés despatched Pedro de Alvarado with 180 cavalry, 300 infantry, crossbows, muskets, 4 cannons and thousands of allied warriors from Tlaxcala, Cholula and other cities of central Mexico; they arrived in Soconusco in 1523. A Kʼicheʼ army was defeated in the Quetzaltenango valley in February 1524 and many Kʼicheʼ nobles were among the dead; local tradition places the death of the prince Tecun Uman in these battles.

In March 1524 Alvarado entered Qʼumarkaj, the Kʼicheʼ capital, at the invitation of its remaining lords. He seized the king Oxib-Keh and the king-elect Beleheb-Tzy in his camp, had the captured lords burnt to death, and then burned the entire city. He then demanded gold in tribute from the Kaqchikel, and by 1526 rebellions had engulfed the highlands. Bartolomé de las Casas charged him with further atrocities in the conquest of the Maya kingdoms.

The same year Alvarado led an expedition against the Pipil province of Cuzcatlán but retreated to Guatemala by July 1524. San Salvador, founded in 1525, was destroyed in a native rising in 1526; Alvarado campaigned again in 1526 and 1528, and the uprising ended in 1528 when the Spanish stormed the native stronghold at the Peñol de Cinacantan. The conquest of Guatemala's other peoples went on until the Petén fell in 1697. Disease, chiefly smallpox and measles, is counted at 1,600,000 dead between 1525 and 1550, and an estimated 33–50% of the highland population perished.

events.title: The conquest of Nicaragua and the shipping of its natives as slaves

events.title: Afonso I of Kongo protests the slave trade
events.description: In 1526 Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo, wrote to the king of Portugal that traders were kidnapping his people, even nobles and his own family, and branding them, and that his land was being depopulated.
events.article:
Kingdom of Kongo

West Central Africa

1526

Documented history

Mvemba a Nzinga, Afonso I, ruled Kongo from 1509 to 1542 or 1543 and made Christianity the royal faith. To pay for Portuguese imports some Kongolese nobles illegally exported slaves, some kidnapping and enslaving freeborn Kongolese, and in 1526 Afonso issued a letter protesting the circumvention of Kongolese law.

events.title: Estevanico crosses the American Southwest

events.title: Manco Inca's rising and the siege of Cusco

Real power rested with the Spaniards, who frequently humiliated him; Juan Pizarro imprisoned him after an attempted escape in November 1535.

Released in January 1536, Manco left Cusco on April 18, 1536, met his military chiefs at Lares, and gathered an army estimated at 100,000 to 200,000 men (some sources say as few as 40,000) around the city, held by 190 Spaniards and several thousand Indian auxiliaries. The Incas seized the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above the city on May 5, 1536; the siege began on 6 May and lasted until March 1537.

Manco coordinated it with a siege of Lima under his captain Quiso Yupanqui; the Incas defeated four relief expeditions sent by Francisco Pizarro, killing nearly 500 Spanish soldiers. When the siege failed, Manco withdrew to Ollantaytambo and then to the remote jungles of Vilcabamba, where he founded the Neo-Inca State in 1537.

In April 1537 they beat the psihipqua Tisquesusa at Funza; in the Iraka Valley the iraca Sugamuxi fell, and the Sun Temple was burned by two of Quesada's soldiers in early September. On August 6, 1538 Quesada founded Bogotá as the capital of the New Kingdom of Granada; Tisquesusa's successor Sagipa allied with the Spanish that month. The conquest lasted until 1540.

Over six years he killed, tortured and enslaved thousands of natives; his policy was to "terrorize the natives with often unprovoked killing, torture, and enslavement", and the Spanish tried to force the natives into servitude through the encomienda.

events.title: The cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576
events.description: Waves of a hemorrhagic fever the Aztecs called cocoliztli, 'pestilence', killed an estimated 5 to 15 million people in sixteenth-century New Spain; it fell most heavily on the Indigenous people.

Documented history

The cocoliztli epidemic, an illness of high fevers and bleeding, caused 5–15 million deaths in New Spain during the 16th century and is often called the worst epidemic in Mexico's history. Its largest outbreaks were in 1545 and 1576; a second large outbreak in 1576 lasted until about 1580 and caused approximately two million deaths. Spanish accounts cite 13 cocoliztli epidemics between 1545 and 1642.

Researchers disagree on the cause: genomic studies point to Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, while others propose an Indigenous viral hemorrhagic fever worsened by drought and by the poor living conditions of the Indigenous peoples after the conquest. The encomendero Gonzalo de Ortiz wrote that God sent such sickness on the Indians that three out of every four perished; the modern consensus is that Indigenous people were the most affected.

events.title: Potosí and the mita: the silver mountain worked by forced labour
events.description: Silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí in 1545; from 1573 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo drafted one in seven adult native men into the mines through the mita, a forced-labour system under which many died and whole communities fled.
events.article:
Potosí (Upper Peru, today Bolivia) and the southern Andes

South America

Documented history

Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, is credited with discovering the Cerro Rico in 1545. Potosí grew to more than 200,000 people, and the mountain produced an estimated 60% of all the silver mined in the world in the second half of the 16th century; the Spanish still say valer un Potosí, 'to be worth a Potosí'. From 1554 the patio process used mercury to extract the silver, and mercury poisoning took the lives of many in the refining.

The Spanish Crown repurposed the Andean mit'a in 1573. Under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, sent to Peru in 1569, communities had to provide one seventh of their male labour force; the first mit'a recruits reached Potosí in 1573, and recruitment came to cover nearly 200,000 square miles of southern Peru and present-day Bolivia. Thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year. Mitayos carried loads of 100 to 300 lbs up ladders in narrow shafts; many died or were seriously injured, and assignment to the mines was considered worse than a death sentence.

Thousands fled their villages and forfeited their land to escape the draft; by the late 17th century Upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its indigenous population compared with a little over a century earlier. A 1603 report counted 58,800 Indians working at Potosí, 5,100 of them mitayos. Potosí was a multiracial society of native Andeans, Spanish settlers and black slaves.

events.title: Philip II's decree against the Moriscos

events.title: The Pequot War and the Mystic massacre
events.description: In 1636–1638 the English colonies of New England and their Narragansett and Mohegan allies destroyed the Pequot nation; at Mystic on May 26, 1637 colonists set the Pequot fort ablaze and killed between 400 and 700 people, and hundreds of captives were enslaved.

The Pequot War was fought from 1636 to 1638 between the Pequot nation and the Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth and Saybrook colonists with their Narragansett and Mohegan allies. On the night of May 26, 1637 a Connecticut force under Captain John Mason, joined by Captain John Underhill and allied Natives, surrounded the fortified Pequot village near the Mystic River; Mason ordered it set ablaze and its two exits blocked, and those who tried to escape over the palisade were shot or killed outside. Between 400 and 700 Pequots were killed. Underhill wrote that “there were about foure hundred soules in this Fort, and not above five of them escaped out of our hands.”

By the end of the war about 700 Pequots had been killed or taken captive. Hundreds of prisoners were enslaved; most were sold to colonists in Bermuda or the West Indies, and others were given as captives to the Narragansett and Mohegan. The Treaty of Hartford of 1638 forbade the Pequots to return to their lands, speak their language or call themselves Pequots, and the colonial authorities classed them as extinct; a western band kept its sovereignty and is today a federally recognized nation.

events.title: The sugar revolution and Barbados's 1661 slave code
events.description: Barbados's planters switched from tobacco and indentured European labour to sugar in the 1640s, and the enslaved African population tripled; in 1661 the island's parliament passed "An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes," the first comprehensive slave code in English America, which classed enslaved people as chattel property and became the model for later codes elsewhere.

Barbadian planters took up sugar cultivation in the 1640s, replacing tobacco and indentured European workers with enslaved Africans; the enslaved population on the island tripled over the decade as the sugar plantations grew.

In 1661 the Parliament of Barbados passed "An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes," the first comprehensive slave code in English America. Its preamble classed enslaved people as "chattel property," required masters to provide only one set of clothing a year with no standard for diet or housing, and let an owner mutilate or burn a slave alive without legal consequence; an enslaved person who struck a white person could be whipped, have the nose slit and the face branded, and be put to death for a second offence.

Historian Russell Menard writes that because Barbados was the first English colony to write a comprehensive slave code, its code was especially influential: Jamaica, South Carolina (1696), Antigua and other colonies adopted or modelled their own slave codes on it, and its influence is traceable even where Virginia's and Maryland's codes were not exact copies.

events.title: The Pueblo Revolt

In 1675 Governor Juan Francisco Treviño arrested forty-seven medicine men for “sorcery”; three were hanged and the rest whipped. Among those released was Popé of Ohkay Owingeh, who spent five years organizing a revolt among the 46 Pueblo towns.

Popé sent runners to the towns carrying knotted cords, one knot to be untied each morning; when the last knot was untied they rose. On August 10, 1680 the Puebloans took the Spaniards’ horses, sealed the roads to Santa Fe and attacked the settlements. A total of 400 people were killed, including 21 of the 33 Franciscan missionaries in New Mexico, and the remaining 2,000 settlers fled the province. The Spaniards returned twelve years later.

events.title: The Code Noir enslaves Saint-Domingue

The Code Noir was promulgated by Louis XIV in March 1685 to govern slavery in France's Caribbean colonies. It was implemented in Martinique on August 6, 1685, Guadeloupe on December 10, 1685, and Saint-Domingue on May 6, 1687; it was later extended to Louisiana (1724) and the Mascarene Islands (1723). Its first article ordered all Jews expelled from the colonies within three months.

The code required enslaved people to be baptized and instructed in the Catholic faith, gave them Sundays and Catholic holy days as rest days, and specified minimum food and clothing. It forbade them to carry weapons, assemble in groups, work on Sundays, or practice any religion but Catholicism, and barred their testimony as legal proof, though they could lodge complaints of mistreatment. Punishments were severe: ear-cropping for a first escape attempt, hamstringing for a second, and death for a third; masters could beat enslaved people but not torture or mutilate them outside the code's own penalties, and killing an enslaved person was technically prosecutable.

events.title: Nanny and the Windward Maroons of Jamaica
events.description: Nanny led the Windward Maroons, formerly enslaved Africans in Jamaica’s mountains, through the First Maroon War against the British, who sued for peace and signed a treaty with the Maroons on 20 April 1740.
events.article:
Blue Mountains, Jamaica (Nanny Town, Moore Town)

Caribbean

First Maroon War c. 1728–1739; treaty 20 April 1740

Documented history

Between 1728 and 1734, during the First Maroon War, Nanny Town and other Maroon settlements were frequently attacked by British colonial forces, who wanted to stop the Maroons’ raids. The Maroons’ guerrilla warfare and knowledge of the terrain played a large part in their successes.

Having failed to defeat them in battle, the British sued for peace and signed a treaty on 20 April 1740. It ended the hostilities, gave the Maroons state-sanctioned freedom and granted 500 acres to Nanny and her followers, where Moore Town (“New” Nanny Town) still stands.

Maroon legend holds that Nanny was born among the Asante people of present-day Ghana. In 1975 Jamaica declared her its only female national hero, and her image is on the Jamaican $500 note.

Many Israelite tribes were on the continent, and most of them came to the Americas as slaves. Queen Nanny of the Maroons was of the Ashanti, and she led the Windward Maroons in a guerrilla war against the British in Jamaica; she fulfilled the prophecy of Deuteronomy 28.

Tacky, who led the revolt in Jamaica in the 1760s, was of the Akan people of the Gold Coast, and Accompong in Jamaica carries an Akan name: the same peoples taken from Ghana are found in the Maroon villages of Jamaica.

events.title: The Antigua slave conspiracy and the execution of Prince Klaas
events.description: In October 1736 Antigua's governor announced he had uncovered a plot by Prince Klaas (Court), an enslaved man said to have been a king in the Gold Coast, to blow up a ball honouring King George II and touch off a general uprising; the colony executed 88 enslaved and free Black people, including Klaas, by burning, breaking on the wheel or gibbeting.
events.article:
Antigua

Caribbean

October–November 1736

Documented history

In 1736 Antigua's authorities said they had discovered a conspiracy led by an enslaved man called Prince Klaas (recorded as "Court" and also called Tackey), said to have been born around 1690 in what is now Ghana and brought to Antigua around 1701. The plan, as the governor described it, was to smuggle a ten-gallon barrel of gunpowder into a building and detonate it during a ball honouring King George II in late October 1736, killing the Europeans gathered there and signalling enslaved people on the surrounding plantations to rise and kill the white population, with the aim of establishing an African-governed state.

On the report of an enslaved informer, Klaas and 132 others were tried. Eighty-eight were executed: 77, including Klaas, were broken on the wheel or burned at the stake, and 6 were gibbeted (left to die in a metal cage); other accounts give 6 hanged and starved and 58 burned at the stake. Klaas was about 45 when he was executed in early November 1736. Some historians have questioned whether the colony's magistrates, in a state of panic, exaggerated or invented the scale of the plot.

events.title: The Guaraní War over the seven missions
events.description: When the 1750 Treaty of Madrid gave the seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River to Portugal, their Guaraní refused to leave; a joint Spanish–Portuguese army defeated them at Caiboaté on February 10, 1756, killing 1,511 Guaraní for four European dead.
events.article:
Misiones Orientales, east of the Uruguay River

South America

1754 – 10 February 1756 (Caiboaté)

Documented history

The Treaty of Madrid set the Uruguay River as the border between Spanish and Portuguese territory, and the seven missions east of it, with 26,362 inhabitants by a Jesuit census, were to be dismantled and moved west. For most of the missions' history the Guaraní had fought Luso-Brazilian slavers, the bandeirantes, who sought to capture them to sell in Brazil.

In 1754 the Jesuits surrendered the missions, but the Guaraní, led by Sepé Tiaraju, refused to relocate; Spanish and Portuguese forces sent in July 1754 failed to remove them. On 10 February 1756, 3,000 Spanish and Portuguese soldiers fought the Guaraní at Caiboaté: 1,511 Guaraní were killed and four Europeans. The army occupied the seven missions; Spain and Portugal annulled the treaty in 1761.

events.title: Tacky's Revolt in Jamaica
events.description: On Easter Monday, 7 April 1760, an enslaved Fante leader named Tacky led an uprising in Jamaica that seized plantations and a fort before being put down over many months; a second rising broke out in the west under Apongo in May, and scattered guerrilla resistance continued into 1761.
events.article:
St. Mary and Westmoreland parishes, Jamaica

Caribbean

7 April 1760 – late 1761

Documented history

On 7 April 1760, Tacky, a Fante royal from present-day Ghana enslaved on a Jamaican plantation, led an uprising that captured the Frontier and Trinity plantations and took nearly four barrels of gunpowder and 40 firearms from Fort Haldane. In May a second rising broke out in Westmoreland led by Apongo. British forces, helped by Jamaican Maroons bound by treaty to suppress revolts, hunted down the rebels; a Maroon marksman named Davy shot Tacky dead, and his head was displayed on a pole in Spanish Town.

About 60 white colonists and 60 free Black people were killed in the uprising; more than 1,100 rebels were killed and over 500 were captured and resold into slavery elsewhere. The revolt fragmented into guerrilla raids from the Cockpit Country that continued through 1761. The colonial assembly passed harsher slave laws afterward and banned the practice of Obeah.

Tacky's plan was to defeat the British and all slave masters and create a Jamaica as a separate and independent Black colony.

Tacky was a Fante king from the Gold Coast (modern Ghana) before he was enslaved on a Jamaican plantation; in 1759, after years of suffering there, he and allies named Yaw, Sobadu and Quao planned a rebellion in a hidden cave, with the support of Queen Nanny, also of Ghanaian descent.

events.title: Cuba's sugar boom and the slave trade that outlived its ban
events.description: After the British occupation of Havana in 1762 and the Haitian Revolution, Cuba became one of the world's largest sugar producers on enslaved African labour; more than a million Africans were brought to the island, and the trade went on until 1867, decades after Spain agreed to end it.
events.article:
Havana, Santiago de Cuba and the sugar districts of western Cuba

Caribbean

1762 – 1867

Documented history

Since the 1550s the Spaniards had relied on the Taíno for enslaved labour; as the Indigenous population declined from disease and warfare they introduced the chattel slavery of West Africans. Just over 40,000 enslaved people had been imported to the island in the 250 years before 1762.

In 1762 British forces under the Earl of Albemarle captured Havana and, during a year-long occupation, expanded the plantation system and imported 4,000 enslaved people from the British West Indies. Santiago de Cuba was authorized from 1789 as a port of arrival for the transatlantic trade. After the Haitian Revolution, Cuba's planters took much of the sugar market formerly held by Saint-Domingue and greatly expanded their imports from Africa: between 1791 and 1805, 91,211 enslaved people entered through Havana.

An Anglo-Spanish treaty of 1817 gained Spain's agreement to end the trade north of the Equator, but 372,449 enslaved people were imported before the trade legally ended and at least 123,775 between 1821 and 1853; lax enforcement brought an estimated 90,000 from 1856 to 1860. The Cuban trade continued until 1867. In all, more than a million enslaved Africans were brought to Cuba, from over 20 African peoples, chief among them Lucumí (Yoruba), Mandingo, Ganga, Arará, Carabalí and Congo.

On the sugar plantations, work days lasted close to 20 hours at harvest; the enslaved were locked at night in barracoons, put in stocks for days or months, and whipped, pregnant women included. The Spanish Black Code of 1789 limited lashings to 25, but planters flouted it.

events.title: Smallpox blankets at Fort Pitt
events.description: During Pontiac’s War, the officers at besieged Fort Pitt gave Native emissaries two blankets and a handkerchief from the fort’s smallpox hospital on June 24, 1763, while the commander-in-chief Jeffery Amherst proposed sending smallpox among the tribes.

Fort Pitt (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania)

North America

June 24, 1763 (Amherst’s letters June–July 1763)

Adair, born in Ireland about 1709, came to South Carolina in 1735, traded with the Catawba and Cherokee and from 1744 lived chiefly among the Chickasaw. He compiled his notes into a book published in London in 1775 by Edward and Charles Dilly.

events.title: The Great Hurricane of 1780
events.description: The Great Hurricane of 9–18 October 1780 tore through the Lesser Antilles with winds estimated near 200 mph, killing about 22,000 people across Barbados, St. Lucia, Martinique and other islands, making it the deadliest hurricane recorded in the Atlantic; enslaved plantation labourers, housed in the flimsiest buildings and given no warning, made up the great majority of the dead.
events.article:
Barbados, St. Lucia, Martinique, St. Vincent, St. Eustatius and Dominica

Caribbean

9–18 October 1780

Documented history

The Great Hurricane struck the Lesser Antilles from 9 to 18 October 1780, reaching Barbados on 10 October with gusts estimated at 200 mph, then moving through St. Vincent, St. Lucia, Martinique, St. Eustatius, Dominica and on to Puerto Rico and Bermuda.

The storm killed roughly 22,000 people in total, the highest death toll of any Atlantic hurricane on record: about 4,300 in Barbados, 6,000 in St. Lucia, 9,000 in Martinique and 4,000–5,000 on St. Eustatius. Martinique's capital, St. Pierre, was almost completely demolished, and a 20-foot storm surge struck St. Vincent. Warring British and French fleets in the region at the time added to the toll.

events.title: The rebellion of Túpac Amaru II
events.description: In November 1780 the kuraka José Gabriel Condorcanqui, taking the name Túpac Amaru II, led Quechua, Aymara and mestizo rebels against Spanish rule and the forced labour of the mita; he was captured and torn apart in Cusco on May 18, 1781, and the rising went on to 1783 at a cost estimated at 100,000 indigenous dead.
events.article:
Cusco, Tinta and the southern Andes, Peru

South America

4 November 1780 – 1783; Túpac Amaru II executed 18 May 1781

Documented history

The rebellion arose against the Bourbon Reforms, which among other things forced the indigenous population to mine under the mita, largely at the Cerro Rico of Potosí; among Túpac Amaru II's proclamations were the freedom of the indigenous people and the abolition of slavery. It began on 4 November 1780 with the seizure of the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, hanged on 10 November before thousands.

Betrayed after defeats at Combapata and Checacupe in April 1781, Túpac Amaru II was sentenced on 15 May and on 18 May forced to watch the execution of his wife, Micaela Bastidas, and one of his children; four horses failed to tear his limbs apart, and he was beheaded in the Plaza de Armas of Cusco. His relatives and Túpac Katari carried on until 1783. The death toll is estimated at 100,000 indigenous people and 10,000–40,000 non-natives. It was the largest revolt in the Americas before the Spanish American wars of independence and the Haitian Revolution.

events.title: Túpac Katari and the siege of La Paz
events.description: The Aymara leader Túpac Katari raised some 40,000 men and besieged La Paz from March 1781; the siege was broken in October, and he was captured and executed by quartering in November 1781, with his wife Bartolina Sisa and his sister Gregoria Apaza later executed too.
events.article:
La Paz and El Alto, Upper Peru (Bolivia)

South America

13 March – November 1781

Documented history

Julián Apasa took the name Túpac Katari to honour the rebels Tomás Katari and Túpac Amaru. In 1781 he raised an army of some 40,000 and laid siege to La Paz on 13 March, holding court with his wife Bartolina Sisa in El Alto; the first siege lasted 109 days, from March until June, and the city held out with troops sent from Buenos Aires.

By 5 August he besieged the city again, joined by Andrés Túpac Amaru; the siege was broken by royalist forces on 17 October 1781. Betrayed by some of his followers, he was captured on the night of 9 November and executed by quartering. His reported last words were 'I die but will return tomorrow as thousand thousands'. Bartolina Sisa and Gregoria Apaza were also executed. In 2005 Bolivia declared Julián Apaza and Bartolina Sisa national Aymara heroes.

events.title: The Haitian Revolution
events.description: Enslaved Africans in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in August 1791 and, after twelve years of war, founded the independent state of Haiti on 1 January 1804, one of the only slave rebellions in history to found a state.
events.article:
Saint-Domingue (Haiti)

Caribbean

21 August 1791 – 1 January 1804

Documented history

The signal for the revolt was given at a ceremony at Bois Caïman in August 1791; within ten days the enslaved held the whole Northern Province. Toussaint Louverture rose to lead the revolution; he was later seized by the French, shipped to France and died months later in prison at Fort-de-Joux.

The war ended with Haitian victory and independence on 1 January 1804. In 1825 France, with warships off the coast, forced Haiti to pay 150 million gold francs to former slaveholders as the condition of recognition; the sum was later reduced to 90 million.

events.title: The Second Maroon War and the deportation of the Trelawny Maroons
events.description: An eight-month war in 1795–1796 between the British and the Trelawny Town Maroons of Jamaica ended with Governor Lord Balcarres deporting about 581 Maroons to Nova Scotia despite the British commander's earlier promise against transportation; after a harsh winter there, the Maroons petitioned to move on and resettled in the new colony of Sierra Leone by the start of the nineteenth century.

events.title: Haiti's founder, Dessalines, is assassinated by his own generals
events.description: Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who had led Haiti's independence in 1804 and declared himself Emperor, was ambushed and killed on October 17, 1806 by a conspiracy of his own officers, including Alexandre Pétion, after his land-redistribution and forced-labor policies turned the new elite and the formerly enslaved population against him.
events.article:

Documented history

After declaring Haiti's independence in 1804, Jean-Jacques Dessalines ruled as Emperor Jacques I and enforced a plantation-labor system to rebuild the devastated economy, a policy the newly freed population experienced as a return to the conditions of slavery. His land-redistribution plans also alienated the mixed-race landowning elite, and senior military officers grew to resent his autocratic rule.

Disaffected officers under his own command, including Alexandre Pétion and Étienne-Élie Gérin, organized a conspiracy against him. On October 17, 1806, Dessalines was ambushed at Pont-Rouge (then called Larnage), just north of Port-au-Prince, and killed; accounts differ on whether he was shot, stabbed, or struck with a sabre, but his body was reportedly dismembered by a mob afterward. A woman named Dédée Bazile gathered his remains and arranged his burial at the Church of Sainte-Anne.

Dessalines's death split Haiti into a northern kingdom under Henri Christophe and a southern republic under Pétion, a division that lasted until Christophe's successor was overthrown and Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified the country in 1820.

events.title: Henri Christophe builds the Kingdom of Haiti and the Citadelle
events.description: After Haiti split following Dessalines's 1806 assassination, Henri Christophe ruled the north, proclaiming himself King Henry I on 28 March 1811 and building the Citadelle Laferrière and the Sans-Souci Palace before his death in 1820 ended the kingdom.

Following the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806, Haiti split between a northern state under Henri Christophe and a southern republic led by Alexandre Pétion. Christophe proclaimed the Kingdom of Haiti on 28 March 1811 and was crowned King Henry I on 2 June 1811.

Christophe's government organized agricultural workers under a military-style system of forced labour, caporalisme agraire, to keep sugar and coffee exports running. He used this labour, along with the kingdom's resources, to build six castles, eight palaces including the Sans-Souci Palace (largely completed by 1813), the Royal Chapel of Milot, and the Citadelle Laferrière, a mountaintop fortress built to defend the north against a feared French invasion to restore slavery.

Christophe suffered a stroke in August 1820 and, facing an uprising, shot himself at the Citadelle on 8 October 1820. His son and heir, Jacques-Victor Henry, was proclaimed king but was hanged by the insurgents ten days later, on 18 October 1820; Jean-Pierre Boyer, who had succeeded Pétion as president of the south in 1818, then reunified the country.

events.description: Andrew Jackson’s army crushed the Red Stick Creeks at Horseshoe Bend on March 27, 1814, killing at least 800 of about 1,000 warriors; the Treaty of Fort Jackson then forced the Creek Nation to give up more than 21 million acres.
events.article:
Alabama and Georgia (Creek country)

North America

1813 – August 1814; Horseshoe Bend, March 27, 1814

Documented history

The Red Sticks, a Muscogee faction resisting US expansion, attacked Fort Mims on August 30, 1813. On March 27, 1814 Jackson’s troops with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies stormed the Red Stick camp at Tohopeka on the Tallapoosa River. The National Park Service counts at least 800 of Chief Menawa’s 1,000 Red Sticks dead, 557 on the field and 200–300 in the river; Jackson lost 49 killed. Afterwards Jackson’s troops cut bridle reins from the skin of the dead and counted bodies by cutting off the tips of their noses.

The wounded Menawa led about 20 survivors across the river to join the Seminole in Spanish Florida. In August 1814 the Treaty of Fort Jackson ended the war and forced the Creek confederacy to surrender its land in what is now southern Georgia and central Alabama; Alabama was carved from it and admitted in 1819.

Quotes and sources

The Native Americans resisted Anglo-American encroachment on their lands after 1800 as best they could, in the Creek wars of 1813 and 1836 and the wars with the Seminoles that lasted into the 1850s: they fought hard and had much integrity. The southeastern nations who tried to imitate the whites, taking up private land and slaves, were called “civilized” for it.

events.title: The Royal Decree of Graces settles Puerto Rico with Europeans
events.description: On 10 August 1815 Ferdinand VII granted free land and incentives to Spaniards and other Catholic Europeans to settle Puerto Rico, to build a loyal population and a plantation economy worked by enslaved Africans and poor jornaleros; it 'whitened' the island into the 1850s.
events.article:
Puerto Rico

Caribbean

10 August 1815; settlement to the 1850s

Documented history

On 10 August 1815 King Ferdinand VII approved a royal decree of graces opening Puerto Rico to trade with countries in good standing with Spain and granting free land and incentives to Spaniards willing to settle. An earlier decree of 1789 had granted Spanish subjects the right to purchase slaves and to take part in the transatlantic slave trade.

By 1825 Spain had lost all its American possessions but Puerto Rico and Cuba. Fearing the native-born mixed-race criollos would follow Haiti and the mainland into independence, the Crown revived the decree and distributed it across Europe to attract settlers who would be more loyal, on condition of loyalty to the Crown and allegiance to the Roman Catholic Church. Corsicans, Italians, French, Portuguese, Irish, Scots, Germans and others came from 1830 onward.

The settlers built sugarcane, coffee and tobacco plantations on enslaved African labour and needy jornaleros. The decree attracted many European immigrants, in effect 'whitening' the island into the 1850s; heavy immigration swelled the population to about one million by the end of the century, decreasing the proportion of Africans. Spain abolished the slave trade to its colonies on 25 June 1835, but slavery was not abolished in Puerto Rico until 1873.

events.title: The destruction of the Negro Fort
events.description: On July 27, 1816 a US force sent on Andrew Jackson’s orders destroyed the Negro Fort on the Apalachicola, a stronghold of free Black people and their Native allies in Spanish Florida, when a heated cannonball struck its powder magazine.
events.article:
Prospect Bluff, Apalachicola River, Spanish Florida

North America

July 27, 1816

Documented history

The British built the fort at Prospect Bluff in 1814 during the War of 1812 and left its arms behind. Fugitive slaves had sought refuge in Florida for generations, received by the Seminoles; the settlement at the fort became “the largest concentration of refugees from chattel slavery in the South between the end of the Revolution and the Civil War”, a Black Seminole stronghold under the command of Garçon, a former slave from Pensacola.

Jackson ordered General Gaines to destroy it and “return the stolen negroes and property to their rightful owners.” Garçon refused to surrender and raised a red flag of no quarter. On July 27, 1816 a heated cannonball landed in the magazine and the explosion was heard more than 100 miles away; almost every source says all but about 60 of the 334 occupants were killed at once, many of them women and children. Garçon and a Choctaw chief, among the few survivors, were handed to the Creek allies, who shot Garçon and scalped the chief.

events.title: Bussa's Rebellion in Barbados
events.description: On 14–16 April 1816 an enslaved African-born man named Bussa led the largest slave revolt in Barbadian history, with about 5,000 enslaved people rising across the island; colonial militia crushed the revolt within three days, killing Bussa and 50 others in battle and executing 214 more afterward.
events.article:
Barbados

Caribbean

14–16 April 1816

Documented history

Bussa, an African-born enslaved man likely of Coromantee or Igbo descent, led a revolt that broke out on 14 April 1816 and lasted until 16 April. About 400 enslaved people fought actively, out of roughly 5,000 who joined the uprising across the island.

British forces lost only one soldier and one civilian. Of the rebels, 50 were killed in the fighting, including Bussa, while the revolt continued briefly under his surviving forces; afterward colonial authorities executed 214 more enslaved people, exiled 170, and mutilated many others. It was the largest slave revolt in Barbadian history and the first of three major revolts (with the Demerara rebellion of 1823 and Jamaica's Baptist War of 1831–1832) that helped push Britain toward abolition.

events.title: The First Seminole War and the taking of Florida
events.description: Andrew Jackson led US forces into Spanish Florida in 1817–1818, burning Seminole, Miccosukee and Black Seminole towns; Spain then ceded Florida to the United States in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819.
events.article:
Spanish Florida

North America

1816–1818; Florida ceded 1819, transferred 1821

Documented history

After the destruction of the Negro Fort, border clashes came to a head in December 1817, when the War Department sent Andrew Jackson to bring the Seminoles under control. Breaking up the maroon communities was one of his major objectives. His forces destroyed Fowltown and other Seminole, Miccosukee and Black Seminole towns across northern Florida in 1818; on April 16, 1818, at the Suwannee River town of the Seminole leader Bolek (Bowlegs), they burned 400 maroon and Seminole homes and destroyed their food supplies. Jackson also seized San Marcos de Apalache and briefly occupied Pensacola.

Spain, no longer able to defend Florida, agreed in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 to cede it to the United States, and the transfer took place in 1821.

events.title: Bolívar's pledge to Pétion and the slow end of slavery from Venezuela to Peru
events.description: In 1816 Simón Bolívar won arms and money from Haiti's president Alexandre Pétion by pledging to free the slaves of the lands he took; yet the republics freed only the newborn at first, and slavery lasted until 1851 in Colombia and Ecuador, 1854 in Venezuela and Peru, and 1869 in Paraguay.
events.article:
Haiti, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Paraguay

South America

1816 (Haiti) – 1854 (Venezuela and Peru)

Documented history

Forced into exile on Jamaica after Spanish forces subdued New Granada in 1815, Bolívar reached Les Cayes in Haiti on 24 December and met Pétion on 2 January 1816; after he pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, Pétion gave him money and military supplies. Realising the importance of Black soldiers, Bolívar declared the abolition of slavery in 1812 and again in 1816.

After independence, the Congress of Cúcuta (1821) passed a law of free womb, manumission and abolition of the slave trade for what is now Colombia and Venezuela. Slavery was finally abolished in Colombia in 1851 and in Ecuador in 1851; in Venezuela on 24 March 1854, when fewer than 24,000 slaves remained; and in Peru in 1854 by President Ramón Castilla. Paraguay adopted a free womb law in 1842 and abolished slavery for all ages in 1869.

events.title: Central America's independence and the abolition of slavery
events.description: Central America declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821 and, after a brief union with Mexico, formed the Federal Republic of Central America, which abolished slavery by federal decree on 17 April 1824.
events.article:
Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica

Central America

September 15, 1821; slavery abolished April 17, 1824

Documented history

The provinces of Central America became independent of the Spanish Empire on 15 September 1821 and of the First Mexican Empire on 1 July 1823. The Federal Republic of Central America, joining Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, adopted its constitution on 22 November 1824; it had 1,287,491 people in 1824 and dissolved in 1839.

Slavery was abolished on 17 April 1824 by federal decree. Indigenous slaves had built and maintained Central America's roads, and their construction and upkeep nearly ended with abolition. Indigenous tribute had been abolished in 1811; in El Salvador in 1833 the Indigenous laborer Anastasio Aquino led 2,000 followers in rebellion after killings of Indigenous people, and was executed that July.

events.title: Sugar slavery in Puerto Rico: Marcos Xiorro's conspiracy and Prim's Bando
events.description: As sugar and slavery grew in 19th-century Puerto Rico, the enslaved conspired and revolted more than twenty times; in 1821 Marcos Xiorro planned a revolt against the planters, and on 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim imposed the Bando contra la Raza Africana to control all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved.
events.article:
Bayamón and across Puerto Rico

Caribbean

July 1821; 31 May 1848

Documented history

In the 19th century Spain established and expanded sugar cane production in Puerto Rico, and slavery increased. By 1873 the enslaved had carried out more than twenty revolts, some of great political importance, such as the Ponce and Vega Baja conspiracies.

In July 1821 the enslaved Marcos Xiorro planned and conspired to lead a revolt against the sugar planters and the Spanish colonial government. The conspiracy was suppressed, but Xiorro achieved legendary status among the enslaved and is part of Puerto Rico's heroic folklore.

Planters, nervous at the number of the enslaved, ordered restrictions on their movement; black Puerto Ricans were made to carry a notebook, the libreta, to move around the island. On 31 May 1848 Governor Juan Prim, fearing an independence or slave revolt, imposed draconian laws, the Bando contra la Raza Africana, to control the behaviour of all black Puerto Ricans, free or enslaved. Juan de la Pezuela replaced Prim that same year. In the Grito de Lares of 1868, free blacks who resented the libreta system burned their notebooks.

They refused to let them go.

There were plantations in Latin America and the Caribbean as in the United States, renamed haciendas: as the southern kingdom was known for cotton, Ephraim's captivity and hard labour was in sugar. For anyone who says Puerto Ricans were not slaves: slavery was abolished in Puerto Rico in 1873, and for slavery to be abolished it had to exist.

planned for 14 July 1822; Vesey hanged 2 July 1822

Likely born into slavery in St. Thomas, Vesey won a lottery and bought his freedom, worked as a carpenter and in 1818 helped found the African Methodist Episcopal congregation now known as Mother Emanuel. He drew on the Bible to inspire hope for freedom.

events.title: Denmark Vesey conspiracy, 1822
events.description: Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter in Charleston, South Carolina, planned a large-scale slave rebellion for June 1822. Though the plot was discovered before it could be executed, Vesey and others were tried, convicted, and executed.
events.article:
Charleston, South Carolina

Southern United States

June 1822

Documented history

Denmark Vesey was a free Black carpenter who lived in Charleston, South Carolina. He had purchased his freedom in 1800 and acquired property and skills that gave him status in the Black community. However, he remained outraged by slavery and the oppression of Black people.

Beginning around 1820, Vesey planned a large-scale rebellion intended to involve thousands of enslaved and free Black people in Charleston and the surrounding area. He planned to seize weapons from a government arsenal and kill white people before escaping to Haiti.

In May 1822, a enslaved house servant revealed the plot to white authorities. A militia company arrested suspected conspirators, and trials began in June 1822. Vesey and five other alleged leaders were convicted and executed by hanging on July 2, 1822. Approximately 35 other Black people were convicted and either executed or transported out of the state.

The Vesey conspiracy terrified white Charlestonians and led to the implementation of even stricter controls on the Black population. Though the rebellion never occurred, Vesey's planning demonstrated significant resistance to slavery.

events.title: Pichincha and Ayacucho: the end of Spanish rule in the Andes
events.description: Bolívar's general Antonio José de Sucre defeated the royalists on the slopes of Pichincha above Quito on May 24, 1822 and at Ayacucho on December 9, 1824, securing the independence of Ecuador within Gran Colombia and of Peru, and ending the Spanish American wars of independence.
events.article:
Quito, Ecuador and Ayacucho, Peru

South America

24 May 1822 (Pichincha) – 9 December 1824 (Ayacucho)

Documented history

Guayaquil proclaimed its independence on October 9, 1820. Sucre, Bolívar's most trusted subordinate, took command of a patriot army there, and on 24 May 1822, on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano 3,500 metres above sea level beside Quito, defeated the royalist army of Melchor Aymerich, liberating Quito and the provinces of its Audiencia, from which Ecuador would emerge. Gran Colombia was dissolved in 1831.

On 9 December 1824 Sucre's independentist army met the royalists at Pampa de Ayacucho near Quinua; Viceroy José de la Serna was wounded, and his second in command signed the capitulation of the royalist army. The battle secured the independence of Peru and is considered in Peru the end of the Spanish American wars of independence.

Invading from Colombia in 1822, the armies of Simón Bolívar and Sucre came to the aid of the Ecuadorian rebels, and on May 24 Sucre won at Pichincha.
