events.title: Haiti unifies Hispaniola under Boyer
events.description: President Jean-Pierre Boyer, who had reunified Haiti in 1820, marched an army of 12,000 into the newly independent Republic of Spanish Haiti and entered Santo Domingo on 9 February 1822, ruling the whole island until Dominican nationalists broke away on 27 February 1844.
events.article:
Santo Domingo and all of Hispaniola

Caribbean

9 February 1822 – 27 February 1844

Documented history

Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified Haiti's north and south in 1820 after Henri Christophe's death. When the Spanish-speaking east briefly declared itself the independent Republic of Spanish Haiti in late 1821, Boyer marched in with 12,000 soldiers in February 1822 and formally entered Santo Domingo on 9 February 1822, unifying the whole island of Hispaniola under Haitian rule for the next twenty-two years.

Boyer's government forbade white elites from owning land and forcibly stripped major Dominican landowning families of their property; it tried and largely failed to force the export-crop production of the 1826 and 1838 Code Rural on the east, and to pay France's 150-million-franc independence indemnity it imposed heavy taxation and let occupying soldiers commandeer food and supplies by force, reducing Dominicans to a position the Code Rural had already made of Haiti's own peasantry.

Boyer lost the support of the Haitian elite and was ousted in 1843, replaced by Charles Rivière-Hérard. On 27 February 1844 Dominican nationalists led by Juan Pablo Duarte and the secret society La Trinitaria seized Santo Domingo and declared the independent Dominican Republic, ending the twenty-two-year unification.

Quotes and sources

Fast forward to 1822, Haiti, trying to protect itself from being invaded or colonized again, occupied the eastern part of the island, which had recently won independence from Spain. This is where the complicated relationship began. At first, some Dominicans were relieved at being free from European rule, but that didn't last long. During Haiti's 22-year occupation, it abolished slavery, redistributed land, broke up the Catholic Church's power, and pushed for French to replace Spanish.

The class frames the 1822-1844 occupation as Haiti protecting itself from being invaded or recolonized again, and credits it with abolishing slavery, redistributing land, breaking the Catholic Church's power in the east, and pushing French to replace Spanish; it marks this occupation as the start of "the complicated relationship" between Haiti and the Dominican Republic that the class traces through to the Parsley Massacre and the 2013 nationality ruling.

events.title: The Demerara rebellion
events.description: On 18–20 August 1823 between 9,000 and 15,000 enslaved people across some 37 plantations in Demerara, British Guiana, rose up under Jack Gladstone and his father Quamina after wrongly believing Parliament had already freed them; colonial forces killed hundreds suppressing the revolt, executed 27 rebels, killed Quamina and left his body on a gibbet, and the death in prison of the missionary John Smith, convicted alongside them, galvanised British abolitionists.
events.article:
Demerara, British Guiana

Caribbean

18–20 August 1823

Documented history

On 18–20 August 1823, between 9,000 and 15,000 enslaved people across about 37 estates on Demerara's east coast rose up, led by Jack Gladstone, an enslaved man on the Success plantation, and his father Quamina, along with other members of their church. The revolt was triggered by a mistaken belief that Parliament in London had already abolished slavery, combined with harsh plantation conditions and religious restrictions.

Colonial forces under Governor John Murray suppressed the rising, killing between 200 and 500 enslaved people; bodies were left on public display for months as a warning. Twenty-seven rebels were executed, out of 45 death sentences handed down. Jack Gladstone was captured on 6 September and deported, probably to Saint Lucia; Quamina was killed by trackers and his body was hung on a gibbet. The English Congregationalist missionary John Smith, tried alongside the rebels and sentenced to death, died in prison awaiting the outcome of his appeal; his case became a rallying point for the British abolitionist movement in the years before the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.

events.title: The Supreme Court’s Indian cases: discovery, dependency and Worcester
events.description: In three cases Chief Justice John Marshall’s court laid down the doctrine of discovery (1823), called the Cherokee a “domestic dependent nation” (1831), and upheld Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia (1832), a ruling that did not save them from removal.
events.article:

North America

February 28, 1823; March 18, 1831; March 3, 1832

Documented history

In Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823) Marshall set out the “discovery doctrine”: a European power gains sovereignty over the land it discovers and the exclusive right to extinguish the Native occupants’ “right of occupancy”. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (March 18, 1831) he held that the Cherokee Nation was not a foreign nation but a “domestic dependent nation”, its relation to the United States like that of “a ward to its guardian”.

In Worcester v. Georgia (March 3, 1832) the Court struck down Georgia’s law barring non-Natives from Cherokee land without a state license, building the foundations of tribal sovereignty. Jackson wrote that the decision “has fell still born”; the words “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it!” are believed to be apocryphal. On December 29, 1835 a few Cherokees without authority signed the removal Treaty of New Echota; Justice Stephen Breyer later observed that the Cherokee nation was the “obvious loser”.

events.title: France extorts a 150-million-franc independence debt from Haiti
events.description: On April 17, 1825, French King Charles X, backing his demand with fourteen warships, ordered Haiti to pay 150 million francs as compensation to former French slaveholders in exchange for recognizing its independence; the debt and the loans taken to pay it burdened Haiti's economy for over a century.
events.article:
Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and Paris, France

Caribbean

April 17, 1825 ordinance; reduced February 12, 1838; last indemnity payment 1883; final related debt retired 1947

Documented history

On April 17, 1825, Charles X issued an ordinance demanding Haiti pay 150 million francs in five annual installments of 30 million, as compensation for the property, including enslaved people, that French colonists had lost in the Haitian Revolution, and requiring Haiti to halve its import duties for French merchants. France delivered the ultimatum by force: Baron de Mackau arrived at Port-au-Prince on July 3, 1825, aboard the warship La Circe, and a fleet eventually totaling fourteen French warships carrying 528 cannons backed the demand. President Jean-Pierre Boyer accepted the terms rather than risk invasion and the restoration of slavery.

Haiti could not pay from its own revenue and borrowed from French banks to make the first payments, compounding the debt with interest -- commonly called Haiti's "double debt." On February 12, 1838, France reduced the remaining balance to 90 million francs, payable over 30 years. Haiti made its last indemnity remittance in 1883, but loans taken to service that debt were not fully repaid, to the National City Bank of New York, until 1947. A 2022 New York Times analysis estimated the debt and its associated loans removed between $21 billion and $115 billion of economic growth from Haiti over two centuries.

events.title: Nat Turner's rebellion and aftermath, 1831
events.description: Nat Turner led an uprising of enslaved people in Southampton County, Virginia, in August 1831, killing approximately 55 white people before being captured and executed. The rebellion shocked the nation and intensified debates over slavery.
events.article:

Southern United States

August 1831

Documented history

Nat Turner was an enslaved preacher in Southampton County, Virginia. He believed himself called by God to end slavery and planned a systematic uprising among enslaved people in the county.

On August 21-22, 1831, Turner and a group of approximately 70 enslaved men and women launched a coordinated attack on white households in Southampton County. Using axes, hatchets, and other weapons, they killed approximately 55 white people, including women and children.

Militia and federal troops were quickly mobilized to suppress the rebellion. Over the following weeks, most of the rebels were captured and executed. Turner remained at large for two months before being captured on October 30, 1831. He was tried, convicted, and executed on November 11, 1831.

The rebellion shocked white Southerners and led to even more repressive measures against Black people and enslaved populations. However, Turner's rebellion became a symbol of resistance to slavery and is remembered as a significant act of defiance against the institution.

Though militarily defeated, the uprising's brutality and scale were widely reported in Britain and accelerated the passage of the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.

Pedro Montes and José Ruiz bought 53 of them and put them on the Amistad; on July 1 the Africans killed the captain and the cook and ordered the two to sail to Africa.

Montes and Ruiz steered north instead, and on August 24, 1839 the U.S. brig Washington seized the ship off Long Island. The Africans were jailed; abolitionists raised money for their defence, and John Quincy Adams argued their case before the Supreme Court, which decided on 9 March 1841 that, kidnapped and transported illegally, they were free and had never been slaves. The Court ordered their release; thirty-five survivors were returned to their homeland, the others having died at sea or in prison.

events.title: Triunvirato and La Escalera: the Year of the Lash
events.description: After a series of slave revolts in 1843, led at the Triunvirato plantation by the Yoruba women Carlota and Fermina, the Spanish authorities claimed to uncover La Escalera, a conspiracy to end slavery, and answered with a terror in which thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished.

In March, May and November 1843 a series of slave revolts occurred in Cuba. On 5 November 1843 the enslaved of the Triunvirato sugar mill in Matanzas rose, led by the African-born Lucumí women Carlota and Fermina with Eduardo, Narciso and Felipe Lucumí and Manuel Gangá; the revolt spread to the neighbouring Acaná estate and reached five plantations. Fermina had been whipped and kept in iron shackles for five months for running away. Carlota died in battle at the end of the revolt.

In December 1843 an enslaved woman, Polonia Gangá, told her master his property was about to be overtaken, and the authorities turned to stopping what they called the Conspiración de La Escalera, an alleged plot to abolish slavery. The British consul David Turnbull, already expelled, was convicted in absentia as its 'prime mover'. Historians have debated whether the conspiracy was real; there now seems to be a consensus that some revolt was planned.

The repression is called the Year of the Lash (Año del Cuero). La Escalera, 'the ladder', alludes to suspects being bound to ladders and whipped during interrogation. Thousands of Afro-Cubans, enslaved and free, were executed, imprisoned or banished; on 29 June 1844 a firing squad in Havana executed accused leaders. In 1912 Pedro Ivonnet of the Independent Party of Color called his party's exclusion "the epilogue of the trial of la Escalera."

events.title: Dred Scott v. Sandford Supreme Court decision, 1857
events.description: On March 6, 1857, the U.S. Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, ruled in Dred Scott v. Sandford that African Americans, whether enslaved or free, were not citizens of the United States and had no right to bring suit in federal court.

Dred Scott was an enslaved man whose master had taken him to Illinois (a free state) and then to the Wisconsin Territory (where slavery was prohibited). Scott later sued for his freedom, arguing that his residence in free territory had made him free.

Scott's case reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 1857. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, writing for the majority, ruled that Scott had no right to sue because African Americans, whether enslaved or free, were not citizens of the United States. Taney further ruled that the Constitution protected the right of slaveholders to hold property (enslaved people) even in free territories.

The Dred Scott decision was widely condemned in the North and contributed to rising tensions over slavery that ultimately led to the Civil War. The ruling was later overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments.

The decision represented a major defeat for African Americans and abolitionists, but it also galvanized opposition to slavery and contributed to the Republican Party's rise to political power.

events.title: The Dakota War and the hanging of the 38 at Mankato

events.title: The Morant Bay rebellion
events.description: On 11 October 1865 the Baptist preacher Paul Bogle led a protest march in Morant Bay, Jamaica, after a trespassing trial turned violent; Governor Edward John Eyre's forces killed more than 400 Black Jamaicans suppressing the rebellion and hanged Bogle and the politician George William Gordon, and the crisis led Britain to strip Jamaica of its elected assembly and rule it directly as a Crown Colony.

On 11 October, Bogle led hundreds of peasants in a march on the Morant Bay courthouse; the volunteer militia shot and killed seven men there, and 25 people died that day in the unrest that followed.

Governor Edward John Eyre declared martial law. Troops killed more than 400 Black Jamaicans and arrested more than 300 more during the suppression. The rebellion led Britain to abolish Jamaica's elected Assembly and govern it directly as a Crown Colony, ending planter political control; in 1969 Bogle and Gordon were both named Jamaican National Heroes.

events.title: 13th Amendment ratified, abolishing slavery nationwide, 1865
events.description: The 13th Amendment, abolishing slavery throughout the United States, was ratified on December 18, 1865. The amendment declared that 'neither slavery nor involuntary servitude' could exist in the United States.
events.article:
United States

United States

December 18, 1865

Documented history

Congress passed the 13th Amendment on January 31, 1865, and it was sent to the states for ratification. The amendment read: 'Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.'

The states ratified the amendment rapidly. Georgia became the final state needed to ratify, providing the three-fourths majority on December 18, 1865. Secretary of State William H. Seward officially proclaimed the amendment ratified on December 18, 1865.

The 13th Amendment legally ended the institution of slavery in the United States, though it permitted involuntary servitude as punishment for crime. This provision was used to justify convict leasing and chain gang labor in the South.

The ratification of the 13th Amendment represented the formal end of slavery but did not end racial discrimination or ensure Black freedom and equality. It was followed by the 14th Amendment (ratified 1868) guaranteeing citizenship and equal protection, and the 15th Amendment (ratified 1870) prohibiting race-based voting restrictions.

events.title: The Occupation of Araucanía
events.description: From 1861 to 1883 Chilean soldiers and settlers advanced into the Mapuche lands of Araucanía, independent through the whole colonial era, and incorporated them into Chile; thousands of Mapuche died by war and disease, chiefly smallpox, and their lands were reduced, plunging many into lasting poverty.

Araucanía had remained de facto independent through the colonial era. Economic and geopolitical reasons, with increasingly negative attitudes towards the Mapuche, led Chile to seek its incorporation by force if necessary. Colonel Cornelio Saavedra Rodríguez planned a state-led colonization influenced by the United States frontier; in 1861 he ordered Major Pedro Lagos to advance to the confluence of the Mulchén and Bureo rivers.

For ten years (1861–1871) the Mapuche could not stop the advance; the war brought famine in the winter of 1869, worsened by smallpox. After a decade of near peace, while Chile fought Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific, a large Chilean army reached the Cautín River in March 1881; a last coordinated Mapuche rising in November 1881 was defeated within days. The conflict killed thousands of Mapuche by warfare and disease, primarily smallpox, and the pillaging of the army and bandits and the reduction of their lands plunged many into poverty that has persisted for generations. It ran alongside Argentina's campaigns against the Mapuche of 1878–1885.

events.title: The Black Codes
events.description: In 1865 and 1866 the legislatures of the former slave states passed Black Codes: laws that limited the freedom of the newly emancipated and forced them back into labor for white employers.
events.article:
Mississippi, South Carolina and the other former Confederate states

Southern United States

1865–1866

Documented history

After chattel slavery was abolished throughout the United States in 1865, the former slave states of the South enacted Black Codes to restrict black citizens, especially the emancipated freedmen. Their defining feature was broad vagrancy laws, and they were particularly concerned with controlling the movement and labor of freedmen.

Mississippi was the first state to pass them. Its law allowed black people to rent land only within cities, required them to present written proof of employment each January, and made the lack of it vagrancy, punishable by arrest. South Carolina, Alabama and Louisiana followed in 1865, and Florida, Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina, Texas, Tennessee and Arkansas at the beginning of 1866.

The codes granted some limited rights, such as owning personal property and marrying, but black people were barred from testifying against white people and faced severe penalties for unemployment. Intense Northern reaction against the Mississippi and South Carolina laws led some later states to remove overt racial language, while keeping vagrancy and apprenticeship laws that worked to the same end.

events.title: Black Codes enacted during Reconstruction, 1865–1868
events.description: Following the Civil War, Southern states enacted Black Codes restricting the freedoms and rights of formerly enslaved people. These laws required freedmen to sign labor contracts, limited their property rights, and restricted their mobility.
events.article:
Southern United States

Southern United States

1865–1868

Documented history

After the Civil War ended in 1865, Confederate states were reconstructed under President Andrew Johnson's lenient Reconstruction policy. One of the first actions of newly reconstructed Southern legislatures was to enact 'Black Codes'—laws designed to control the newly freed population and restore white economic dominance.

Black Codes required freedmen and freedwomen to sign labor contracts with white employers, often for terms of a year or more. Laborers who left before the contract expired could be arrested and fined. Convict labor provisions allowed impoverished freedmen to be arrested and forced to work.

The codes restricted freedmen's property rights: in some states, freedmen could own property only in restricted areas. Curfews prevented freedmen from gathering after dark. Vagrancy laws authorized the arrest of unemployed freedmen. In some areas, freedmen were barred from owning weapons or attending school.

Northern Republicans condemned the Black Codes as a betrayal of the Civil War's purpose and the freedmen's expectations. The codes contributed to the rise of Radical Reconstruction and Reconstruction Act of 1867.

Pulaski, Tennessee

Southern United States

December 24, 1865 (founding); weakened by federal prosecutions from 1871

Documented history

The first Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, on December 24, 1865, by six former officers of the Confederate Army: Frank McCord, Richard Reed, John Lester, John Kennedy, J. Calvin Jones and James Crowe. It began as a fraternal social club.

It carried out widespread violence against black voters, officeholders and their white allies to undermine the Republican state governments and restore white Democratic control in the South. Federal Enforcement Acts and prosecutions beginning in 1871 significantly weakened it.

A second Klan was founded in 1915 atop Stone Mountain, Georgia, by William Joseph Simmons, drawing on the film The Birth of a Nation; it peaked in the 1920s and spread beyond the South. The earlier Klan had not worn white costumes or burned crosses; those elements came from Thomas Dixon's 1905 novel The Clansman, on which the film was based.

events.title: Forty acres taken back and the Freedman's Bank fails
events.description: Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 set aside land in plots of up to 40 acres for freed families, but President Andrew Johnson reversed the policy in 1865; the Freedman's Savings Bank, chartered the same year, failed in 1874 with the savings of its depositors.
events.article:
Sea Islands and coast of Georgia and South Carolina; Washington, D.C.

Southern United States

January 16, 1865 (Field Order No. 15) to 1874 (failure of the Freedman's Bank)

Documented history

On January 16, 1865, General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15, instructing officers to settle freed refugees on the Sea Islands and inland: 400,000 acres divided into plots of no more than 40 acres. Mules were not mentioned in the order, though some beneficiaries received them from the army.

Freed people widely expected to claim 40 acres of land. In 1865 Abraham Lincoln's successor, Andrew Johnson, tried to reverse the intent of the order and of similar provisions in the second Freedmen's Bureau bills; as one of the first acts of Reconstruction he ordered all land under federal control returned to the owners from whom it had been seized.

The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company was chartered by Congress on March 3, 1865, to collect deposits from Black people, especially the formerly enslaved. It opened 37 branches in 17 states and Washington, D.C., and collected funds from over 67,000 depositors, holding more than $3.7 million at its height in 1872. Its growth rested on false claims, mismanagement and fraud: its white officials made speculative and insider loans, and its advertising implied a government guarantee it did not have.

In March 1874 the trustees deposed its president, John W. Alvord, and elected Frederick Douglass. The bank failed in 1874, destroying the savings of many African Americans and, historians believe, their trust in financial institutions.

events.title: Convict leasing
events.description: Using the Thirteenth Amendment's exception for punishment of crime, Southern states leased prisoners, the great majority of them Black men convicted under the Black Codes and vagrancy laws, to planters and companies.
events.article:
The Southern states

Southern United States

Expanded after 1865; peaked about 1880; phased out after December 12, 1941

Documented history

Louisiana leased out convicted people as early as 1844, and the system expanded throughout most of the South with emancipation in 1865. Its constitutional basis was the 1865 Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude “except as a punishment for crime”.

Black Codes, pig laws and vagrancy laws criminalized unemployment, homelessness and changes of employment, creating a new criminal class of freed people. By the 1880s Black people made up 80 to 90 percent of those incarcerated in the South.

The system was highly lucrative: in 1898, 73 percent of Alabama's annual state revenue came from convict leasing. The practice peaked about 1880 and was gradually phased out after Attorney General Francis Biddle's Circular No. 3591 of December 12, 1941. In February 2018 the remains of 95 people, victims of convict leasing, were unearthed on a former sugar plantation in Sugar Land, Texas.

events.title: Sharecropping and the crop lien
events.description: After the Civil War most freed people, with no land, worked white-owned land for a share of the crop, bound by debt to the landowner or merchant.
events.article:
The cotton South

Southern United States

Widespread from Reconstruction (1865–1877); declined from the late 1930s and 1940s

Documented history

Under sharecropping, landowners provided land, housing, tools and seed, and merchants supplied food on credit; at the end of the season the cropper paid the owner a share of the crop, typically one-half to two-thirds. If what was left came to less than what he owed, he remained in debt. Under the crop lien the planter or merchant took the year's crop as collateral and settled the debt when it was sold.

Sharecropping became widespread in the South during Reconstruction (1865–1877), after President Johnson returned the land set aside by Sherman's Field Order No. 15. In Mississippi by 1900, 85 percent of black farmers were tenants or sharecroppers. Around Elaine, Arkansas, landowners kept sharecroppers in debt through plantation-store prices and underpayment for crops, and it was an unwritten law that a sharecropper could not leave until his debts were paid.

Traditional sharecropping declined after farm mechanization became economical in the late 1930s and early 1940s, and many sharecroppers moved to the cities.

events.title: The Buffalo Soldiers and the Indian Wars
events.description: From 1866 the U.S. Army raised all-black regiments, later called the Buffalo Soldiers, who served on the frontier and fought in the Western Indian Wars.
events.article:
The American West

Western United States

1866 (10th Cavalry formed September 21, 1866); Western Indian Wars 1867–1896

Documented history

Buffalo Soldiers were United States Army regiments composed exclusively of Black American soldiers, formed during the 19th century to serve on the American frontier. On September 21, 1866, the 10th Cavalry Regiment was formed at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Congress established them as the first all-black Army regiments in peacetime, and they were racially segregated.

They fought in the Western Indian Wars from 1867 to 1896, and also served in Cuba, the Philippines, Hawaii and Mexico. According to legend the name was given by the Apache and Cheyenne; 23 Buffalo Soldiers received the Medal of Honor during the Indian Wars.

In the 21st century their employment in the American Indian Wars has led some to call for a critical reappraisal of the regiments, seen by some as accessories to settler-colonial and westward expansion.

events.title: El Grito de Lares
events.description: On 23 September 1868 some 400–600 rebels of the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico took Lares and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; the revolt was crushed within a day and hundreds were imprisoned.
events.article:
Lares and San Sebastián del Pepino, Puerto Rico

Caribbean

23 September 1868

Documented history

Ramón Emeterio Betances and Segundo Ruiz Belvis founded the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico in exile in the Dominican Republic on 6 January 1868. Its cells, organized by Mathias Brugman, Mariana Bracetti and Manuel Rojas, brought together landowners, merchants, professionals, peasants and the enslaved; the economy, slavery and Spanish repression were the catalysts. Betances's arms ship was seized in Saint Thomas, and the plot was discovered in Camuy, so the leaders moved the date forward.

Some 400 to 600 rebels gathered at Manuel Rojas's estate and took Lares around midnight on 23 September 1868. In the church they placed the Lares flag on the altar and proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico under Francisco Ramírez Medina, offering freedom to the enslaved who joined them; free blacks burned their libretas. The next morning the rebels were repulsed at San Sebastián del Pepino; four of them died.

Spanish forces arrested more than 800 suspects; some 475 rebels were imprisoned in Arecibo, where they were tortured and humiliated, and on 17 November a military court sentenced them all to death, though they were later amnestied. The revolt failed, but Spain granted more political autonomy. The Lares flag is recognized as the first flag of Puerto Rico.

events.title: The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments and Black office-holders
events.description: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made the freed people citizens with equal protection of the laws, and the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote on account of race, colour or previous servitude; within decades Southern states had stripped most black men of the vote again.
events.article:
United States

United States

July 9, 1868 (14th); February 3, 1870 (15th)

Documented history

The Fourteenth Amendment was adopted on July 9, 1868, as one of the Reconstruction Amendments, a response to issues affecting freed slaves after the Civil War. Its Citizenship Clause superseded Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), which had held that Americans descended from African slaves could not become citizens.

The Fifteenth Amendment prohibits the federal government or any state from denying or abridging a citizen's right to vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." It was ratified on February 3, 1870, the third and last of the Reconstruction Amendments; no Democrat in either house voted for it.

Late nineteenth-century Supreme Court decisions read the amendment narrowly, and from 1890 to 1910 Southern Democrats adopted new state constitutions and Jim Crow laws that raised barriers to voter registration, removing most black voters from the rolls.

events.title: The Opelousas and Colfax massacres
events.description: Two of the bloodiest massacres of Reconstruction struck black Republicans in Louisiana: at Opelousas in 1868 and at the Colfax courthouse on Easter Sunday 1873.
events.article:
St. Landry Parish and Colfax, Grant Parish, Louisiana

Southern United States

September 28, 1868 (Opelousas); April 13, 1873 (Colfax)

Documented history

The Opelousas massacre in St. Landry Parish began on September 28, 1868, as tensions rose between white Democrats and Black Republicans after Louisiana's 1868 constitution gave Black men the vote. The white supremacist Knights of the White Camelia was thought to have 3,000 members in the parish. Estimates of the dead vary widely: Democratic papers reported 100 or fewer, Republicans 200 to 300, and other estimates 150 to 300 Black people and 30 to 50 whites.

On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, after the contested 1872 election, armed white men with rifles and a small cannon overpowered the Black freedmen and state militia holding the Grant Parish courthouse in Colfax. Between 62 and 153 Black men were murdered while surrendering, nearly another 50 of them later that night after being held prisoner. Many bodies were thrown into the Red River.

The federal convictions of a few perpetrators were appealed, and in United States v. Cruikshank (1876) the Supreme Court ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment's protections did not apply to individuals acting privately, ending federal prosecution of paramilitary groups such as the White League under the Enforcement Act of 1870.

Black families were shot in public, killed in their homes, hanged and drowned in the Red River at Colfax.

events.title: The Ten Years' War and the Protest of Baraguá
events.description: On 10 October 1868 Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves and proclaimed Cuba's independence, beginning a ten-year war; at its end Antonio Maceo refused, in the Protest of Baraguá, a peace that neither freed Cuba nor abolished slavery.
events.article:
Oriente and Camagüey, Cuba

Caribbean

10 October 1868 – 28 May 1878

Documented history

In the early morning of 10 October 1868 the sugar-mill owner Carlos Manuel de Céspedes issued the cry of independence at La Demajagua, freed his slaves and asked them to join the struggle, calling on men of all races to fight. It was the first of Cuba's three wars of liberation against Spain. Céspedes was killed by a Spanish patrol on 27 February 1874. Spain sent more troops after 1876, until they numbered more than 250,000.

The Pact of Zanjón of 10 February 1878 ended most of the fighting; its most significant reform was freedom for the enslaved who had fought on either side. Antonio Maceo and other Mambises met General Martínez Campos at Los Mangos de Baraguá on 15 March 1878 and rejected it, because it won neither independence nor the abolition of slavery. Maceo fled to Jamaica in May, and hostilities ended on 28 May 1878.

Losses are estimated at 50,000 dead on the Cuban side and 81,248 Spanish dead, 75,000 of them from disease.

events.title: Robert Smalls takes his seat in Congress
events.description: Robert Smalls, born enslaved in Beaufort in 1839, became a delegate to South Carolina's 1868 constitutional convention, a state legislator and a five-term congressman.
events.article:
Beaufort, South Carolina; Washington, D.C.

Southern United States

State offices 1868–1874; U.S. House 1875–1879, 1882–1883, 1884–1887

Documented history

Robert Smalls was born in Beaufort, South Carolina, on April 5, 1839, and served as a pilot in the United States Navy throughout the Civil War after he escaped slavery in 1862.

He was a member of the state constitutional convention in 1868, served in the South Carolina house from 1868 to 1870 and the state senate from 1870 to 1874, and was elected to Congress as a Republican, serving from March 4, 1875, to March 3, 1879. He was convicted of bribery in 1877 and fully pardoned by the governor in 1879. He served again from July 19, 1882, to March 3, 1883, after contesting an election, and from March 18, 1884, to March 3, 1887.

He was collector of the port of Beaufort from 1897 to 1913 and died there on February 23, 1915.

Quotes and sources

He was illiterate until the 1860s, learned to read in a couple of years as an adult, and became a successful politician who changed policies for black people during the time of Jim Crow. His story should be in every history book.

events.title: The Moret Law: free wombs in Cuba and Puerto Rico
events.description: The Moret Law of 4 July 1870 freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, the elderly and those who served Spain, beginning a gradual abolition in Cuba and Puerto Rico while owners were compensated.

4 July 1870

Documented history

After the U.S. Civil War, international pressure pushed Spain to end slavery in its last American colonies. The Moret Law, named after Segismundo Moret, Spain's Minister of Overseas Territories, was approved on 4 July 1870 for Cuba and later Puerto Rico; Spain also passed it hoping to preempt the independence movements.

It freed children born to enslaved mothers after 18 September 1868, and children under 14 were not to be separated from their mothers. It also freed the enslaved who served in the Spanish army, those over 60 and those owned by the government. The Spanish government compensated owners 125 pesetas for each person freed. Slavery was abolished in Puerto Rico, but not in Cuba, in 1873, and without exceptions in 1886.

events.description: Industrial-scale hide hunting, encouraged by the federal government to drive the Plains nations onto reservations, cut the bison herds that had numbered 25–30 million to fewer than 100 in the wild by the late 1880s.

events.title: Elijah McCoy, inventor of automatic lubrication, c.1844–1929
events.description: Elijah McCoy (c.1844–1929) was an African American inventor who created an automatic lubrication device for steam engines. His invention revolutionized railroad and steam-powered machinery maintenance and made him one of the most prolific Black inventors of the nineteenth century.
events.article:
United States

United States

c.1872–1920

Documented history

Elijah McCoy was born around 1844 in Colchester, Ontario, Canada, the son of enslaved people who had escaped to freedom. His family moved to Michigan when he was a boy. Lacking access to formal education suitable for Black students, McCoy worked as a fireman on railroad locomotives and observed the inefficiency of manually lubricating moving machinery.

In 1872, McCoy patented an automatic oilcup (lubricating device) that could oil moving machinery without shutting down the equipment. This invention dramatically improved the efficiency of steam engines and railroad locomotives. Over his lifetime, McCoy received at least 50 patents for his lubricating devices and other innovations, many of which were used widely by American industries.

McCoy's work was so well-regarded that railroad companies and manufacturers developed a reputation for demanding 'the real McCoy'—his genuine products—rather than inferior imitations. His success as an inventor and entrepreneur made him one of the most successful African American businessmen of the nineteenth century, though his race prevented him from receiving widespread public recognition during his lifetime.

events.title: The Little Bighorn and the taking of the Black Hills
events.description: After Custer announced gold in the Black Hills promised to the Sioux by the 1868 treaty, the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho destroyed his 7th Cavalry at the Little Bighorn on June 25–26, 1876; Congress then starved the Sioux into giving up the Black Hills.
events.article:
Little Bighorn River, Montana Territory; the Black Hills

North America

June 25–26, 1876; Black Hills taken February 28, 1877

Documented history

The Fort Laramie Treaty of April 29, 1868 set the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills, apart “for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians.” In 1874 Custer led an expedition into the Black Hills and announced the discovery of gold. On June 25–26, 1876 the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho, led by Crazy Horse and Gall and inspired by Sitting Bull’s visions, overwhelmed the 7th Cavalry on the Little Bighorn; 268 soldiers were killed.

Congress answered with what the Sioux call the “sell or starve” rider, cutting off all rations until they ceded the Black Hills, and the Act of February 28, 1877 removed the Black Hills from the reservation. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled that “a more ripe and rank case of dishonorable dealings will never, in all probability, be found in our history” and ordered compensation; the Sioux refused the money, which was worth over $1 billion by 2011, seeking the return of the land.

Crazy Horse was a man of war fit for the battle

The Gadites were men of war fit for the battle, with faces like lions, their war paint, swift as the roes upon the mountains, and able to bear buckler and sword and shoot with the bow.

The battle came because the government encroached on Native land after gold was found in the Black Hills, sacred to the Lakota.

events.title: The end of Reconstruction and the Jim Crow laws
events.description: The Compromise of 1877 ended federal military oversight of the South, and white-dominated legislatures enacted Jim Crow laws that segregated public life and took the vote from black citizens into the mid-20th century.
events.article:
Southern United States

Southern United States

1877 (Compromise of 1877) to the mid-20th century

Documented history

The Compromise of 1877 was an informal deal that settled the disputed 1876 presidential election: Democrats ended their filibuster of the certified results in exchange for the Republicans' ending military oversight of the South. When Rutherford B. Hayes took office he withdrew the last federal troops from the South, which historians largely regard as the end of Reconstruction. No written evidence of such a deal has ever been found.

The Jim Crow laws were state and local laws introduced in the Southern United States from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century that enforced racial segregation. They were enacted by white-dominated legislatures (Redeemers) to disenfranchise and remove the political and economic gains made by African Americans during Reconstruction, and were upheld in 1896 in Plessy v. Ferguson.

Facilities for African Americans were consistently inferior and underfunded, and companion laws excluded most African Americans from the vote in the South.

events.title: Carlisle and the Indian boarding schools

The United States Indian Industrial School at Carlisle, Pennsylvania, was founded in 1879 by Lieutenant Richard Henry Pratt under U.S. government authorization, in the Carlisle Barracks, and was the flagship Indian boarding school until 1918. events.title: Slavery ends in Cuba: the patronato and the decree of 1886
events.description: In 1880 Spain abolished slavery in Cuba gradually, binding the freed to work for their former masters for years at wages too low to live on; slavery was finally abolished by royal decree on 7 October 1886, making Cuba one of the last places in the hemisphere to end it.

Caribbean

In 1880 the Spanish legislature abolished slavery in Cuba in a form of gradual abolition: the law required the enslaved to continue to work for their masters for a number of years, in a kind of indentured servitude, for wages so low the freed could barely support themselves.

Slavery was abolished by Spanish royal decree on 7 October 1886, ahead of the schedule of 1888 promised at Zanjón, making Cuba one of the last countries in the Western Hemisphere, before only Brazil, to abolish it. Former slaves joined the ranks of farmers and the urban working class. More than 100,000 Chinese indentured workers had been brought in to replace African labour, and slave traders turned to other sources such as the Indians of Yucatán.

United States

United States

c.1880–1900

Documented history

Lewis Howard Latimer was born in 1848 in Chelsea, Massachusetts, to former enslaved parents. He worked his way from a humble background into technical work, learning drafting and engineering skills.

In 1880, Latimer patented an improved carbon filament for electric light bulbs, making them more efficient and longer-lasting than Thomas Edison's earlier design. His improvement, using a carbon rod instead of carbon paper, extended the filament's lifespan significantly.

Latimer worked for both Edison's company and the United States Electric Lighting Company, where he helped develop and commercialize electric lighting systems. He was also employed by Alexander Graham Bell, for whom he prepared technical drawings for patenting innovations.

Latimer's work was crucial to making electric lighting practical for widespread use. He authored 'Incandescent Electric Lighting,' a technical manual that became an industry standard. His contributions helped establish the electrical industry in America.

events.title: The Selkʼnam genocide in Tierra del Fuego

Companies paid their employees and hunters such as Julius Popper to kill or capture Selkʼnam people, and the Chilean and Argentine militaries attacked them during exploratory voyages.

The population fell from about 4,000 in the 1880s to a few hundred by the early 1900s; by 1930 only 100 Selkʼnam were alive.

events.title: The Berlin Conference divides Africa
events.description: At the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 fourteen colonial powers agreed the rules for claiming African territory, formalizing the Scramble for Africa.
events.article:
Berlin, Germany

Africa

November 15, 1884 – February 26, 1885

The Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 was a meeting of colonial powers that concluded with the signing of the General Act of Berlin, an agreement regulating European colonisation and trade in Africa. The conference of fourteen countries was organised by Otto von Bismarck at the request of Leopold II of Belgium. It met on 15 November 1884 and concluded on 26 February 1885.

The attendees agreed a common framework for recognising European "effective occupation" of African territory, and after the conference European claims on Africa increased with international legal recognition. The General Act can be seen as formalizing the Scramble for Africa and is sometimes cited as responsible for the "carve-up of Africa", though some scholars warn against overstating its role.

From 1885 to 1908 many atrocities were committed in the Congo Free State under the absolute rule of King Leopold II of Belgium, particularly associated with the labour policies used to collect natural rubber for export. At the Berlin Conference the European powers recognized the claims of a supposedly philanthropic organisation run by Leopold to most of the Congo Basin.

Dissenters were beaten or whipped, hostages were taken to ensure prompt collection, and punitive expeditions destroyed villages that refused. A central instrument of terror was the chicotte, a whip of raw hippopotamus hide. Combined with disease, famine, displacement and falling birth rates, the atrocities contributed to a sharp decline in the Congolese population; modern estimates range from 1.2 million to 10 million people. On 15 November 1908, under international pressure, Belgium annexed the territory as the Belgian Congo.

events.title: The Dawes Act breaks up reservation land
events.description: The General Allotment (Dawes) Act of February 8, 1887, authorized the President to break up tribal reservation land into individual allotments.
events.article:
United States (reservations west of the Mississippi)

Western United States

February 8, 1887

On February 8, 1887, Congress passed the Dawes Act, named for Senator Henry Dawes of Massachusetts and also known as the General Allotment Act. It authorized the President to break up reservation land, held in common by the members of a tribe, into small allotments for individuals registered on a tribal roll: a quarter-section to each head of a family, an eighth to each single person over eighteen.

The act treated Native Americans as individuals rather than as members of tribes, and the United States held each allotment in trust for twenty-five years.

events.title: Granville Woods, railroad telegraph innovations, 1887–1901
events.description: Granville Woods (1852–1910) was an African American inventor who developed electrical improvements for railroads, including the synchronous multiplex railway telegraph. He received more than 60 patents and competed directly with Thomas Edison.
events.article:
United States

United States

1887–1901

Documented history

Granville T. Woods was born in 1852 in Columbus, Ohio. He began his career as a railroad worker and gained practical knowledge of railroad operations and electrical systems.

In 1887, Woods invented the synchronous multiplex railway telegraph, which allowed train operators to communicate with each other and with stations. This innovation improved railroad safety by reducing collisions and enabling better coordination between trains.

Over his career, Woods received more than 60 patents for electrical and mechanical innovations, many related to railroads and electrical systems. Some of his patents were so valuable that Edison's company attempted to purchase them. Woods's work contributed significantly to the development of modern electrical systems.

Woods's life demonstrated both the technical brilliance of African American inventors and the racial barriers they faced. Despite his achievements, Woods remained largely unknown to the general public during his lifetime.

Arturo Alfonso Schomburg (24 January 1874 – 10 June 1938) was born in Santurce to Mary Joseph, a freeborn black midwife from St. Croix, and a merchant of German descent. When a grade-school teacher claimed that black people had no history, heroes or accomplishments, he determined to document the accomplishments of Africans and the diaspora.

He moved to New York in 1891, joined the Revolutionary Committee of Puerto Rico and in 1892 co-founded Las Dos Antillas, a club for the independence of Cuba and Puerto Rico. He became an important figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

In 1926 the New York Public Library's 135th Street branch bought his private collection of more than 4,000 books for $10,000, funded by the Carnegie Corporation; it became the basis of the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture in Harlem.

events.title: Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise address, 1895
events.description: On September 18, 1895, Booker T. Washington delivered his famous Atlanta Compromise address, advocating accommodation with segregation and focusing on economic self-improvement rather than political rights.
events.article:
Atlanta, Georgia

Southern United States

September 18, 1895

Documented history

Booker T. Washington was the principal of Tuskegee Institute, an African American educational institution in Alabama. He advocated a controversial approach to race relations based on economic development and vocational education rather than political activism.

On September 18, 1895, Washington addressed the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta. In his speech, which became known as the Atlanta Compromise, he argued that African Americans should focus on economic advancement and education rather than demand political and social equality immediately.

Washington's speech included the famous metaphor: 'In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.' This statement was interpreted as accepting segregation.

Washington's approach was controversial. Some, including W. E. B. Du Bois, criticized his accommodation with segregation as a betrayal of Black rights. Others praised his pragmatism. Washington's philosophy dominated Black education and leadership for a generation.

events.title: Cuba's War of Independence and Weyler's reconcentration camps
events.description: Cuba's last war against Spain began on 24 February 1895; to cut the rebels off from the people, General Valeriano Weyler forced the rural population into fortified towns, where at least 170,000 Cubans, about one in ten, died of disease and hunger.
events.article:
Cuba

Caribbean

24 February 1895 – 1898

Documented history

The insurrection organized by José Martí and Máximo Gómez began on 24 February 1895. Martí was killed soon after landing, on 19 May 1895 at Dos Ríos, but Gómez and Antonio Maceo carried the war across the island, reaching its western tip on 22 January 1896. Maceo, the 'Bronze Titan', was killed on 7 December 1896 in Havana province. Spain sent 220,285 soldiers to Cuba, the largest army to cross the Atlantic until World War II.

General Valeriano Weyler answered with periodic executions, mass exile, the destruction of farms and crops, and the reconcentration policy: rural Cubans had eight days to move into camps in fortified towns, and all who failed to obey were to be shot. Housing was decaying, food scarce and disease spread; by 1898 a third of the population had been moved into the camps. Historian John Lawrence Tone estimates that 155,000 to 170,000 civilians died, nearly 10% of the population; the policy is remembered as the first construction of modern concentration camps.

Weyler was dismissed in 1897 after the assassination of Prime Minister Cánovas; the policy was kept until March 1898. The final months of the war became the Spanish–American War.

events.title: The Foraker Act and the Insular Cases make Puerto Rico an 'unincorporated territory'
events.description: The Foraker Act of 12 April 1900 gave Puerto Rico a civil government whose governor, executive council and judges were appointed in Washington; in 1901 the Supreme Court's Insular Cases held that the Constitution did not fully apply there, calling the islands' peoples 'alien races'.
events.article:

Documented history

The Foraker Act, signed by President McKinley on 12 April 1900 and effective 1 May, replaced military rule with a civil government: a governor and an 11-member Executive Council appointed by the U.S. President, a 35-member elected House of Delegates, judges appointed by the President, and a non-voting Resident Commissioner in Congress. Congress could annul any law the island passed. It created a Puerto Rican citizenship and imposed tariffs on goods shipped to the United States.

In six opinions decided on 27 May 1901, among them Downes v. Bidwell, the Supreme Court held that full constitutional protection does not automatically extend to all places under American control, so that the people of unincorporated territories such as Puerto Rico, even if U.S. citizens, may lack some constitutional rights. Downes called the people of the insular areas 'alien races', and DeLima v. Bidwell termed them 'savage tribes'; the cases are widely considered racist.

events.title: The Platt Amendment and Guantánamo Bay
events.description: As the price of withdrawing its troops, the United States made Cuba write into its constitution, and then into a 1903 treaty, a U.S. right to intervene in Cuban affairs and a lease of land for naval bases, which the U.S. still holds at Guantánamo Bay.

Documented history

The Platt Amendment, part of the Army Appropriations Act signed by President McKinley on 2 March 1901, set seven conditions for the withdrawal of U.S. troops remaining in Cuba and an eighth that Cuba sign a treaty accepting them. Cuba amended its constitution to contain the seven demands word for word.

Its third article gave the United States the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence and a government adequate for the protection of life, property and individual liberty; another required Cuba to sell or lease land for coaling and naval stations. After U.S. troops withdrew in 1902, Cuba signed the Cuban–American Treaty of Relations on 22 May 1903 and leased land at Guantánamo Bay, which the U.S. still controls. The treaty was used to justify the second occupation of Cuba in 1906; in 1934 a new treaty dropped three of the seven pledges.

In 1912 the Independent Party of Color appealed to the third article for protection against the Cuban government's forces; the United States did not accept the plea.

France began the canal in 1881 with a labor force of about 40,000 by 1888, nine-tenths of them Afro-Caribbean workers from the West Indies; an estimated 22,000 men died before the French effort failed in 1889. The United States took over in 1904 and opened the canal on 15 August 1914.

Skilled workers and managers, almost all from the United States, were paid in gold on the 'gold roll'; the great majority of laborers were West Indians paid in local silver on the 'silver roll', and housing, transport, health care and even post offices were segregated by roll. Between 1905 and 1908 the system was tightened to enforce racial segregation; skilled West Indians were demoted to the silver roll and the gold roll was limited to U.S. and Panamanian citizens. About 5,600 workers died from disease and accidents during the U.S. construction; the great majority were West Indian laborers, particularly from Barbados, and about 350 were Americans. The U.S. controlled the canal and its Zone until the Torrijos–Carter Treaties; Panama took full control in 1999.

events.title: The massacre of the Independent Party of Color
events.description: Black veterans of the independence war founded the Partido Independiente de Color in 1908; banned under the Morúa law, it rose in Oriente in May 1912 and was crushed by the Cuban army with U.S. Marines guarding American property, with estimates of up to 6,000 dead.
events.article:
Oriente and Las Villas provinces, Cuba

Caribbean

7 August 1908 – 27 June 1912

Documented history

The Partido Independiente de Color (PIC) was founded on 7 August 1908 by black and mixed-race veterans of the War of Independence, after no black politician was elected in the elections of 1 August 1908. Its platform called for equal treatment regardless of race, free university education, guaranteed public employment and land for veterans. It is described as the first black political party in the Western Hemisphere. Since the war, U.S. businesses had been taking up land in Oriente, where most Afro-Cubans lived.

President José Miguel Gómez had the party outlawed under the Morúa law, which banned parties based on race. The PIC petitioned President Taft under the Platt Amendment against "outrages against our persons and our rights"; the U.S. refused. Newspapers such as El Día cast the movement as a racist uprising of blacks.

On 20 May 1912 the rebels attacked the Cuban Army, mainly in Oriente. The government met them with severe repression and appealed to the United States, whose Marines moved to protect U.S.-owned property, railroads and mines. Evaristo Estenoz was killed on 27 June. Rebel forces had numbered at least 3,000; by June about 1,800 were left alive, and some sources cite as many as 6,000 deaths including civilians. Many Afro-Cubans were killed whether or not they were involved, and the party was disbanded. Pedro Ivonnet called the party's exclusion "the epilogue of the trial of la Escalera."

events.title: Marcus Garvey and the UNIA
events.description: Marcus Garvey founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in Jamaica in 1914 and built it into a mass movement from Harlem; convicted of mail fraud in 1923, he was imprisoned and deported in 1927.

Marcus Mosiah Garvey Jr. was born on August 17, 1887, in Saint Ann's Bay, Jamaica. He launched the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League in July 1914, moved to the United States in 1916 and launched a New York branch in Harlem in May 1917. Membership grew rapidly in 1918.

The Bureau of Investigation's J. Edgar Hoover decided that Garvey was politically subversive and should be deported. After his appeal failed in February 1925 he was imprisoned in the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary. President Calvin Coolidge commuted his sentence and he was deported to Jamaica in 1927. He moved to London in 1935 and died there on June 10, 1940, aged 52, after two strokes. President Joe Biden granted him a posthumous pardon on January 19, 2025.

events.title: The British West Indies Regiment and the Taranto Mutiny
events.description: Some 15,600 West Indian volunteers served in the British West Indies Regiment in the First World War, mostly in Palestine, while being denied the pay and promotions given white soldiers; in December 1918, after the armistice, battalions gathered at Taranto, Italy mutinied over the discrimination, leading to disbandment, courts martial and one execution, but also to the founding of the Caribbean League, which demanded self-determination for the West Indies.
events.article:
Palestine, France, Flanders, Italy; Taranto, Italy

Caribbean / Europe / Middle East

1915–1918

Documented history

The British West Indies Regiment formed in 1915, its 1st Battalion mustering at Seaford, Sussex, on 1 October 1915 with recruits from Jamaica (about two-thirds of the roughly 15,600 men who served), British Guiana, Trinidad, Barbados, the Bahamas, British Honduras, the Leeward Islands, Saint Lucia and St Vincent. The regiment served mainly against Ottoman forces in Palestine and Jordan, with some battalions in France, Flanders and Italy; 262 men died, 105 of them in combat and 157 of disease, and 573 were wounded, while the regiment earned 81 medals for bravery and 49 mentions in despatches.

After the armistice, BWIR battalions gathered at Taranto, Italy to demobilise. Resentment grew when the men discovered white soldiers had received pay rises they were denied, despite being made to do menial labour — loading ships, fatigue duty and latrine work. On 6 December 1918 the 9th Battalion refused orders and 180 sergeants petitioned against the unequal pay and promotions; the 10th Battalion also refused work on 9 December. Over four days a Black NCO was killed and an officer assaulted before the Worcestershire Regiment restored order. The 9th Battalion was disbanded, about 60 men were court-martialled for mutiny and given sentences of three to five years (one got 20 years, and one was executed). On 17 December 1918 about 60 NCOs formed the Caribbean League, demanding equal rights and self-determination for the West Indies.

events.title: The United States occupies the Dominican Republic, 1916-1924
events.description: US Marines occupied the Dominican Republic from May 15, 1916 to September 18, 1924, to force repayment of debts to European and American creditors, installing a military government that controlled Dominican finances through the National City Bank of New York while a guerrilla movement, the gavilleros, resisted in the eastern provinces.

The US military government built roads connecting Santo Domingo to Santiago, Azua and San Pedro de Macorís, created the Dominican Constabulary Guard to replace partisan militias, balanced the budget and reduced debt, while controlling Dominican finances through the National City Bank of New York.

Political pressure from Warren Harding's 1921 campaign led to the 1922 Hughes-Peynado agreement; after Horacio Vásquez won the March 1924 election, US forces withdrew on September 18, 1924, transferring police authority to the Dominican National Guard, the force a young officer named Rafael Trujillo would rise through.

events.title: Great Migration of African Americans, 1916–1970
events.description: During the Great Migration, approximately 6 million African Americans moved from the South to northern and western cities between 1916 and 1970, seeking economic opportunity and escape from Jim Crow segregation.
events.article:
United States

United States

1916–1955

Documented history

Beginning around 1916, African Americans began migrating from the South in large numbers, drawn by job opportunities in northern factories and cities and seeking to escape the harsh conditions of Jim Crow segregation.

World War I labor demand accelerated the migration: northern factories needed workers for military production, and Southern cotton remained devastated by the boll weevil infestation. An estimated 500,000 African Americans migrated north during World War I alone.

The migration continued through the 1920s, 1930s, and beyond. By the 1970s, approximately 6 million African Americans had relocated from the rural South to urban centers in the North and West, including Chicago, Detroit, Pittsburgh, New York, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

The Great Migration transformed American cities. It led to the development of vibrant African American neighborhoods and cultural centers. However, migrants also faced discrimination in housing, employment, and public services in the North, leading to residential segregation through redlining and police violence in many Northern cities.

events.title: The Jones Act binds Puerto Rico's shipping
events.description: The Merchant Marine Act of 1920, whose Section 27 is the Jones Act, requires goods shipped between U.S. ports, including Puerto Rico, to travel on U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed ships.
events.article:
United States; Puerto Rico

Documented history

The Merchant Marine Act of 1920 was introduced by Senator Wesley Jones and signed by President Woodrow Wilson on June 5, 1920. Its Section 27, the Jones Act, deals with cabotage: all goods carried by water between U.S. ports must travel on ships built in the United States, flying the U.S. flag, owned by U.S. citizens and crewed by U.S. citizens and permanent residents.

The act prevents foreign-flagged ships from carrying cargo between the contiguous United States and Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska and Guam. Critics say it more than doubles shipping costs to Puerto Rico; a 2013 government study found the exact effect on freight rates hard to isolate.

events.title: Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association, 1920s
events.description: Marcus Garvey led the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in the 1920s, promoting Black nationalism, African repatriation, and economic self-sufficiency. His movement influenced millions of Black Americans.

United States

Documented history

Marcus Garvey, born in Jamaica, founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914. He migrated to the United States in 1916 and established the UNIA in Harlem, New York, in 1917.

Garvey's movement promoted Black nationalism, pride in African heritage, and economic independence. He established the Black Star Line, a shipping company intended to facilitate commerce and repatriation to Africa. He advocated for Black businesses and educational institutions.

At its peak in the 1920s, the UNIA claimed millions of members across the United States, Africa, and the Caribbean. Garvey held massive meetings in New York and other cities, attracting tens of thousands of supporters.

In 1927, Garvey was deported to Jamaica following conviction on fraud charges related to the Black Star Line. Despite his deportation, his movement inspired pan-African consciousness and influenced subsequent civil rights and Black nationalist movements.

Albizu Campos, born in Ponce in 1893 to Juliana Campos, a domestic worker of African ancestry, graduated from Harvard Law School in 1921; animus towards his African heritage led professors to delay two of his exams to keep him from graduating on time. He joined the party in 1924 as vice president and was elected president on 11 May 1930. In 1934 he led a sugar cane workers' strike, which the source describes as failed.

Under Governor Blanton Winship the party faced harsh repression. After the revolts of October 1950 he was sentenced to eighty years; 3,000 independence supporters were arrested across the island.

In prison he alleged he was the subject of human radiation experiments and wrapped wet towels around his head; guards mocked him as 'the King of the Towels', and officials suggested mental illness. Other prisoners at La Princesa said they felt the radiation too, and Dr. Orlando Daumy, president of the Cuban Cancer Association, concluded from examining him that his sores were radiation burns. The FBI investigated doctors who planned to visit him. He suffered a stroke in prison in 1956, was pardoned on 15 November 1964 and died on 21 April 1965; more than 75,000 Puerto Ricans accompanied his remains. In all he spent twenty-six years in prison.

events.title: Garrett Morgan's traffic signal patent, 1923
events.description: Garrett Morgan received a patent for an improved three-position traffic signal in 1923. Morgan, an African American inventor, created a device that improved traffic safety in urban areas where automobile traffic was increasing.
events.article:
United States

United States

1923

Documented history

Garrett Morgan (1877–1963) was an African American inventor born in Paris, Kentucky. In the early twentieth century, as automobile traffic increased, the need for better traffic control became apparent. Existing traffic signals, which consisted of simple red and green lights, were inadequate for managing the growing complexity of urban intersections.

Morgan designed an improved traffic signal with three positions: 'stop,' 'all go,' and a 'caution' mode that stopped traffic in all directions temporarily, allowing pedestrians and vehicles to clear the intersection safely. His design was a significant improvement over existing systems.

Morgan received a patent for his traffic signal design in 1923 (U.S. Patent No. 1,475,024). The device was later purchased by the General Electric Company and used in many American cities. Morgan's traffic signal became a model for modern traffic control systems.

In 1924 the Virginia General Assembly enacted the Racial Integrity Act, pushed by Walter Plecker, registrar of the Virginia Bureau of Vital Statistics. It required that all birth and marriage certificates in Virginia record the person's race as either "white" or "colored", and it classified all non-whites, including Native Americans, as colored.

It prohibited interracial marriage. A 1930 act defined anyone with even a trace of sub-Saharan African ancestry as black, codifying the so-called one-drop rule. Its proponents were spurred on by Native groups such as the Chickahominy and Rappahannock asserting their identities, and racialization became a tool for dispossession. The Supreme Court overturned the act in 1967 in Loving v. Virginia.

events.title: The Napalpí massacre
events.description: On July 19, 1924 police and ranchers massacred hundreds of Toba (Qom) and Mocoví people at the Napalpí reserve in the Chaco, who had struck against a 15% tax on their cotton; in 2019 an Argentine federal court declared it a crime against humanity.

events.title: The Mexican Repatriation
events.description: During the Great Depression the United States deported and pressured into leaving hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many of them U.S.-born citizens.
events.article:
United States, especially California and Texas

Southwestern United States

1929–1939

Documented history

The Mexican Repatriation was the repatriation or deportation of Mexicans and Mexican Americans from the United States during the Great Depression, between 1929 and 1939. About 82,000 people were formally deported and others left under pressure; estimates of the number who moved to Mexico range from 300,000 to 2 million, most between 500,000 and 1 million.

An estimated forty to sixty percent of those repatriated were citizens of the United States, overwhelmingly American-born children. Some scholars tie the large number of deportations between 1929 and 1933 to the policy of the Hoover administration.

California apologized in 2005 through the Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program, recognizing the unconstitutional removal and coerced emigration of U.S. citizens and legal residents of Mexican descent; Los Angeles County apologized in 2012.

events.title: The Marion lynching and “Strange Fruit”
events.description: On August 7, 1930, a mob of thousands lynched Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith in Marion, Indiana; the photograph of their bodies inspired the poem and song “Strange Fruit.”
events.article:
Marion, Indiana; New York

United States

August 7, 1930 (lynching); 1937 (poem); 1939 (Billie Holiday's recording)

Documented history

On August 7, 1930, Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith, two young African-American men held as suspects in an attack on a white couple, were taken from their cells by a crowd with sledgehammers, beaten and hanged from a tree in the county courthouse square in Marion, Indiana. Police officers in the crowd cooperated. A third prisoner, 16-year-old James Cameron, narrowly escaped.

A local photographer, Lawrence Beitler, photographed the bodies surrounded by a crowd estimated at 5,000, including women and children, and sold thousands of copies in ten days. Abel Meeropol cited the photograph as the inspiration for his poem, published as “Bitter Fruit” in January 1937 in a teachers' union magazine; Billie Holiday recorded “Strange Fruit” in 1939.

The Tuskegee Institute recorded the lynchings of 3,446 Blacks and 1,297 Whites between 1882 and 1968, with the peak in the 1890s; lynchings declined considerably by the Great Depression.

events.title: Rafael Trujillo's dictatorship and dominicanidad
events.description: Rafael Trujillo, risen through the US-created National Guard, seized power in August 1930 and ruled the Dominican Republic for 31 years through a personality cult and a secret police that killed an estimated 25,000 to over 50,000 people, while promoting "dominicanidad," an official anti-Black, anti-Haitian national ideology, and "blanqueamiento," the whitening of the population.
events.article:
Ciudad Trujillo (Santo Domingo), Dominican Republic

Caribbean

August 1930 - 1955 (regime continued to May 1961)

Documented history

Rafael Trujillo rose through the ranks of the US-created Dominican National Guard during the American occupation. In 1930 he made a secret arrangement with rebel leader Rafael Estrella Ureña: Trujillo kept his troops in their barracks while Estrella's forces marched on the capital, and Trujillo then stood for the presidency, officially winning with an implausible 99 percent of the vote. He renamed the capital Ciudad Trujillo and built a personality cult ("Dios y Trujillo"; churches required to display "God in Heaven, Trujillo on Earth"); government employees were required to donate 10 percent of their salaries to the state. His secret police, the SIM, killed an estimated 25,000 to over 50,000 opponents and civilians over his rule.

Trujillo's regime, initially backed by the United States, promoted "dominicanidad," an official ideology distinguishing Dominican from Haitian identity and portraying Haiti as a threat; his government rewrote Dominican history to cast Haitians as constant aggressors. He promoted "blanqueamiento," the whitening of the population, wore skin-lightening makeup himself, and had many Afro-Dominicans reclassified as "indio" to distance them from Blackness, even though his own grandmother was Haitian. This ideology directly preceded and justified his October 1937 Parsley Massacre of Haitians on the border.

events.title: The Scottsboro Boys
events.description: In 1931 nine black teenagers taken off a freight train in Alabama were accused of raping two white women and all but the youngest were sentenced to death, despite no medical evidence of rape.
events.article:
Scottsboro, Alabama

Southern United States

All but 14-year-old Roy Wright were convicted and sentenced to death, though there was no medical evidence that rape had taken place. In Powell v. Alabama (1932) the Supreme Court ordered new trials. Charges were finally dropped for four of the nine; the others received long sentences. On November 21, 2013, Alabama's parole board granted posthumous pardons to the three who had not yet been pardoned or had their convictions overturned.

events.title: The Rhoads letter in Puerto Rico
events.description: In November 1931 Rockefeller Institute pathologist Cornelius Rhoads wrote a letter from Puerto Rico calling Puerto Ricans a degenerate race and claiming he had killed eight and transplanted cancer into others; Pedro Albizu Campos made it public in 1932.
events.article:
San Juan, Puerto Rico

Caribbean

November 10, 1931 (letter); early 1932 (made public)

Documented history

In 1931 Cornelius P. Rhoads joined the Rockefeller Anemia Commission at Presbyterian Hospital in San Juan, where the group had more than 200 patients, primarily clinical subjects. On November 10, 1931, he wrote an unmailed letter calling Puerto Ricans “the dirtiest, laziest, most degenerate and thievish race of men ever inhabiting this sphere” and claiming he had furthered their extermination by killing eight and transplanting cancer into several more.

In early 1932 a lab assistant gave the letter to the nationalist leader Pedro Albizu Campos, who publicized it and charged that Rhoads was part of a U.S. plot to exterminate Puerto Ricans. An investigation by the Puerto Rican Attorney General reviewed the files of 257 patients, including 13 who died, and found no evidence of the crimes described; Rhoads called his words a joke.

Rhoads went on to lead Memorial Hospital and Sloan-Kettering and appeared on the cover of Time in 1949. In 2002 an investigation led by Jay Katz for the American Association for Cancer Research found no evidence of unethical human experimentation but judged the letter so offensive that the association removed Rhoads's name from its award.

Dr. Cornelius Rhoads, sponsored by the Rockefeller Institute, deliberately infected Puerto Ricans with cancer cells and wrote that he had killed eight; they take delight in the abuse and torture of our people. events.title: The Tuskegee syphilis study begins
events.description: In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service began a study of untreated syphilis in 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, deceiving them and withholding treatment for forty years.
events.article:
Macon County, Alabama

Southern United States

1932 (begins; continued until 1972)

Documented history

In 1932 the U.S. Public Health Service, working with the Tuskegee Institute, began a study to record the natural history of syphilis, the “Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male.” It enrolled 600 impoverished Black sharecroppers, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. Their informed consent was not collected; they were told they were being treated for “bad blood” and promised free medical care.

The men were told the study would last six months; it lasted forty years. By 1943 penicillin was the treatment of choice, and by 1947 it was standard, but the men were not offered it, and researchers kept them from treatment elsewhere.

The study ended in 1972 after an Associated Press story. By then 28 of the men had died of syphilis and 100 of related complications, 40 of their wives had been infected, and 19 of their children had been born with congenital syphilis. President Bill Clinton apologized on May 16, 1997.

Quotes and sources

The Tuskegee syphilis experiments were one of the curses that the Most High God placed upon the so-called negro here in the Americas to show that they are the children of Israel.

The study was conducted from 1932 to 1972: the men were only told they were receiving free health care, and they were deceived with placebos disguised as treatment.

events.title: Leonard Howell and the rise of Rastafari in Jamaica
events.description: Leonard Percival Howell, deported from the United States in 1932 after working with Marcus Garvey's UNIA, began preaching in Jamaica from 1933 that the newly crowned Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie I was the returned Black Messiah, becoming one of the first teachers of what grew into the Rastafari movement; convicted of sedition for it, he went on to found the Pinnacle commune at Sligoville, St Catherine, in 1940, which the colonial and Jamaican authorities raided and eventually destroyed.
events.article:
Jamaica

Kingston and St Catherine Parish

1933–1940

Documented history

Howell, born in Clarendon, Jamaica, in 1898, migrated to the United States and became a lieutenant in Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association before being deported back to Jamaica in December 1932. Inspired by the November 1930 coronation of Ras Tafari Makonnen as Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia, Howell began preaching from January 1933 that Selassie was the incarnation of God and the returned Black Messiah for the African diaspora. He founded the King of Kings Mission, appointed himself Selassie's representative in Jamaica, and was prosecuted for sedition for preaching doctrines the colonial authorities judged anti-Church and anti-government; he wrote the movement's first text, 'The Promised Key', in prison.

In 1940 Howell founded Pinnacle, a communal settlement on about 400 acres at Sligoville in St Catherine Parish, where several hundred followers farmed, traded and governed themselves largely outside colonial authority. Jamaican police raided Pinnacle more than once in the years that followed and ultimately cleared and destroyed it in the 1950s; sources differ on the exact years of the later raids, Howell's further imprisonment and Pinnacle's final destruction (see disagreements). Howell died in Kingston in 1981.
