Leonard P. Howell, he made up the Rastafarian religion. I don't care if he is Black, it ain't biblical. Don't make up your own religions.

events.title: Jesse Owens wins four gold medals at 1936 Berlin Olympics
events.description: African American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, breaking world records and disproving Nazi racial theories. His achievements were a significant moment in sports and racial progress.
events.article:
Berlin, Germany

Europe

August 1936

Documented history

Jesse Owens was born in 1913 in Alabama. He became an exceptional track and field athlete, breaking multiple world records in high jump, long jump, and sprint events.

At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, held in Nazi Germany, Owens competed for the United States. He won four gold medals: in the 100 meters, 200 meters, long jump, and 4x100 meter relay. He set Olympic records in three of these events.

Owens's achievements were historically significant for two reasons. First, they demonstrated the athletic excellence of African Americans despite segregation and discrimination in the United States. Second, they contradicted Nazi theories of racial superiority, though Hitler did not acknowledge Owens's achievements.

events.title: The 1937 Trinidad oilfield riots at Fyzabad

events.title: The Frome and Kingston labour riots in Jamaica, and the Moyne Commission
events.description: Labour unrest that broke out at the Tate & Lyle-owned Frome sugar estate in Westmoreland in 1938 spread to Kingston and across Jamaica, leaving 46 dead and at least 429 injured; the unrest, part of a wave across the British West Indies from 1934 to 1939, led Britain to appoint the Moyne Commission, whose findings produced the Colonial Development and Welfare Act of 1940 and fed the rise of Jamaica's trade unions and political parties.
events.article:
Frome, Westmoreland, and Kingston, Jamaica

Caribbean

May–June 1938 riots; Moyne Commission 1938–1939; Colonial Development and Welfare Act, July 1940

Documented history

In the 1930s the British firm Tate & Lyle bought the Frome estate in Westmoreland, Jamaica, and in May 1937 formed the West Indies Sugar Company with £600,000 of capital, consolidating several plantations and leaving many sugar workers without jobs. That grievance fed labour riots at the Frome factory in 1938, where police killed four protesters and wounded nine; unrest spread from Frome east to Kingston, and across Jamaica the 1938 unrest left 46 dead and at least 429 injured, with thousands detained and prosecuted.

Jamaica's 1938 unrest was part of a wider wave of labour disturbances across the British West Indies from 1934 to 1939, including Trinidad's 1937 riots and a 1937 Barbados uprising that killed between 14 and 22 people. The British government responded by appointing the West India Royal Commission, chaired by Lord Moyne, which investigated conditions from November 1938 to February 1939 and reported on housing, agriculture, health, prisons and schools; its findings led to the Colonial Development and Welfare Act of July 1940, which committed £5 million a year for ten years to colonial development and £500,000 a year indefinitely for colonial research. The unrest also strengthened Jamaica's trade unions and fed the growth of the People's National Party (1938) and the Jamaica Labour Party (1943).

events.title: Operation Bootstrap and the Great Migration of Puerto Ricans
events.description: From 1947 Puerto Rico's Operation Bootstrap lured U.S. corporations with tax exemptions and cheap labour, while planned emigration sent Puerto Ricans north by air: some 31,000 a year moved to New York from 1946 to 1950, in what is called the Great Migration.
events.article:

Documented history

In May 1947 Puerto Rico's legislature passed the Industrial Incentives Act, eliminating corporate taxes to draw U.S. investment, with a ten-year exemption from many taxes; the Administration of Economic Development encouraged factories, and the economy turned from agriculture to industry. According to Virginia Sánchez Korrol of the Center for Puerto Rican Studies, Bootstrap rested on three elements: industrialization by tax inducements to American corporations, a cheap labour pool educated in English under a U.S.-imposed curriculum, and the proposed emigration of over a third of the island's population.

Air travel was one of the principal factors in the largest wave of Puerto Rican migration to New York City in the 1950s, 'the Great Migration'; the decision to migrate was generally rooted in the island's poverty and in public policies that sanctioned migration. In 1948 the Migration Division of Puerto Rico's Department of Labor opened its office in New York. An estimated 31,000 migrants a year went to New York from 1946 to 1950; nearly 40,000 settled in the city in 1946 and 58,500 in 1952–53.

In New York, Lolita Lebrón recalled restaurant signs reading "No dogs or Puerto Ricans allowed."

events.title: The Windrush generation arrives in Britain

The acquittal shocked the nation and galvanized the civil rights movement. Till's murder became a symbol of racial violence and the failure of the justice system.

events.title: Montgomery bus boycott, 1955–1956
events.description: On December 5, 1955, African Americans in Montgomery, Alabama, began a boycott of the city's segregated bus system following Rosa Parks's arrest for refusing to give up her seat. The 381-day boycott became a pivotal moment in the civil rights movement.
events.article:
Montgomery, Alabama

Southern United States

December 5, 1955 – December 20, 1956

Documented history

On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a 42-year-old seamstress and civil rights activist, boarded a Montgomery bus. When a white passenger boarded, the driver ordered Parks to give up her seat, as required by Montgomery's segregation laws. Parks refused and was arrested and charged with violating the city's segregation ordinance.

Word of Parks's arrest spread quickly through the Black community. Civil rights activists, including a young minister named Martin Luther King Jr., organized a response. On December 5, 1955, Montgomery's African American citizens began a boycott of the city's bus system, refusing to ride the buses until segregation was ended.

The boycott lasted 381 days. Despite economic hardship and harassment, Black residents found alternative transportation, carpooling and walking rather than riding segregated buses. The boycott attracted national attention and brought King to prominence as a civil rights leader.

On December 20, 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Browder v. Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional, forcing Montgomery to desegregate its buses. The boycott's success demonstrated the power of nonviolent direct action and became a model for future civil rights campaigns.

events.title: The birth control pill is tested on Puerto Rican women

Rosa Louise McCauley Parks was born in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1913. She grew up in a household that valued education and racial dignity despite the constraints of Jim Crow segregation.

Parks became a seamstress and activist in Montgomery, Alabama. She worked with the NAACP and the Women's Political Council, organizations fighting for civil rights.

Parks became a national symbol of resistance to segregation. She remained active in civil rights work throughout her life, speaking and writing about the movement. She received numerous honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996. She died in 2005 at age 92.

events.title: Little Rock integration crisis, 1957
events.description: Nine African American students attempted to attend Little Rock Central High School on September 4, 1957, challenging segregation. Arkansas governor Orval Faubus mobilized the National Guard to prevent their entry, and President Eisenhower eventually dispatched federal troops to enforce desegregation.
events.article:
Little Rock, Arkansas

Southern United States

September 1957

Documented history

On September 4, 1957, nine African American students—later known as the 'Little Rock Nine'—arrived at Little Rock Central High School to integrate the school following the Brown v. Board decision. The school's principal, Jess Matthews, and the city's superintendent were instructed by Governor Orval Faubus, who had announced he would use the National Guard to prevent integration.

Governor Faubus mobilized the Arkansas National Guard on September 3, 1957, declaring his intent to prevent the integration. When the nine students arrived, the National Guard turned them away. The incident drew national media attention and provoked a constitutional crisis between state and federal authority.

President Dwight Eisenhower, reluctant to intervene, eventually sent U.S. Army troops and the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock on September 24, 1957, to enforce the students' right to attend the school. The troops escorted the students into the school and remained stationed in the city throughout the school year.

events.title: The Duvalier dynasty and the Tonton Macoutes

François Duvalier was president of Haiti from October 22, 1957, until his death on April 21, 1971. In 1959 he formed the Militia of National Security Volunteers, known as the Tonton Macoutes, an unsalaried paramilitary and secret-police force that grew to roughly twice the size of the army by 1961 and eventually numbered in the hundreds of thousands; its members financed themselves through extortion and violence against Duvalier's opponents. In June 1964 a fraudulent referendum (reported as 99.9 percent in favor, with ballots premarked "yes") declared him president for life. Estimates of those killed or disappeared under his rule range from 30,000 to 60,000.

On Duvalier's death in 1971 his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier succeeded him and ruled for 15 more years, continuing widespread torture and killing while hundreds of thousands emigrated. Popular revolts beginning in Gonaïves in 1985 spread nationwide by early 1986; under pressure from the Reagan administration, Jean-Claude Duvalier fled Haiti for France aboard a U.S. Air Force aircraft on February 7, 1986, ending 29 years of Duvalier rule. He returned to Haiti in January 2011, was charged with corruption and human-rights abuses, and died in Haiti on October 4, 2014.

events.title: The West Indies Federation
events.description: The West Indies Federation, uniting ten British Caribbean territories under one government from 3 January 1958, collapsed after a September 1961 Jamaican referendum voted to leave; Jamaica's withdrawal on 6 August 1962 led Trinidad's premier Eric Williams to declare that "one from ten leaves nought," and the federation was formally dissolved on 31 May 1962.
events.article:
British Caribbean

Caribbean

3 January 1958 – 31 May 1962

Documented history

The West Indies Federation was established on 3 January 1958, joining ten territories — Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, Antigua, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla, with the Cayman Islands and Turks and Caicos administratively attached to Jamaica — under a single federal government.

Jamaica, the largest member, resented having a smaller share of federal parliamentary seats than its population warranted and feared its bauxite wealth would be drained to support poorer members; many Jamaicans were also unhappy that Kingston was not made the federal capital. A September 1961 referendum produced a 54% vote to leave the federation, against the opposition of Jamaican premier Norman Manley. Jamaica formally withdrew on 6 August 1962, and Trinidad's premier, Eric Williams, responded that "one from ten leaves nought," judging the federation no longer viable without its two largest economies; it was formally dissolved on 31 May 1962.

events.title: Lunch counter sit-ins begin, 1960
events.description: On February 1, 1960, four African American college students sat at a segregated lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, refusing to leave until served. This act of nonviolent civil disobedience sparked a nationwide movement of sit-ins that spread to hundreds of cities.
events.article:

Southern United States

February 1, 1960

Documented history

On February 1, 1960, four freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College—Ezell Blair Jr., David Richmond, Franklin McCain, and Joseph McNeil—entered the Woolworth's Five and Dime store in Greensboro, North Carolina. They purchased items at other counters, then sat at the segregated lunch counter and requested service. The waitress refused, citing the store's segregation policy, but the four remained seated until closing time.

Word of the sit-in spread quickly. On February 2, the group returned with more students; by February 3, nearly 70 students participated; by February 5, over 300 students sat in at the Greensboro Woolworth's and other lunch counters downtown. Similar sit-ins began in other North Carolina cities and soon spread throughout the South.

Within two months, sit-ins had been organized in approximately 100 cities across the South and the Border states, involving an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 young people of both races. Though arrests and violence occurred, the sit-in movement demonstrated the power of nonviolent mass action and revitalized the civil rights movement.

events.title: The United States embargo against Cuba
events.description: After Cuba's nationalizations, the United States cut off trade from 1960 and in 1962 extended the embargo to almost all Cuban trade; reinforced in 1992 and 1996, it is the most enduring trade embargo in modern history and has been condemned by the UN General Assembly since 1992.

Documented history

The U.S. launched an arms embargo against Cuba in 1958 and targeted its energy and agricultural sectors in 1960. After nationalizations and Cuba's seizure of American assets, including oil refineries, in October 1960, the U.S. retaliated with a total embargo on Cuban trade, with exceptions for food and medicine. The Foreign Assistance Act of 4 September 1961 authorized a complete trade embargo; on 7 September 1962 Kennedy formally expanded it to all Cuban trade except the non-subsidized sale of food and medicines, and the Cuban Assets Control Regulations followed on 8 July 1963.

The embargo was reinforced by the Cuban Democracy Act of 1992 and the Helms–Burton Act of 1996, which penalizes foreign companies that do business in Cuba. It was loosened during the thaw of 2015–2017 and tightened sharply thereafter. It is the most enduring trade embargo in modern history, and the United Nations has formally condemned it since 1992 for its impact on Cubans.

events.title: Freedom Rides begin, 1961
events.description: The Freedom Rides began on May 4, 1961, when civil rights activists boarded buses in Washington, D.C., traveling through the Deep South to challenge segregation of interstate transportation. The riders faced violent mobs and police arrests throughout the journey.
events.article:
Southern United States

Southern United States

Documented history

The Freedom Rides began on May 4, 1961, when a group of interracial civil rights activists, organized by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), departed Washington, D.C., on two buses bound for the Deep South. Their goal was to test compliance with the 1960 Supreme Court decision Boynton v. Virginia, which had ruled that segregation of interstate bus terminals was unconstitutional.

The riders encountered violent opposition in Alabama. In Anniston, Alabama, on May 14, a mob of approximately 200 white residents attacked one of the buses with a firebomb, forcing the driver to abandon it. In Birmingham, on May 15, another mob attacked the second bus, and riders were beaten by white assailants while police made no attempt to intervene.

Despite the violence, the Freedom Rides continued, with hundreds of additional riders joining subsequent journeys throughout the summer and fall of 1961. The riders were arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, and imprisoned in the state penitentiary, but their courage and persistence brought national attention to the segregation of interstate transportation.

The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom took place on August 28, 1963, in the nation's capital. It was organized by a coalition of civil rights, labor, and religious organizations and called for immediate passage of the Civil Rights Act, voting rights legislation, federal enforcement of school desegregation, and a major federal program to address unemployment.

Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his now-famous 'I Have a Dream' speech, in which he expressed his vision of racial equality and harmony. The March is credited with galvanizing public opinion in favor of civil rights legislation, and Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 the following year.

In early 1965, civil rights organizations led by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) launched a voting rights campaign in Selma.

On March 7, 1965, approximately 600 marchers, led by SNCC chairman John Lewis and SCLC official Hosea Williams, gathered to march toward Montgomery. As they crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge, state police and Alabama National Guard troops blocked their path. The officers, led by Major John Cloud, ordered the marchers to disperse. When they refused, troopers advanced on the crowd, clubbing marchers with billy clubs and whips, while releasing tear gas into the crowd. Seventeen marchers were hospitalized, and dozens more were injured.

The violence, broadcast on national television, shocked Americans and accelerated support for voting rights legislation. A week later, King led a successful march of about 3,200 people from Selma to Montgomery, protected by federalized Alabama National Guard troops ordered by President Johnson. The march culminated in a speech by King at the state capitol in Montgomery on March 25, 1965, when he announced: 'I know you are asking today, "How long will it take?"'

The Voting Rights Act was signed into law by President Johnson on August 6, 1965, suspending literacy tests and authorizing federal examiners to register voters in areas with patterns of discrimination.

events.title: Balaguer's "Twelve Years": repression after the 1965 war
events.description: Returning from exile with U.S. backing after the 1965 civil war, Joaquín Balaguer won the 1966 election and ruled for twelve years through a period of systematic political repression -- jailings, torture, disappearances and killings estimated at between about 3,000 and 11,000 -- before losing the 1978 election to Antonio Guzmán.

Balaguer was reelected in 1970 and 1974, largely through intimidation of the opposition. His bid for a fourth term in 1978 failed when election returns favored Antonio Guzmán; despite initial military interference with the vote count, Guzmán's victory stood, the first defeat of Balaguer's career.

events.title: The 1970 Black Power Revolution in Trinidad and Tobago

events.title: The Mariel boatlift
events.description: After 10,000 Cubans sought asylum at the Peruvian embassy, Castro let anyone who wished leave from Mariel; between 15 April and 31 October 1980 about 125,000 Cubans reached Florida, between 20% and 40% of them black.

events.title: Antigua and Barbuda's independence
events.description: Antigua and Barbuda became independent from the United Kingdom on 1 November 1981, with Vere Cornwall Bird sworn in as its first prime minister, after a constitutional process in which the British refused Barbuda's bid to separate from Antigua as its own territory and instead gave Barbuda increased local autonomy.
events.article:
Antigua and Barbuda

Caribbean

1 November 1981

Documented history

Antigua, an associated state of the United Kingdom from 1967, moved toward full independence after its government signalled the intention in 1978 and the pro-independence party won 13 of 17 seats in the April 1980 election. A constitutional conference at Lancaster House in December 1980 addressed outstanding issues, including a Barbudan delegation's wish to separate from Antigua as its own territory, which the British refused on grounds of Barbuda's small population; the compromise instead amended the Barbuda Local Government Act to give the island greater autonomy.

Antigua's House of Representatives passed a resolution consenting to the termination of its association with Britain on 23 April 1981, and the Senate passed it on 1 May 1981. The British House of Lords approved the independence order on 8 July 1981 by a vote of 75 to 7, and Queen Elizabeth II signed both the termination and constitution orders on 31 July 1981. Antigua and Barbuda became independent on 1 November 1981, and Vere Cornwall Bird was sworn in as its first prime minister.

Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla became an associated state of the United Kingdom with full internal self-government in 1967. Anguilla, resentful of domination by St Kitts, unilaterally declared independence from the arrangement that same year and was formally separated from it in 1980, remaining a British overseas territory. A constitutional conference was held in London in 1982; the resulting Constitution of Saint Kitts and Nevis was adopted on 23 June 1983, giving Nevis the right to secede from the federation if a referendum produced a two-thirds majority in favour.

events.title: The Jamaat al Muslimeen coup attempt in Trinidad
events.description: On 27 July 1990, about 114 members of the Jamaat al Muslimeen, led by Imam Yasin Abu Bakr, stormed Trinidad and Tobago's Parliament at the Red House and the state television station, holding Prime Minister A. N. R. Robinson and much of his cabinet hostage for six days before surrendering on 1 August 1990; 24 people died, and the government's later amnesty for the insurgents was upheld by the Court of Appeal and then invalidated by the Privy Council, though none were re-arrested.

On 27 July 1990, roughly 114 members of the Jamaat al Muslimeen, an Afrocentric Black Muslim organisation led by Imam Yasin Abu Bakr (born Lennox Phillips) and Bilaal Abdullah, attempted to overthrow the government of Trinidad and Tobago. Forty-two of them stormed the Red House, the seat of Parliament, taking Prime Minister A. N. R. Robinson and most of his National Alliance for Reconstruction cabinet hostage, while 72 others attacked the Trinidad and Tobago Television (TTT) station. A car bomb exploded at Police Headquarters on St Vincent Street.

The standoff lasted six days of negotiation before the insurgents surrendered on 1 August 1990. Twenty-four people died in the uprising, and the government later estimated millions of dollars in property losses from the accompanying looting and arson. The insurgents were charged with treason, but an amnesty agreement reached to secure their surrender was upheld by the Court of Appeal and they were released; the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council later invalidated that amnesty, though none of the insurgents were re-arrested.

events.title: The Dominican Republic expels Haitian cane workers, 1991
events.description: On 13 June 1991 President Joaquín Balaguer issued Decree 233-91 ordering the expulsion of foreign sugar-plantation workers; Dominican authorities used it to drive out Haitian cane cutters and their families, separating families and beating and detaining people without due process.
events.article:
The bateyes of the Dominican sugar plantations

Caribbean

13 June 1991 (decree); 18 June – September 1991 (expulsions)

Documented history

On 13 June 1991, days after international media exposed the conditions of Haitian cane cutters on Dominican sugar plantations, President Joaquín Balaguer issued Decree 233-91, ordering the "repatriation" of undocumented foreign workers under 16 and over 60 from the plantations, and warned that the Dominican Republic risked "losing its identity as a nation" to what he called a "peaceful invasion" of Haitian migrants.

Beginning 18 June 1991, Dominican authorities carried out mass expulsions of Haitian sugar workers and their Dominican-born children without regard to legal residency, separating families, denying people the chance to collect belongings or wages or to notify relatives, and in some cases beating detainees. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 1999 country report states the decree authorized the expulsion of more than 35,000 Haitians over 1991; Human Rights Watch's contemporary report describes several thousand summarily expelled between June and September, with tens of thousands more fleeing to Haiti on their own to avoid forced deportation.

events.title: Haitian boat refugees are interdicted at sea and the HIV-positive among them held at Guantánamo
events.description: After the September 1991 coup against Jean-Bertrand Aristide, the US Coast Guard interdicted tens of thousands of Haitians fleeing by boat and, under a policy upheld by the Supreme Court in 1993, returned most of them to Haiti without a hearing; those found HIV-positive were instead held for up to twenty months behind razor wire at Guantánamo Bay until a federal court ordered the camp closed in June 1993.

Under a 1981 US-Haitian agreement, the US Coast Guard intercepted vessels carrying undocumented Haitians and screened passengers at sea for asylum claims before returning the rest to Haiti. After the September 1991 military coup against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, the number of Haitians fleeing by boat rose sharply, overwhelming the screening capacity on Coast Guard cutters; thousands were instead taken to a tent camp at the US Naval Base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for processing.

In 1992, the Bush administration ordered the Coast Guard to repatriate intercepted Haitians directly to Haiti without any screening for asylum claims, a policy the incoming Clinton administration continued. Haitians who tested positive for HIV were segregated from the rest of the Guantánamo camp and held in a separate, fenced compound -- the only known refugee camp in the world made up entirely of HIV-positive detainees -- some for as long as twenty months.

The Haitian Centers Council and other plaintiffs sued over conditions at the HIV camp; on June 8, 1993, federal judge Sterling Johnson Jr. ordered the camp closed, writing that although the government called it a "humanitarian camp," it was in substance "an HIV prison camp," and ordered the remaining detainees released into the United States. Haitian Centers Council (decided June 21, 1993), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that the President's power to order the Coast Guard to repatriate undocumented aliens intercepted on the high seas was not limited by US immigration law or international refugee conventions; Justice Blackmun dissented alone.

events.title: Rodney King acquittal and LA uprising, 1992
events.description: On April 29, 1992, a jury acquitted four Los Angeles police officers charged in the beating of motorist Rodney King, despite video evidence of the assault. The acquittals sparked the LA uprising, in which thousands of residents protested police violence through six days of unrest.
events.article:
Los Angeles, California

Western United States

April-May 1992

Documented history

On March 3, 1991, Los Angeles police officers pulled over Rodney King, a 25-year-old African American motorist. After a high-speed chase, officers struck King repeatedly with batons, fracturing his skull and breaking numerous bones. Nearby resident George Holliday recorded the beating on video, capturing approximately 81 seconds of the assault.

The LAPD officers involved were charged with assault. However, on April 29, 1992, a predominantly white jury in Simi Valley acquitted three of the four officers and deadlocked on the fourth. The acquittals, despite the video evidence, sparked immediate and widespread anger among Los Angeles residents.

Beginning that evening, residents in South Los Angeles and surrounding areas took to the streets in protest. Over the following six days, the uprising spread across the city, involving thousands of residents. Fires were set, stores were looted, and clashes erupted between protesters and police. The National Guard and federal troops were mobilized to suppress the unrest.

By May 4, 1992, the uprising had subsided. The violence resulted in 63 deaths, over 2,000 injuries, and approximately $1 billion in property damage. The incident exposed tensions over police brutality and racial justice that had long simmered in Los Angeles and other American cities.

events.title: Aristide demands $21 billion in reparations from France
events.description: On April 7, 2003, President Jean-Bertrand Aristide demanded France pay Haiti over $21 billion, which he said was the present-day equivalent of the 90 million gold francs Haiti had been forced to pay Paris after independence; French and Haitian officials later told the New York Times the demand helped drive the push to remove him in the 2004 coup, and his successor called it "illegal" and dropped it.

events.title: Hurricane Jeanne drowns Gonaïves
events.description: Although its center passed north of Haiti, Hurricane Jeanne dropped heavy rain from September 17 to 19, 2004 that flooded the deforested hillsides above Gonaïves under 16 feet of water, killing roughly 3,000 people nationwide -- most of them in that one city -- just months after the February 2004 coup that drove Jean-Bertrand Aristide from office.
events.article:
Gonaïves, Haiti

Caribbean

Documented history

Hurricane Jeanne passed north of Haiti in September 2004 without making landfall there, but its outer bands dropped roughly 330 millimeters of rain over about 36 hours, from September 17 to 19. Decades of deforestation had stripped the hillsides above the port city of Gonaïves of the tree cover that would otherwise have slowed the runoff, and floodwaters reaching about 16 feet deep inundated roughly 80 percent of the city of around 100,000 people.

Haiti's Directorate of Civil Protection and international relief agencies recorded approximately 3,006 deaths nationwide, with 2,826 of them in Gonaúves alone, making Jeanne one of the deadliest Atlantic hurricanes on record for Haiti. About 5,490 homes were destroyed across the country, and roughly 300,000 people were left homeless in the Nord-Ouest department.

The flooding struck seven months after the armed rebellion that forced President Jean-Bertrand Aristide from office in February 2004, while the country was still under a transitional government and the newly arrived UN peacekeeping mission (MINUSTAH), compounding a humanitarian crisis already underway.

events.title: UN peacekeepers' sexual abuse and exploitation in Haiti
events.description: Across MINUSTAH's 2004-2017 deployment, UN peacekeepers sexually abused and exploited Haitians, including at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers accused of running a child sex ring from 2004 to 2007 and, separately, Quebec police officers accused of sexual misconduct investigated from 2013; none of the Sri Lankan soldiers was ever criminally convicted.

In November 2007 the UN repatriated 108 members of the roughly 950-member Sri Lankan contingent, including three officers, on disciplinary grounds. Separately, a 2013 case investigated by UN investigator Rob Hotston involved a Canadian peacekeeper -- recruited from Quebec's Sûreté du Québec for the Haiti mission -- accused of picking up a Haitian sex worker, assaulting her and pointing his UN-issued firearm at her; she escaped with his UN identification badge, which identified him. events.title: The 2010 Haiti earthquake
events.description: A magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck near Léogâne, 25 kilometers from Port-au-Prince, on January 12, 2010; estimates of the dead range from about 46,000 to over 300,000, some 1.5 million people were displaced, and the American Red Cross was later found to have built only six houses in Haiti despite raising almost $500 million.
events.article:
Léogâne and Port-au-Prince, Haiti

Caribbean

Documented history

On January 12, 2010, at 16:53 local time, a magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck roughly 25 kilometers west of Port-au-Prince near Léogâne, at a depth of 13 kilometers. Death-toll estimates vary enormously by source: the Haitian government cited 220,000 to 316,000; the Inter-American Development Bank estimated 200,000-250,000 in February 2010; a University of Michigan study put it near 160,000; a Radio Netherlands investigation found about 92,000; and a 2011 USAID draft report estimated 46,000-85,000. A UN official said at the time, "I do not think we will ever know what the death toll is from this earthquake." The International Federation of Red Cross estimated 3 million people affected; USAID put displacement at about 1.5 million, with 550,000 still without permanent shelter as of January 2012. Total damage was estimated at $7.8-8.5 billion, with roughly 250,000 homes and 30,000 commercial buildings destroyed or severely damaged.

An NPR/ProPublica investigation published in June 2015 found that the American Red Cross raised nearly $488 million for Haiti earthquake relief but built only six permanent homes, despite initially planning about 700; much of the money went to other organizations that took their own overhead, and the Red Cross disputed the account.

events.title: UN peacekeepers bring cholera to Haiti
events.description: Nine months after the 2010 earthquake, a cholera epidemic traced to sanitation failures at a UN base housing Nepalese peacekeepers infected roughly 820,000 Haitians and killed nearly 10,000; the United Nations publicly apologized and pledged $400 million in assistance only in December 2016.

Documented history

The first confirmed cholera case in Haiti's modern history was recorded on October 21, 2010, nine months after the January earthquake, with the outbreak spreading rapidly along the Artibonite River. Investigators, including journalist Jonathan M. Katz and epidemiologist Renaud Piarroux, traced the source to a UN base housing Nepalese peacekeepers whose waste from outhouses flowed into the Artibonite; DNA testing matched the outbreak strain to those found in South Asia. By 2013 more than 6 percent of Haiti's population had been infected; the outbreak eventually accounted for an estimated 820,000 cases and nearly 10,000 deaths, and represented 57 percent of all cholera cases and 45 percent of all cholera deaths recorded worldwide in 2010-2011.

The United Nations resisted acknowledging responsibility for years. In December 2016, Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon formally apologized and pledged $400 million toward a response, though only a small fraction of that pledge had materialized in the years that followed.

events.title: The Dominican Republic strips citizenship from Dominicans of Haitian descent
events.description: The Dominican Republic's Constitutional Court ruled in 2013 that anyone born after 1929 to parents the state classified as "in transit," overwhelmingly Dominicans of Haitian descent, had never held Dominican nationality, rendering an estimated 200,000 people stateless; a 2014 law offered a path to regularize some of them.
events.article:
Dominican Republic

Caribbean

September 23, 2013 (Sentencia TC/0168/13); May 2014 (Law 169-14)

Documented history

In Sentencia TC/0168/13, the Dominican Republic's Constitutional Court ruled that anyone born in the country after June 21, 1929 to foreign parents classified as "in transit" -- a category long applied to undocumented Haitian laborers regardless of how many years or generations they had lived in the country -- had never legally held Dominican nationality, and ordered authorities to audit birth records back to that date. An estimated 200,000 people, overwhelmingly of Haitian descent, faced statelessness as a result; Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights all condemned the ruling.

In response, the government passed Law 169-14 in 2014, creating two categories: about 55,000 people with Civil Registry birth records received an amnesty and Dominican identity documents; about 53,000 people without such records had to register as foreigners and apply to naturalize by a 2015 deadline, of whom only 8,755 successfully registered. A further group born 2007-2010 had to register as foreigners and could seek ordinary naturalization after two years.

events.title: Puerto Rico's debt crisis, PROMESA and 'la junta'
events.description: When Puerto Rico's bonds were cut to junk in 2014, Congress passed PROMESA in 2016 and set over the island a federally appointed oversight board, 'la junta', which cut health care, pensions and education to repay creditors; students struck against a $450 million cut to the university in 2017.

Documented history

The crisis began in 2014 when three major credit agencies downgraded Puerto Rico's bonds to junk status. In 2016 Congress enacted PROMESA, a custom-made bankruptcy law that established a Financial Oversight and Management Board, known in Puerto Rico as 'la junta', with ultimate control over the Commonwealth's budget; all seven voting members were appointed by the U.S. President. Governor García Padilla suspended payments due on 1 July 2016.

The board's austerity plan for 2017–2026 cut deeply into health care, pensions and education. By May 2017 the government and its corporations owed $123 billion, and the board sought a federal judge for 'the largest bankruptcy case in the history of the American public bond market'; a 2018 report counted $74 billion in bond debt and $49 billion in unfunded pensions. Puerto Rico exited bankruptcy on 15 March 2022.

On 28 March 2017 students at the University of Puerto Rico's Río Piedras campus began a strike against a $450 million budget cut to the public university under PROMESA; it spread to most of the system's eleven campuses and ended on 7 June 2017.

events.title: Standing Rock and the Dakota Access Pipeline
events.description: From April 2016 thousands joined the Standing Rock Sioux to stop the Dakota Access Pipeline under Lake Oahe, near their water source and sacred sites; protesters were met with attack dogs, pepper spray and water cannon, and the camps were cleared in February 2017.

Standing Rock Sioux Reservation and Lake Oahe, North Dakota

North America

Documented history

The pipeline runs from North Dakota’s Bakken oil fields to Illinois, crossing under Lake Oahe near the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation; the tribe feared for the Missouri River, its water source, and for sacred and burial sites. In April 2016 youth from Standing Rock began a campaign to stop it. On September 3, 2016 the company bulldozed ground the tribe had identified as containing possible burial sites; private security used attack dogs and pepper spray, and at least six protesters were treated for dog bites. A United Nations expert said the tribe had been excluded from consultation.

In November 2016 police used tear gas and water cannon on protesters in freezing weather. On December 4, 2016 the Army said it would not grant the easement under Lake Oahe, but in early 2017 the Army Corps of Engineers granted it. The last protesters were evicted by the National Guard and police on February 23, 2017.

events.title: Hurricane María
events.description: Hurricane María struck Puerto Rico on 20 September 2017, destroying the power grid and leaving all 3.4 million residents without electricity in the worst blackout in U.S. history; an estimated 2,975 people died in Puerto Rico, and more than 130,000 left for the mainland by December.
events.article:

Documented history

María, the deadliest storm of the 2017 season, weakened to a high-end Category 4 by the time it struck Puerto Rico on 20 September 2017. It completely destroyed the island's power grid, leaving all 3.4 million residents without electricity, the worst blackout in U.S. history, which lasted months; about 80% of the island's agriculture was lost and 95% of cell networks were down. Three months later 45% of Puerto Ricans still had no power.

Puerto Rico accounted for an estimated 2,975 of the storm's 3,059 deaths, after a recount by George Washington University; a Harvard study had estimated 793 to 8,498 excess deaths. By 5 November more than 100,000 people had left for the mainland, and by mid-December 130,000.

Visiting the island, President Trump distributed canned goods and paper towels at a relief shelter and told residents they had thrown the budget "a little out of whack".

events.title: "Where is the PetroCaribe money?": corruption and mass protest under Jovenel Moïse
events.description: A Haitian Senate probe found that officials across three administrations, including then-president Jovenel Moïse, had embezzled an estimated 3.8 billion dollars raised through Venezuela's discounted PetroCaribe oil program; a viral #PetroCaribeChallenge launched in August 2018 by Gilbert Mirambeau Jr. helped drive waves of protest in October-November 2018 and again in 2019 that killed dozens and nearly toppled Moïse's government.
events.article:
Port-au-Prince and nationwide, Haiti

Caribbean

August 2018 – October 2019

Documented history

Haiti joined the Venezuelan-financed PetroCaribe program, which let member states buy oil on credit at below-market rates and redirect the savings toward development projects. A Haitian Senate investigation released in November 2017, covering the years 2008 to 2016, found an estimated 3.8 billion dollars of PetroCaribe funds had been embezzled or misused by officials spanning three presidential administrations, including then-president Jovenel Moïse's own company.

On August 14, 2018, Haitian-Canadian activist Gilbert Mirambeau Jr. tweeted a photo of himself blindfolded holding a sign reading, in Haitian Creole, "Kot kòb PetwoKaribe a?" ("Where is the PetroCaribe money?"), launching the #PetroCaribeChallenge that spread rapidly online and became the public face of Haiti's anti-corruption movement.

Fuel-price increases in July 2018 had already triggered unrest; anger over the PetroCaribe revelations then drove protests through the autumn, including a week of demonstrations in November 2018 that left about 10 people dead. Haiti's Superior Court of Auditors released further findings in early 2019 documenting payments for projects that were never built, contracts awarded in a dead person's name, and large undocumented disbursements to officials, igniting a fresh wave of protests from February through October 2019 that the United Nations said killed at least 42 people and injured 86 between mid-September and October alone.

events.title: The murder of Joy Morgan, and the charges laid against the church
events.description: Joy Morgan, a 20-year-old midwifery student and member of IUIC’s UK branch, was murdered after a church celebration on December 26, 2018; fellow member Shohfah-El Israel was convicted on August 5, 2019, and coverage of the case carried her family’s and the SPLC’s charges against the church, which IUIC denied.
events.article:
Ilford, Hatfield and Stevenage, England

Europe

Last seen December 26, 2018; conviction August 5, 2019; inquest 2021

Documented history

Joy Morgan, born February 12, 1998, was a midwifery student at the University of Hertfordshire. She joined the UK branch of Israel United in Christ in Ilford, east London, in January 2016, ran its children’s group, and two weeks before she went missing said in a video, “IUIC is my family and like the best family that I’ve ever had.” She was last seen alive on December 26, 2018 at a church celebration in Ilford. She was reported missing on February 7, 2019, after her housemates had not seen her since Christmas.

Police arrested fellow member Shohfah-El Israel (born Ajibola Shogbamimu) on February 9, 2019 on the M25; he was charged with murder on February 27. He admitted spending two nights alone with her at his Cricklewood flat, which broke the church’s rule against women being alone with men other than their husbands. A jury at Reading Crown Court convicted him on August 5, 2019, and he was sentenced to life with a minimum of 17 years; he refused to say where her body was. Her remains were found in woodland near Stevenage in October 2019. A 2021 coroner’s inquest could not establish how she died.

The coverage carried charges against the church. Her mother Carol said her daughter had been turned into a racist by the church and called it a cult, and her family said she had grown distant and called her mixed-race younger sister a “demon” and a “white devil.” Former members told the BBC of harsh discipline and of being told to cut off unbelieving family. The prosecutor described a strict hierarchy in which women had no rank. The SPLC described IUIC as a “hate group” and “a black nationalist group.”

IUIC denied these claims. It told the BBC that former members who speak against it are “disgruntled,” that claims it encourages members to cut off their families are “lies,” and that “at no point do we teach against the laws of the land or authorities.” The church described Shohfah-El Israel as an “enthusiastic” member and said he had once been demoted from the rank of soldier over his behaviour. Evidence given at the trial indicated that Joy Morgan had a good relationship with the church and its congregants, and police found no reliable indication that she wanted to leave it.

Quotes and sources

Years after her death, other camps print Joy Morgan’s picture and teach in the street that IUIC had something to do with her death, all the way over in England, while they say nothing of a 13-year-old girl abused by a man who called himself a Hebrew Israelite. All Israelite groups are not the same, and IUIC has no affiliation with those groups.

So the chief priests and Pharisees followed Christ’s camp and sought to lay hands on him, but feared the multitude: digging into a member’s personal life is to turn the multitude against us.

events.title: The Mapuche conflict, Catrillanca, and the rejected plurinational constitution
events.description: Mapuche communities' struggle for their ancestral lands, lost in the Occupation of Araucanía, sharpened after police shot Camilo Catrillanca in 2018 and Chile sent troops to Biobío and Araucanía in 2021; in 2022 voters rejected, 61.89% to 38.11%, a constitution that would have made Chile a plurinational state.
events.article:
Araucanía and Biobío, Chile

South America

2018 – 4 September 2022

Documented history

The Mapuche conflict intensified with the return of democracy in the 1990s, as activists sought to recover the 'ancestral territory' lost in the Occupation of Araucanía and the Conquest of the Desert; its period of violence began in December 1997, and some groups have used violent tactics since 1998 while others negotiate. In 1993 the Chilean government passed the Indigenous Peoples Act recognizing Mapuche land, cultural and development rights. In 2018 Camilo Catrillanca, grandson of a local Indigenous leader, was shot in the head during a police operation near Ercilla; in October 2021 President Sebastián Piñera declared a state of emergency and deployed troops to Biobío and Araucanía.

The constitution drafted after the 2020 plebiscite declared that 'Chile is a Plurinational and Intercultural State'; the plurinational state and indigenous justice were among its most debated provisions. On 4 September 2022 it was rejected by 61.89% to 38.11%, winning also in communes with large indigenous populations, and the 1980 constitution of the dictatorship era remained in force.

events.title: Murder of George Floyd, Minneapolis, 2020
events.description: On May 25, 2020, George Floyd, a 46-year-old African American man, was killed by Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin. Floyd's murder sparked the largest racial justice protests in American history.
events.article:
Minneapolis, Minnesota

May 25, 2020

Documented history

On May 25, 2020, Minneapolis police officers responded to a report of a counterfeit $20 bill at a grocery store. They detained George Floyd, a 46-year-old man known in the neighborhood.

During the detention, officer Derek Chauvin pinned Floyd to the ground and pressed his knee against Floyd's neck for approximately 9 minutes and 29 seconds, even as Floyd said he could not breathe and became unresponsive. Paramedics pronounced Floyd dead at the hospital.

Video recordings of Floyd's killing were widely shared on social media. The footage sparked immediate protests in Minneapolis and across the country, with demonstrations in all 50 states and internationally. The protests called for police accountability and systemic racial justice.

Officer Chauvin was arrested and charged with murder and manslaughter. He was convicted on April 20, 2021, of second-degree murder, third-degree murder, and second-degree manslaughter, and sentenced to 22.5 years in prison. Floyd's death became a watershed moment in conversations about police violence and systemic racism.

events.title: McGirt v. Oklahoma
events.description: On July 9, 2020 the Supreme Court held that the reservation promised to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and remains Indian country, so Oklahoma could not prosecute Native people for major crimes there.
events.article:
Eastern Oklahoma (the Muscogee reservation)

North America

July 9, 2020

Documented history

Before statehood in 1907 about half of Oklahoma, including Tulsa, belonged to the Five Tribes: the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek and Seminole. The case was brought by Jimcy McGirt, an enrolled member of the Seminole tribe. Writing for a 5–4 majority, Justice Gorsuch held that the Muscogee domain remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act: “Because Congress has not said otherwise, we hold the government to its word.” He rejected the argument that “the price of keeping” the promises “has become too great.”

Oklahoma’s Court of Criminal Appeals applied McGirt to rule that nine other nations’ reservations had not been disestablished, but held it was not retroactive. In Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) the Supreme Court held that the state shares jurisdiction over crimes by non-Natives against Natives in Indian country.

events.title: Gangs seize Port-au-Prince as the state collapses
events.description: After the 2021 assassination of Jovenel Moïse, armed gangs led by Jimmy "Barbecue" Chérizier formed the Viv Ansanm coalition, stormed Haiti's prisons and forced Prime Minister Ariel Henry to resign in March 2024; by 2025 the coalition held about 80 percent of Port-au-Prince despite a Kenya-led, UN-authorized multinational police mission.
events.article:
Port-au-Prince and nationwide, Haiti

Caribbean

2 October 2023 (UN authorizes the mission) – October 2025 (Gang Suppression Force)

Documented history

The UN Security Council authorized a Kenya-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission for Haiti on 2 October 2023 (Resolution 2699). On 29 February 2024, Haiti's two largest gang umbrellas, the G9 Family and Allies and G-Pèp, united as the Viv Ansanm coalition under spokesman Jimmy "Barbecue" Chérizier, a former police officer, and launched coordinated attacks on police stations, government buildings and the international airport.

On 2-3 March 2024, Viv Ansanm stormed Haiti's largest prisons at Croix-des-Bouquets and the National Penitentiary, freeing roughly 4,700 inmates, then seized the main airport to block Prime Minister Ariel Henry's return from abroad. Henry announced his resignation on 11 March 2024, and a nine-member Transitional Presidential Council was sworn in on 25 April 2024.

Kenya's first contingent of 400 police officers landed in Port-au-Prince on 25 June 2024 under the MSS mission, which was authorized for up to 2,500 personnel but had only about 991 actually deployed by June 2025. In October 2025 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2793, transforming the MSS into a Gang Suppression Force with an expanded mandate and authorization for up to 5,500 personnel. By then Viv Ansanm controlled an estimated 80 percent of metropolitan Port-au-Prince.

events.title: The Dominican Republic's mass deportations of Haitians
events.description: Under a policy set by President Luis Abinader's National Security and Defense Council to remove up to 10,000 undocumented Haitians a week, the Dominican Republic deported more than 276,000 people in 2024 and well over 100,000 more in 2025, including hundreds of pregnant and breastfeeding women, drawing UN condemnation.
events.article:
Dominican Republic and the Dominican-Haitian border

Caribbean

2024-2025 (ongoing)

Documented history

The Dominican Republic's National Security and Defense Council, headed by President Luis Abinader, ordered immigration authorities to remove up to 10,000 undocumented Haitians per week. The country deported more than 276,000 people in 2024, including over 94,000 in the final three months of the year alone. Deportations continued to accelerate into 2025: more than 119,000 Haitians had been deported by mid-2025, a 71 percent increase over the same period in 2024, and reporting later in the year put the figure above 145,000 Haitians deported, with nearly 20,000 repatriated between April and May 2025 alone, the highest two-month total on record.

The United Nations publicly condemned the deportation of about 900 pregnant or breastfeeding Haitian women in a several-month span, with the Secretary-General's spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric calling the practice a violation of international standards. Human-rights organizations including Amnesty International characterized the campaign as racially targeted.

events.title: Cuba's blackouts and the U.S. fuel blockade
events.description: From 2024 Cuba's failing power plants and fuel shortages brought repeated blackouts, including a total nationwide blackout from 18 October 2024; in February 2026 the United States began blocking oil tankers bound for Cuba, its first effective blockade since 1962, and by May 2026 Cuba said it had run out of oil and diesel.
events.article:
Cuba

Caribbean

February 2024 – 2026

Documented history

Blackouts began in February 2024, affecting 45% of the country on 13 February; in March outages of up to 18 hours a day brought protests in Santiago de Cuba. From 18 October 2024 a total nationwide blackout followed the failure of the Antonio Guiteras power plant in Matanzas, the largest. Blackouts continued through 2025 and into 2026, attributed to fuel and spare-part shortages, failing plants and, by some, the U.S. embargo.

In February 2026 the United States began blocking oil tankers heading to Cuba, targeting companies such as Mexico's Pemex; The New York Times called it the first effective U.S. blockade of Cuba since the Missile Crisis. On 13 March 2026 Miguel Díaz-Canel confirmed talks with the United States over the blockade, which had left Cuba with crippling fuel shortages and widespread outages; Cuba released 51 political prisoners and, on 3 April, more than 2,000 prisoners. On 14 May 2026 Cuba's energy ministry warned that the country had run out of oil and diesel.

events.title: An academic dictionary’s entry on Israel United in Christ
events.description: On August 30, 2026 the Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements published Michael T. Miller’s entry on Israel United in Christ, which calls it the most populous Black Hebrew Israelite group and charges its teaching with conspiracy theory, selective misreading and an expectation of race war.
events.article:
Online

Europe

August 30, 2026

Documented history

The entry, by Michael T. Miller in the Critical Dictionary of Apocalyptic and Millenarian Movements (edited by James Crossley and Alastair Lockhart), was published on August 30, 2026. It describes IUIC as the most populous group of the Black Hebrew Israelite movement and the most successful One West camp, with an estimated 10,000 members, led by Bishop Nathanyel Ben Israel.

It records charges in its own words: that IUIC’s eschatology predicts “the imminent ‘awakening’ of the true Israelites, followed by a race war and the enslavement/destruction of all non-Israelites”; that the group is a purveyor of “conspiracy theory in religion,” almost “conspiracy theory as religion”; that its history rests on “wild speculation” like a pseudohistory; and that “selective and seemingly deliberate misreading is also common.” It notes that IUIC, One West and Bishop Nathanyel “have been repeatedly accused of hatred, antisemitism, homophobia, conspiracy theories, and various other prejudices.”

The entry also records IUIC’s answer and its work: that IUIC “vociferously refute” the hate-group designation, open many videos with “We are not a hate group,” citing Romans 12:18, and tell members to notify the authorities of any plot to cause harm, citing Leviticus 5:1 and Romans 13:1. It writes that IUIC brings “a radically new message of race consciousness and dignity,” motivates people to improve their lives and commit to family, and does waste cleanup, youth and crisis support and prison outreach.

Answer

Romans 12:18
IUIC’s own answer, as the entry records it: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” No race war is taught by those who read this.

Leviticus 5:1
Cited by IUIC, as the entry records, for reporting any plot to harm anyone.

Acts 24:14
“After the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets.” Read in the classes against the names cult and heresy.

Acts 28:22
“As concerning this sect, we know that every where it is spoken against.” The apostles’ teaching was spoken against everywhere; the classes read it of themselves.

Wisdom of Solomon 2:12-16
The ungodly say of the righteous: “He professeth to have the knowledge of God… He is grievous unto us even to behold… We are esteemed of him as counterfeits.” The ring: a people who call themselves the children of the Lord are charged with fantasy.

Deuteronomy 28:37
“A proverb, and a byword, among all nations”: the curse names the people’s story being made a byword.

Sources

events.title: The United States strikes Venezuela and seizes Maduro
events.description: On January 3, 2026 U.S. forces bombed northern Venezuela and captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, flying them to New York; about 80 people died, and the Trump administration made access to Venezuela's oil a core reason for the action.
events.article:
Caracas and northern Venezuela

South America

3 January 2026

Documented history

Operation Absolute Resolve began around 2 a.m. on 3 January 2026 with strikes on air defences across northern Venezuela while a force attacked Maduro's compound in Caracas. Approximately 80 Venezuelan and Cuban military personnel and civilians died; Cuba said 32 of its personnel were killed. Maduro and Flores were indicted in New York on drug trafficking charges and pleaded not guilty. UN officials and international law experts said the raid violated the UN Charter and Venezuela's sovereignty.

Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as acting president on 5 January. The U.S. announced a 50-million-barrel oil deal, a new law gave private companies control of oil production, and the administration collected more than $13 billion from Venezuelan oil sales; according to The New York Times, Venezuela has since been a de facto puppet state, with the U.S. State Department under Marco Rubio controlling core parts of its government.

Quotes and sources

America never overthrow them with somebody in the inside. He's always a traitor.

“There is no new thing under the sun.” What just happened in Venezuela is not new: America has been doing this for over a hundred years. America pushes laws but respects no laws; it is a bully.

Every government America overthrows, it overthrows with somebody on the inside, a traitor, a trusted adviser: “mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted”. Maduro is no different, Venezuela is no different, and it will not be over until Christ comes and takes them down.

DESTROYED BY FAMILIAR HANDS — 2026-01-10 — 7:14

https://youtu.be/tmB8z0qSYo4?t=434

paraguay 1954, brazil 1964, peru 1968, chile 1973, uruguay 1973, argentina 1976

Here is every South American country whose government the CIA overthrew since 1947: Guatemala 1954, El Salvador 1979, Nicaragua 1981, Panama 1989, Paraguay 1954, Brazil 1964, Peru 1968, Chile 1973, Uruguay 1973, Argentina 1976 and Venezuela in 2002. That is South America alone; Africa is not on the list, and the islands are not there. America has always overthrown governments with a traitor on the inside.

https://youtu.be/tmB8z0qSYo4?t=4559

events.title: The Chocó earthquake of 2026
events.description: On August 10, 2026 a magnitude 7.4–7.5 earthquake centred near San José del Palmar in Chocó struck western Colombia, killing at least 335 people, injuring more than 4,600 and leaving 111 missing.
events.article:
Chocó and western Colombia

South America

10 August 2026

Documented history

The earthquake struck at 07:34 with its epicentre 20 km from San José del Palmar in the department of Chocó; it was felt across western and central Colombia and in Ecuador and Panama, and caused extensive damage in Cali, Pereira, Quibdó, Manizales, Armenia and Buenaventura. At least 335 people were killed, more than 4,600 injured and 111 left missing; at least 107 died in Pereira, and in Chocó at least 14 deaths and 119 injuries were recorded.

President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a state of national disaster and three days of mourning; the United States announced US$26.5 million in relief.

Quotes and sources

Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees.

“Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees”: unrighteous laws against the people, for the destruction of the people and of the land. When they take the precious minerals out of the earth the tectonic plates move and earthquakes happen; the minerals are in the earth for a reason.

They turn aside the needy from judgment and take away the right of the poor of my people, the rightful owners of the land. Chocó, Colombia's most Afro-Colombian department, was at the epicentre and paid the price for generations of government neglect: the people affected are our people, the indigenous and the Afro-descendants, and they are not getting help.

ABYA YALA UNDER FIRE — 2026-08-29 — 1:56:39

https://youtu.be/FSUFtJ08joo?t=6999

Scriptural application

Isaiah 10:1-2
Woe to them that decree unrighteous decrees and take away the right from the poor: the laws and mining that strip the land, and the neglect of the people of Chocó.
